case_summary.text: INCOME TAX: Where assessee-trust registered under section 12A derived income from letting out property, royalty, and allied activities and applied such income for charitable purposes, with no finding of non-genuineness or misapplication of income, such receipts could not be treated as commercial activity merely by their nature and exemption under section 11 was allowable.

INCOME TAX: Where assessee-trust earned rental income from leasing property but trust deed only enabled trustees to hold and manage property for charitable objects without treating leasing as an independent object, and receipts including rental income were applied solely to charitable activities, exemption under sections 11 and 12 could not be denied since leasing was only incidental to charitable purpose

INCOME TAX : Payment of remuneration to managing trustee of major philanthropic trust like assessee and an important part of India's most prestigious and credible business house, was not at all so unusual as to warrant further inquiries about its reasonableness more so when similar payments to him did not invoke provisions of section 13(2) in earlier years

IT : Once income derived from property held under by assessee-trust was applied in accordance with charitable objects in view of specific exemption granted by a special order issued by CBDT, there would be no violation of section 13(1)(d) so as to deny exemption

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust entered into an agreement with a private limited company for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to it, since object of transfer agreement was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally and purpose of charity was not violated, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 could not be denied

INCOME TAX: Where assessee-trust registered under section 12A/12AB carried out environmental protection activities and earned receipts mainly from contractual arrangements incidental to its objects, application of such receipts wholly for charitable purposes did not alter their charitable character, and exemption under section 11 could not be denied merely because income arose from such arrangements

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust, registered under section 12A, and engaged in providing medical help, education help and relief to poor had let out its halls and buildings for earning rental income so as to fund its charitable objects, proviso to section 2(15) would not be attracted and assessee could not be denied exemption under section 11

INCOME TAX : Where funds of assessee-charitable trust were managed by member of trustees headed by District Collector and audit report was submitted before competent authorities before completion of assessment proceedings, since there was sufficient compliance to claim exemption under section 10(23C)(v), claim could not be denied merely on ground that assessee generated surplus income

IT : Where all members of assessee-trust were engaged in whole time management activities of Trust and as regular time teachers and were being paid salaries from earning of these schools and were not being paid any extra salary for management work, there was no violation of provisions of section 13(2)(c) and assessee was entitled to benefit of exemption under section 11

INCOME TAX : Where assessee educational trust was denied exemption under section 11 on ground that remunerations paid to two trustees as a professor and an administrative officer respectively were not in proportion to pay scale of professors and administrative officers and it was done to divert funds by assessee-trust, thus, section 13(1)(c) was breached, revenue cannot sit in armchair of assessee and decide pattern of working of trust and cannot manage or control managerial affairs of trust, accordingly, impugned denial of exemption by making reference to section 13(1)(c) was unjustified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee charitable trust was not registered under section 12A, voluntary donations received by it with a specific direction to be formed part of corpus of trust would fall within ambit of income of a trust derived from property held under trust and, hence, includible in total income of trust

IT : Director (Exemption) having allowed accumulation of income of assessee-trust in terms of section 11(2) after being satisfied with objects of trust, exemption under section 11 could not be denied to assessee on ground of non-application of income for charitable purpose
Activities of trust could not be held non-charitable on mere fact that trust has earned certain revenue

INCOME TAX : Where assessee charitable trust, engaged into health and human services for purpose of improving quality of life in society, earned revenue from organizing event of garba during navratri festival, since profit making was not an objective of assessee and said income generated by it was utilized fully for purposes of objects of trust, assessee would not be hit by proviso to section 2(15) and assessee was to be granted exemption under section 11

IT: Exclusion of amounts received by virtue of section 10(22A) is not subject-matter of section 13(1) or any of its further conditions where assessee society duly registered under Indian Societies Act was entitled in law to claim exemption of its income under section 10(22A), fact that managing trustee/founder director in trust was participating in profits of income of trust would not disentitle institution to claim aforesaid exemption

EXCISE/ST/VAT : Where Venture Capital Funds (VCFs) established as trust were managing funds of contributors and thereby rendering service to contributors, in view of fact that they had violated principles of mutuality by concerning themselves in commercial activities and had discretion over distribution of dividend/profit to entities other than subscribers, they could no longer be treated as trusts for purposes of taxation statutes and thus, said services rendered by trust squarely fell under Asset Management as applicable under Banking and Other Financial Services leviable to service tax

IT: Property (i.e. Kalyanamandapams) built by assessee society from its income, subsequent to its formation, on land, which was part of original settlement, was to be considered as property under trust and income therefrom was income from property under trust

INCOME TAX : Where Commissioner cancelled registration of assessee-trust as granted under section 12A(a) on grounds that activities of trust were not genuine and property and income of trust had been used for personal benefits of trustees, since activities of trust were charitable in nature and benefit that trustees were getting could not be a sole reason to cancel registration of trust, cancellation of registration of assessee to be quashed

INCOME TAX : Assessee-trust formed for limited purpose of managing statutory obligations in form of gratuity payable to employees of parent trust would fall within ambit of advancement of general public utility and, hence, its activities was to be considered as a charitable as defined under section 2(15) and, accordingly, assessee was to be granted registration under section 12AA

INCOME TAX : SLP granted against High Court ruling that where assessee-trust, engaged in business of publishing newspaper, did not run any school or college but utilized surplus of income from business for donation to a trust which was running educational institution, earnings of assessee being spent for charitable purpose, registration granted to it could not be cancelled

INCOME TAX : Where assessee trust was engaged in providing asylum/shelter to cows and maintaining gaushalas and famine relief centres to provide proper treatment and fodder to needy stray cows, merely because assessee earned certain revenue from sale of milk, milk product, cattle feed etc., it could not be said that activities of assessee were not charitable so as to cancel its registration under section 12A
No denial of sec. 11 exemption if trust earning rental income to fund its charitable objects: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust engaged in running educational institutions, earned income from letting out of community hall, Kalyana Mandapam and Gnanvapi and utilized surplus income from letting out for objects of trust i.e. running educational institution and providing medical relief to poor, assessee-trust is entitled to exemption under section 11

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust, engaged in business of publishing newspaper, did not run any school or college but utilized surplus of income from business for donation to a trust which was running educational institution, earnings of assessee being spent for charitable purpose, registration granted to it could not be cancelled
IT: Where aims and objects of assessee-trust were charitable and profit earned from said activities was incidental in nature, assessee was not hit by proviso to section 2(15)

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust was engaged in business of publishing newspaper, though assessee did not run any school or college, surplus of income from business was utilized for donation to a particular assessee-trust which was running educational institution and in earlier years, it was confirmed that amounts which were earned by assessee-trust was spent for a charitable purpose, registration granted to assessee-trust could not be cancelled
IT : Where aims and objects of assessee-trust were charitable and profit earned from said activities was incidental in nature, assessee was not hit by proviso to section 2(15)

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust established with main object of establishing educational institutions and providing scholarships, was also running Kalyana Mandapam within boundaries set out in trust deed and surplus generated out of this activity had been utilized by assessee in furtherance of other charitable purposes viz. payment of school fees, contribution to relief funds etc., assessee's claim of deduction under section 11 could not be usurped merely on finding that assessee's activities resulted into surplus funds for assessee

IT : When there was substantial growth in trust on account of services rendered by trustees, to trustes payment made to trustees for such services was not in violation of section 13 and benefit under section 11 was available

INCOME TAX : Once income of a trust was computed under provision of section 11, income derived from trust property was to be taken into account and actual expenditure incurred for objects of trust must be considered as application of income

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, a charitable trust, was a public body, there was no question of its beneficiaries being individual members, whose shares had to be defined and, thus, section 167B prescribing maximum marginal rate would not apply

IT: Fee charged by trust for processing subsidy applications could not be deemed as commercial receipts if it was incidental to its charitable objectives. Thus, assessee-trust was entitled to exemption under Section 10(23C)(iv).

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust established with main object of establishing educational institutions and providing scholarships, was also running Kalyan Mandapam within boundaries set out in trust deed and surplus generated out of this activity had been utilized by assessee in furtherance of other charitable purposes viz., payment of school fees, contribution to relief funds etc.,

IT : Where Assessing Officer disallowed a part of remuneration paid to trustee by assessee-trust taking a view that it was excessive, in view of fact that assessee-trust earned income and paid remuneration to trustee who had also offered tax on remuneration received by her, impugned disallowance was to be deleted
IT: Where genuineness of trust and objects of trust being charitable had not been disputed even if trustees had mismanaged or misutilised funds, exemption under section10(22) could not be denied

INCOME TAX :Where assessee-trust made donations to other charitable trusts out of accumulated income, since said donations were in any case reversed and had been advanced only for an extremely short duration, same would not be hit by provisions of Explanation 2 to section 11(1) as same applies only to amounts credited or paid to certain categories of institutions
IT: Where assessee-trust was a venture capital fund, trusteeship and management fees incurred as per terms of deed could not be disallowed

IT : Any voluntary contribution received by a Charitable or religious trust shall be deemed to be income derived from property held under Trust to extent said contributions are used for charitable purposes even though assessee fails to disclose names and addresses of donors

IT: Where remuneration paid to trustee who was rendering services as full time secretary of trust was about 1 per cent of total value of activities of trust, it could not be said to be excessive or unreasonable
Trust earning sizeable income from incidental activities will get registration if its main object is charitable

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust, set up to address national issues relating to real estate sector, earned revenue from activities of holding conventions, exhibitions etc., since activities that were carried out by assessee were with sole intent of attaining object for which trust was established, activities of assessee would not be hit by exclusion carved out in definition of 'charitable purpose' in section 2(15) and as such, assessee was eligible for exemption under section

IT : Where assessee-trust claimed exemption under section 11 in respect of income earned from a business carried on by it and primary objects of trust were charitable in nature, it was eligible for exemption

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust made donations to other charitable trusts out of accumulated income, since said donations had been advanced only for an extremely short duration, same would not be hit by provisions of Explanation 2 to section 11(1) as same applies only to amounts credited or paid to certain categories of institutions

INCOME TAX : Interest income earned by assessee-charitable trust on its funds which were deposited in bank, would be income directly arising from property of trust and would be exempt under section 11(1)(a)

INCOME TAX: Where assessee-trust paid salary to a specified person, being relative of trustee and holding senior functional role, increase in remuneration being attributable to enhanced roles and responsibilities and his having about 25 years’ experience in sports and 15 years in related sports industry, remuneration was not excessive or unreasonable so as to attract section 13 and exemption under section 11 was allowable

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-association of third party administrators (ATPA) was engaged in primary aim and objective to organise and arrange all licensed third party administrators (TPAs) to be members of trust for mutual betterment of TPA business, merely because certain benefits accrued to TPA members and certain objects of trust were for advancement of business of TPA, it would not ipso facto render trust to be non-charitable

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust paid remuneration to specified person (CEO of trust) who had relevant qualification for job and there was no material brought on record to substantiate that salary or remuneration paid was excessive, provisions of section 13(1)(c) could not be invoked to deny exemption under section 11

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, charitable trust registered under section 12A, filed return claiming exemption under section 11 including accumulation under section 11(2), and filed prescribed Form No. 10 within due date referring to trustees’ resolution setting out specific charitable purposes within objects of trust, income could not be said to have escaped assessment and reassessment notices alleging non-compliance with section 11(2) were unsustainable
IT: Deduction as to repairs and maintenance expenses incurred on trust property being meant for objects of charitable trust, was to be allowed in computing income available for application
Trust not hit by proviso to sec. 2(15) just because it earned incidental income while rendering services

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1946-47 to 1948-49 - Assessee executed a deed of trust whereby they settled certain amount on various charities and appointed themselves as trustees - Later, in accordance with terms of trust deed, trustees assessees were appointed as managing agents of a company - Before Income-tax authorities, trustee claimed that income derived from managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Revenue authorities, however, held that income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Whether word "property" in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend "business," and if question fell to be decided solely on terms of that sub-section, managing agency formed by assessees/trustees must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether fact that trustees had option at any time to throw up managing agency was no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

FACT: 'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation. It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

[Matter remanded to High Court]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether section 4(3)(i) relates to income from business held under trust and section 4(3)(ia) relates to income from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution where that business itself is not held on trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, where business of managing agency was held in trust, it could be concluded that business carried on by trustees fell under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

The Tribunal also held that before the income of a trust for charitable purposes was exempt from tax, it must satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i), i.e., and in the instant case the business not being carried on the course of carrying out the primary purpose of the trust, the income was not exempt form liability to pay tax.

On reference : HELD: By the Insurance Act, 1938, a "principal agent" is defined as meaning "a person, who, not being a salaried employee of an insurer, in consideration of any commission, (i) performs any administrative and organizing functions for the insurer and (ii) procures general insurance business whether wholly or in part by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents of behalf of the insurer". Evidently a principal agent by the definition does not merely render personal service but is concerned with performing certain administrative and organizing functions and the procuring of general insurance business by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents. Such an agent by the very definition will be regarded as carrying on the business of a principal agent. He is not merely an employee engaged for rendering services of a personal nature: he is invested with the right as an agent to perform the administrative organizing functions for the insurer and to procure general insurance business by employing, directly or indirectly, insurance agents. By section 42A of the Insurance Act principal agents are required to obtain a certificate from the Controller of Insurance or an officer authorized by him entitling them to conduct the business of principal agency, and the certificate remains in operation for a period of twelve months only from the date of issue but is liable to be renewed. It is also true that under Part A of the Sixth Schedule to the Insurance Act certain terms are deemed to be included in every contract between an insurer carrying on general insurance business and a principal agent. Under clause 2 of Part A of the Sixth Schedule the principal agent has to procure or cause to be procured through insurance agents such an amount of general insurance business as will yield a gross premium income of not less than Rs. 20,000 in each calendar year. Under clause 4, in the event of the principal agent failing to comply with the requirements of clause 2 in any two successive calendar years, the contract shall, without prejudice to the provisions of clause 3, terminate on the 31st day of March immediately following the second calendar year. Under clause 3 the agency is also liable to be forfeited in the events set out in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) thereof. By clause 5 certain restriction are placed upon the principal agent but an account of these provisions, which impose certain restrictive conditions upon the principal agent it could not be said that the appointment of a principal agent gave rise to a bare service agreement and that the remuneration paid was not for the conduct of a business but for performance of personal service. The circumstance that the appointment was liable to be terminated at short notice and the agency was not permanent and was liable to be forfeited in the events set out hereinbefore would not, affect the character of the agency as business. Following the observation made by the Supreme Court in J.K. Trust's case [1957] 32 ITR 535 the principal agency conducted by the assessee was a business and, therefore, "property" within the meaning of section 4(3)(i). Being property which was capable of being settled upon trust by the deed of trust, dated 17-2-1951, it was lawfully settled upon trust for charitable purposes. The taxing authorities are primarily concerned with the question whether the income sought to be taxed in income from property, which is held on trust for religious or charitable purpose. If the business of the principal agency was transferred to the trustees under a deed of settlement, and from that business income was received, the income will fall within section 4(3)(i) and be exempt from tax in the hands of the trustees. Therefore, under the terms of appointment made with the company firm became the principal agents conducting a business and that business was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i ) and that the alteration, sometime after their appointment as principal agents, in the constitution of the from did not alter the character of the income earned in the course of the business. The income which is liable to be included in the total income of the assessee, was income derived from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution, unless that income fulfils the conditions prescribed by clause (b). The expression "such income" in the proviso refers to the income derived from property (which expression includes a business) held for religious or charitable purposes. But that did not justify the submission that the business which was referred to in clause (b) of the proviso must be business which is held for charitable or religious purposes. The business referred to in clause (b) of the proviso need not be business which is held for religious or charitable purposes, provided it is business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution.

On further appeal, the Tribunal also rejected the claim and confirmed the view of the ITO and the AAC, holding that the true effect of the payments to the hereditary pujaris was the application of the income and it had no direct or indirect relation to the services, if any, rendered by them. HELD: The nature of payment to the trustees-cum - pujaris could not be otherwise than for the services rendered by them, since their tenure of office was linked with their good conduct and they held the offices of trustees-cum-pujaris under the scheme framed under the Bombay Public Trusts Act and were liable to be removed on any of the permissible grounds under the said Act. It was, no doubt, true that the payment had been linked up with the net income of the trust. Nonetheless, the real question was what was the consideration for the payment ? This consideration was the various duties and obligations which the pujaris or the trustees had to carry out under the scheme. The Tribunal, without assigning any reason, had ignored the weighty opinion of the Bombay High Court in Second Appeal No. 565 of 1942 mentioned above supporting this view of the nature of the payments. The Tribunal had also failed to consider the duties to be performed by the trustees-cum-pujaris under the earlier or the present scheme. The Tribunal had, therefore, committed an error of law in reaching the conclusion that the impugned payments were not remuneration for the services rendered by the trustees-cum -pujaris and were merely application of the income of the trust.

The Tribunal had also not borne in mind the clear distinction between the provisions of section 11(1)(a ) relating to income from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes and section 11(1)(b ) relating to income from property held under trust in part only for such purposes. It could not be gainsaid that the trust properties in the instant case were wholly set apart for religious and charitable purposes and it was nobody's case that only a part of the properties had been so set apart. Consequently, having regard to the nature of payments made to the trustees-cum - pujaris, the consideration for which the payment was made and the judicial decisions in that behalf, it could not be urged successfully that this was a case of sharing of income fur a non-charitable object. The Tribunal was, therefore, clearly in error in holding that the case of the assessee-trust fell under section 11(1 )(b) and not under section 11(1)(a ).

HEADNOTE: Section 11(1)(a) and (b) of the Income-tax act, 1961 [as it stood before 1-4-1971]-Charitable or religious trust-Exemption of income from property held for charitable or religious purposes-Assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64-Under scheme of assessee-trust framed under the Bombay public trust act, 50 per cent of its surplus income was to be set apart for reserve fund and remaining 50 per cent was to be divided equally between two heriditary trustees-cum-pujaris-Whether tribunal right in holding that case of trust fell under section 11(1)(b) and not under section 11(1)(a)-Held, on facts, no

FACT: The assessee was a public religious and charitable trust registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. A scheme for this trust was originally framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad way back in 1960 after finding in a suit that the suit properties were part of a public religious , trust and that the defendants were in possession as trustees for and on behalf of the general worshippers of the temple. The Court gave directions setting down the duties and obligations of the pujaries who, as trustees and managers of the temple, were allowed two-thirds of the income of the trust properties for purposes of their maintenance and temple expenses. Subsequently, in Second Appeal No. 565 of 1942, by a judgment-creditor of the then pujari-trustees, the Bombay High Court had occasion to observe that the original scheme framed by the District Court lent strong support to the view that the remuneration payable to the trustees or managers was for the services rendered by them and was their personal property. The present scheme of the trust was framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad in 1960. Under clauses 12, 13 and 14 of this scheme, after meeting outgoings on account of rates, taxes, assessment and expenses incidental to the administration of the trust and worship of the deity of the temple and also current repair and upkeep charges, the trustees were under obligation to distribute the surplus income by setting apart 50 per cent thereof for reserve fund and dividing the remaining 50 per cent equally between the two hereditary trustees, which was to be treated as their absolute property. The amount standing to the credit of the reserve fund was to be invested according to the provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, but out of the annual contribution to the fund, 20 per cent was to be utilised for religious, educational and/or medical purposes with the sanction of the District Court. In the assessment for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64, the previous years being Samvat Years 2017 and 2018, respectively, the trust claimed that the entire income from its property should be exempt from tax under section 11(1)(a). The ITO disallowed the claim holding that the properties of the trust were not held wholly for religious and charitable purposes, since the payment of 50 per cent of the surplus income to the two hereditary trustees was not for charitable purposes, inasmuch as it was not by way of remuneration or salary for the services rendered by them as employees and what they received was out of the income of the trust. According to the ITO, the only income which was entitled to be exempt under section 11(1)(b) would be the amount actually spent for religious purposes and 20 per cent of the amount of contribution set apart as reserve fund. On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's view that the case would fall under section 11(1)(b) as the income was only partly applied for religious purposes. He also rejected the alternative claim of the trust that the said payments must be treated as allowable expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal also rejected the claim and confirmed the view of the ITO and the AAC, holding that the true effect of the payments to the hereditary pujaris was the application of the income and it had no direct or indirect relation to the services, if any, rendered by them.

HEADNOTE: Section 10(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(viii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Agricultural income - Assessment year 1950-51 - Assessee executed a deed of trust settling certain properties including agriculture lands in trust for maintenance of certain temples - Under covenant in trust deed, he received 15 per cent of net income from trust as remuneration for management of trust - Assessee had no beneficial interest in lands which were subject-matter of trust nor was he given a right to receive and appropriate to himself income of properties or a part thereof in lieu of any beneficial interest in that income - Whether both source and character of income in question was altered when a part of income of trust was appropriated by assessee under covenant in deed of trust as remuneration for services rendered and therefore, remuneration not being received as rent or revenue of agricultural lands under a title, legal or beneficial in property from which income was received, it was not income exempt under section 4(3)(viii) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee executed a deed of trust settling certain lands and the rents of lands for the maintenance of certain temples. He as a legal trustee received 15 per cent of net income of the trust as remuneration. The ITO sought to tax the income received by the assessee from the trust as well as remuneration received as shebait on the ground that same was not an agriculture income. In the view of the ITO, the trust was not a public religious trust and the income derived from properties not used for agriculture was not exempt from liability to pay tax in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC held that the income coming to the hands of the assessee from the trust properties was not taxable as private income of the assessee, but the remuneration computed at the rate of 15 per cent on the net income of the trust properties in the year in question not being agricultural income in the assessee's hands was liable to be taxed. On appeal to the Tribunal, the order passed by the AAC in so far as it related to remuneration received by the assessee was affirmed.

On reference, the High Court agreed with the Tribunal that the remuneration was received by the assessee under a contract, and it was not agricultural income.

On appeal to the Supreme Court, the assessee submitted that the remuneration which by the covenant contained in the deed of trust he had received was also exempt under section 4(3)(viii) because, when he appropriated a fraction of the rent or revenue of agricultural lands towards his remuneration, the original character of the income was not altered.

HELD: The assessee had no beneficial interest in the lands which were the subject-matter of the trust: nor was he given under the trust a right to receive and appropriate to himself the income of the properties or a part thereof in lieu of any beneficial interest in that income. The source of the right in which a fraction of the net income of the trust was to be appropriated by the assessee as his remuneration was not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands, but rested in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The income of the trust appropriated by the assessee as remuneration was not received by him as rent or revenue of land; the character of the income appropriated as remuneration due was again not the same as the character in which it was received by the assessee as trustee. Both the source and character of the income were, therefore, altered when a part of the income of the trust was appropriated by the assessee as his remuneration, and that was so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration was made as a percentage of the income, a substantial part whereof was derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. The remuneration not being received as rent or revenue of agricultural lands under a title, legal or beneficial in the property from which the income was received, it was not income exempt under section 4(3)(viii).

In the instant case, the assessee had no beneficial interest in the trust property. The assessee so far as his remuneration was concerned was not the direct recipient of the income of the trust, the source and the character of the income were both altered when agricultural income was appropriated under the covenant in the deed of trust as remuneration for services rendered.

Hence, the amount paid to the assessee in his character of a shebait of the trust properties was not exempted from taxation.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1951-52 to 1954-55 - A partnership firm was formed by four brothers - Firm was appointed as chief agent of an insurance company - Subsequently, brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming trustees would hold said business of chief agency of said company and all benefits and profits to arise from said business upon trust for public charitable purposes - Whether principal agency conducted by assessee-trust was a business and, therefore, "property" within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which was capable of being settled upon trust - Held, yes - Whether income of assessee-trust not being one which was not governed by proviso to section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as amended by Act 25 of 1953, but was governed by operative part of section 4(3)(i), it was exempt from tax - Held, yes

FACT: A partnership firm was formed by four brothers. No deed of partnership was said to have been executed in respect of this firm. The firm was appointed the chief agent an insurance company as from 1-9-1950. On 17-2-1951, the aforesaid brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming the trustees would hold the said business of the chief agency of the said company and all the benefits and profits to arise from the said business upon trust for public charitable purposes. The said declaration of trust was registered with the Registrar of Assurances.

The assessee claimed that as from 17-2-1951, the income from agency business should be assessed in the hands of the trustees and should be allowed exemption under section 4(3)(i). The ITO, however, made the assessment in the status of an unregistered firm. The ITO held that there was no charitable trust created by the deed dated 17-2-1951. On appeal, the AAC reversed the findings of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no proper and valid contract between the insurance company and the trustees as such; that the letter of appointment was only a service agreement; that there had been no transfer of property to the trustees wholly for charitable purposes; that the alleged transfer of the agency agreement did not amount to the transfer of property. The Tribunal also held that before the income of a trust for charitable purposes was exempt from tax, it must satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i), i.e., and in the instant case the business not being carried on the course of carrying out the primary purpose of the trust, the income was not exempt form liability to pay tax.

On reference :

On reference, the High Court held that it was a voluntary resignation for which under the agency agreement the assessee was not entitled to any compensation, therefore, the compensation received for surrendering the agency was remuneration received on account of conducting the business, and was income.

On appeal to the Supreme Court : HELD: The managing agency was not, except in the circumstances set out in clause 2 of the agreement, liable to be determined at the instance of the company, unless the assessee by giving notice of three weeks voluntarily resigned the agency. At the date of termination the agency had five more years to run, and the Companies Act did not prohibit renewal of the agency in favour of the assessee, after the expiry of the initial period of twenty years. The assessee was formed for the object, amongst others (vide clause 3(2) of the memorandum of association of the appellant) of carrying on the business of managing agencies. The assessee was entitled under the terms of the agreement to receive so long as the agency enured ten per cent of the profits of the company's working, three per cent on all purchases of stores and machinery abroad, and a monthly remuneration of Rs. 3,000. The assessee submitted its resignation in exercise of the power reserved under clause 8 of the managing agency agreement, but that resignation was, it was common ground, part of the arrangement. Under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the principal company was not obliged to pay any compensation to the assessee for voluntary resignation of the agency, but in consideration of the assessee parting with its shareholding and submitting resignation of the managing agency so as to facilitate the appointment of 'M' as managing agent, the latter purchased the shareholding of the assessee, undertook to make available Rs. 3,50,000 for payment to the assessee and to discharge the debt due by the company to the assessee. Payment of Rs. 3,50,000, was therefore an integral part of an arrangement for transfer of managing agency. A managing agency of a company is in the nature of a capital asset; that is not denied. It is true that it is not like an ordinary asset capable of being transferred from one person to another. Theoretically, the power to appoint or dismiss the managing agent may lie with the directors of the company, but in practice the power lies with the person or persons having a controlling interest in the shareholding of the company. 'M' was anxious to be appointed managing agents of the principal company; and for that purpose the assessee had to be persuaded to agree to a premature termination of its agency. This was secured for a triple consideration: sale of shares held by the assessee at an agreed price, stipulation to discharge the liability of the company to repay the loans due by the company, and payment of Rs. 3,50,000 as compensation for termination of the assessee's agency. The assessee was formed with the object, among others, of acquiring managing agencies of companies and to carry on the business and to take part in the management, supervision or control of the business or operations of any other company, association, firm or person and to make profit out of it. That only authorised the assessee to acquire as a fixed asset, if a managing agency may be so described, and to exploit it for the purpose of profit. But there was no evidence that the company was formed for the purpose of acquiring and selling managing agencies and making profit by those transactions of sale and purchase. A managing agency is not an asset for which there is a market, for it depends upon the personal qualifications of the agent. In truth the amount of Rs. 3,50,000 was received by the assessee from 'M' in consideration of the former agreeing to forgo the agency which it held and which 'M' was anxious to obtain. It was in a business sense a sale of such rights as the assessee possessed in the agency. This was supported by the recitals made in clause 2 of the agreement that if at any time within six months after the completion of such sale 'M' was unable to exercise the voting rights attached to the shares purchased by them, the assessee would appoint any person nominated by to attend and vote for them at any meeting of the company or the holders of any class of shares to be held within such period in such manner as 'M' might decide. The object underlying the agreement was therefore to transfer the managing agency to 'M' or at least to effectuate their appointment in place of the assessee as managing agent of the company. All the stipulations and the covenants of the agreement, viewed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, did stamp the transaction as one of surrender of the rights of the assessee in the managing agency so that corresponding rights may arise in favour of 'M'. It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts

The Tribunal's view was that the surrender by 'B' was valid under section 58 of the Indian Trusts Act, and, consequently, after that deed was executed, the properties were held wholly for charitable purposes and the income was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court also decided the matter in favour of the assessee - trust.

On appeal to the Supreme Court: HELD: Whenever a valid trust is executed, the property vests in the trustees, and the income accruing from those properties is the income of the trust and not of the beneficiaries. For purposes of income-tax law, however, the income under section 41(1) of the Act 1922 is treated as received by the trustees on behalf of the beneficiaries, but is to be taxed in the hands of the trustees in the like manner and to the same amount as it would be leviable upon the person on whose behalf such income is receivable. The liability of the income to tax is, therefore, independent of the income actually being received by the beneficiaries and it may be subjected to tax as soon as it is earned by the trust. The exception is that, where the trust properties are held wholly for charitable or religious purposes, in so far as such income is applied or accumulated for application to such religious or charitable purposes, it is exempt from income-tax. In the instant case, therefore, in dealing with the question referred to the High Court, any assumption that the income of the trust properties was received by 'B' would not be correct. The income during her lifetime was clearly taxable as income in the hands of the trustees received by them on behalf of 'B'.

Under section 4(3)(i ) of 1922 Act, the income from trust properties, held wholly for charitable or religious purposes, is exempt from tax under two circumstances. The first is when that income is actually applied for such religious or charitable purposes, and the second is when it is accumulated for application to such religious or charitable purposes. In instant case, as soon as 'B' executed the deed of surrender, her rights under clause 7 completely ceased and all the income from the trust properties remained with the trustees to be applied in accordance with the other terms of the deed of trust. If it could be held that clause 8 came into operation and permitted the application of that income to the charitable purposes mentioned in it as soon as B's rights ceased, even though she remained alive, there would be no difficulty in holding that section 4(3)(i ) of 1922 Act would have exempted the income from income-tax.

The instant appeal was to be dismissed accordingly.

The case was decided in favour of respondent/assessee.
