Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Property held under trust) - Assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015 - Whether once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, property so acquired will be property held under trust and income from such property will be income from property under trust - Held, yes - Assessee society was having income from two Kalyanamandapams - According to Assessing Officer these properties were not settled by settlor as trust property and hence could not be considered as properties held under trust and thus he held that income earned by assessee from its Kalyanamandapams could not be treated as income from house property but only as income from business - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Assessing Officer holding that Kalyanamandapams having being built by assessee subsequent to its formation could not be considered as property under trust - However, assessee submitted that land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of original settlement and buildings were built therein by assessee from its income - Whether thus, rental income received by assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT: Property (i.e. Kalyanamandapams) built by assessee society from its income, subsequent to its formation, on land, which was part of original settlement, was to be considered as property under trust and income therefrom was income from property under trust  IT: Where predominant activity of assessee society was charity, it would be eligible for exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Hindu undivided family - Assessable as - Assessment year 1939-40 - Assessee was karta of HUF - He entered into partnership representing beneficial interest of HUF - Said partnership firm purchased a mill - Later on, partnership firm promoted a company which took over said mill - Company so promoted, appointed partnership firm as its managing agent - Pursuant to said agreement, firm received managing agency commission from company time to time which was divided between partners thereof - During assessment year in question, assessee claimed that his share of managing agency commission belonged to him individually, and therefore, it could not be included in his assessment made as karta of HUF - Revenue authorities rejected assessee's claim - Whether since managing agency was acquired with assistance of HUF's property, i.e. mill in which assessee as karta was beneficially interested, income derived by him from managing agency was to be regarded as income of HUF of which he was karta - Held, yes

Section 11, read with section 13(1)(c)(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1978-79, 1979-80 and 1980-81 - Two cinemas, being property of assessee-trust, were given on hire to a company - Company further gave management and control of cinemas to a firm which consisted of two partners being wife and son of trustee of assessee-trust - Whether income of trust property was diverted to prohibited persons and, thus, exemption of income of trust derived from these cinemas was hit by provisions contained in section 13(1)(c)(ii) - Held, no.

Section 11, read with section 2(15), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property. Held for charitable or religious purposes - Main objects of assessee-association were to promote cultural, social and educational developments, to encourage development of arts, agriculture, horticulture and industry, to improve cattle breeding, to promote physical culture and public health, etc. - None out of said objects was dominant and trustees could utilise trust income for any such objects - It derived income from shop rents, cattle registration fees, wrestling matches and music sammelans, etc. - Whether assessee held property within the meaning of section 11(1)(b) and consequently eligible for exemption thereunder in respect of amounts actually spent on charities - Held, on facts, no - Whether assessee's income was not exempt under section 11(1)(a) - Held, on facts, yes - Whether assessee's object of holding agricultural and industrial exhibitions involved an activity for profit within the meaning of section 2(15) - Held, on facts, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income form property held under - Assessment year 1982-83 - ITO disallowed part of expenses claimed by assessee-trust - Whether question whether expenses incurred by assessee trust for maintaining horses, carriages and motor cars and allowances paid to trustees and others to extent disallowed by authorities below were also part and parcel of amount applied for religious and charitable purposes and were in any event bona fide and legitimate expenditure wholly and exclusively incurred for purpose of earning income, was a question of fact which required cosideration - Held, yes - Whether since ITO did not go into question whether said expenses were incurred for religious and charitable purposes, matter was to be remanded back - Held, yes

Section 11, read with section 2(13) and section 12, of the Income-tax 
Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1978-79 to 1980-81 - Hyderabad Race Club created assessee-trust - Main objects of assessee-trust were advancement and propagation of education, medical aid and relief 
to poor, etc. - Assessee-trust obtained licence from State Government 
for conduct of races and inter-venue betting and derived income from such activities - Whether since assessee-trust had conducted stray activities, i.e., conducting races and inter-venue betting for purpose 
of achieving its primary objects, activities undertaken by assessee-
trust could be called ‘business’ within meaning of section 2(13) and income derived from such activities could be called as ‘business income’ - 
 Held, no - Whether, therefore, income derived by assessee-trust was exempted under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether even if income was not treated as income from property held under trust, it could be treated as voluntary contribution given by Hyderabad Race Club to assessee-trust as contemplated in section 12 - Held, yes

II. Section 11, read with  section 12, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1966-67 - Whether membership fee and subscription amounts received by trust/society from its members cannot be characterized as voluntary contribution within meaning of expression 'fund' in section 12 - Held, yes - Whether said subscription has to be considered as income derived from property held under trust and therefore, is exempt under section 11 - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Hindu undivided family - Assessable as - Two brothers 'M' and 'C', who were members of joint Hindu family, entered into a partnership and were appointed as managing agents of 'D' mill under an agreement - After death of 'C' fresh managing agency agreement was entered into between 'D' mill and 'M' and four sons of 'C' - Revenue authorities claimed that income earned by each of four sons of 'C' under managing agency agreement was joint family income and not their individual income - Whether since in terms of managing agency agreement there was no obligation on part of managing agents either to advance money or keep any of assets in hands of mills as a condition precedent for exercising their rights under agreement or for continuance of agreement, there was no legal basis for coming to conclusion that income earned by four sons of 'C' under managing agency agreement was joint family property and not their individual income - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Whether in view of facts stated under heading ‘Charitable purpose’ and the fact that income was derived from commercial activities, income accumulated by assessee could be 
 held as income accumulated only for charitable purposes and assessee was entitled to exemption of amount accumulated by it - Held, no (matter remanded back)

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with section 19 of Bombay Trust Act, 1950 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1964-65 to 1969-70, 1972-73 and 1973-74 - Lands of some villages were said to have been granted by one Mughal Emperor for upkeep of Roza in year 1670 under a Sanad and grants were confirmed by sanads issued during British regime - A suo motu enquiry was started under section 19 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 - As a result of that inquiry, Dy. Charity Commissioner made an order directing that assessee- Roza Trust be registered as a Public Trust - On appeal Charity Commissioner confirmed order of Dy. Charity Commissioner - He held that assessee-trust was a public trust and lands of villages were properties of said trust - Question for consideration was as to whether income from lands in question was income of assessee-Roza Trust assessable in hands of said trust and exempt under section 11 or whether it was assessable in hands of Sajjadanashin of Trust i.e., ‘SM’, as income from his private property - Tribunal on material before it, which included orders made by Dy. Charity Commissioner and Charity Commissioner, documents such as Sanad issued by Mughal Emperor and Sanads of Government, Survey Settlement register and historical account given in text-books, came to finding that these lands of four villages belonged to assessee-trust - Whether while it is true that tax authority, during assessment proceedings, can always inquire into question of ownership of property and decide issue in context of relevant provisions of said Act, in order to ascertain income of the assessee for bringing it to tax, it will not be open for tax authorities to ignore relevant evidence of statutory registration of a public trust and fact of the properties having been registered as properties of such public trust under provisions of Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 - Held, yes - Whether finding of Charity Commissioner in an inquiry 
under section 19 of Bombay Public Trust operates as findings in rem and cannot be ignored by authorities under Income-tax Act - Held, yes - Whether Sajjadanashin of Roza Trust was spiritual leader and integral part of Roza Trust and, therefore, provision for Sajjadanashin was not a provision for man but for institution and therefore, expenses incurred on 
 Sajjadanashin by assessee-trust could not be held to be expenses for private property - Held, yes - Whether Tribunal was justified in holding that income from lands in question was assessable in hands of assessee-trust and not in hands of Sajjadanashin and further that trust was entitled to exemption in respect of income spent as ‘Madad-E-Maash’ on maintenance of Sajjadanashin, his family and descendants - Held, yes - Whether amount received by Sajjadanashin was to be taxed as income in his hands - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1977-78 to 1979-80 - Assessee-trust was denied exemption under section 11 as it derived income from letting out its hall as Kalyana Mandapam and furniture, utensils and decorative items, etc., at commercial rates - Whether since objects of assessee-trust were education and other objects of general utility and letting out of Kalyana Mandapam was not one of objects of assessee but was only activity carried on to fulfil its objects and income therefrom was not its business income but property income, Tribunal was correct in holding that assessee was entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

Section 57,  read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income from other sources - Deductions - Whether following decision in CIT v. Trustees of H.E.H. The Nizam's Miscellaneous Trust [1986] 160 ITR 253 (AP), the High Court was right in dismissing revenue's application under section 256(2) and holding that 7½ per cent of net receipts of income of trust after deducting from its total income remuneration paid to trustees, constituted reasonable expenditure for administering trust under sections 57(i) and 19(i) - Held, yes

SECTION 11 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CHARITABLE OR RELIGIOUS 
TRUST-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDER TRUST-
WHETHER HANDING OVER OF ACCUMULATED INCOME TO ANOTHER CHARIT-
ABLE TRUST WOULD AMOUNT TO APPLICATION OF INCOME FOR CHARITABLE PURPOSES-HELD, YES

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable and Religious Trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1994-95 - Whether, if a property, including running business, was held for charitable and religious purposes and fulfilled all conditions envisaged under section 11 and did not come under any of exceptional clauses under section 13 then 
 Assessing Officer cannot deny benefit provided to such trust under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether for carrying on charitable purpose trust could have activity of profit as well as property which could give income so as to maintain and execute its basic aim and objects, with only exception that profit earning should not be real object - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) – Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under – Assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56 – Claim of assessee trust for exemption of its income under section 4(3)(i) was rejected by ITO on ground that business of trust carried on by managing trustee on behalf of trust fell within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and hence its business income was not exempt from taxation – Whether where trust carries on business and business itself is held in trust and income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for purpose of religious or charitable character, conditions prescribed under section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and income is exempt from taxation - Held, yes – Whether claim of exemption cannot be denied even if business were to be conducted by someone else acting on behalf of trust, and proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to such businesses as are not held under trust and, therefore, field of its operation is distinct and separate from that covered by main provision of section 4(3)(i) – Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, assessee being a religious and charitable trust, was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act for assessment years in question – Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Religious or charitable trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies created a trust and purported to endow it with share held by him in certain transport companies - Contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately but companies in which N was interested were to have benefit of assets set apart by him - N was managing trustee and empowered to borrow to any extent on properties conveyed to trust not only for trust but for his own use trustees were empowered, so long as N held office of managing trustee, to sell immovable properties belonging to trust for purpose of floating other companies - Foundation of institution was apparently to be left over until companies had made sufficient money for purpose - N also reserved right to revoke trust at any time - Whether on facts properties in question were not held under trust for charitable purpose within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(ii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1946-47 - Assessee was appointed Mahant of a temple under a deed of trust, whereunder offerings made by devotees were completely under his control and he could spend them as he liked without consent of managing committee subject to condition that such spending would not be against his position as Mahant and against tenets of their religion - ITO treated said offerings as taxable income of assessee - Assessee claimed that as income was applicable solely to religious or charitable purposes, it was exempt under section 4(3)(ii) - Whether income could not be said to be applicable solely to religious or charitable purposes and as such, offerings were not exempt from tax under section 4(3)(ii) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11, read with section 164 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i), read with section 41(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1940-41 and 1941-42 - Settlor-trustee created a trust by two deeds in favour of certain family deities which were shown in three groups - Under trust deed, trustee was directed to meet in first place out of income received by him public charges, cost of litigation and for preservation and improvement of trust properties and in next place pay to shebait or trustee for time being as his commission or remuneration- Balance of income remaining after meeting such expenses was to be held by trustee for benefit of deities and same was to form part of corpus of trust properties - Whether on terms of deed, it must be held that property was vested in various deities and not in trustee even though in very nature of things shebait or trustee must have full control over income and expenditure always subject to directions in deeds of trust - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income of trust properties in question in hands of trustee was not to be assessed at maximum rate under first proviso to section 41(1) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether since provisions of trust deed did not contain any direction that any part of income should be spent on specific public charitable purposes, amount spent by assessee-trustee on public charitable objects amounted merely to application of part of income but would not entitle assessee to claim that part of income should be exempt from taxation - Held, yes

Section 11, read with section 13 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income, from property held under - Assessment year 1995-96 - Assessing Officer disallowed exemption claimed by assessee-
 trust under section 11 on two grounds, namely, (a) that even though assessee’s buildings were being used by other societies of same group for charitable activities, such use could not be treated as use by assessee for carrying out its own charitable activities; and (b) that major expenditure was on account of agricultural and dairy activities carried on by it which was not in nature of application of its income for charitable purpose - Commissioner (Appeals), however, upheld assessee’s claim - Whether where buildings of assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature, such use could very well be treated as use by assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for purpose of exemption under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether since agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by assessee-society as separate business activities, same constituted ‘property held under trust’ as provided in section 11(4) and in any case income of said activities was to be determined after deducting expenditure incurred in connection with said business - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, gross income being more than sufficient to cover expenses incurred in connection with said activities, allowance of same by Commissioner  (Appeals) as application of its income hardly made any difference in ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to revenue - Held, yes
Circulars and Instructions - CBDT’s Circular No. 1132, dated 5-1-1978

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 2004-05 - Whether a voluntary contribution would qualify to form a part of income of recipient trust; however, only exception is where such income is directed to form part of corpus of trust or institution and it is in that case, in view of specific provisions of section 11(1)(d), it cannot be applied for charitable purposes, and, hence, for claiming exemption - Held, yes [Matter remanded]

Section 11(1)(a) and (b) of the Income-tax act, 1961 [as it stood before 1-4-1971]-Charitable or religious trust-Exemption of income from property held for charitable or religious purposes-Assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64-Under scheme of assessee-trust framed under the Bombay public trust act, 50 per cent of its surplus income was to be set apart for reserve fund and remaining 50 per cent was to be divided equally between two heriditary trustees-cum-pujaris-Whether tribunal right in holding that case of trust fell under section 11(1)(b) and not under section 11(1)(a)-Held, on facts, no

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1949-50 and 1950-51 - Taking up managing agency along with secretaryship to plantation company and other trading rights was part of assessee's normal trading activities - Assessee dealt with, among other things, export of tea produced in India - Managing agencies, assessee obtained were liable to termination, in which event assessee received compensation it was entitled to by agreement - Such agreement was not a contract for securing simpliciter managing agency for company but was a composite agreement securing other rights as well to assessee, which helped it in its trading activities in tea - Assessee's business in tea proceeded apace notwithstanding termination of such agreements - Whether termination of agreement with tea company could be said to have been brought about in ordinary course of business of assessee and money paid to assessee as a result of or in connection with termination of such agreements should certainly be regarded as money received in ordinary course of business of assessee and, therefore, it was a trading receipt - Held, yes

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1950-51 - Managing agents of assessee company decided to voluntarily forgo part of its remuneration - In matter of assessment of managing agents High Court held that amount voluntarily forgone by managing agents could not be allowed as revenue deduction and accordingly, taxed entire amount of remuneration in their hands - Whether liability incurred by assessee company was not lesser amount but whole amount payable as remuneration and, hence, assessee was entitled to deduction of whole amount as managing agency remuneration - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1961-62 to 1963-64 - An association of persons, chiefly engaged in horse racing, declared and made a trust - As per said trust deed, surplus funds were to be disposed of, (i) by making improvements to racing facilities, and/or (ii) by making donations at discretion of trustees to any recognised institution for social, cultural and physical benefits of people - Whether surplus funds really emanated from a property which was not a subject-matter of trust and as such in absence of any legal obligation fastened thereto, no exemption could be allowed under section 11 - Held, yes - Whether further, since trustees had indefeasible alternative right to apply funds to other purposes, without making any donation to charitable purposes no part of its income was exempt from tax - Held, yes

Section 28(ii) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(5A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Compensation - Assessment year 1960-61 - Assessee-company was allowed in terms of an agreement, a compensation for loss of managing agency of managed company as a consequence of its takeover by State Government - ITO taxed compensation amount treated it as a capital receipt - Tribunal held that entire receipt to which provisions of section 10(5A) were attracted was a taxable income - Whether words "termination...of his managing agency agreement" as used in section 10(5A) of 1922 Act, contemplated termination of agency agreement, in several manners contemplated under Contract Act and by other statutes, and meant cessation of mutual rights and obligations of either party under agency agreement and, therefore, it could not be said that managing agency contract can be terminated only by out of parties and in no other manner - Held, yes - Whether business of assessee was to carry on managing agency business multiple in nature, there was no material to show that assessee was not carrying on such business, after State Government had taken over G managed company and business could not be read in restricted sense taking into consideration only that business to which compensation related - Held, yes - Whether section 10(5A) of 1922 Act speaks of compensation being due to or received by a managing agent to be deemed to be profits and gains of a business carried on by managing agent, as such compensation is paid or becomes payable on cessation of business, section provides that it shall be deemed to be income even after termination - Held, yes - Whether therefore, compensation received by assessee company was taxable profit within meaning of section 10(5A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1965-66 to 1967-68 - Whether section 11 requires consideration of objects of trust and also of income derived from property held in trust -Held, yes - Whether so long as expenditure had to be incurred out of income earned by trust, even if such expenditure is for capital purposes on objects of trust, income would be exempt - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, mere improvement of a property held under trust would not by itself come within scope of application of income for charitable purposes without investigating as to whether by incurring said expenditure assessee promoted objects of trust - Held, yes

Section 11, read with section 13(2), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1973-74 to 1981-82 - Whether income received by trust from a business is by itself not a ground to deny benefit of section 10(22) - Held, yes - Whether 
 fact that trustees happened to be partners of firms and that they had assigned to trust irrevocably their share income would not result in any diversion of funds by trust to trustees - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1950-51 - Whether on facts under head 'Business expenditure - Allowability of' amount voluntarily given up by managing agents and received as such by assessee could not be treated as receipt or income in hands of assessee and, hence, was not liable to income-tax - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under Assessment year 1984-85 - Whether donation made by a charitable trust to another charitable trust would tantamount to application of income for charitable purposes and, hence, was eligible for exemption - Held, yes - Whether assessee, a charitable trust, was exempt, from tax, under section 11(1A), on capital gains arising from sale of certain immovable property held by it - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to Section 4(3)(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Settlor created a trust in respect of certain shares declaring in trust deed that income from trust property was to be belonged to him during his life time and after his death to his wife and after death of both, income was to go to certain charitable trusts created by him - During his life time settlor modified said trust deed and relinquished his entire life interest in that property - Up to death of settlor income from trust fund was paid to his wife - After death of settlor, his wife also executed a deed on 20-5-1955 whereby she in turn relinquished and surrendered her life interest with a view to accelerating subsequent trust in favour of charity - After that deed that 20-5-1955, assessee, (trustees), claimed that income derived from property held under trust was wholly religious and charitable purpose and was to exempted from tax - However, ITO on observation that interest for life allowed by settlor to his wife was restricted in asmuch as it was laid down that she had no power to anticipate or alienate her interest, therefore declaration made by her in said deed was void and income of property held under trust was not for charitable purpose - Whether in view of decision of Supreme Court in CIT v. Kasturbai Walchand Trust [1967] 63 ITR 656 (SC) income that accrued or arose to trustees from trust properties from 20-5-1953 onwards, was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the Act 1922 - Held, yes

facts.text:
'P; 'L' and 'LS' executed a deed of trust whereby they settled a sum on various charities specified therein and appointed themselves and two others as trustees. The trust deed provided inter alia that the trustees mights with the help of the trust fund, for and on behalf of and for the benefit of the trust, carry on such business including the taking up and conducting the managing agency or selling agency of any company in such name or names as they in their absolute discretion might think fit and proper. Later the trustees were appointed as managing agents of a company. The agency was to be for a period of 20 years; but it was open to the trustees to throw it up on giving three months' notice. The managing agents were to get a remuneration of 10 per cent of the net annual profits. Before the Income-tax authorities, the assessee/trustees claimed that the income derived from the managing agency was income derived from property held under trust to be applied wholly for charitable purposes, and was, in consequence, exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The Income-tax authorities held that the income in question was remuneration for services rendered, and was not derived from any property, and that, therefore, it did not fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court held that no part of the sum of Rs. 1,00,000 which was the only property settled on trust was actually invested in the managing agency business, which could not, therefore, be regarded as trust property, and that the income received from that business was not within the exemption enacted in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

Under a trust deed dated the 15-6-1945, according to the decision of the Privy Council the business of a managing agency was held in trust. Therefore, the income derived from managing agency was held by the Supreme Court as falling with section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act since the word "property" in that sub-section includes business as well. But it was contended before the Supreme Court that although the income might appear to fall within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act as the language of that section is wide enough to include the income, the scope of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act has been narrowed down by the provision in section 4(3)(ia) which deals with income from business and, therefore, the Sub-section that really applies to the determination of the question as to whether the income sought to be taxed in the hands of the trustees was exempt from tax in section 4(3)(ia) and not section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. It was common ground that if section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act was the section under which the exemption claimed was to be determined, the conditions laid down in that sub-section for the purpose of granting an exemption were not satisfied and, therefore, the assessees would not be entitled to an exemption. The question was, therefore, of vital importance to the assessees as to whether their case fell within section 4(3)(i) of section 4(3)(ia) of 1922 Act.

On reference:

The assessee was a public religious and charitable trust registered under the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. A scheme for this trust was originally framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad way back in 1960 after finding in a suit that the suit properties were part of a public religious , trust and that the defendants were in possession as trustees for and on behalf of the general worshippers of the temple. The Court gave directions setting down the duties and obligations of the pujaries who, as trustees and managers of the temple, were allowed two-thirds of the income of the trust properties for purposes of their maintenance and temple expenses. Subsequently, in Second Appeal No. 565 of 1942, by a judgment-creditor of the then pujari-trustees, the Bombay High Court had occasion to observe that the original scheme framed by the District Court lent strong support to the view that the remuneration payable to the trustees or managers was for the services rendered by them and was their personal property. The present scheme of the trust was framed by the District Judge, Ahmedabad in 1960. Under clauses 12, 13 and 14 of this scheme, after meeting outgoings on account of rates, taxes, assessment and expenses incidental to the administration of the trust and worship of the deity of the temple and also current repair and upkeep charges, the trustees were under obligation to distribute the surplus income by setting apart 50 per cent thereof for reserve fund and dividing the remaining 50 per cent equally between the two hereditary trustees, which was to be treated as their absolute property. The amount standing to the credit of the reserve fund was to be invested according to the provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, but out of the annual contribution to the fund, 20 per cent was to be utilised for religious, educational and/or medical purposes with the sanction of the District Court. In the assessment for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64, the previous years being Samvat Years 2017 and 2018, respectively, the trust claimed that the entire income from its property should be exempt from tax under section 11(1)(a). The ITO disallowed the claim holding that the properties of the trust were not held wholly for religious and charitable purposes, since the payment of 50 per cent of the surplus income to the two hereditary trustees was not for charitable purposes, inasmuch as it was not by way of remuneration or salary for the services rendered by them as employees and what they received was out of the income of the trust. According to the ITO, the only income which was entitled to be exempt under section 11(1)(b) would be the amount actually spent for religious purposes and 20 per cent of the amount of contribution set apart as reserve fund. On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's view that the case would fall under section 11(1)(b) as the income was only partly applied for religious purposes. He also rejected the alternative claim of the trust that the said payments must be treated as allowable expenditure. On further appeal, the Tribunal also rejected the claim and confirmed the view of the ITO and the AAC, holding that the true effect of the payments to the hereditary pujaris was the application of the income and it had no direct or indirect relation to the services, if any, rendered by them.

The assessee company carried on business in hides and skins, minerals, tobacco and other commodities, and also acted as managing agents for the 'N' and for two other companies. 'T', 'M' and 'C' were directors of the company. The assessee was appointed by the Central Government as its agent for buying, checking, weighing, leaf drying, storing, transporting, retaining and reselling tobacco under and in accordance with the directions issued from time to time and agreed to pay to the assessee price of the tobacco purchased, charge at the rate of one anna per 1b. for tobacco not redried, and at the rate of two annas per 1b. for tobacco redried, and commission on all purchases. Subsequently assessee passed a resolution placing 'T' 'special charge' for arranging purchases of tobacco on credit, inspecting tobacco at Guntur and at Madras Port, and for supervising shipment of tobacco, and agreed to pay him 30 per cent of the net profit as remuneration. Under the contract with the Government of India, certain amount became due to the assessee as commission in the account year ending 31-3-1952. After providing for expenses, 30 per cent of the balance was paid to 'T' as commission and was claimed in the assessment year 1952-53 as a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act. The ITO accepted that the expenditure for payment of remuneration for attending to the contract was laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee but reduced the stipulated rate to 10 per cent on two grounds : that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of the company, bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the contract.

Further, the managing agency agreement of the assessee with the 'N' was terminated, when the Government of the State of Madras in exercise of the powers conferred upon it by the Electrical Undertakings Acquisition Act, 1949, compulsorily acquired the undertaking of that company, and the assessee was paid sum as compensation for premature termination of its agency. The ITO observed that the 'assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end', the assessee still continues as 'managing agents of other companies'. Even after surrender of one of the agencies, the assessee carried on business as before, its structure not being affected' and therefore the receipt is to be considered as revenue.

On appeal, both the AAC as well the Tribunal upheld the order of the ITO.

On reference, the High Court allowed the assessee's claim.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee executed a deed of trust settling certain lands and the rents of lands for the maintenance of certain temples. He as a legal trustee received 15 per cent of net income of the trust as remuneration. The ITO sought to tax the income received by the assessee from the trust as well as remuneration received as shebait on the ground that same was not an agriculture income. In the view of the ITO, the trust was not a public religious trust and the income derived from properties not used for agriculture was not exempt from liability to pay tax in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC held that the income coming to the hands of the assessee from the trust properties was not taxable as private income of the assessee, but the remuneration computed at the rate of 15 per cent on the net income of the trust properties in the year in question not being agricultural income in the assessee's hands was liable to be taxed. On appeal to the Tribunal, the order passed by the AAC in so far as it related to remuneration received by the assessee was affirmed.

On reference, the High Court agreed with the Tribunal that the remuneration was received by the assessee under a contract, and it was not agricultural income.

On appeal to the Supreme Court, the assessee submitted that the remuneration which by the covenant contained in the deed of trust he had received was also exempt under section 4(3)(viii) because, when he appropriated a fraction of the rent or revenue of agricultural lands towards his remuneration, the original character of the income was not altered.

Durgha consecrated to Hazerath Sayed receives large income from immovable properties endowed to it and the offerings in cash and kind made by the devotees. The Durgha and its properties were being administered under a scheme settled by the High Court under which the management of the administration of the affairs of the said Durgha vested hereditarily in 8 trustees called nattamaigars, who constitute a board of trustees. The said board of trustees would from among themselves elect one as a managing trustee and he would hold office for a term of 3 years. The managing trustee would at the end of each Fasli prepare a balance-sheet verified by the manager and ascertain the net amount of surplus available for payment to kasupangudars, who are the descendants of foster-son of the saint. The managing trustee would declare the amount due to each of the kasupangu (share) and would allocate the amount to each kasupangudar (sharer) in the list to be prepared for that purpose in each year. He would pay the amount to each kasupangudar in accordance with the list.

The ITO assessed the surplus income in the hands of the managing trustee as an association of persons. The AAC, on appeal, confirmed the same. On further appeal, the Tribunal took the same view.

On reference, the High Court held that the managing trustee qua the surplus income managed the property and derived the income on behalf of the kasupangudars and that the assessment should be made on the said managing trustee to the extent of the interest of each of the kasupangudars in the income received by him. Thus, the provision of section 41 of the 1922 Act could be said to apply to the assessee.

On appeal :

One 'S' and his wife 'B', settled certain properties in a trust. The trustees were both of them themselves and three brothers of 'S'. The provisions of the trust, laid down that, after defraying the expenses for management of the trust properties and certain other expenses, such as, rents, rates, etc. the trustees were to pay 'B' during her lifetime, the income arising from the trust funds and properties. Further, 'S', himself and 'B', during their lifetime, had the right of residence in some of the house property, free of rent and without any obligation for payment of any outgoings or moneys in respect thereof. The next provision contained in clause 8 of the deed was that, from and after the death of 'B', the trustees were directed to apply the net rents, profits and income of the properties and trust funds, at their discretion, on charitable purposes enumerated in the deed of trust. It was not disputed that all the charitable purposes mentioned in the trust constituted public charities, 'S' died and, thereafter, 'B', on 21-7-1955, executed a deed, under which she surrendered, released and transferred the interest in the aforesaid properties in favour of the trustees, with the liberty that the trustees would utilise the same for charitable purposes. For the assessment years 1956-57 to 1959-60, it was claimed by the trust that, during these previous years, those properties were held under a trust wholly for charitable purposes, and, consequently, the income was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The ITO, however, held that the deed executed by 'B' did not amount to a renouncement of her rights under the trust deed, and that it really amounted to a transfer of the income received by her for purposes of the use of the trust. Since the income of the trust was receivable by 'B', it could not be held that the trust properties were held wholly for charitable purposes. On appeal, the AAC disagreed with the ITO and accepted the submission made by the respondent, holding that the income received by the trust, after the execution of the deed of surrender by 'B' was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act in view of the applicability of section 9 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. The Tribunal, on further appeal, upheld the same decision, but on a slightly different ground. The Tribunal's view was that the surrender by 'B' was valid under section 58 of the Indian Trusts Act, and, consequently, after that deed was executed, the properties were held wholly for charitable purposes and the income was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court also decided the matter in favour of the assessee - trust.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

‘N’ was the karta of a joint Hindu family. The joint family properties included a building which had been set apart for use of pilgrims visiting the town. Subsequently the family properties were partitioned under a partition deed between ‘N’ and his adopted son, ‘R’ as also minor, ‘D’ the adopted some of his pre-deceased son. Under that partition the building in question was directed to be maintained by ‘N’ with the income from certain lands over which he had been given a life-interest. Later on N died. At the time of his death he was a partner in the firm having a 3/16th share in the profits and losses of the said firm. The accountable persons filed an estate duty return admitting a net dutiable estate including the share capital and the share of profit and interest of the deceased in the managing agency firm, but did not include the value of the share of the deceased in the goodwill of the said managing agency firm. It also did not include the value of the building. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty, however, proposed to value of building at Rs. 62,000 and 3/16th share in the goodwill of the firm and to include the same in the estate of the deceased. The accountable persons objected to this proposal and contended that the value of the building could not be included in the estate of the deceased because it had been set apart only for charitable purposes, with regard to the goodwill, it was contended that in the case of managing agency business, there was no goodwill at all, and that in fact the accountable persons had not obtained any amount from the firm towards the value of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the firm. The Assistant Controller, however, overruled these objections and held that the building was not a trust property and that it was owned by the deceased at the time of his death, and, therefore, its value was includible in the estate of the deceased. On the question of goodwill, the Assistant Controller held that the managing agency firm did possess goodwill and on the death of the deceased the accountable persons were entitled to 3/16th share in the goodwill of the business of the firm and as such a sum being the value of the 3/16th share had to be included in the estate of the deceased.

On appeal, the Appellate controller upheld the order of the assistant controller and reduced the value of the building.

On further appeal the Tribunal upheld the order of the Appellate Controller in respect of inclusion of value of building holding that a mere provision for the maintenance of the building by the deceased and thereafter by others could not amount to creation of a trust with reference to the building and that the exclusive use of the building from 1942 to 1958, for religious and charitable purposes did not amount to a permanent dedication of the building as a trust property. As regards the inclusion representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm, the Tribunal held that goodwill cannot be associated with the business of managing agency firm because the managing agency business is governed by the terms of the agreement between the managing agency firm and the company and the right of managing agency was more personal and could not pass on to a successor. The Tribunal also held that no share in the goodwill of the business passed to the accountable persons on the death of the deceased and that in any event no amount was actually paid to the accountable persons by way of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the business. In that view the Tribunal deleted the sum representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm.

It was proposed to treat the said receipts as income for the purpose of assessment. The assessee contended that the income in question was derived from the property held under trust wholly for charitable purposes and, therefore, was exempted under section 11(1)(a). The assessee-company was the trustee of a religious and charitable trust within the meaning of section 11. Its affairs were managed by another trust association to whom it paid Rs. 10,000 as management charges and claimed the same as an admissible deduction. The ITO rejected the claim on the grounds (i ) that the exact amount actually incurred for such management was not ascertainable; and (ii ) that there was no necessity for any other expenditure (apart from salary allowances, legal charges, postage and other incidental charges) for its management, especially, when its sources were only income from rent and interest. On appeal, the AAC confirmed the ITO's order. On further appeal, the Tribunal upheld the assessee's claim, holding (i) that the assessee was governed by the Charitable and Religious Trust Act, 1922 (and not by the Indian Trust Act, 1882) and the Act did not place any restriction on payment of remuneration to the trustees for managing the trust affairs; and (ii) that the impugned payment was for the purpose of the trust and was for the services rendered.

On reference:

The assessee trust was constituted under a trust deed dated 27-8-1963. As per the trust deed, the objects of the trust, were relief of the poor, advancement of education, medical relief, promotion of science, art and of literature and any other object of general public utility for the benefit of the public. The powers of the trustees, as per the deed, included power to hold any business undertaking upon trust and to administer and manage the same. Clause(5) of the deed provided that after paying all costs and expenses, the trustees would utilise the net income of the trust for aforesaid charitable objects or purposes at such time or times and in such manner and on such proportions as the trustees might in their discretion think fit. During the relevant assessment years the assessee had earned commission as area managers of a company, but did not show the income in its return on the ground that the income earned was not liable to income-tax as the same had been derived from a business undertaking held under trust for charitable purposes, and had been applied to such purposes in India in terms of section 2(15) and section 11. The ITO, however, did not agree with the assessee and assessed the income derived by the assessee from its business activity. The AAC allowed the appeals and held that the assessee was entitled to exemption from income-tax under section 2(15) and 11.

On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order of the AAC and restored that of the ITO holding that the business undertaking carried on by the assessee was one of the objects of the trust, and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 2(15), read with section 11.

On reference:

Maharaja of Darbhanga created a public religious trust on 16-03-1949 in favour of certain deities endowing certain properties with himself as the sole trustee. The trust deed provided for trustee's remuneration at the rate of fifteen per cent of the income from the trust properties. On 5-10-1950, the assessee executed a deed of relinquishment stipulating that as the net income from trust properties was not sufficient for puja path, bhog of the deities and for proper repair of the temples and as he was anxious to maintain the deities and the temple property, his remuneration should be distributed proportionately amongst the beneficiary deities. On 3-11-1959 the trust properties vested in the State by virtue of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. Section 24(3) of the said Act provided that in the case of a charitable or religious trust, without any reservation of pecuniary benefit to any individual, the compensation payable for such vesting would be a perpetual annuity equal to the net income of the trust estate. Accordingly, the net income of the trust estate continued to be paid to the assessee as the sole trustee.

The ITO sought to assess the remuneration in the hands of the assessee, being the trustee, in the assessment years 1959-60, 1960-61 and 1961-62. The assessee contended that the same was not assessable in his hands on the grounds, viz., ( i) that he had relinquished his right to receive remuneration by the deed dated 5-10-1950; and (ii) that, after vesting of the properties in the State, only net income was being received which did not admit of further deduction towards trustee's remuneration. Relying on the Tribunal's decision for the earlier year 1957-58, the ITO rejected these contentions and assessed the remuneration in the assessee's hands. Both the AAC and the Tribunal rejected the assessee's appeal on the ground (i ) that there was no statutory bar to payment of such remuneration to a trustee; and (ii) that the said Act, in fact, provided for payment of remuneration not exceeding fifteen per cent of the net trust income.

On reference, the assessee also claimed on behalf of the trust estate that the perpetual annuity received from the State was not income but only capital receipt being compensation for the loss of assets.

The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

The respondent/assessee firm was under agreement appointed as the managing agent of a company. Under the agreement the assessee was entitled to receive from the managed company commission payable on sale price of all cotton yarn and cloth sold and on sale proceeds of all material yarn and fabrics manufactured from other fibres and sold by company and certain per centage on net profits from ginning or pressing operations. On 28-12-1950 the managed company passed a resolution modifying the terms of the managing agency agreement in regard to the commission and added a proviso that for the years 1950 and 1951 if the directors of the company having regard to the result of the working were of the opinion that a lesser remuneration than that given in the agreement should be paid to the managing agents then the directors would have the right, in their absolute discretion, to fix such lesser remuneration payable either by way of lump sum or at a reduced percentage rate. The said modification had been agreed to by the managing agents. The managed company, on 8-4-1951, resolved that the managing agents should be paid Rs. 1,00,000 less than the commission calculated at the rates mentioned in the original agreement and on 31-12-1950, an entry to that effect was made in the books of the company. The income-tax authorities held that entire sum of commission which the assessee was entitled under the original agreement, was taxable income having accrued as commission during previous year and that Rs. 1,00,000 was mere voluntary surrender which could not affect the taxability of whole amount of commission accruing to managing agents. On appeal, the Tribunal held that as a result of the agreement between the managing agents and the managed company the right of the managing agents to claim full remuneration, had been taken away as from 1-1-1950, and it was not a voluntary relinquishment on the part of the managing agents and, therefore, the amount of Rs. 1,00,000 out of the commission due according to the original agreement was not income in the hands of the managing agents which was liable to taxation. On reference, the High Court agreed with the view taken by the Tribunal.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

By an indenture of trust dated 23-8-1954, one ‘D’ and his wife settled upon trust two maternity hospitals which were run by them and an immovable property for the purposes and objects contained in the said deed of trust. The assessee were the trustees under the said trust. The primary object of the trust was to carry on and promote the educational, health, cultural, literary, social and economic interests of the people, particularly of the backward and poorer classes. The important recitals in the trust deed were to the effect that the net annual income from the said hospitals, after deducting all the expenses for maintaining and running the hospitals including a sum of Rs. 750 per month which should be paid regularly to ‘D’s wife for managing the said hospitals for and on behalf of the trust during her lifetime, should accrue to the trust from year to year and that Dr. Divekar and Dr. Nalini Divekar did transfer the above said property and both the hospitals to the Trustees. And that the monies and properties of the trust were to be applied, firstly in payment of the expenses of carrying out of the trust and then in carrying out the other objects. The assessee claimed exemption under section 43(1)(i) of the 1922 Act. Even though the ITO accepted that the business in maternity homes was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act, he however took the view that its income was not exempt under the said section because it did not fulfil the requirements of proviso (b) thereto. This view was arrived at by him because he took the view that the primary purpose in conducting or running the two maternity homes or hospitals was not to give free medical facilities but charge the patients and then to apply the income for certain objects. Even the amount paid to D’s wife claimed as a deduction was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that the same was paid by the association of persons to one of its own members.

On appeal, the AAC held that the income from the trust was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and that the salary paid was an allowable deduction in computation of the assessees’ income.

On revenue’s further appeal, the Tribunal took the view that there was no actual transfer of immovable properties to the trustees if regard be had to the language employed in the document. On the assumption that the properties were considered to have been managed on behalf of a charitable institution the Tribunal took the view that the conditions laid down in proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) were not satisfied in the case and the income was, therefore, not exempt from tax.

It, however, affirmed the finding of the AAC that salary to ‘D’s wife was an allowable deduction.

On reference:

A partnership firm was formed by four brothers. No deed of partnership was said to have been executed in respect of this firm. The firm was appointed the chief agent an insurance company as from 1-9-1950. On 17-2-1951, the aforesaid brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming the trustees would hold the said business of the chief agency of the said company and all the benefits and profits to arise from the said business upon trust for public charitable purposes. The said declaration of trust was registered with the Registrar of Assurances.

The assessee claimed that as from 17-2-1951, the income from agency business should be assessed in the hands of the trustees and should be allowed exemption under section 4(3)(i). The ITO, however, made the assessment in the status of an unregistered firm. The ITO held that there was no charitable trust created by the deed dated 17-2-1951. On appeal, the AAC reversed the findings of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no proper and valid contract between the insurance company and the trustees as such; that the letter of appointment was only a service agreement; that there had been no transfer of property to the trustees wholly for charitable purposes; that the alleged transfer of the agency agreement did not amount to the transfer of property. The Tribunal also held that before the income of a trust for charitable purposes was exempt from tax, it must satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i), i.e., and in the instant case the business not being carried on the course of carrying out the primary purpose of the trust, the income was not exempt form liability to pay tax.

On reference :

There were two groups of partners who constituted the managing agency firm BK. The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

The assessee was a trustee of a trust. Under a clause of the trust-deed, one-third of the income of the trust was to be paid to the trustees as their remuneration. The trustees had, however, by a resolution given up their right to receive the remuneration and had resolved that, that part of the income of the trust be also spent on the charitable objects of the trust. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal had reversed the order of the AAC holding that the ITO was justified in initiating reassessment proceedings under section 147(a) and that the matter be restored to the AAC to decide on merits the question of includibility of the remuneration payable to the assessee as a trustee.

On reference :

On 24-10-1944, the settlor, executed a trust deed in respect of shares of certain company. The provisions of the trust deed were that the income from the trust property was to belong to him during his lifetime. On his death the income was to go to the wife if she survived him. By clause 1(b) of the trust deed, settler's wife was entitled to the net income 'during her lifetime without power of anticipation or alienation'. After the death of the survivor of the settlor and his wife, the net income was to go, after payment of certain remuneration to the trustees, to certain charitable trusts which the settlor had created previously for the maintenance of those trusts. If after the utilisation of the income from the trust properties for the benefit of those specified charitable trusts, any income was available, it was to be utilised for the maintenance of any nursing home, hospital or any institution for medical relief. The trust deed came to be modified on 15-7-1953, by which the settlor relinquished his entire life interest in the income from the trust properties.

After this relinquishment the income from the trust fund was continued to be paid to his wife until the death of settlor. No amount was paid to settler's wife after the death of the settlor.

On 20-5-1955, the wife of settler executed a deed whereby she in her turn relinquished and surrendered her life interest with a view to accelerating the subsequent trust in favour of charity.

In these circumstances the assessee trustees claimed that the income derived from the property had under trust was wholly for religious and charitable purpose and therefore clearly covered under provisions of section 4(3)(i) of the Act of 1922 and applied for refund. However the ITO observed that the interest for life allowed by the settlor to his wife, was of a restricted nature inasmuch as it was definitely laid down that she had no power to anticipate or alienate her interest, though she would be perfectly justified in refusing to become a beneficiary in her place. He therefore, he held that the declaration dated 25-5-1955 made by her was void and, as such, the income of the trust would, in law, revert to the executors/legal heirs of the settlor. On revenue’s appeal :

The deceased had executed a will under which he created a trust in respect of all his properties and appointed the Official Trustee as the sole executor and trustee he directed that all his properties would vest in the Official Trustee on his death; who would sell his properties and invest the net realizations in Government approved securities and pay certain legacies out of the income from the investment. On the deceased's death, the assessee (i.e. Official Trustee) applied for and granted probate of the will.

The assessee's claim that for the assessment years 1962-63 to 1964-65 and 1966-67, he should be assessed only as a trustee and that income derived by him from the properties held for charitable purposes, could not be assessed was disallowed by the ITO who held that since all the immovable properties of the deceased had not been sold during the assessment years, the assessee could not be said to have discharged the executorial functions, and that, therefore, the assessee having acted only as an executor under the will of the deceased during the years in question the income was liable to be taxed in his hands only, under section 168, and not as a trustee. On appeal, the AAC observed that the deceased had clearly stated in the will that the assessee was to be the sole executor, that he should sell all the properties and the net realisations including the cash should be invested in Government securities and that, therefore, the assessee could not shed his character as an executor so long as he had not completed the sale of the properties. On further appeal, the Tribunal allowed assesee's claim holding that where the official trustee was appointed as a trustee by a testator under his will, there was no question of an executor functioning at all, that even if there was any executor he had to transfer the properties subject to the trust after obtaining the probate of the will to the trustee, that the directions contained in the will regarding the sale of the properties merely amounted to a direction for conversion of the properties from one kind to another, that the official trustee was bound to pay the legatees, carry out the duties such as discharge of the debt and payment of legacies, etc., as a trustee and that, therefore, the properties of the deceased had become vested in the assessee as trustee from the very inception and that in any event after the official trustee obtained probate of the will of the deceased he had ceased to be an executor and had assumed the character of a trustee. The Tribunal also upheld the claim of the assessee that the income from the properties held by him in trust in so far as it related to religious and charitable purposes was exempt from tax under section 11. It also held that the official trustee was a representative assessee as contemplated in sections 160(1)(iii) and 160(1)(iv) and as such he had to be assessed only in the manner indicated in section 161(1) and that the amounts disbursed by him to the various relatives of the deceased as per the terms of the will could not be aggregated together for the purpose of ascertaining the tax and that tax on such amounts had to be levied separately and the aggregate-tax had to be recovered from the assessee.

The assessee-firm contended before the ITO that the minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 could be claimed by the assessee only if there was no loss to the managed company after charging such commission in the profit and loss account of the managed company, that in the assessment year in question, i.e., 1954-55, the managed company did not make any profit, and that no commission was, therefore, paid to the assessee-firm. But, on a scrutiny of the profit and loss account of the managed-company, the ITO found that the managed company made in the relevant year a profit of Rs. 5,571 before charging any commission payable to its managing agent, i.e., the assessee-firm. The ITO, therefore, held in his assessment order dated 30-3-1959, that, according to clause 2(b) of the managing agency agreement, the assessee-firm was entitled to a minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 from the managed company, that the assessee firm had earned the commission, and that if the assessee-firm chose not to claim the minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 from the managed company, it only meant a voluntary surrender of the amount by the assessee firm for extra-commercial consideration. A second contention was urged before the AAC that, even if it was held that the minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 had accrued to the assessee-firm under clause 2(b) of the agreement, the said sum should have been held to be an admissible deduction, as the amount was surrendered or waived by the assessee-firm on grounds of commercial expediency. The AAC rejected this contention also on the ground that the surrender of managing agency commission was merely a gratuitous act in the circumstances of the case.

The Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the assessee.
