Concurring view

Per Chagla, J

"Agricultural income" is defined in section 2(1) of 1922 Act as any rent or revenue derived from land which is used for agricultural purposes, and the question, therefore, which arose for determination was whether any portion of the remuneration received by the assessee was rent or revenue derived from land which was used for agricultural purposes. It was clear that the remuneration received by the assessee was under a contract between it and the principal company for services to be rendered by the assessee as the managing agents of the principal company. That contract had nothing whatever to do with the income earned by the principal company from agricultural sources. It was also clear from the contract that what the principal company contracted with the managing agents was to pay them a sum of Rs. 10,000 or ten percent of the profits computed in a particular manner whichever sum was larger.

In the instant case, it was perfectly evident that what the assessee was going to share in was an artificial fund which first came into existence. They received ten per cent of that fund. After that had been ascertained the usefulness of that fund disappeared and a new fund came into existence by a different computation which was to be divisible amongst the shareholders as their own profits.

If the income is agricultural income, it bears an indelible impression upon it and is exempt from tax. But on the construction of the contract, the remuneration of the assessee was for its services as the managing agents of the principal company; that was the character of its income. The character of its income was not that part of it was rent or revenue from land which was used for agricultural purposes. Therefore, the income received by the assessee from the principal company which was proportionate to the agricultural income earned by the principal company was not agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act 1922, and was not exempt from assessment under the provision of section 4(3)(viii) of the 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 11(1)(a), read with sections 11(4) and 28(iii), of the Income-tax act, 1961-charitable or religious trust-exemption of income from property held under trust-objects of assessee, a registered society, included promotion and development of hosiery industry and it used to procure, allocate and distribute to its members woollen hosiery yarn on no-profit-no-loss basis-assessee used to charge subscription, and allocation charges from its members-before tribunal, assessee claimed allocation charges received by it to be exempt from tax-whether tribunal correct in holding that although assessee's activity fell within the definition of "charitable purposes", yet its income was covered by section 28(iii) and was not income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a) and was hence not entitled to exemption-held, on facts, no

FACT: The assessee, a registered society, was established, inter alia, (a) to promote, organise and encourage scientific research in the hosiery manufacturers, inventions, investments and design, (b ) to find out way and means of progress, development and improvement of hosiery industry and to safeguard and to protect its investments, (c) to procure, encourage and formulate means for collective buying of industrial raw materials and machinery on a no-profit-no-loss basis, (d) to encourage and formulate ways and means for collective selling of hosiery products, (e) to make arrangements for setting up of woollen hosiery yarn spinning plant on co-operative basis in order to provide the industry its basic raw materials on fair prices, and (f) to procure, allocate, distribute to hosiery manufacturers woollen hosiery yarn, their basic raw material, on a no-profit-no-loss basis. To meet its office and administrative expenses, the assessee charged annual subscription, special subscription and allocation charges (i.e., charges for allocation of raw yarn) from its members. For the assessment years 1969-70 and 1970-71, the ITO treated the allocation charges as the assessee's income under section 28(iii) and taxed the same. He also repelled the assessee's contention that it was entitled to exemption under section 11 (1)(a). On appeal, the AAC sustained the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal sustained the AAC's order, holding that although the activity of the assessee was covered by the definition "charitable purposes" as contemplated in section 2(75), yet the assessee's income which was covered by section 28(iii), was not income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a), so that it was not entitled to exemption from tax.

On reference:

HELD: By virtue of section 11(4) "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, it could not be accepted that the income derived by the assessee was not income from property as envisaged under section 11(1)(a). That apart, a perusal of the aims and objects of the assessee-society led to the conclusion that the income derived by it was income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a). Accordingly, the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the amount received by the assessee on account of allocation charges was not income from property held under trust.

HEADNOTE: Section 2(24) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Properties held under trust vested in the state by law and trustee continued to receive perpetual annuity equal to income from trust properties from the state as compensation-Trustee relinquished remuneration receivable for pooja path, etc., of beneficiary deities-Whether annuity received was income in nature-Held, on facts, yes-Whether remuneration receivable by trustee was his income-Held, on facts, yes, as it was merely diversion of income after it accrued to him

FACT: Maharaja of Darbhanga created a public religious trust on 16-03-1949 in favour of certain deities endowing certain properties with himself as the sole trustee. The trust deed provided for trustee's remuneration at the rate of fifteen per cent of the income from the trust properties. On 5-10-1950, the assessee executed a deed of relinquishment stipulating that as the net income from trust properties was not sufficient for puja path, bhog of the deities and for proper repair of the temples and as he was anxious to maintain the deities and the temple property, his remuneration should be distributed proportionately amongst the beneficiary deities. On 3-11-1959 the trust properties vested in the State by virtue of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. Section 24(3) of the said Act provided that in the case of a charitable or religious trust, without any reservation of pecuniary benefit to any individual, the compensation payable for such vesting would be a perpetual annuity equal to the net income of the trust estate. Accordingly, the net income of the trust estate continued to be paid to the assessee as the sole trustee.

The ITO sought to assess the remuneration in the hands of the assessee, being the trustee, in the assessment years 1959-60, 1960-61 and 1961-62. The assessee contended that the same was not assessable in his hands on the grounds, viz., ( i) that he had relinquished his right to receive remuneration by the deed dated 5-10-1950; and (ii) that, after vesting of the properties in the State, only net income was being received which did not admit of further deduction towards trustee's remuneration. Relying on the Tribunal's decision for the earlier year 1957-58, the ITO rejected these contentions and assessed the remuneration in the assessee's hands. Both the AAC and the Tribunal rejected the assessee's appeal on the ground (i ) that there was no statutory bar to payment of such remuneration to a trustee; and (ii) that the said Act, in fact, provided for payment of remuneration not exceeding fifteen per cent of the net trust income.

On reference, the assessee also claimed on behalf of the trust estate that the perpetual annuity received from the State was not income but only capital receipt being compensation for the loss of assets.

HELD: 1. The trust was receiving income out of certain assets which had been endorsed to the deities. Even after the vesting of the assets to the State, the income from those assets continued to flow for the purposes of the trust. It was not a case of capital value of asset being paid in annual instalments but a case of payment of income from the assets, as envisaged in section 24(3 ) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act. The annuity, therefore, continued to have the character of income.

2. The deed of relinquishment clearly showed that the remuneration payable to the assessee shall, instead of being paid to him, be used in a particular manner as per directions contained in the trust deed. It was a clear case of diversion of income after it accrued to the assessee. There is no merit in the argument that since the State was paying only net income, the question of payment of fifteen per cent out of it to the trustee did not arise.

Bihar Land Reforms Act did not bar such payment out of annuity paid. The remuneration was, accordingly, assessable in the hands of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 161 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 41 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Representative assessee - Liability of - Assessment years 1953-54 and 1954-55 - Under a scheme sanctioned by High Court, management and administration of a Durgh of a saint vested hereditarily in trustees called nattamingars from whom was elected a managing trustee - Managing trustee was to allocate surplus due to Kasupangudars (shares) who were descendants of foster son of saint - ITO assessed surplus income in hands of managing trustee as an association of persons - Whether even if nattamaigars were trustees in whom properties of Durgha vested, they should be deemed to have received income only on behalf of kasupangudars in definite shares - Held, yes - Whether in terms of section 41 of 1922 Act nattamaigars were managers of properties on behalf of others and were entitled to receive income therefrom on behalf of them and therefore income which they held on behalf of kasupangudars could be assessed only in their hands in manner prescribed thereunder - Held, yes - Whether what vests in nattamaigars was not properties of the Durgha but management and administration thereof and, therefore, provisions of section 41 of 1922 Act could be said to apply to assessee - Held, yes

FACT: Durgha consecrated to Hazerath Sayed receives large income from immovable properties endowed to it and the offerings in cash and kind made by the devotees. The Durgha and its properties were being administered under a scheme settled by the High Court under which the management of the administration of the affairs of the said Durgha vested hereditarily in 8 trustees called nattamaigars, who constitute a board of trustees. The said board of trustees would from among themselves elect one as a managing trustee and he would hold office for a term of 3 years. The managing trustee would at the end of each Fasli prepare a balance-sheet verified by the manager and ascertain the net amount of surplus available for payment to kasupangudars, who are the descendants of foster-son of the saint. The managing trustee would declare the amount due to each of the kasupangu (share) and would allocate the amount to each kasupangudar (sharer) in the list to be prepared for that purpose in each year. He would pay the amount to each kasupangudar in accordance with the list.

The ITO assessed the surplus income in the hands of the managing trustee as an association of persons. The AAC, on appeal, confirmed the same. On further appeal, the Tribunal took the same view.

On reference, the High Court held that the managing trustee qua the surplus income managed the property and derived the income on behalf of the kasupangudars and that the assessment should be made on the said managing trustee to the extent of the interest of each of the kasupangudars in the income received by him. Thus, the provision of section 41 of the 1922 Act could be said to apply to the assessee.

On appeal :

HELD: Under section 41(1) of the 1922 Act, the income of properties receivable by the enumerated persons for the benefit of others is liable to be assessed to tax in their hands in the like manner and to the same amount as it would be leviable upon and recoverable from the person or persons on whose behalf such income is receivable. This section centres on the basic fact that the person in whose hands the income is assessable shall be entitled to receive the same on behalf of any person; if he is not so entitled, the provisions of the section cannot be invoked. So, it was contended that, as the properties vested in the managing trustee and he received the income in his own right and not on behalf of the beneficiaries, though for their benefit, the said income in the hands of the managing trustee fell outside the scope of section 41 of the 1922 Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1956-57 to 1959-60 - One 'S' and his wife 'B' settled certain properties in a trust - Trustees were both of them and three brothers of 'S' - Under trust deed trustees after meeting certain expenses were liable to pay to 'B' for her benefit income arising from trust properties - After death of 'S', 'B' executed a deed under which she surrendered and transferred trust properties in favour of trustees to utilise same for charitable purposes mentioned in settlement - Whether, subsequent to execution of deed by 'B', income arising from trust properties was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act in hands of trust - Held, yes

FACT: One 'S' and his wife 'B', settled certain properties in a trust. The trustees were both of them themselves and three brothers of 'S'. The provisions of the trust, laid down that, after defraying the expenses for management of the trust properties and certain other expenses, such as, rents, rates, etc. the trustees were to pay 'B' during her lifetime, the income arising from the trust funds and properties. Further, 'S', himself and 'B', during their lifetime, had the right of residence in some of the house property, free of rent and without any obligation for payment of any outgoings or moneys in respect thereof. The next provision contained in clause 8 of the deed was that, from and after the death of 'B', the trustees were directed to apply the net rents, profits and income of the properties and trust funds, at their discretion, on charitable purposes enumerated in the deed of trust. It was not disputed that all the charitable purposes mentioned in the trust constituted public charities, 'S' died and, thereafter, 'B', on 21-7-1955, executed a deed, under which she surrendered, released and transferred the interest in the aforesaid properties in favour of the trustees, with the liberty that the trustees would utilise the same for charitable purposes. For the assessment years 1956-57 to 1959-60, it was claimed by the trust that, during these previous years, those properties were held under a trust wholly for charitable purposes, and, consequently, the income was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act. The ITO, however, held that the deed executed by 'B' did not amount to a renouncement of her rights under the trust deed, and that it really amounted to a transfer of the income received by her for purposes of the use of the trust. Since the income of the trust was receivable by 'B', it could not be held that the trust properties were held wholly for charitable purposes. On appeal, the AAC disagreed with the ITO and accepted the submission made by the respondent, holding that the income received by the trust, after the execution of the deed of surrender by 'B' was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act in view of the applicability of section 9 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882. The Tribunal, on further appeal, upheld the same decision, but on a slightly different ground. The Tribunal's view was that the surrender by 'B' was valid under section 58 of the Indian Trusts Act, and, consequently, after that deed was executed, the properties were held wholly for charitable purposes and the income was exempt from tax under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court also decided the matter in favour of the assessee - trust.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(2)(xv) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1952-53 - Assessee was appointed by Central Government as its agent for buying, checking, weighing, leaf drying, storing, transporting, retaining and reselling tobacco under and agreed to pay to assessee price of tobacco purchased, and commission on all purchases – Subsequently assessee passed a resolution placing 'T' in 'special charge' for arranging purchases of tobacco on credit, and agreed to pay him 30 per cent of net profit as remuneration – Under contract with Government of India, certain amount became due to assessee as commission after providing for expenses, 30 per cent of balance was paid to 'T' as commission and was claimed as a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act - ITO reduced stipulated rate to 10 per cent. on two grounds that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of company, bound to attend to all activities of company including contract - Whether since there was no evidence that agreement was motivated by considerations other than strictly business considerations as a director 'T' was bound to attend to all activities of company including special contract with Central Government, disallowance of a sum out of remuneration paid to 'T' was not justifiable - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as – Assessment year 1952-53 – Assessee was acting as managing agents for 'N' - Subsequently, agreement was terminated when Government of State of Madras in exercise of powers conferred upon it by Electrical Undertakings Acquisition Act, 1949, compulsorily acquired undertaking of that company, and assessee was paid as compensation for premature termination of its agency - The ITO observed that assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end, assessee still continued as 'managing agents of other companies' and therefore receipt was to be considered as revenue - Whether such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of assessee, was a capital receipt, therefore, same was not liable to tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee company carried on business in hides and skins, minerals, tobacco and other commodities, and also acted as managing agents for the 'N' and for two other companies. 'T', 'M' and 'C' were directors of the company. The assessee was appointed by the Central Government as its agent for buying, checking, weighing, leaf drying, storing, transporting, retaining and reselling tobacco under and in accordance with the directions issued from time to time and agreed to pay to the assessee price of the tobacco purchased, charge at the rate of one anna per 1b. for tobacco not redried, and at the rate of two annas per 1b. for tobacco redried, and commission on all purchases. Subsequently assessee passed a resolution placing 'T' 'special charge' for arranging purchases of tobacco on credit, inspecting tobacco at Guntur and at Madras Port, and for supervising shipment of tobacco, and agreed to pay him 30 per cent of the net profit as remuneration. Under the contract with the Government of India, certain amount became due to the assessee as commission in the account year ending 31-3-1952. After providing for expenses, 30 per cent of the balance was paid to 'T' as commission and was claimed in the assessment year 1952-53 as a permissible deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the 1922 Act. The ITO accepted that the expenditure for payment of remuneration for attending to the contract was laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee but reduced the stipulated rate to 10 per cent on two grounds : that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of the company, bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the contract.

, transporting and shipping the goods might have resulted in serious losses to the assessee. The ITO accepted that the expenditure for payment of remuneration for attending to the contract was laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee, but reduced the stipulated rate to 10 per cent on two grounds that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of the company, bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the contract. There was no evidence that the agreement was motivated by considerations other than strictly business considerations. There was also no evidence that as a director 'T' was bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the special contract with the Central Government. The duties which the director was bound to perform for earning the remuneration of Rs. 400 per month were not on the record, but even in the opinion of the taxing authorities the duties of 'T' as director did not cover attendance to the contract with the Government. 'T' and 'M' were brothers, but that by itself is not sufficient to justify an inference that unreasonable or excessive remuneration was agreed to be paid. The person who was called upon to attend to a contract of this magnitude was required to have expert knowledge of the business, apply his time exclusively thereto, travel from time to time, maintain supervision and control at the stage of purchase, redrying, packing, transport and loading for shipment. Presumably 'T' was such a person, and that is why he was selected for earning for the assessee a large amount of commission by duly performing the contract.

An analysis of the reasons given by the ITO disclosed no grounds to support the view that remuneration at a rate exceeding 10 per cent of the net profit was excessive or unreasonable. The contract with the Government was for the assessee an important contract requiring constant and vigilant application and supervision by a person well acquainted with the practical details of the business. If the management of the assessee as prudent businessman for advancing the interest of the assessee bona fide regarded 30 per cent of the net profits as reasonable remuneration, the revenue authorities were not justified in reviewing their opinion and reducing the rate of remuneration. It was true that if, on a consideration of the relevant materials, the Tribunal was of the opinion that a particular remuneration stipulated to be paid was not bona fide or is unreasonable, the High Court in exercising its advisory jurisdiction had no power to interfere with that opinion. But the material circumstances relating to the nature of the contract, the services to be performed and the nature of the duties by the employee were not at all taken into account by the Tribunal and the income-tax authorities. Therefore, the disallowance of a sum of out of the remuneration paid to 'T' was not justifiable ?

The contract under which the assessee was appointed managing agent for the 'N' was to enure till 1960, but it had to be prematurely terminated because the Government of Madras exercising its powers under 1949 Act had compulsorily acquired the electricity undertaking. With the acquisition of that undertaking the right of the assessee as managing agent ceased. Under section 15 of the 1449 Act, the Government was bound to pay compensation which would include compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement. The assessee received sum as compensation for termination of the agency, computed in the manner laid down in section 15 of that Act. Prima facie, such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of the assessee, was a capital receipt.

Turning to the facts of the instant case, it must in the first instance be observed that it was for the revenue to establish that a particular receipt was income liable to tax, and beyond stating that the assessee was the managing agent of the 'N' and of two other companies, there was no other evidence about the nature of the business of the two other companies of which the assessee was the managing agent, about their relative importance qua the managing agency of the 'N' and whether by reason of the extinction of the managing agency of the 'N' any enduring asset was lost to the assessee, or its trading organisation was adversely affected. The ITO observed that the 'assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end', the assessee still continues as 'managing agents of other companies'. Even after surrender of one of the agencies, the assessee carried on business as before, its structure not being affected' and therefore 'the receipt was to be considered as revenue'.

Hence, the compensation received for taking over the 'N' was a capital receipt not liable to be taxed, and on the materials placed the Supreme Court did not disagree with the High Court.

The appeal therefore failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with section 2(1A), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i), read with section 2(1), of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1930-31 - Petitioner, a horse breeding farm, was founded by a commanding of army - Management of farm was in hands of officer commanding officer - Income derived from agriculture, securities and other sources was utilized to finance breeding of horses, majority of horses thus bred were supplied to army department on payment and stallions and brood mares were also imported and any stock found unsustainable as remounts were sold publicly - Said farm covered certain villages, residents of which cultivate lands as tenants to assessee and assessee also raised agricultural produce by cultivation - Assessee also levied weighing charges called ‘dharat’ upon tenants in addition to rent received from them - Whether since commanding officer was in receipt and control of income of farm, he was assessee under Act - Held, yes - Whether ‘dharat’ would clearly fall within definition of agricultural income under section 2(1)(b)(ii) of 1922 Act and was, therefore, exempt from provisions of Act - Held, yes - Whether since officer commanding, had discretion in matter of making disbursements it could not be said that property in trust was held wholly or partly or charitable purposes - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, income of trust was not exempt from taxation within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The petitioner, a horse breeding farm, was founded by a commanding officer of army by obtaining grant of certain lands from the Government. The management of the farm remained in the hands of the officer commanding, who worked as an honorary trustee. The income derived from agriculture, securities, and other sources was utilized to finance the breeding of horse; the main object of the institution was to provide remounts for the regiment and the improvement of horse breeding in India; the majority of the horses thus, bred were supplied to the Army Department on payment and stallions and brood mares were also imported; and any stock found unsustainable as remounts were sold publicly. The instrument of lease executed between the Government and the officer commanding, did not definite the purpose for which the lease of land was granted, but the lessee had to pay the yearly rent by way of land revenue and malikhan and all rates and cesses. The farm covered certain village, the residents of which cultivate lands as tenants to the assessee and the assessee also raised agricultural produce by cultivation. It was a custom among cultivators, especially where the produce was to be accounted for between the landlord and the tenants, that the agricultural produce was got weighed or measured through a separate agency, called Dharwais, who were paid at certain stipulated rates for the job. Instead of allowing each tenant to engage his own Dharwais independently of the assessee, the farm appointed this own Dharwais for the entire farm by selling out the monopoly or right of weighing by public auction. In return for the auction purchase price, the Dharwais were allowed to charge certain rates. The ITO held that the assessee was an association of individuals and that the property was not held for the advancement of an object of general public utility because the entire benefits went to the members of that particular regiment. He further held that the income from Dharat could not be regarded as exempt under section 2(1)(b) of the 1922 Act because it was not rent or revenue derived from land which was used or agricultural purposes and, therefore, he assessed the total income of the farm and levied a tax thereon accordingly. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case the person in receipt and control of the income was undoubtedly the officer commanding. Therefore, he was an assessee under the Act. ‘Dharat’ means weighing charges which in the instant case were levied by the assessee from the tenants of the land in addition to the rent which he received from them. It was admitted that they formed part of an agreement entered into with the tenants in that behalf. Section 2(1) of the 1922 Act defines agricultural income, which includes the performance by a cultivator, or receiver of rent in kind of any process ordinarily employed by a cultivator or receiver of rent-in-kind to render the produce raised or received by him fit to be taken to market. Accordingly, dharat income would clearly fall within the provision of this sub-clause and was, therefore, exempt from the provisions of the Act.

The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

As regards the question whether the impugned income from the race meets and inter-venue betting was income from property or income from business it would be difficult to accept that the assessee was conducting a business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter- venue betting on two or three occasions in a year. Even if the receipts did not constitute the corpus, there was certainly no quid pro quo in the arrangement between the assessee and the HRC as the asses- see was getting, from the said race meets and inter-venue betting, on almost certain profit from the HRC at practically no risk or cost to itself. The assessee had obtained a licence from the Government to conduct the races and inter-venue betting on the basis of a letter from the HRC. This licence itself could be treated as property and such property was obtained with the consent of the settlor-club and was contemplated even at the inception of the assessee-trust. Since the expression ‘property’ has the widest import for income-tax purposes, the impugned income would be income from property held under trust.

Alternatively. even if the impugned income was not income from property, it could only be treated as a voluntary contribution given by the HRC to the assessee. Though the form of such contribution indicated that the assessee itself had to conduct the races, the actual conduct was done by the HRC on behalf of the assessee merely as a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contribution did not have the character of income but was a capital receipt. The facts of the case did not justify the inference that the assessee-trust was in business for conducting horse races. It had neither the horses nor organisation nor any other equipment for that purpose. Consequently, since the impugned income was not income from business, the question of applicability of section 13(1)(bb ) did not arise.

For the foregoing reasons, the assessee-trust was an institution which satisfied the conditions of section 2(15) read with section 11. Since the ITO had not considered the requirements of accumulation, if there had been such accumulation, or application of sections 12, 12A and 13, the assessments were set aside for consideration of these aspects.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessee, who was one of partners of managing agency firm and was director of managed company, received his share of compensation from managed company in terms of arbitration award for premature termination of managing agency agreement - Assessee claimed amount so received to be capital receipt and hence not liable to tax - Whether amount in question was capital receipt and not revenue receipt because (i) under managing agency agreement termination of agency was contemplated only in case of winding up of managed company and compensation was paid not in pursuance of terms of agreement but was independent of it; (ii) compensation was paid not for past services but for wrongful termination of agency; (iii) managing agency contracts were not ordinary contracts but were regarded as capital asset and termination of managing agency was destruction of capital asset and compensation received therefor was also capital receipt - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under (Property held under trust) - Assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015 - Whether once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, property so acquired will be property held under trust and income from such property will be income from property under trust - Held, yes - Assessee society was having income from two Kalyanamandapams - According to Assessing Officer these properties were not settled by settlor as trust property and hence could not be considered as properties held under trust and thus he held that income earned by assessee from its Kalyanamandapams could not be treated as income from house property but only as income from business - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld order of Assessing Officer holding that Kalyanamandapams having being built by assessee subsequent to its formation could not be considered as property under trust - However, assessee submitted that land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of original settlement and buildings were built therein by assessee from its income - Whether thus, rental income received by assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT: Property (i.e. Kalyanamandapams) built by assessee society from its income, subsequent to its formation, on land, which was part of original settlement, was to be considered as property under trust and income therefrom was income from property under trust  IT: Where predominant activity of assessee society was charity, it would be eligible for exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)

Section 2(15), read with sections 11 and 12A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable purpose (Objects of general public utility) - Assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015 - Assessee a society registered under section 12A had claimed exemption under section 11(1) - From objects of assessee as they appeared in its Memorandum of Association, it was clear that assessee could purchase, build and let out properties for its other purposes - Assessee was having income from its two kalyanamandapams and it was also having properties from which a school, a health centre and a library were run - All activities of assessee were either in field of education or in field of medical care - Further, assessee had given donations to a trust having section 12A registration which was pursuing an object of medical relief, education or relief to poor - Whether this would be equivalent to using money for charitable purposes - Held, yes - Whether therefore, predominant activity of assessee being charity, it would be eligible for exemption claimed by it under section 11(1) - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12][In favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee a society registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860 and having registration under section 12A had claimed exemption under section 11(1), in the returns filed for the impugned assessment years 1987-88, 1991-92, 1997-98, 1998-99, 2006-07 and 2008-09 to 2014-2015. The assessee was having income from two Kalyanamandapams.

According to the Assessing Officer, these properties were not settled by the settlor as trust property and hence could not be considered as properties held under trust. The Assessing Officer submitted that by running these Kalyanamandapams, business was being carried on since this was its predominant activity. Hence, Assessing Officer denied exemption claimed by the assessee under section 11 (1). For assessment years 2008-09 to 2014-15, the Assessing Officer also applied proviso to section 2(15) for denying such exemption.The Assessing Officer took a view that income earned by the assessee from its Kalyanamandapams could not be treated as income from house property but only as income from business.

were being meant for achieving primary objects of trust and could not be called a business. The natural corollary that followed was that the income derived from such transactions could not be called an income from the business. Assuming that it was a business as contemplated under section 2(13), the same was exempted under section 11. Further, the submission that the income would be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust could not also be disbelieved. [Para 12] The licence to run races and betting itself could be treated as property and the said property was obtained with the consent of the Hyderabad Race Club. The term ‘property’ itself has got widest import for income-tax purposes and inclusive of holding a licence. But, it is not every case of business which can be treated as property. If it were to be so treated, section 13(1)(bb) would lose its meaning. It may be that a business itself may be settled in trust of the trustees who may conduct a business on their own under the powers given to them in the trust deed. In the instant case, it was difficult to accept that the assessee-trust was conducting the business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter-venue betting for few occasions in a year. Thus, there could not be any doubt that the income derived by the trust for the relevant assessment years was from the property held under trust and as such it was exempted under section 11.

Assuming even if it was not treated as income from the property held under the trust, it could be treated as voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee-trust as contemplated under section 12. The conduct of the Hyderabad Race Club in respect of the transaction was only a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contributions could be characterized only as a capital receipt in the assessee’s hands. Thus, it could not be held that there had been business in the normal sense in such arrangement and in the facts and circumstances, it was not such a business which would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). It was only an activity which could constitute the property or an arrangement involved in transfer of funds from Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee’s institution in a form recognized by law and not shown to be colourable exercise or otherwise as contended by the revenue. Since it could not be said to be a business and the income derived could not be said to be a business income, the provisions of section 13(1)(bb) were not attracted. The assessee-trust was an institution, which satisfied the conditions under section 2(15), read with section 11 and as such, conclusion reached by the Tribunal should be upheld. [Para 13]

None of the objects of the trust could be said to be non-charitable in nature. Rather the objects of the trust were purely of a charitable nature. The main objects of the trust were advancement and propagation of education, medical aid and relief to the poor. In fact, promotion of sports and games was also one of the charitable objects. Merely because a discretion was vested in the trustees to utilize the income for any one or more of the objects would not make any difference. HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01 - Assessee-society was formed, inter alia, with main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard - It was duly registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860 - It was also registered under section 12A - Assessee claimed exemption under section 11 - Assessing Officer denied exemption holding that, assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return, and, thus, it was earning profit and not doing any charity - However, it was found from records that assessee was duly recognised by HNB Garhwal University and strictly following university regulations with regard to admission charging of fees and course curriculum and had on its governing body nominee of State Government, HNB University and AICTE functioning under Human Resources Ministry and, thus, in fact Government managed and moreover, any surplus arising to society was utilized into activities of society and did not find its way to pocket of persons who were running society/institution - Whether, in view of said facts, it could be said that assessee was not a profit making institution and it was rendering services of education to general public and was eligible for exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-society was formed, inter alia, with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. It was duly registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. It was also registered under section 12A. For the relevant assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01, the assessee claimed exemption under section 11. The Assessing Officer denied the exemption holding that the assessee was not deriving any income out of the property held under trust, and that the income of the assessee was from fee charged from the students on account of tuition fee and other charges and whatever property had been acquired subsequently was as a result of application of this income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessee was a registered society duly incorporated and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1862. The society was formed with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. The income which the assessee received in the form of tuition fee and other receipts could not have been received but for the organization and, therefore, the tuition fee and other receipts derived from other organizations was income derived from property held under trust. Such tuition fee and other receipts, received by the assessee were directly and substantially arising from the organization, which was the property held under the trust. The Assessing Officer's assertion that whatever property in the shape of office building, furniture, computer was simply an application of income was not sustainable. It is well-settled that property acquired by an organization from its own income is also a property held under trust. Thus, fixed assets and current assets held by the assessee as on 31-3-1999 and 31-3-2000 were properties held under trust. Further, the Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case vide order dated 15-12-2003 had held that department cannot guide a charitable institution as to how it should carry on its charity. It is sufficient compliance with the relevant provisions of law in case surplus of the institution is utilized into activities of the institution and does not find its way to the pocket of the persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity.

’ is a saleable commodity. In the instant case, the material found during the course of survey operation clearly established the collection of money over and above the fee prescribed by the Government for admission of a student. Therefore, it was a clear case of sale of education by the assessee-society. Thus, the assessee could not be considered as a charitable institution under section 2(15 ). Therefore, the assessee was not eligible for exemption under section 11. [Para 9] Any income derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose, should not be included in the total income. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee was not holding any property under trust for charitable purpose. It was also not the case of the assessee that any income was derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose. Moreover, it was also not the case of the assessee that any income in the form of voluntary contributions was received with a specific direction to form part of the corpus of the society. The assessee-society was running educational institution and deriving income from such institution. The assessee had also collected money over and above the fees prescribed for admitting students under management quota. In other words, the educational institution was used as a tool/apparatus for collecting money over and above the fees prescribed. The assessee-society had no other source of income/receipt. The society owned the educational institution. The Legislature has visualized two situations. One is religious and another is charitable. Section 11 provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust for charitable and religious purpose. ‘Education’ falls within the definition of charitable purpose. Therefore, any income derived from property held under trust for charitable purpose and applied for education, is eligible for exemption under section 11. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee had not derived any income from any property held under trust. The only source of receipt was the education itself, i.e., from educational institution. [Para 11]

The next question that fell for consideration was whether the educational institution owned by the assessee-society would be regarded as a property held under trust by the society. Section 11 speaks of the property held under trust. The Legislature visualized two situations. One is income derived from the property held under trust and another is application of that income derived from the property held under trust for a charitable purpose. Therefore, there is a clear distinction between the property held under trust and the charitable activity. In the instant case, the assessee-society was carrying on charitable activity by establishing educational institution. Therefore, the charitable activity of the assessee was education. The income, if any, derived from the property held under the Trust and applied for the educational activity, would be construed as application of income for the purpose of charitable purpose. Therefore, the expenditure incurred in establishing the educational institution, namely, acquisition of land, construction of building, etc., are all application of income for charitable activity. If any income was generated in the course of educational activity, the said income would be construed as if it was generated in the course of carrying on the charitable activity. Therefore, such receipt/income received in the course of carrying on charitable activity was also eligible for exemption, provided the same was applied or set apart for educational purposes. However, such receipt/income cannot be construed as derived from property/business held under trust. Since such receipt/income is inevitable or consequential while carrying on the activity of education, such income also becomes eligible for exemption. The educational institution is an apparatus for carrying out the charitable activity. Therefore, the educational institution or charitable activity itself cannot be construed as the property held under trust. The establishment of an educational institution is an activity of charity. Therefore, by any stretch of imagination, the charitable activity, cannot be held as the property held under trust, even though the income/receipt incidental to such activity is eligible for exemption. However, the money collected over and above the prescribed fee for admitting students cannot be construed as income derived from/incidental to the activity of carrying on charitable activity. [Para 12]

It is a well-settled principle of law that a business held under a trust is also a property. Section 11(4) also makes it very clear that the property held under the trust includes a business undertaking. If the assessee-society runs a business incidental to the attainment of the object of the society and separate books of account are maintained by the assessee, the income derived from such business, shall be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust. The Apex Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/ 115 Taxman 126 considered the provisions of section 11(4A) and held that if the business income is derived from business held under the trust and the same is utilized by the institution for achieving object of the institution, then it could be said that such income is applied for charitable purpose. The assessee-society in question had no property or business whatsoever under trust. Moreover, it was not the claim of the assessee that any income was derived from the property or business held under trust. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Whether an amount paid as solatium for cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt - Held, yes - Assessee company under an agreement had been appointed as managing agents by 'M' mills for a period of 20 years - After about two years, assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs - Whether amount paid by 'M' mills to assessee for surrendering its rights as managing agents was a capital receipt, not assessable as business income of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

Concurring view

[Per Cunliffe, J.] The maxim in equity which considers as done that which ought to be done is almost invariably applied to cases in which some default or fraud has taken place for which reason the assistance of the Court is asked. The whole of this transaction could be regarded as being nothing more or less than executory trust. The deposit of the draft so-called trust deed was in law a direction to create an executory trust. Executory trusts are exceedingly common in the United Kingdom. The directions to create them are usually found in wills and marriage settlements and often covenants to settle after acquired property have been confirmed. Where too, the creator of the trust nominates himself as a trustee for the cesti que trust, the Courts have always looked generously upon the intention of the declaration. It is quite true that covenants to settle usually only effect corpus and not income, but effect has been given where a plain intention is shown to trusts with income alone; for trusts and legal estates are governed by the same rules. It is quite true that a voluntary covenant to create a trust is not enforceable, but if the whole of the circumstances of the instant case, were examined, it would be seen that there was a valid contract between the Government and the assessee enforceable in law from which this voluntary trust sprang and the true test was whether, on the whole construction of the letters passing between the parties and also of the draft trust deed, there was an intention to give third parties immediate equitable rights. That test was fulfilled.

The Commissioner, however, contended that any question of a trust in India is controlled by the provisions of the Indian Trusts Act of 1882. That was quite true if the trust in question did not happen to be a charitable trust. But the preamble to that Act has been interpreted to exclude all charitable trusts from the operation of the statute. The arrangement in question came well within the definition of a charitable trust.

It was true that the assessee having regard to his covenant with the Chief Secretary received his salary and his position in a fiduciary capacity alone, but as that salary was not income derived from property held on trust he could not be considered as able to obtain the benefit of exemption. It was with reluctance that this assessment was upheld.

[Per Pratt, CJ]

Under the circumstances, it was clear that the money was the personal income of the assessee and only became trust money, if at all, when paid into the separate account for the purposes of the boat club.

The exemption set forth in sub-section (3)(i ) of section 4 of the 1922 Act had no application since the emoluments in question were not income derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes.

The position would have been different had he accepted the office on condition that he should draw no salary. It was open to him to accept the appointment without pay, and to leave the University with liberty to devote the emoluments, which would ordinarily be paid to a Lecturer and Professor to charitable purposes, if they thought fit.

He made no such agreement.

He could not, therefore, claim as of right exemption from income-tax with respect to a portion of his income, which he devoted to charitable purposes under an agreement with the Local Government, even if he had created a trust with respect thereto.

HEADNOTE: Section 11, read with  section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1967-68 to 1970-71 - Assessee - Trust was formed with objects of providing relief to poor, advancement of education, medical relief, promotion of science, art and literature and any other object of general pubic utility for benefit of pubic - As per trust deed, trustees had power to hold any business undertaking and administer and manage it only for purpose of achieving object of general benefit - It was further mentioned that profit from business activity must feed charitable purpose under terms of trust - Whether, on construction of terms of trust deed, it could not be said that there was any profit-making object of assessee - Trust in carrying on business activities - Held, yes - Whether therefore, income derived by assessee - Trust was eligible for exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee trust was constituted under a trust deed dated 27-8-1963. As per the trust deed, the objects of the trust, were relief of the poor, advancement of education, medical relief, promotion of science, art and of literature and any other object of general public utility for the benefit of the public. The powers of the trustees, as per the deed, included power to hold any business undertaking upon trust and to administer and manage the same. Clause(5) of the deed provided that after paying all costs and expenses, the trustees would utilise the net income of the trust for aforesaid charitable objects or purposes at such time or times and in such manner and on such proportions as the trustees might in their discretion think fit. During the relevant assessment years the assessee had earned commission as area managers of a company, but did not show the income in its return on the ground that the income earned was not liable to income-tax as the same had been derived from a business undertaking held under trust for charitable purposes, and had been applied to such purposes in India in terms of section 2(15) and section 11. The ITO, however, did not agree with the assessee and assessed the income derived by the assessee from its business activity. The AAC allowed the appeals and held that the assessee was entitled to exemption from income-tax under section 2(15) and 11.

On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order of the AAC and restored that of the ITO holding that the business undertaking carried on by the assessee was one of the objects of the trust, and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 2(15), read with section 11.

On reference:

HELD: In AddI. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1980] 121 ITR 1 (SC) it has been held by the Supreme Court that if the dominant or primary purpose of the assessee trust was charitable, the subsidiary objects would not militate against its charitable character and the purpose of the assessee would not be any the less charitable. It is not necessary that the accomplishment of the object or the means to carry out the object should not involve an activity for profit.

As laid down by the Supreme Court an activity involved in carrying out charitable purpose must not be motivated by a profit objective but it must be undertaken for the purpose of advancement or carrying out the charitable purposes. It would not be correct to draw invariably an inference that whenever an activity is carried on which yields profit, the activity must be deemed to be for profit and the charitable purpose involves a carrying on of activity for profit. In other words, the object must be of general public utility, that is, it must not involve the carrying on of any activity for profit, but if for advancement of that object it becomes necessary to carry on any activity for profit, such an activity could not detract from the charitable purpose. That the Legislature did not intend to debar a trust created for charitable purpose from holding property under trust including a business undertaking is clearly borne out by the language of section 11(4) which lays down that for the purpose of this section property held under trust includes a business undertaking so held. Thus, taking into consideration the provisions of section 11(4), it is clear that a business undertaking can be held for charitable purpose but the object of the trust must not be the carrying on of any activity for profit.

In the instant case, the question as to what were the object of the trust was to be decided on the interpretation of the various clauses of the trust deed itself.
