It was contended before the ITO by the assessee-trust that only an annual amount of Rs. 1,80,000 should be appor-tioned amongst the three beneficiaries and the balance of income should be allocated to J Trust. The ITO however, held that the beneficiaries were not empowered to part with any portion of their rights under the original trust deed and that the income first accrued to the beneficiaries and thereafter was applied for charitable purposes and, therefore, it was a case of application of income and not of diversion of income by an over-riding title in favour of J Trust. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) the assessee contended, inter alia, that in view of section 11 and section 58 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, beneficiaries had the power to part with any portion of their interest and in fact the interest of the beneficiaries in the balance income of the assessee-trust in excess of Rs. 1,80,000 was effect-ively diverted at source and, therefore, it no longer belonged to them. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee's contention and set aside the ITO's order.

On appeal by the revenue :

The assessee, a registered firm, was appointed as the managing agents of a company. The duration of the managing agency period was 20 years. The managing agency agreement provided that the company would pay each year to the managing agents 5 per cent commission on the proceeds of the total sales of yarn and of all cloth sold by the company or three pies per pound avoirdupois on the sale, whichever the managing agents chose; that the company would also pay 10 per cent on the proceeds of sales of all other materials; that the mills were to pay to the managing agents each year after December 31, or such other date which the directors of the company may choose for the closing of the accounts. There was a further clause that if the net profits of the managed company were not sufficient to enable the directors to recommend a dividend of 8 per cent per annum on the paid up capital, then the managing agents were bound to forgo a portion of their commission up to one-third. On 9-12-1950, the managing agency agreement was modified as to the commission payable under it and that the managing agents had agreed to charge 3 per cent on sales instead of 5 per cent, for the year ending 31-12- 1950. A resolution was passed at the annual general meeting of the managed company on 22-4-1951, and it was ratified at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed company on 7-10-1951. For the assessment years 1951-52 and 1952-53, the managing agents were taxed by the income-tax authorities on the basis that in those two years they had voluntarily relinquished a sum. These sums were added to the income of the managing agents for the purpose of income-tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the agreement between the managing agents and the managed company to receive remuneration at 3 per cent on the total sales was a valid one and took effect as from 1-1-1950. It also held that commission did not accrue as the managing agents were to get the amount of commission after the whole profit was determined at the end of the year. On reference, the High Court decided in favour of the managing agents.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

The assessee, a limited company, had a sugar mill and also ran an agricultural farm for growing sugarcane used for the production of sugar in the mill. Under a managing agency agreement, the assessee were appointed as the managing agents for a period of ten years on the remuneration of 10 per cent of the net profit project to minimum of Rs. 20,000. The ITO held that the assessee was entitled to claim as deduction from the profits only the remuneration at 10 per cent, of the profits which were subjected to income-tax and, therefore, disallowed the agricultural profits out of the managing agency remuneration. The Tribunal confirmed the order of the ITO. It also held that as the profit of arising out of the agricultural farm was not assessable to income-tax, the expenditure attributable to earning of the said agricultural income could not be allowed while ascertaining the profits of the sugar mill under section 10 of 1922 Act.

On reference:

Two brothers of 'M' and 'C', who were members of joint Hindu family, entered into a partnership and were appointed as managing agents of a 'D' mill under an agreement, 'C' died in 1945. Thereafter there was a fresh agreement of managing agency between 'D' mills and 'M' and the four sons of 'C'. The revenue authorities claimed that the income earned by each of the four sons of 'C' under the managing agency agreement was the joint family property and was not their individual income.

On reference :

The assessee society was a Charitable Institution registered under section 12AA. The main objects of the society were to provide education, medical relief to the poor and objects of general public utility. It was running lodging accommodations at two places and had two auditoriums and a ground, which had a commercial value to be let out for public functions, exhibitions, etc. The society maintained a swimming pool, recreation centers and gymnasium. Two schools and a home were also formed and maintained for the deprived children. Relief activities in times of flood and other natural calamities were also being carried out by the society. The Auditorium and the hall were let out to members and non-members. Rooms were also let out to members and non-members, which included providing of food.

The Assessing Officer held that the assessee was carrying on business activities. As regards the letting out of the Auditoriums, the ground and letting of rooms the society was charging rent as well as providing food and beverages to the persons, who were occupying such rooms. The assessee took contention that the income from these activities was not business income but income from the property. However, the contention of the assessee was rejected holding the view that letting out of the hall and the open space and hiring out rooms amounted to business and, hence, the income therefrom was assessable as business income. Thus, the Assessing Officer viewed that the assessee would be ineligible for exemption under sections 11 and 12.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) agreed with the assessee that the receipts from letting off of the rooms and the Auditorium constitute income from a house property and thus directed the Assessing Officer to grant the benefit under section 11.

On second appeal the Tribunal held that the question as to whether the assessee was earning income as incidental to the activities of the society or whether the assessee was really engaged in business activity was required to be examined by the Assessing Officer and for this the matter was deserved to be remitted back to the Assessing Officer to examine afresh in all these aspects.

On appeal to High Court the assessee contended that the Tribunal had not considered the view of the Commissioner(Appeals) that the income earned was an income from house property and the remand order had not referred to this but ordered an open remand, such open remand would prejudice the assessee and hence submitted that the same may be clarified herein by directing the Assessing Officer to consider the question as to whether the income earned had to be assessed as income from house property or of business income, keeping in mind the objects of the trust.

The assessee was a charitable trust enjoying exemption from tax in the earlier assessment years. During relevant assessment year, the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee was earning rental income from sub-letting the properties. According to the Assessing Officer, the said exercise done by the assessee for earning income was not incidental to the attainment of the object of the trust and, thus, income so earned was to be assessed as income from business by applying the provisions of section 11(4A).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the provisions of section 11(4A) were not attracted and income earned from sub-letting the property was for the charitable object and hence, the exemption under section 11 was to be allowed. On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal held that to enable the trust to carry out its charitable object in effective manner if rental income was received by way of sub-letting, for that reason, the exemption could not have been denied by the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal :

Sassoon & Company (Sasoons) were the managing agents of three companies. The Sassoons transferred their managing agencies of the said companies to other companies. The Sassoons executed in favour of the transferee companies formal deeds of assignment and transfer and received from them the net consideration of Rs. 75,77,693. This was taken by them to the "Capital Reserve Account". The accounts of the managing agency commission payable by the respective companies to the managing agents for the year 1943 were made up in the year 1944 and the transferee companies received from managed companies certain amounts as and by way of such commission.

For the assessment year 1944-45 the original income-tax assessment of the Sassoons were made on a total income of Rs. 46,48,483. This income however did not include any part of the managing agency commission received by the transferees. The entire amounts of the managing agency commission received by the transferees were assessed by the ITO for the assessment year 1945-46 as the income of the transferees. The Tribunal accepted the transferees' contention that the managing agency commission received by them should be apportioned on a proportionate basis and the transferees should be made liable to pay tax only on the commission earned by them during the period that they had worked as the managing agents of the respective companies.

The ITO discovered that the amounts of the managing agency commission earned by the Sassoons prior to the dates of the respective transfers were not brought to tax and therefore issued on 29-6-1946, notice under section 34 of 1922, Act upon the Sassoons on the ground that their income from the managing agency had escaped assessment, the amount proposed to be included was Rs. 28,51,934. According to ITO, such managing agency commission had accrued to the Sassoons for services rendered upto the dates of transfers so that on the dates on which the agencies were transferred the Sassoons were entitled to such remuneration from the managed companies. In spite of the objection of the Sassoons the ITO determined the said sum as their escaped incomes and assessed them accordingly. The AAC dismissed assessee's appeals. The Tribunal relied upon its order in the case of the transferees and confirmed the orders of the AAC. The Tribunal was of the opinion that the managing agency commission was earned for services rendered and therefore, it was taxed in the hands of the person who carried on the business of the managing agency and not in the hands of the person to whom it was assigned, and that therefore so far as the Sassoons were concerned the managing agency commission should be apportioned between them and their transferees. On references by the assessee and the Department, the decision of the High Court was against the contentions which had been urged both by the Sassoons and the Commissioner. The High Court adopted test of the services rendered by the Sassoons as well as the transferees during the whole of the year and considered the proportions of the services rendered by the Sassoons and the transferees as the managing agents of the companies as decisive of the portions of the managing agency commission earned respectively by each. The High Court held in substance that (1) the managing agency remuneration for the year in question accrued as the joint income of the both the assignor and the assignee and was apportionable between them, and (2) the assignee-companies received the assignor's share of the joint income by virtue of the assignments of the assignor's share and hence to that extent it was not their taxable income but continued to be the taxable income of the assignor. The income was held assessable to tax not on the basis of receipt but on the basis of accrual.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee, a trust existing for charitable purposes, gave interest-free loans to needy persons. When the loans were repaid, the ITO treated the repayments of such loans, received back by the assessee, as the assessee's income for the years in which sum repayments were made. On appeal, the AAC set aside the ITO's order on the ground that repayments of the loans did not constitute taxable income of the assessee and on further appeal, the Tribunal upheld the AAC's order.

On reference, the assessee contended that the money received from or returned by the beneficiaries could not be deemed to be the income derived from the property held under trust in the absence of any deeming provision in section 11.

held.text:
The 'property' is a term of the widest import, and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context might require, it signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire, hold and enjoy. Business would undoubtedly be property, unless there is something to the contrary in the enactment. There is nothing in language of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act which restricts in any manner the normal and accepted meaning of the word 'property', and excludes business from its connotation.

It is true that a public charity is perpetual in character, and that means that it is capable of enforcement, so long as there is any property left which can be appropriated for its objects. And even if some or all of the objects become incapable of fulfilment, the trust properties will be devoted to the performance of similar or allied charitable purposes on the doctrine of cy-pres. But so far as the trust properties themselves are concerned, they will be held only on the incidents to which they are subject under the law. Thus, if the property is a leasehold interest, it must cease on the termination of the lease. Likewise, if trust property is alienated under circumstances binding on the trust, it will go out of the trust. But that does not operate as an extinction of the trust, unless there is no property at all left, with which the trust could be carried out. That is the principle enacted in section 77(c) of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, which in terms, however, applies only to private trusts. Therefore, the fact that the trustees have the option at any time to throw up the managing agency is no legal impediment to its being property which could be held on trust.

In the result, it could be held that the word 'property' in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act is of sufficient amplitude to comprehend 'business', and if the question fell to be decided solely on the terms of that sub-section, the managing agency must be treated as property held on trust within section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act.

With aforesaid observation, the case was remanded to High Court for a fresh disposal on merits.

[Matter remanded to High Court]

The nature of payment to the trustees-cum - pujaris could not be otherwise than for the services rendered by them, since their tenure of office was linked with their good conduct and they held the offices of trustees-cum-pujaris under the scheme framed under the Bombay Public Trusts Act and were liable to be removed on any of the permissible grounds under the said Act. It was, no doubt, true that the payment had been linked up with the net income of the trust. Nonetheless, the real question was what was the consideration for the payment ? This consideration was the various duties and obligations which the pujaris or the trustees had to carry out under the scheme. The Tribunal, without assigning any reason, had ignored the weighty opinion of the Bombay High Court in Second Appeal No. 565 of 1942 mentioned above supporting this view of the nature of the payments. The Tribunal had also failed to consider the duties to be performed by the trustees-cum-pujaris under the earlier or the present scheme. The Tribunal had, therefore, committed an error of law in reaching the conclusion that the impugned payments were not remuneration for the services rendered by the trustees-cum -pujaris and were merely application of the income of the trust.

The Tribunal had also not borne in mind the clear distinction between the provisions of section 11(1)(a ) relating to income from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes and section 11(1)(b ) relating to income from property held under trust in part only for such purposes. It could not be gainsaid that the trust properties in the instant case were wholly set apart for religious and charitable purposes and it was nobody's case that only a part of the properties had been so set apart. Consequently, having regard to the nature of payments made to the trustees-cum - pujaris, the consideration for which the payment was made and the judicial decisions in that behalf, it could not be urged successfully that this was a case of sharing of income fur a non-charitable object. The Tribunal was, therefore, clearly in error in holding that the case of the assessee-trust fell under section 11(1 )(b) and not under section 11(1)(a ).

The High Court observed that m view of its judgment given above, the question whether the payments made to the hereditary trustees-cum-pujaris were allowable as expenditure did not survive for consideration.

By the Insurance Act, 1938, a "principal agent" is defined as meaning "a person, who, not being a salaried employee of an insurer, in consideration of any commission, (i) performs any administrative and organizing functions for the insurer and (ii) procures general insurance business whether wholly or in part by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents of behalf of the insurer". Evidently a principal agent by the definition does not merely render personal service but is concerned with performing certain administrative and organizing functions and the procuring of general insurance business by employing or causing to be employed insurance agents. Such an agent by the very definition will be regarded as carrying on the business of a principal agent. He is not merely an employee engaged for rendering services of a personal nature: he is invested with the right as an agent to perform the administrative organizing functions for the insurer and to procure general insurance business by employing, directly or indirectly, insurance agents. By section 42A of the Insurance Act principal agents are required to obtain a certificate from the Controller of Insurance or an officer authorized by him entitling them to conduct the business of principal agency, and the certificate remains in operation for a period of twelve months only from the date of issue but is liable to be renewed. It is also true that under Part A of the Sixth Schedule to the Insurance Act certain terms are deemed to be included in every contract between an insurer carrying on general insurance business and a principal agent. Under clause 2 of Part A of the Sixth Schedule the principal agent has to procure or cause to be procured through insurance agents such an amount of general insurance business as will yield a gross premium income of not less than Rs. 20,000 in each calendar year. Under clause 4, in the event of the principal agent failing to comply with the requirements of clause 2 in any two successive calendar years, the contract shall, without prejudice to the provisions of clause 3, terminate on the 31st day of March immediately following the second calendar year. Under clause 3 the agency is also liable to be forfeited in the events set out in sub-clauses (i) and (ii) thereof. By clause 5 certain restriction are placed upon the principal agent but an account of these provisions, which impose certain restrictive conditions upon the principal agent it could not be said that the appointment of a principal agent gave rise to a bare service agreement and that the remuneration paid was not for the conduct of a business but for performance of personal service. The circumstance that the appointment was liable to be terminated at short notice and the agency was not permanent and was liable to be forfeited in the events set out hereinbefore would not, affect the character of the agency as business. Following the observation made by the Supreme Court in J.K. Trust's case [1957] 32 ITR 535 the principal agency conducted by the assessee was a business and, therefore, "property" within the meaning of section 4(3)(i). Being property which was capable of being settled upon trust by the deed of trust, dated 17-2-1951, it was lawfully settled upon trust for charitable purposes. The taxing authorities are primarily concerned with the question whether the income sought to be taxed in income from property, which is held on trust for religious or charitable purpose. If the business of the principal agency was transferred to the trustees under a deed of settlement, and from that business income was received, the income will fall within section 4(3)(i) and be exempt from tax in the hands of the trustees. Therefore, under the terms of appointment made with the company firm became the principal agents conducting a business and that business was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i ) and that the alteration, sometime after their appointment as principal agents, in the constitution of the from did not alter the character of the income earned in the course of the business. The income which is liable to be included in the total income of the assessee, was income derived from business carried on behalf of religious or charitable institution, unless that income fulfils the conditions prescribed by clause (b). The expression "such income" in the proviso refers to the income derived from property (which expression includes a business) held for religious or charitable purposes. But that did not justify the submission that the business which was referred to in clause (b) of the proviso must be business which is held for charitable or religious purposes. The business referred to in clause (b) of the proviso need not be business which is held for religious or charitable purposes, provided it is business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution.

The assessee had no beneficial interest in the lands which were the subject-matter of the trust: nor was he given under the trust a right to receive and appropriate to himself the income of the properties or a part thereof in lieu of any beneficial interest in that income. The source of the right in which a fraction of the net income of the trust was to be appropriated by the assessee as his remuneration was not in the right to receive rent or revenue of agricultural lands, but rested in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The income of the trust appropriated by the assessee as remuneration was not received by him as rent or revenue of land; the character of the income appropriated as remuneration due was again not the same as the character in which it was received by the assessee as trustee. Both the source and character of the income were, therefore, altered when a part of the income of the trust was appropriated by the assessee as his remuneration, and that was so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration was made as a percentage of the income, a substantial part whereof was derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. The remuneration not being received as rent or revenue of agricultural lands under a title, legal or beneficial in the property from which the income was received, it was not income exempt under section 4(3)(viii).

In the instant case, the assessee had no beneficial interest in the trust property. The assessee so far as his remuneration was concerned was not the direct recipient of the income of the trust, the source and the character of the income were both altered when agricultural income was appropriated under the covenant in the deed of trust as remuneration for services rendered.

Hence, the amount paid to the assessee in his character of a shebait of the trust properties was not exempted from taxation.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

Whenever a valid trust is executed, the property vests in the trustees, and the income accruing from those properties is the income of the trust and not of the beneficiaries. For purposes of income-tax law, however, the income under section 41(1) of the Act 1922 is treated as received by the trustees on behalf of the beneficiaries, but is to be taxed in the hands of the trustees in the like manner and to the same amount as it would be leviable upon the person on whose behalf such income is receivable. The liability of the income to tax is, therefore, independent of the income actually being received by the beneficiaries and it may be subjected to tax as soon as it is earned by the trust. The exception is that, where the trust properties are held wholly for charitable or religious purposes, in so far as such income is applied or accumulated for application to such religious or charitable purposes, it is exempt from income-tax. In the instant case, therefore, in dealing with the question referred to the High Court, any assumption that the income of the trust properties was received by 'B' would not be correct. The income during her lifetime was clearly taxable as income in the hands of the trustees received by them on behalf of 'B'.

Under section 4(3)(i ) of 1922 Act, the income from trust properties, held wholly for charitable or religious purposes, is exempt from tax under two circumstances. The first is when that income is actually applied for such religious or charitable purposes, and the second is when it is accumulated for application to such religious or charitable purposes. In instant case, as soon as 'B' executed the deed of surrender, her rights under clause 7 completely ceased and all the income from the trust properties remained with the trustees to be applied in accordance with the other terms of the deed of trust. If it could be held that clause 8 came into operation and permitted the application of that income to the charitable purposes mentioned in it as soon as B's rights ceased, even though she remained alive, there would be no difficulty in holding that section 4(3)(i ) of 1922 Act would have exempted the income from income-tax.

The instant appeal was to be dismissed accordingly.

The case was decided in favour of respondent/assessee.

By virtue of section 11(4) "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, it could not be accepted that the income derived by the assessee was not income from property as envisaged under section 11(1)(a). That apart, a perusal of the aims and objects of the assessee-society led to the conclusion that the income derived by it was income from property within the meaning of section 11(1)(a). Accordingly, the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the amount received by the assessee on account of allocation charges was not income from property held under trust.

Under the agreement the managing agents could be participators in profits, if they divided in a stated percentage an agreed fund. They could not be participators of the profits divisible amongst the shareholders constituted one fund and they got a percentage of a fund which was differently calculated and, therefore, in fact a different fund. The ten per cent, were not necessarily payable out of the profits. The annual net profits. The net profits were again, not what one ordinarily finds in the company's balance sheets. They are net profits only for the purpose of calculation, to be worked out strictly on the lines specifically mentioned in that clause. It was obvious that several deductions which are not permitted under the clause would be made in preparing the balance sheet and ascertaining the net profits of a commercial corporation. Moreover, the commission was not in any year to amount to a sum less than Rs. 10,000. Therefore, if in any year the company made no profits, the sum had to be paid by the principal company, even out of its capital. If in any given year there was no agricultural income, the remuneration, with a minimum of Rs. 10,000, will still have to be paid out of the profits earned through the other activities of the principal company. It was therefore clear that, on the face of this clause itself, there was nothing to connect it necessarily with the agricultural income of the principal company.

In the instant case, the managing agents would receive the remuneration irrespective of the nature of the business of the principal company. They were paid for their work as managing agents. The assets of the principal company were not vested in them. They were not the persons who could sue for amounts due to the principal company in their own name. They were only agents for management. It seemed therefore clear that, under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the balance of the agricultural income in the hands of the principal company was not to be divided between the principal agency and the managing agents in a stated proportion.

Therefore, the conclusion of the Tribunal was correct. On the true construction of the clause in question it could not be stated that the managing agents received any portion of the agricultural income, when they received remuneration for services rendered for managing the affairs of the principal company, only one part of whose business was held to be agricultural.

Concurring view

Per Chagla, J

"Agricultural income" is defined in section 2(1) of 1922 Act as any rent or revenue derived from land which is used for agricultural purposes, and the question, therefore, which arose for determination was whether any portion of the remuneration received by the assessee was rent or revenue derived from land which was used for agricultural purposes. It was clear that the remuneration received by the assessee was under a contract between it and the principal company for services to be rendered by the assessee as the managing agents of the principal company. That contract had nothing whatever to do with the income earned by the principal company from agricultural sources. It was also clear from the contract that what the principal company contracted with the managing agents was to pay them a sum of Rs. 10,000 or ten percent of the profits computed in a particular manner whichever sum was larger.

In the instant case, it was perfectly evident that what the assessee was going to share in was an artificial fund which first came into existence. They received ten per cent of that fund. After that had been ascertained the usefulness of that fund disappeared and a new fund came into existence by a different computation which was to be divisible amongst the shareholders as their own profits.

If the income is agricultural income, it bears an indelible impression upon it and is exempt from tax. But on the construction of the contract, the remuneration of the assessee was for its services as the managing agents of the principal company; that was the character of its income. The character of its income was not that part of it was rent or revenue from land which was used for agricultural purposes. Therefore, the income received by the assessee from the principal company which was proportionate to the agricultural income earned by the principal company was not agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act 1922, and was not exempt from assessment under the provision of section 4(3)(viii) of the 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

There was no doubt, that the opportunity of becoming and of being actually appointed managing agents arose directly from the asset which was sold to the new company, viz., the mills, which in part was joint family property.

It was provided by the articles of association of the new company that the firm, should be appointed managing agents, and that this arrangement was part and parcel of the arrangements, whereby the Mills, in which the assessee admittedly held a share as karta, were sold by the partnership to the new company. If the partners should sell or assign their right to remuneration, as per clause 14 of the managing agency agreement it could not be said that the portion of the proceeds of sale attributable to HD's share, did not pass to him as joint family property. The managing agency was derived from or acquired with the assistance of joint family property, that is to say, the mills in which HD as karta was beneficially interested.

Accordingly, share income received by 'HD' from managing agency was income of HUF of which he was karta.

Decision was in favour of revenue.

The managing agency was not, except in the circumstances set out in clause 2 of the agreement, liable to be determined at the instance of the company, unless the assessee by giving notice of three weeks voluntarily resigned the agency. At the date of termination the agency had five more years to run, and the Companies Act did not prohibit renewal of the agency in favour of the assessee, after the expiry of the initial period of twenty years. The assessee was formed for the object, amongst others (vide clause 3(2) of the memorandum of association of the appellant) of carrying on the business of managing agencies. The assessee was entitled under the terms of the agreement to receive so long as the agency enured ten per cent of the profits of the company's working, three per cent on all purchases of stores and machinery abroad, and a monthly remuneration of Rs. 3,000. The assessee submitted its resignation in exercise of the power reserved under clause 8 of the managing agency agreement, but that resignation was, it was common ground, part of the arrangement. Under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the principal company was not obliged to pay any compensation to the assessee for voluntary resignation of the agency, but in consideration of the assessee parting with its shareholding and submitting resignation of the managing agency so as to facilitate the appointment of 'M' as managing agent, the latter purchased the shareholding of the assessee, undertook to make available Rs. 3,50,000 for payment to the assessee and to discharge the debt due by the company to the assessee. Payment of Rs. 3,50,000, was therefore an integral part of an arrangement for transfer of managing agency. A managing agency of a company is in the nature of a capital asset; that is not denied. It is true that it is not like an ordinary asset capable of being transferred from one person to another. Theoretically, the power to appoint or dismiss the managing agent may lie with the directors of the company, but in practice the power lies with the person or persons having a controlling interest in the shareholding of the company. 'M' was anxious to be appointed managing agents of the principal company; and for that purpose the assessee had to be persuaded to agree to a premature termination of its agency. This was secured for a triple consideration: sale of shares held by the assessee at an agreed price, stipulation to discharge the liability of the company to repay the loans due by the company, and payment of Rs. 3,50,000 as compensation for termination of the assessee's agency. The assessee was formed with the object, among others, of acquiring managing agencies of companies and to carry on the business and to take part in the management, supervision or control of the business or operations of any other company, association, firm or person and to make profit out of it. That only authorised the assessee to acquire as a fixed asset, if a managing agency may be so described, and to exploit it for the purpose of profit. But there was no evidence that the company was formed for the purpose of acquiring and selling managing agencies and making profit by those transactions of sale and purchase. A managing agency is not an asset for which there is a market, for it depends upon the personal qualifications of the agent. In truth the amount of Rs. 3,50,000 was received by the assessee from 'M' in consideration of the former agreeing to forgo the agency which it held and which 'M' was anxious to obtain. It was in a business sense a sale of such rights as the assessee possessed in the agency. This was supported by the recitals made in clause 2 of the agreement that if at any time within six months after the completion of such sale 'M' was unable to exercise the voting rights attached to the shares purchased by them, the assessee would appoint any person nominated by to attend and vote for them at any meeting of the company or the holders of any class of shares to be held within such period in such manner as 'M' might decide. The object underlying the agreement was therefore to transfer the managing agency to 'M' or at least to effectuate their appointment in place of the assessee as managing agent of the company. All the stipulations and the covenants of the agreement, viewed in the light of the surrounding circumstances, did stamp the transaction as one of surrender of the rights of the assessee in the managing agency so that corresponding rights may arise in favour of 'M'. It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts

, transporting and shipping the goods might have resulted in serious losses to the assessee. The ITO accepted that the expenditure for payment of remuneration for attending to the contract was laid out for the purpose of the business of the assessee, but reduced the stipulated rate to 10 per cent on two grounds that 'T' was the brother of 'M', and that he was, as a director of the company, bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the contract. There was no evidence that the agreement was motivated by considerations other than strictly business considerations. There was also no evidence that as a director 'T' was bound to attend to all the activities of the company including the special contract with the Central Government. The duties which the director was bound to perform for earning the remuneration of Rs. 400 per month were not on the record, but even in the opinion of the taxing authorities the duties of 'T' as director did not cover attendance to the contract with the Government. 'T' and 'M' were brothers, but that by itself is not sufficient to justify an inference that unreasonable or excessive remuneration was agreed to be paid. The person who was called upon to attend to a contract of this magnitude was required to have expert knowledge of the business, apply his time exclusively thereto, travel from time to time, maintain supervision and control at the stage of purchase, redrying, packing, transport and loading for shipment. Presumably 'T' was such a person, and that is why he was selected for earning for the assessee a large amount of commission by duly performing the contract.

An analysis of the reasons given by the ITO disclosed no grounds to support the view that remuneration at a rate exceeding 10 per cent of the net profit was excessive or unreasonable. The contract with the Government was for the assessee an important contract requiring constant and vigilant application and supervision by a person well acquainted with the practical details of the business. If the management of the assessee as prudent businessman for advancing the interest of the assessee bona fide regarded 30 per cent of the net profits as reasonable remuneration, the revenue authorities were not justified in reviewing their opinion and reducing the rate of remuneration. It was true that if, on a consideration of the relevant materials, the Tribunal was of the opinion that a particular remuneration stipulated to be paid was not bona fide or is unreasonable, the High Court in exercising its advisory jurisdiction had no power to interfere with that opinion. But the material circumstances relating to the nature of the contract, the services to be performed and the nature of the duties by the employee were not at all taken into account by the Tribunal and the income-tax authorities. Therefore, the disallowance of a sum of out of the remuneration paid to 'T' was not justifiable ?

The contract under which the assessee was appointed managing agent for the 'N' was to enure till 1960, but it had to be prematurely terminated because the Government of Madras exercising its powers under 1949 Act had compulsorily acquired the electricity undertaking. With the acquisition of that undertaking the right of the assessee as managing agent ceased. Under section 15 of the 1449 Act, the Government was bound to pay compensation which would include compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement. The assessee received sum as compensation for termination of the agency, computed in the manner laid down in section 15 of that Act. Prima facie, such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of the assessee, was a capital receipt.

Turning to the facts of the instant case, it must in the first instance be observed that it was for the revenue to establish that a particular receipt was income liable to tax, and beyond stating that the assessee was the managing agent of the 'N' and of two other companies, there was no other evidence about the nature of the business of the two other companies of which the assessee was the managing agent, about their relative importance qua the managing agency of the 'N' and whether by reason of the extinction of the managing agency of the 'N' any enduring asset was lost to the assessee, or its trading organisation was adversely affected. The ITO observed that the 'assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end', the assessee still continues as 'managing agents of other companies'. Even after surrender of one of the agencies, the assessee carried on business as before, its structure not being affected' and therefore 'the receipt was to be considered as revenue'.

Hence, the compensation received for taking over the 'N' was a capital receipt not liable to be taxed, and on the materials placed the Supreme Court did not disagree with the High Court.

The appeal therefore failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Under the scheme the assessee had only powers of management of the wakf estate and that these powers were limited in certain respects by the control of a committee of management. The recovery of the rent depends on the rights of the wakf estate, and on the assessee's performance of his duties of management as Mutawalli, and the amount of his remuneration did not depend either on the nature of the properties or assets which constitute the wakf estate, nor on the amount of the income derived therefrom by the wakf estate. If, as might possibly happen, the whole or a portion of the wakf property ceased to be represented by agricultural lands, it was clear that the remuneration fixed by article 15 of the scheme would not be affected.

Thus, the High Court was right in holding that, albeit the income received by the wakf estate was within the definition of agricultural income in section 2(1), the sums drawn therefrom as remuneration by the assessee were not agricultural income received by the assessee.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

The assessee was a registered society duly incorporated and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1862. The society was formed with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. The income which the assessee received in the form of tuition fee and other receipts could not have been received but for the organization and, therefore, the tuition fee and other receipts derived from other organizations was income derived from property held under trust. Such tuition fee and other receipts, received by the assessee were directly and substantially arising from the organization, which was the property held under the trust. The Assessing Officer's assertion that whatever property in the shape of office building, furniture, computer was simply an application of income was not sustainable. It is well-settled that property acquired by an organization from its own income is also a property held under trust. Thus, fixed assets and current assets held by the assessee as on 31-3-1999 and 31-3-2000 were properties held under trust. Further, the Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case vide order dated 15-12-2003 had held that department cannot guide a charitable institution as to how it should carry on its charity. It is sufficient compliance with the relevant provisions of law in case surplus of the institution is utilized into activities of the institution and does not find its way to the pocket of the persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity.

The educational institution being run by the assessee was for the general benefit of the public and not for the benefit of any class or section of the public, as (a ) the institution was duly recognized by HNB Garhwal University and strictly followed all procedures with regard to admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum as laid down by the university, and (b) the nominees of State Government, HNB University and AICTE (functioning under the Human Resources Ministry) were on the governing body of the society and, therefore, the assessee had no choice in matters of admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum. The institute, was, in fact, State Government managed.

It was also found that the working system of the assessee was as per the guidelines laid down by the University. In respect of fixing and charging fees from students, the society management had no powers. Fee was being charged from students strictly as specified and laid down by the University. The governing body of the society had no powers to workout the cost and thereafter to add on the element of overheads and profits. Therefore, there was no question of building huge margins of profits in the fees structure as conceived by the Assessing Officer.

From a plain reading of the main objects given in the Memorandum, it could very well be discerned that the society had been formed with the sole objective of imparting and spreading computer education. Further, the assessee-society was virtually Government managed. Therefore, the question of functioning like a commercial profit making institution was totally unfounded. Thus, the fees charged by the assessee was simply receipt in the hands of the society and not profit.

Further, the assessee was rendering services of education to the general public. Therefore, its activities clearly fell within the ambit of charitable purpose as defined under section 2(15). Charging of fees does not in anyway dilute the aspect of charitable purpose. It is the end use and spirit and objective which matters.

In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had not been able to appreciate the difference in the words 'charitable purposes' as are used in the Act and the word 'charity' as had been used by the Assessing Officer in his order. The word 'charity' as used in English language and recognized in English law, implies as an act motivated by pity and may require benevolence to manifest it. However, exemption under section 11 has been prescribed with reference to 'charitable purposes' and not 'charity'. The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act.

Where a settlor creates a trust, it lies within his power to also make a provision as to the management of the trust property. It is perfectly permissible for a settlor to nominate any person as trustees for first trustees and where there were more than one trustee, a managing trustee. It is also within his power to regulate the appointment of trustees in future as well as the managing trustee. There is no prohibition in law if the settlor himself takes over the function of the managing trustee after the trust has come into being. When the settlor himself becomes a trustee or managing trustee a change undergoes in his capacity from one of an owner of property to that of trustee holding the trust property for the benefit of the beneficiaries or for the purpose of working out the directions in the deed of trust. If for such work, any remuneration is provided for by the terms of the trust deed, that would not, amount to the reservation of any interest for the purposes of section 12(1).

The Department was, therefore, not entitled to rely on clauses 6 and 19 to contend that there was reservation of interest of the trust property and, therefore, the value of Kale Bhawan was liable to be treated as a part of the dutiable estate.

There could hardly be any doubt that clause 23 of the trust deed was a repository of the express power of revocation which could be exercised after the period of 10 years from the date specified therein and if the trust could not function for any reason. It could not be held that merely because in the case of a public trust a power to revoke is reserved by the settlor, such property must be deemed to pass on the death of the settlor for the purposes of section 12(1). When section 12(1) refers to the reservation by the settlor of the right to exercise the power of revocation, it obviously presupposes that such a power of revocation can be validly and legally reserved by the settlor. In other words, even if the document of trust does contain a clause expressly reserving the power of revocation if in law such a power of revocation is impossible to the either reserved or exercised, the Department would not be entitled to rely on the latter part of section 12(1) merely because in the settlement the settlers purported to reserve the power of revocation.

It cannot be disputed that once a trust for a charitable purpose is created in a given case, the trust fund can grow and grow to a size much larger than what was endowed originally by the settlement in the given case. Donations may be given to the trust or immovable property may be gifted to the trust by persons who want their property to be utilized for the same purpose for which the trust is created. Whether the trust is in favour of an idol and is of a religious nature or whether the trust is intended to achieve charitable purposes would in that context be wholly irrelevant. The real question is whether in such a case, it would be permissible for a settlor to revoke the trust so as to undo the trust itself and thus affect not only the trust property settled by him but certain other properties also which may have been endowed in favour of the trust or dedicated to that charity. There is no express provision of law permitting this to be done. On first principles, permitting such a power to be exercised by the settlor would open the floodgates of a device which would enable people to use the creation of the trust as a means for getting back larger property than what was originally settled as trust property.

There is unanimity in the view that in the case of a charitable endowment or trust once the dedication is completed there is no power of revocation left with the settlers. Even though in a given case the settlor has reserved the power to revoke the trust, such a reservation would be wholly invalid and the power cannot be invoked so as to undo the settlement.

Apart from the general principle that in the case of a public trust, where dedication is complete, a power of revocation does not vest in the settlor, in so far as the instant trust was concerned there could not be any ground which could be wholly irrelevant because there were overriding provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act under which a public trust was not being given effect to, the Charity Commissioner could step in and see that the trust funds were applied to a charitable purpose. It was, therefore, clear that the so-called power of revocation was wholly redundant and ineffective. If the power of revocation was redundant and ineffective and indeed wholly invalid the mere reservation of a power by a clause in the trust deed could not attract the applicability of the provisions of section 12(1).

Under section 41(1) of the 1922 Act, the income of properties receivable by the enumerated persons for the benefit of others is liable to be assessed to tax in their hands in the like manner and to the same amount as it would be leviable upon and recoverable from the person or persons on whose behalf such income is receivable. This section centres on the basic fact that the person in whose hands the income is assessable shall be entitled to receive the same on behalf of any person; if he is not so entitled, the provisions of the section cannot be invoked. So, it was contended that, as the properties vested in the managing trustee and he received the income in his own right and not on behalf of the beneficiaries, though for their benefit, the said income in the hands of the managing trustee fell outside the scope of section 41 of the 1922 Act.

There were two answers to that contention. The doctrine of vesting is not germane to that contention. In some of the enumerated persons in the section the property vests and in others it does not vest, but they only manage the property. In general law the property does not vest in a receiver or manager but it vests in a trustee, but both trustees and receivers are included in section 41 of the 1922 Act. The common thread that passes through all of them is that they function legally or factually for others: they manage the property for the benefit of others. That the technical doctrine of vesting is not imported in the section is apparent from the fact that a trustee appointed under a trust deed is brought under the section though legally the property vests in him. In the case of a Muslim wakf the property vests in the Almighty; even so the mutawallis are brought under the section. A reasonable interpretation of the section is that all the categories of persons mentioned therein are deemed to receive the income on behalf of another person or persons or manage the same for his or their benefit. None of them has any beneficial interest in the income; he collects the income for the benefit of others. In that view, even if the nattamaigars were trustees in whom the properties of the Durgha vested, they should be deemed to have received the income only on behalf of the kasupangudars in definite shares.

The nattamaigars were only the managers of the properties in which the Durgha and the kasupangudars had beneficial interests. The properties did not vest in them. They receive the income therefrom on behalf of both of them. In terms of section 41 of the 1922 Act the nattamaigars were the managers of the properties on behalf of others and were entitled to receive the income therefrom on behalf of them. With the result, the income which they held on behalf of the kasupangudars could be assessed only in their hands in the manner prescribed thereunder.

What vested in the nattamaigars was not the properties of the Durgha but the management and administration thereof. It was therefore, held that the scheme did not vest the properties of the Durgha in the nattamaigars .

In the result, it was held that the High Court was right in holding that section 41 of the 1922 Act applied to the assessee. The appeals failed and were dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The only possible view was that the liability incurred by the company was not the lesser amount but the whole amount and if that be the position, then the Department was justified in withholding full deduction.

The finding of the High Court in the earlier reference relating to the assessment of the managing agents was that the managing agents were not compelled under the provisions of any, agreement to give up the amount but it was voluntarily given up by them. That being the position, it was extremely difficult to see how that amount which was voluntarily given up by the managing agents and received as such by the company could be treated as receipt or income in the hands of the company.

Therefore, the assessee company was entitled to a deduction of the whole amount as managing agency remuneration and on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the payment made by the managing agents was not a revenue receipt of the assessee company and was not liable to income-tax.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

In the instant case, the material found during the course of survey operation clearly established the collection of money over and above the fee prescribed by the Government for admission of a student. Therefore, it was a clear case of sale of education by the assessee-society. Thus, the assessee could not be considered as a charitable institution under section 2(15 ). Therefore, the assessee was not eligible for exemption under section 11. [Para 9] Any income derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose, should not be included in the total income. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee was not holding any property under trust for charitable purpose. It was also not the case of the assessee that any income was derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose. Moreover, it was also not the case of the assessee that any income in the form of voluntary contributions was received with a specific direction to form part of the corpus of the society. The assessee-society was running educational institution and deriving income from such institution. The assessee had also collected money over and above the fees prescribed for admitting students under management quota. In other words, the educational institution was used as a tool/apparatus for collecting money over and above the fees prescribed. The assessee-society had no other source of income/receipt. The society owned the educational institution. The Legislature has visualized two situations. One is religious and another is charitable. Section 11 provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust for charitable and religious purpose. ‘Education’ falls within the definition of charitable purpose. Therefore, any income derived from property held under trust for charitable purpose and applied for education, is eligible for exemption under section 11. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee had not derived any income from any property held under trust. The only source of receipt was the education itself, i.e., from educational institution. [Para 11]

The next question that fell for consideration was whether the educational institution owned by the assessee-society would be regarded as a property held under trust by the society. Section 11 speaks of the property held under trust. The Legislature visualized two situations. One is income derived from the property held under trust and another is application of that income derived from the property held under trust for a charitable purpose. Therefore, there is a clear distinction between the property held under trust and the charitable activity. In the instant case, the assessee-society was carrying on charitable activity by establishing educational institution. Therefore, the charitable activity of the assessee was education. The income, if any, derived from the property held under the Trust and applied for the educational activity, would be construed as application of income for the purpose of charitable purpose. Therefore, the expenditure incurred in establishing the educational institution, namely, acquisition of land, construction of building, etc., are all application of income for charitable activity. If any income was generated in the course of educational activity, the said income would be construed as if it was generated in the course of carrying on the charitable activity. Therefore, such receipt/income received in the course of carrying on charitable activity was also eligible for exemption, provided the same was applied or set apart for educational purposes. However, such receipt/income cannot be construed as derived from property/business held under trust. Since such receipt/income is inevitable or consequential while carrying on the activity of education, such income also becomes eligible for exemption. The educational institution is an apparatus for carrying out the charitable activity. Therefore, the educational institution or charitable activity itself cannot be construed as the property held under trust. The establishment of an educational institution is an activity of charity. Therefore, by any stretch of imagination, the charitable activity, cannot be held as the property held under trust, even though the income/receipt incidental to such activity is eligible for exemption. However, the money collected over and above the prescribed fee for admitting students cannot be construed as income derived from/incidental to the activity of carrying on charitable activity. [Para 12]

It is a well-settled principle of law that a business held under a trust is also a property. Section 11(4) also makes it very clear that the property held under the trust includes a business undertaking. If the assessee-society runs a business incidental to the attainment of the object of the society and separate books of account are maintained by the assessee, the income derived from such business, shall be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust. The Apex Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/ 115 Taxman 126 considered the provisions of section 11(4A) and held that if the business income is derived from business held under the trust and the same is utilized by the institution for achieving object of the institution, then it could be said that such income is applied for charitable purpose. The assessee-society in question had no property or business whatsoever under trust. Moreover, it was not the claim of the assessee that any income was derived from the property or business held under trust. [Para 13]

In the instant case the J.K. Charitable Trust made the donations to both the petitioner-trusts with the specific direction that they would constitute part of the corpus of the donee-trust, and the petitioners accepted the donations subject to that condition. These donations were hence outside the purview of section 12(2) and could not themselves be deemed to be income from property held under trust within the meaning of section 11. Now, voluntary contributions to be of any use of section 11 or 12 must have money value; they will either be of money or money's worth in the shape of shares, securities, movable or immovable properties. If the legislative intent was to exempt income earned from property received by a trust in the form of voluntary contributions, there was no point in enacting section 12(1), because income from such property held by a trust would be income from property held under trust within the meaning of section 11 and 'would be liable to be delt with thereunder income from property held under trust exempt under section 11(1) only to the extent to which it is applied for charitable or religious purposes, except to the limited extent to which accumulation is permitted by that section. Reading section 12(1) to deal with the same kind of income, namely, income from property held under trust, would nullify the conditions and limitations placed by section 11, because under section 12(1) such income is unconditionally exempt from being included in the total income. This will create an impasse in the working of the Act. A construction which creates serious difficulties and anomalies in the working of inter-linked provisions of a statute is to be avoided.

The fact that section 12(1) is confined to voluntary contributions only does not advance the argument, because in the case of a charitable trust the constitution of its endowment or initial corpus is also from voluntary contributions. When a charitable or religious trust is created, the properties which constitute its initial corpus come by way of voluntary contributions from the settlors. The income of all such properties is already with in the purview of section 11.

The construction placed on section 12 is in consonance with the scheme underlying Chapter III. Sections 4(3)(i) and (ii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, exempted income from property of charitable and religious trusts without any restriction upon accumulation of income. The Act of 1961 engrafted restrictions upon accumulation of income. Section 11(1) granted exemption to such income as was actually applied or utilised for religious or charitable purposes. Accumulation was permitted to a limited extent on certain conditions. In order to prevent evasion by a trust of the restrictions upon accumulation, by instead of actually applying its income to religious or charitable purpose, it making a voluntary contribution of its income to other similar trusts, section 12(2) was enacted. Without it, a trust, by making voluntary contribution to a charitable or religious trust, could claim exemption under section 11(1) by saying that it had actually applied its income for religious and charitable purposes though that income remained accumulated in the hands of the receiving trust. The receiving trust, although accumulating the income so received would claim exemption under section 12(1) on the ground that it was derived from a voluntary contribution. To defeat this device for accumulating income, section 12(2) provided that contributions constituting income will be deemed to be income from property within the meaning of section 11, so that such contributions may become subject to the purview of section 11. The idea was to catch accumulations of income. Section 12(2) did not seek to convert a capital receipt into an income receipt. It has no application where what is received is, in its true nature and character, capital in the hands of the receiving trust. Sub-section (2) of section 12 speaks of contributions, and deems the contributions themselves to be income from property under section 11. In other words, what was income in the shape of voluntary contributions under section 12(1) is converted by sub-section (2) into income from property for purposes of section 11.

The contributions made by the J.K.Charitable Trust to the petitioner-trusts . formed part of the petitioners’ capital or corpus. They did not constitute income in the hands of the petitioners within the meaning of section 12(1). These contributions were not covered by section 12(2), and could not themselves be dealt with as if they were income from property held under trust for purposes of section 11. Of course, the income that the petitioners might earn or derived from the properties which constituted these contributions would be income from property held under trust and would be directly governed by section 11. The dividend income received by the petitioner-trust on the shares initially donated by the J.K. Charitable Trust to the petitioners would be governed by section 11.

In the result both the petitions succeed and were allowed. The ITO was directed not to include the value of the shares, etc., received by the petitioners by way of donations from the J.K. Charitable Trust as petitioners’ income, but to treat the dividend income as governed by section 11.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

A perusal of section 13 would indicate that if the assessee society has availed the services or purchased any object from any specified person contemplated in sub-clause (3) and paid to such specified person in excess of what may be paid reasonably for such service in open market, then excess would be disallowed. In other words, for example, if assessee society has availed the services of an Engineer who happened to be a specified person under sub-clause (3) and paid him the service charges which he could not command in the open market, then such excess amount will be disallowed to the assessee and benefit of Section 11 would not be available on such an amount. It will be taxable. For example, assessee can purchase an item for Rs.100 but from a specified person, it has purchased at Rs.120, then this excess Rs.20 will be added to the taxable income of the assessee and benefit of section 11 will not be available to the assessee Society. A perusal of the complete assessment order reveals that Assessing Officer has nowhere made analysis of the remuneration/ honorarium paid to the members of the Management Committee vis-à-vis their services utilized for the benefit of the Society. All the persons are qualified persons, they have devoted their time for managing the affairs of the Society and it has paid only honorarium, not regular salary. In other words, in assessment year 2015-16, a little higher amount is being incurred by the assessee because the member of the Management Committee has to travel outside India for inspection of a plane which was to be used in Aviation Wing of the Engineering College. The Assessing Officer has not examined this aspect as to how this type of facilities can be availed from the open market and the price of such services. He has simply narrated that these persons are gainfully implied in their other activities also and therefore, payment of honorarium to these persons is not in accordance with law. This cannot be a logic for denying the benefit to them. The intention of the section is not as such. It is the assessee who has to manage its affairs and to decide what is necessary for its functioning. The Assessing Officer can only examine whether excess is being paid or not, but he has not carried out any Investigation in that area. The Assessing Officer has not assigned any reason as to why he is departing from the principle of consistency where such honorarium has been allowed to these per sons. Similarly Traveling Expenses has been allowed to the assessee in earlier years. It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts . It may be broadly stated that what is received for loss of capital is a capital receipt: what is received as profit in a trading transaction is taxable income. But the difficulty arises in ascertaining whether what is received in a given case is compensation for loss of a source of income, or profit in a trading transaction. Cases on the borderline give rise to vexing problems. The Act contains no real definition of income; indeed it is a term not capable of a definition in terms of a general formula. Section 2(6C) of 1922 Act catalogues broadly certain categories of receipts which are included in income. It need hardly be said that the form in which the transaction which gives rise to income is clothed and the name which is given to it are irrelevant in assessing the exigibility of receipt arising from a transaction to tax. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. In the absence of a statutory rule, payment made by an employer in consideration of the employee releasing him from his obligations under a service or agency agreement or a payment made voluntarily as compensation for determination of right to office arises not out of employment, but from cessation of employment and may not generally constitute income chargeable under sections 10 and 12 of 1922 Act.

It was contended by the revenue that the assessees were established with profit motive because they were not rendering free services but were charging cess/fees for their services and, therefore, they were not established for charitable purposes. There was no merit in that contention. The cess/fees were charged by the assessees from the purchasers in the market area at the rate prescribed by the State Government for the purpose of carrying out the object of the Act. As held by the Apex Court in the cases of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Mfrs. Association [1980] 121 ITR 1/[1979] 2 Taxman 501 and DIT v. Bharat Diamond Bourse [2003] 259 ITR 280/ 126 Taxman 365 , where the dominant purpose of a trust/institution is charitable, incidentally if some profit is made and the said profit is used for charitable purposes, the said trust/institution does not cease to be established for charitable purposes. In the case of the assessees, the dominant object was to regulate procurement and supply of agricultural and some other produce and to meet the expenses required for achieving the said object, the Legislature has empowered the assessees to levy cess/fees. Moreover, surplus remaining in the market fund was ploughed back for carrying out the object for which those mandi samitis was established. Thus, the surplus remaining in the market fund was neither distributed nor accumulated as profit. In those circumstances, it could not be said that the assessees were established with profit motive so as to deny registration under section 12A/12AA. [Para 41]

It is pertinent to note that prior to 1-4-1984, the words used in section 2(15) were "advancement of any other object of general public utility not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit". By the Finance Act, 1983 with effect from 1-4-1984, the Legislature has omitted the words "not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit" from section 2(15 ). Thus, after 1-4-1984, even if there is some profit in the activity carried on by the trust/institution, so long as the dominant object is of general public utility, it cannot be said that said trust/institution is not established for charitable purposes. [Para 42]

The word ‘property’ in section 11 includes immovable and movable property like money, shares, securities, etc. Therefore, where a trust/institution fulfils all the conditions mentioned in section 12A/12AA, registration cannot be denied on the ground that some conditions of sections 11 and 12 are not fulfilled. Even after registration, unless the conditions set out in sections 11 and 13 are complied with, no benefit would be available to the registered trusts or institutions. Therefore, in the facts of the instant case, the decision of the Tribunal that the assessees, who had fulfilled all the conditions, were entitled to registration, could not be faulted. The contention of the revenue that the assessees were not registered as institution and, hence, not entitled to registration, was also without any merit, because there is no requirement under the Act that an institution constituted for advancement of any object of general public utility must be registered as a trust.
