No prayer was made in the said application to attach the offerings and emoluments paid to the trustees. Since the executing court rejected the application, the matter was carried in appeal before the District Court where also it met with the same fate. In the second appeal, it was urged that the decree was executable against the joint family property which had passed to the son of the deceased by survivorship and also under the pious obligation of the sons to pay the debts. A Division Bench of the Bombay High Court consisting of Kania, Actg. C.J., and Gajendrakadkar J. (as they then were) while confirming the conclusion of the lower courts considered the nature of the income of the deceased. The Division Bench in this behalf observed:

"………The character of the receipts must be determined according to all the circumstances of the case. The first thing to be noticed in this connection is that under the scheme the defendants and their heirs during their good conduct are to be trustees and managers. They could therefore be removed if the appointing authorities considered that they were guilty of misconduct. Secondly, the express words do not show that the office is hereditary. Again, under clause 6, the two-thirds share is not given to the trustees and managers for their own use. It is provided that 'out of the remaining income……….the temple expenses had to be defrayed and the managers had to maintain themselves'. It is, therefore, clear that the whole of the two-thirds in no event belongs to the trustees. The temple expenses have first to be defrayed…… We do not propose to determine the exact meaning of the words of these clauses, but read together they do not support the contention that this is a hereditary office with the right to receive the emoluments attached thereto as understood in Hindu law. It will again be noticed that under clause 11 the whole scheme may be altered by the District Court. That right of alteration does not reserve to the defendants and their heirs a right to be trustees and managers…….

The scheme framed by the District Court strongly lends support to the view taken by the learned district judge that the remuneration payable to the trustees or managers is for the service rendered by them and is their personal property……"

The appeal of the judgment-creditor was, therefore, dismissed. It is against this backdrop that we have to decide whether the Tribunal was right in reaching the conclusion that the payments made to the two hereditary trustees-cum-pujaris were not remuneration for the services rendered. In the ultimate analysis, it is the consideration of the payment which will determine the entire dispute between the assessee-trust and the revenue. According to the present scheme, the trustee-cum-pujaris were under obligation to render the following services:

(1)To maintain and administer the trust properties.

(2)To maintain regular accounts of all income and expenditure of the trust properties and get them audited.

(3)To submit the balance-sheet to the court and the Charity Commis sioner every year.

(4)To lease out the properties.

(5)To carry out the worship of the deity.

(6)To maintain proper system of worship.

(7)To see that the doors of the temple open and close at specified hours.

(8)To pay all taxes, rates, assessments and all costs, charges and expenses incidental to the administration and management of the trust properties.

(9)To keep the trust properties in proper repairs.

Under the scheme the assessee had only powers of management of the wakf estate and that these powers were limited in certain respects by the control of a committee of management. The recovery of the rent depends on the rights of the wakf estate, and on the assessee's performance of his duties of management as Mutawalli, and the amount of his remuneration did not depend either on the nature of the properties or assets which constitute the wakf estate, nor on the amount of the income derived therefrom by the wakf estate. If, as might possibly happen, the whole or a portion of the wakf property ceased to be represented by agricultural lands, it was clear that the remuneration fixed by article 15 of the scheme would not be affected.

Thus, the High Court was right in holding that, albeit the income received by the wakf estate was within the definition of agricultural income in section 2(1), the sums drawn therefrom as remuneration by the assessee were not agricultural income received by the assessee.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

The assessee was a registered society duly incorporated and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1862. The society was formed with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. The income which the assessee received in the form of tuition fee and other receipts could not have been received but for the organization and, therefore, the tuition fee and other receipts derived from other organizations was income derived from property held under trust. Such tuition fee and other receipts, received by the assessee were directly and substantially arising from the organization, which was the property held under the trust. The Assessing Officer's assertion that whatever property in the shape of office building, furniture, computer was simply an application of income was not sustainable. It is well-settled that property acquired by an organization from its own income is also a property held under trust. Thus, fixed assets and current assets held by the assessee as on 31-3-1999 and 31-3-2000 were properties held under trust. Further, the Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case vide order dated 15-12-2003 had held that department cannot guide a charitable institution as to how it should carry on its charity. It is sufficient compliance with the relevant provisions of law in case surplus of the institution is utilized into activities of the institution and does not find its way to the pocket of the persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity.

The educational institution being run by the assessee was for the general benefit of the public and not for the benefit of any class or section of the public, as (a ) the institution was duly recognized by HNB Garhwal University and strictly followed all procedures with regard to admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum as laid down by the university, and (b) the nominees of State Government, HNB University and AICTE (functioning under the Human Resources Ministry) were on the governing body of the society and, therefore, the assessee had no choice in matters of admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum. The institute, was, in fact, State Government managed.

It was also found that the working system of the assessee was as per the guidelines laid down by the University. In respect of fixing and charging fees from students, the society management had no powers. Fee was being charged from students strictly as specified and laid down by the University. The governing body of the society had no powers to workout the cost and thereafter to add on the element of overheads and profits. Therefore, there was no question of building huge margins of profits in the fees structure as conceived by the Assessing Officer.

From a plain reading of the main objects given in the Memorandum, it could very well be discerned that the society had been formed with the sole objective of imparting and spreading computer education. Further, the assessee-society was virtually Government managed. Therefore, the question of functioning like a commercial profit making institution was totally unfounded. Thus, the fees charged by the assessee was simply receipt in the hands of the society and not profit.

Further, the assessee was rendering services of education to the general public. Therefore, its activities clearly fell within the ambit of charitable purpose as defined under section 2(15). Charging of fees does not in anyway dilute the aspect of charitable purpose. It is the end use and spirit and objective which matters.

In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had not been able to appreciate the difference in the words 'charitable purposes' as are used in the Act and the word 'charity' as had been used by the Assessing Officer in his order. The word 'charity' as used in English language and recognized in English law, implies as an act motivated by pity and may require benevolence to manifest it. However, exemption under section 11 has been prescribed with reference to 'charitable purposes' and not 'charity'. The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act.

‘N’ was the karta of a joint Hindu family. The joint family properties included a building which had been set apart for use of pilgrims visiting the town. Subsequently the family properties were partitioned under a partition deed between ‘N’ and his adopted son, ‘R’ as also minor, ‘D’ the adopted some of his pre-deceased son. Under that partition the building in question was directed to be maintained by ‘N’ with the income from certain lands over which he had been given a life-interest. Later on N died. At the time of his death he was a partner in the firm having a 3/16th share in the profits and losses of the said firm. The accountable persons filed an estate duty return admitting a net dutiable estate including the share capital and the share of profit and interest of the deceased in the managing agency firm, but did not include the value of the share of the deceased in the goodwill of the said managing agency firm. It also did not include the value of the building. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty, however, proposed to value of building at Rs. 62,000 and 3/16th share in the goodwill of the firm and to include the same in the estate of the deceased. The accountable persons objected to this proposal and contended that the value of the building could not be included in the estate of the deceased because it had been set apart only for charitable purposes, with regard to the goodwill, it was contended that in the case of managing agency business, there was no goodwill at all, and that in fact the accountable persons had not obtained any amount from the firm towards the value of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the firm. The Assistant Controller, however, overruled these objections and held that the building was not a trust property and that it was owned by the deceased at the time of his death, and, therefore, its value was includible in the estate of the deceased. On the question of goodwill, the Assistant Controller held that the managing agency firm did possess goodwill and on the death of the deceased the accountable persons were entitled to 3/16th share in the goodwill of the business of the firm and as such a sum being the value of the 3/16th share had to be included in the estate of the deceased.

On appeal, the Appellate controller upheld the order of the assistant controller and reduced the value of the building.

On further appeal the Tribunal upheld the order of the Appellate Controller in respect of inclusion of value of building holding that a mere provision for the maintenance of the building by the deceased and thereafter by others could not amount to creation of a trust with reference to the building and that the exclusive use of the building from 1942 to 1958, for religious and charitable purposes did not amount to a permanent dedication of the building as a trust property. As regards the inclusion representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm, the Tribunal held that goodwill cannot be associated with the business of managing agency firm because the managing agency business is governed by the terms of the agreement between the managing agency firm and the company and the right of managing agency was more personal and could not pass on to a successor. The Tribunal also held that no share in the goodwill of the business passed to the accountable persons on the death of the deceased and that in any event no amount was actually paid to the accountable persons by way of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the business. In that view the Tribunal deleted the sum representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm.

Where a settlor creates a trust, it lies within his power to also make a provision as to the management of the trust property. It is perfectly permissible for a settlor to nominate any person as trustees for first trustees and where there were more than one trustee, a managing trustee. It is also within his power to regulate the appointment of trustees in future as well as the managing trustee. There is no prohibition in law if the settlor himself takes over the function of the managing trustee after the trust has come into being. When the settlor himself becomes a trustee or managing trustee a change undergoes in his capacity from one of an owner of property to that of trustee holding the trust property for the benefit of the beneficiaries or for the purpose of working out the directions in the deed of trust. If for such work, any remuneration is provided for by the terms of the trust deed, that would not, amount to the reservation of any interest for the purposes of section 12(1).

The Department was, therefore, not entitled to rely on clauses 6 and 19 to contend that there was reservation of interest of the trust property and, therefore, the value of Kale Bhawan was liable to be treated as a part of the dutiable estate.

There could hardly be any doubt that clause 23 of the trust deed was a repository of the express power of revocation which could be exercised after the period of 10 years from the date specified therein and if the trust could not function for any reason. It could not be held that merely because in the case of a public trust a power to revoke is reserved by the settlor, such property must be deemed to pass on the death of the settlor for the purposes of section 12(1). When section 12(1) refers to the reservation by the settlor of the right to exercise the power of revocation, it obviously presupposes that such a power of revocation can be validly and legally reserved by the settlor. In other words, even if the document of trust does contain a clause expressly reserving the power of revocation if in law such a power of revocation is impossible to the either reserved or exercised, the Department would not be entitled to rely on the latter part of section 12(1) merely because in the settlement the settlers purported to reserve the power of revocation.

It cannot be disputed that once a trust for a charitable purpose is created in a given case, the trust fund can grow and grow to a size much larger than what was endowed originally by the settlement in the given case. Donations may be given to the trust or immovable property may be gifted to the trust by persons who want their property to be utilized for the same purpose for which the trust is created. Whether the trust is in favour of an idol and is of a religious nature or whether the trust is intended to achieve charitable purposes would in that context be wholly irrelevant. The real question is whether in such a case, it would be permissible for a settlor to revoke the trust so as to undo the trust itself and thus affect not only the trust property settled by him but certain other properties also which may have been endowed in favour of the trust or dedicated to that charity. There is no express provision of law permitting this to be done. On first principles, permitting such a power to be exercised by the settlor would open the floodgates of a device which would enable people to use the creation of the trust as a means for getting back larger property than what was originally settled as trust property.

There is unanimity in the view that in the case of a charitable endowment or trust once the dedication is completed there is no power of revocation left with the settlers. Even though in a given case the settlor has reserved the power to revoke the trust, such a reservation would be wholly invalid and the power cannot be invoked so as to undo the settlement.

Apart from the general principle that in the case of a public trust, where dedication is complete, a power of revocation does not vest in the settlor, in so far as the instant trust was concerned there could not be any ground which could be wholly irrelevant because there were overriding provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act under which a public trust was not being given effect to, the Charity Commissioner could step in and see that the trust funds were applied to a charitable purpose. It was, therefore, clear that the so-called power of revocation was wholly redundant and ineffective. If the power of revocation was redundant and ineffective and indeed wholly invalid the mere reservation of a power by a clause in the trust deed could not attract the applicability of the provisions of section 12(1).

FACT: The petitioner, a horse breeding farm, was founded by a commanding officer of army by obtaining grant of certain lands from the Government. The management of the farm remained in the hands of the officer commanding, who worked as an honorary trustee. The income derived from agriculture, securities, and other sources was utilized to finance the breeding of horse; the main object of the institution was to provide remounts for the regiment and the improvement of horse breeding in India; the majority of the horses thus, bred were supplied to the Army Department on payment and stallions and brood mares were also imported; and any stock found unsustainable as remounts were sold publicly. The instrument of lease executed between the Government and the officer commanding, did not definite the purpose for which the lease of land was granted, but the lessee had to pay the yearly rent by way of land revenue and malikhan and all rates and cesses. The farm covered certain village, the residents of which cultivate lands as tenants to the assessee and the assessee also raised agricultural produce by cultivation. It was a custom among cultivators, especially where the produce was to be accounted for between the landlord and the tenants, that the agricultural produce was got weighed or measured through a separate agency, called Dharwais, who were paid at certain stipulated rates for the job. Instead of allowing each tenant to engage his own Dharwais independently of the assessee, the farm appointed this own Dharwais for the entire farm by selling out the monopoly or right of weighing by public auction. In return for the auction purchase price, the Dharwais were allowed to charge certain rates. The ITO held that the assessee was an association of individuals and that the property was not held for the advancement of an object of general public utility because the entire benefits went to the members of that particular regiment. He further held that the income from Dharat could not be regarded as exempt under section 2(1)(b) of the 1922 Act because it was not rent or revenue derived from land which was used or agricultural purposes and, therefore, he assessed the total income of the farm and levied a tax thereon accordingly. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the ITO.

HELD: In the instant case the person in receipt and control of the income was undoubtedly the officer commanding. Therefore, he was an assessee under the Act. ‘Dharat’ means weighing charges which in the instant case were levied by the assessee from the tenants of the land in addition to the rent which he received from them. It was admitted that they formed part of an agreement entered into with the tenants in that behalf. Section 2(1) of the 1922 Act defines agricultural income, which includes the performance by a cultivator, or receiver of rent in kind of any process ordinarily employed by a cultivator or receiver of rent-in-kind to render the produce raised or received by him fit to be taken to market. Accordingly, dharat income would clearly fall within the provision of this sub-clause and was, therefore, exempt from the provisions of the Act.

As regards the question whether the impugned income from the race meets and inter-venue betting was income from property or income from business it would be difficult to accept that the assessee was conducting a business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter- venue betting on two or three occasions in a year. Even if the receipts did not constitute the corpus, there was certainly no quid pro quo in the arrangement between the assessee and the HRC as the asses- see was getting, from the said race meets and inter-venue betting, on almost certain profit from the HRC at practically no risk or cost to itself. The assessee had obtained a licence from the Government to conduct the races and inter-venue betting on the basis of a letter from the HRC. This licence itself could be treated as property and such property was obtained with the consent of the settlor-club and was contemplated even at the inception of the assessee-trust. Since the expression ‘property’ has the widest import for income-tax purposes, the impugned income would be income from property held under trust.

Alternatively. even if the impugned income was not income from property, it could only be treated as a voluntary contribution given by the HRC to the assessee. Though the form of such contribution indicated that the assessee itself had to conduct the races, the actual conduct was done by the HRC on behalf of the assessee merely as a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contribution did not have the character of income but was a capital receipt. The facts of the case did not justify the inference that the assessee-trust was in business for conducting horse races. It had neither the horses nor organisation nor any other equipment for that purpose. Consequently, since the impugned income was not income from business, the question of applicability of section 13(1)(bb ) did not arise.

For the foregoing reasons, the assessee-trust was an institution which satisfied the conditions of section 2(15) read with section 11. Since the ITO had not considered the requirements of accumulation, if there had been such accumulation, or application of sections 12, 12A and 13, the assessments were set aside for consideration of these aspects.

Under section 41(1) of the 1922 Act, the income of properties receivable by the enumerated persons for the benefit of others is liable to be assessed to tax in their hands in the like manner and to the same amount as it would be leviable upon and recoverable from the person or persons on whose behalf such income is receivable. This section centres on the basic fact that the person in whose hands the income is assessable shall be entitled to receive the same on behalf of any person; if he is not so entitled, the provisions of the section cannot be invoked. So, it was contended that, as the properties vested in the managing trustee and he received the income in his own right and not on behalf of the beneficiaries, though for their benefit, the said income in the hands of the managing trustee fell outside the scope of section 41 of the 1922 Act.

There were two answers to that contention. The doctrine of vesting is not germane to that contention. In some of the enumerated persons in the section the property vests and in others it does not vest, but they only manage the property. In general law the property does not vest in a receiver or manager but it vests in a trustee, but both trustees and receivers are included in section 41 of the 1922 Act. The common thread that passes through all of them is that they function legally or factually for others: they manage the property for the benefit of others. That the technical doctrine of vesting is not imported in the section is apparent from the fact that a trustee appointed under a trust deed is brought under the section though legally the property vests in him. In the case of a Muslim wakf the property vests in the Almighty; even so the mutawallis are brought under the section. A reasonable interpretation of the section is that all the categories of persons mentioned therein are deemed to receive the income on behalf of another person or persons or manage the same for his or their benefit. None of them has any beneficial interest in the income; he collects the income for the benefit of others. In that view, even if the nattamaigars were trustees in whom the properties of the Durgha vested, they should be deemed to have received the income only on behalf of the kasupangudars in definite shares.

The nattamaigars were only the managers of the properties in which the Durgha and the kasupangudars had beneficial interests. The properties did not vest in them. They receive the income therefrom on behalf of both of them. In terms of section 41 of the 1922 Act the nattamaigars were the managers of the properties on behalf of others and were entitled to receive the income therefrom on behalf of them. With the result, the income which they held on behalf of the kasupangudars could be assessed only in their hands in the manner prescribed thereunder.

What vested in the nattamaigars was not the properties of the Durgha but the management and administration thereof. It was therefore, held that the scheme did not vest the properties of the Durgha in the nattamaigars .

In the result, it was held that the High Court was right in holding that section 41 of the 1922 Act applied to the assessee. The appeals failed and were dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The assessee trust was constituted under a trust deed dated 27-8-1963. As per the trust deed, the objects of the trust, were relief of the poor, advancement of education, medical relief, promotion of science, art and of literature and any other object of general public utility for the benefit of the public. The powers of the trustees, as per the deed, included power to hold any business undertaking upon trust and to administer and manage the same. Clause(5) of the deed provided that after paying all costs and expenses, the trustees would utilise the net income of the trust for aforesaid charitable objects or purposes at such time or times and in such manner and on such proportions as the trustees might in their discretion think fit. During the relevant assessment years the assessee had earned commission as area managers of a company, but did not show the income in its return on the ground that the income earned was not liable to income-tax as the same had been derived from a business undertaking held under trust for charitable purposes, and had been applied to such purposes in India in terms of section 2(15) and section 11. The ITO, however, did not agree with the assessee and assessed the income derived by the assessee from its business activity. The AAC allowed the appeals and held that the assessee was entitled to exemption from income-tax under section 2(15) and 11.

On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order of the AAC and restored that of the ITO holding that the business undertaking carried on by the assessee was one of the objects of the trust, and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 2(15), read with section 11.

Maharaja of Darbhanga created a public religious trust on 16-03-1949 in favour of certain deities endowing certain properties with himself as the sole trustee. The trust deed provided for trustee's remuneration at the rate of fifteen per cent of the income from the trust properties. On 5-10-1950, the assessee executed a deed of relinquishment stipulating that as the net income from trust properties was not sufficient for puja path, bhog of the deities and for proper repair of the temples and as he was anxious to maintain the deities and the temple property, his remuneration should be distributed proportionately amongst the beneficiary deities. On 3-11-1959 the trust properties vested in the State by virtue of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. Section 24(3) of the said Act provided that in the case of a charitable or religious trust, without any reservation of pecuniary benefit to any individual, the compensation payable for such vesting would be a perpetual annuity equal to the net income of the trust estate. Accordingly, the net income of the trust estate continued to be paid to the assessee as the sole trustee.

The ITO sought to assess the remuneration in the hands of the assessee, being the trustee, in the assessment years 1959-60, 1960-61 and 1961-62. The assessee contended that the same was not assessable in his hands on the grounds, viz., ( i) that he had relinquished his right to receive remuneration by the deed dated 5-10-1950; and (ii) that, after vesting of the properties in the State, only net income was being received which did not admit of further deduction towards trustee's remuneration. Relying on the Tribunal's decision for the earlier year 1957-58, the ITO rejected these contentions and assessed the remuneration in the assessee's hands. Both the AAC and the Tribunal rejected the assessee's appeal on the ground (i ) that there was no statutory bar to payment of such remuneration to a trustee; and (ii) that the said Act, in fact, provided for payment of remuneration not exceeding fifteen per cent of the net trust income.

The natural corollary that followed was that the income derived from such transactions could not be called an income from the business. Assuming that it was a business as contemplated under section 2(13), the same was exempted under section 11. Further, the submission that the income would be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust could not also be disbelieved. [Para 12] The licence to run races and betting itself could be treated as property and the said property was obtained with the consent of the Hyderabad Race Club. The term ‘property’ itself has got widest import for income-tax purposes and inclusive of holding a licence. But, it is not every case of business which can be treated as property. If it were to be so treated, section 13(1)(bb) would lose its meaning. It may be that a business itself may be settled in trust of the trustees who may conduct a business on their own under the powers given to them in the trust deed. In the instant case, it was difficult to accept that the assessee-trust was conducting the business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter-venue betting for few occasions in a year. Thus, there could not be any doubt that the income derived by the trust for the relevant assessment years was from the property held under trust and as such it was exempted under section 11.

Assuming even if it was not treated as income from the property held under the trust, it could be treated as voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee-trust as contemplated under section 12. The conduct of the Hyderabad Race Club in respect of the transaction was only a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contributions could be characterized only as a capital receipt in the assessee’s hands. Thus, it could not be held that there had been business in the normal sense in such arrangement and in the facts and circumstances, it was not such a business which would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). It was only an activity which could constitute the property or an arrangement involved in transfer of funds from Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee’s institution in a form recognized by law and not shown to be colourable exercise or otherwise as contended by the revenue. Since it could not be said to be a business and the income derived could not be said to be a business income, the provisions of section 13(1)(bb) were not attracted. The assessee-trust was an institution, which satisfied the conditions under section 2(15), read with section 11 and as such, conclusion reached by the Tribunal should be upheld. [Para 13]

None of the objects of the trust could be said to be non-charitable in nature. Rather the objects of the trust were purely of a charitable nature. The main objects of the trust were advancement and propagation of education, medical aid and relief to the poor. In fact, promotion of sports and games was also one of the charitable objects. Merely because a discretion was vested in the trustees to utilize the income for any one or more of the objects would not make any difference. Since there was no payment of club’s funds to the trust, there was no scope for the retrieval of the funds of the race club from the assessee-trust. Thus, it satisfied the test that the objects of the trust were not only charitable in nature, but also of general public utility and as such, attracted the provisions of section 11 and, therefore, the income derived by the trust was exempted under section 11. [Para 14]

Thus, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the assessee was an institution which satisfied the conditions of section 2(15), read with section 11 and the derived income was from the property held under the trust and even otherwise, it could only be treated as a voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club and it could not be said that the activities carried on by the assessee constituted a business and even if it were to be a business, it was not such a business as would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01 - Assessee-society was formed, inter alia, with main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard - It was duly registered under Societies Registration Act, 1860 - It was also registered under section 12A - Assessee claimed exemption under section 11 - Assessing Officer denied exemption holding that, assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return, and, thus, it was earning profit and not doing any charity - However, it was found from records that assessee was duly recognised by HNB Garhwal University and strictly following university regulations with regard to admission charging of fees and course curriculum and had on its governing body nominee of State Government, HNB University and AICTE functioning under Human Resources Ministry and, thus, in fact Government managed and moreover, any surplus arising to society was utilized into activities of society and did not find its way to pocket of persons who were running society/institution - Whether, in view of said facts, it could be said that assessee was not a profit making institution and it was rendering services of education to general public and was eligible for exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-society was formed, inter alia, with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. It was duly registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. It was also registered under section 12A. For the relevant assessment years 1999-2000 and 2000-01, the assessee claimed exemption under section 11. The Assessing Officer denied the exemption holding that the assessee was not deriving any income out of the property held under trust, and that the income of the assessee was from fee charged from the students on account of tuition fee and other charges and whatever property had been acquired subsequently was as a result of application of this income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessee was a registered society duly incorporated and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1862. The society was formed with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. The income which the assessee received in the form of tuition fee and other receipts could not have been received but for the organization and, therefore, the tuition fee and other receipts derived from other organizations was income derived from property held under trust. Such tuition fee and other receipts, received by the assessee were directly and substantially arising from the organization, which was the property held under the trust. The Assessing Officer's assertion that whatever property in the shape of office building, furniture, computer was simply an application of income was not sustainable. It is well-settled that property acquired by an organization from its own income is also a property held under trust. Thus, fixed assets and current assets held by the assessee as on 31-3-1999 and 31-3-2000 were properties held under trust. Further, the Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case vide order dated 15-12-2003 had held that department cannot guide a charitable institution as to how it should carry on its charity. It is sufficient compliance with the relevant provisions of law in case surplus of the institution is utilized into activities of the institution and does not find its way to the pocket of the persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity.

The respondent/assessee firm was under agreement appointed as the managing agent of a company. Under the agreement the assessee was entitled to receive from the managed company commission payable on sale price of all cotton yarn and cloth sold and on sale proceeds of all material yarn and fabrics manufactured from other fibres and sold by company and certain per centage on net profits from ginning or pressing operations. On 28-12-1950 the managed company passed a resolution modifying the terms of the managing agency agreement in regard to the commission and added a proviso that for the years 1950 and 1951 if the directors of the company having regard to the result of the working were of the opinion that a lesser remuneration than that given in the agreement should be paid to the managing agents then the directors would have the right, in their absolute discretion, to fix such lesser remuneration payable either by way of lump sum or at a reduced percentage rate. The said modification had been agreed to by the managing agents. The managed company, on 8-4-1951, resolved that the managing agents should be paid Rs. 1,00,000 less than the commission calculated at the rates mentioned in the original agreement and on 31-12-1950, an entry to that effect was made in the books of the company. The income-tax authorities held that entire sum of commission which the assessee was entitled under the original agreement, was taxable income having accrued as commission during previous year and that Rs. 1,00,000 was mere voluntary surrender which could not affect the taxability of whole amount of commission accruing to managing agents. On appeal, the Tribunal held that as a result of the agreement between the managing agents and the managed company the right of the managing agents to claim full remuneration, had been taken away as from 1-1-1950, and it was not a voluntary relinquishment on the part of the managing agents and, therefore, the amount of Rs. 1,00,000 out of the commission due according to the original agreement was not income in the hands of the managing agents which was liable to taxation. On reference, the High Court agreed with the view taken by the Tribunal.

In the instant case, the material found during the course of survey operation clearly established the collection of money over and above the fee prescribed by the Government for admission of a student. Therefore, it was a clear case of sale of education by the assessee-society. Thus, the assessee could not be considered as a charitable institution under section 2(15 ). [Para 9] Any income derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose, should not be included in the total income. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee was not holding any property under trust for charitable purpose. It was also not the case of the assessee that any income was derived from the property held under trust for charitable purpose. Moreover, it was also not the case of the assessee that any income in the form of voluntary contributions was received with a specific direction to form part of the corpus of the society. The assessee-society was running educational institution and deriving income from such institution. The assessee had also collected money over and above the fees prescribed for admitting students under management quota. In other words, the educational institution was used as a tool/apparatus for collecting money over and above the fees prescribed. The assessee-society had no other source of income/receipt. The society owned the educational institution. The Legislature has visualized two situations. One is religious and another is charitable. Section 11 provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust for charitable and religious purpose. ‘Education’ falls within the definition of charitable purpose. Therefore, any income derived from property held under trust for charitable purpose and applied for education, is eligible for exemption under section 11. In the instant case, admittedly, the assessee had not derived any income from any property held under trust. The only source of receipt was the education itself, i.e., from educational institution. [Para 11]

The next question that fell for consideration was whether the educational institution owned by the assessee-society would be regarded as a property held under trust by the society. Section 11 speaks of the property held under trust. The Legislature visualized two situations. One is income derived from the property held under trust and another is application of that income derived from the property held under trust for a charitable purpose. Therefore, there is a clear distinction between the property held under trust and the charitable activity. In the instant case, the assessee-society was carrying on charitable activity by establishing educational institution. Therefore, the charitable activity of the assessee was education. The income, if any, derived from the property held under the Trust and applied for the educational activity, would be construed as application of income for the purpose of charitable purpose. Therefore, the expenditure incurred in establishing the educational institution, namely, acquisition of land, construction of building, etc., are all application of income for charitable activity. If any income was generated in the course of educational activity, the said income would be construed as if it was generated in the course of carrying on the charitable activity. Therefore, such receipt/income received in the course of carrying on charitable activity was also eligible for exemption, provided the same was applied or set apart for educational purposes. However, such receipt/income cannot be construed as derived from property/business held under trust. Since such receipt/income is inevitable or consequential while carrying on the activity of education, such income also becomes eligible for exemption. The educational institution is an apparatus for carrying out the charitable activity. Therefore, the educational institution or charitable activity itself cannot be construed as the property held under trust. The establishment of an educational institution is an activity of charity. Therefore, by any stretch of imagination, the charitable activity, cannot be held as the property held under trust, even though the income/receipt incidental to such activity is eligible for exemption. However, the money collected over and above the prescribed fee for admitting students cannot be construed as income derived from/incidental to the activity of carrying on charitable activity. [Para 12]

It is a well-settled principle of law that a business held under a trust is also a property. Section 11(4) also makes it very clear that the property held under the trust includes a business undertaking. If the assessee-society runs a business incidental to the attainment of the object of the society and separate books of account are maintained by the assessee, the income derived from such business, shall be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust. The Apex Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 247 ITR 785/ 115 Taxman 126 considered the provisions of section 11(4A) and held that if the business income is derived from business held under the trust and the same is utilized by the institution for achieving object of the institution, then it could be said that such income is applied for charitable purpose. The assessee-society in question had no property or business whatsoever under trust. Moreover, it was not the claim of the assessee that any income was derived from the property or business held under trust. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from properties held under - Assessment year 1956-57 - By an indenture of trust, ‘D’ and his wife both doctors, settled upon trust an immovable property and two maternity hospitals which were run by them - Primary object of trust was to carry on and promote educational, health, cultural, social and economic interest of people particularly of backward and lower classes - Substance of indenture of trust itself was that all trust properties were transferred by both settlers to trustees and trustees made declaration that they would hold properties for objects of trust from date of deed - One of recitals clearly indicated that it was business of conducting two maternity homes that had been settled upon trust, because net annual income which was to accrue to trust from said hospitals to be arrived at after deducting all expenses for maintaining and running hospitals and after making payment to ‘D,’ s wife as provided in trust deed for managing said hospitals for and on behalf of trust during her lifetime - Whether as trust deed was duly registered it was sufficient in law to effect a valid transfer - Held, yes - Whether since business of running and conducting maternity homes itself was settled upon trust, conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act were fulfilled and, hence income from maternity homes was exempt from taxation - Held, yes - Whether for conducting maternity hospitals presence of a doctor was essential and therefore, amount paid to wife of ‘D’ was a part of normal expenditure of conducting and managing said hospitals which was allowable as admissible deduction in computation of income of trust in hands of trustees as association of persons - Held, yes

FACT: By an indenture of trust dated 23-8-1954, one ‘D’ and his wife settled upon trust two maternity hospitals which were run by them and an immovable property for the purposes and objects contained in the said deed of trust. The assessee were the trustees under the said trust. The primary object of the trust was to carry on and promote the educational, health, cultural, literary, social and economic interests of the people, particularly of the backward and poorer classes. The important recitals in the trust deed were to the effect that the net annual income from the said hospitals, after deducting all the expenses for maintaining and running the hospitals including a sum of Rs. 750 per month which should be paid regularly to ‘D’s wife for managing the said hospitals for and on behalf of the trust during her lifetime, should accrue to the trust from year to year and that Dr. Divekar and Dr. Nalini Divekar did transfer the above said property and both the hospitals to the Trustees. And that the monies and properties of the trust were to be applied, firstly in payment of the expenses of carrying out of the trust and then in carrying out the other objects. The assessee claimed exemption under section 43(1)(i) of the 1922 Act. Even though the ITO accepted that the business in maternity homes was property within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act, he however took the view that its income was not exempt under the said section because it did not fulfil the requirements of proviso (b) thereto. This view was arrived at by him because he took the view that the primary purpose in conducting or running the two maternity homes or hospitals was not to give free medical facilities but charge the patients and then to apply the income for certain objects. Even the amount paid to D’s wife claimed as a deduction was disallowed by the ITO on the ground that the same was paid by the association of persons to one of its own members.

On appeal, the AAC held that the income from the trust was exempt under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and that the salary paid was an allowable deduction in computation of the assessees’ income.

On revenue’s further appeal, the Tribunal took the view that there was no actual transfer of immovable properties to the trustees if regard be had to the language employed in the document. On the assumption that the properties were considered to have been managed on behalf of a charitable institution the Tribunal took the view that the conditions laid down in proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) were not satisfied in the case and the income was, therefore, not exempt from tax.

It, however, affirmed the finding of the AAC that salary to ‘D’s wife was an allowable deduction.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Whether an amount paid as solatium for cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt - Held, yes - Assessee company under an agreement had been appointed as managing agents by 'M' mills for a period of 20 years - After about two years, assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs - Whether amount paid by 'M' mills to assessee for surrendering its rights as managing agents was a capital receipt, not assessable as business income of assessee - Held, yes

FACT: The 'M' mills had appointed company 'H' as its managing agents for several years, and on 28-6-1943, a new managing agency agreement was entered into between the mills and company 'H'. This agreement was transferred by a deed of transfer to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944. On 3-4-1946, the assessee surrendered its rights as managing agents of the company for a sum of Rs. 25 lakhs. The taxing department treated this receipt as income and brought it to tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the aforesaid payment was not taxable as income of the assessee.

On reference :

HELD: Looking at the agreement, it was clear that it was a composite agreement and it was not a simple agreement which, one often comes across of a company appointing some one as its managing agents. In other words, this was not a simple managing agency agreement. This was an agreement under which Company 'H' was appointed managing agents and as such certain rights, conferred upon them and, therefore, this agreement deals with the integrated rights which were conferred upon the managing agents. The agreement casted an obligation upon the managed company to employ only the managing agents as muccadums and brokers. It was a right which belonged to the managing agents under this agreement not only to act as managing agents of the company but also to act as muccadums and brokers. Therefore, it was clear on a true construction of this agreement that the 'M' mills appointed company 'H' as the managing agents and in that capacity company 'H' were given further rights as muccadums and brokers and selling agents. It was not open to the mills to deprive the managing agents of the right as muccadums and brokers or selling agents, nor was it permissible to the managing agents to continue as muccadums and brokers and selling agents if they ceased to be managing agents. Thereafter, the rights of 'H' were transferred to the assessee-company on 21-7-1944 and a deed of transfer was executed. The Act fortunately or unfortunately is not concerned with moral considerations. It is only concerned with finding out what is the income of a person and subjecting that income to tax, and if the assessee succeeded in satisfying that this sum of Rs. 25,00,000 was not income, it must be held that the Tribunal was right in coming to the conclusion that it did that this amount was not liable to tax.

The amount had been paid by the 'M' Mills to the assessee in order to bring about a cessation of the assessee-company's business as managing agents, and it is well settled that an amount paid as solatium for the cessation of a business activity constitutes a capital receipt and not income receipt.

The source of income is the congeries of rights conferred upon the assessee under the deed and those rights must be looked upon as integrated rights. It was by reason of the fact that the assessee enjoyed the status or office of the managing agents that these other rights were conferred upon it and one could not look upon these rights as separate and distinct as constituting separate and distinct sources.

The managing agency was productive of profit or income and as such it must be looked upon as a capital asset, one among others, which the assessee possessed for the purpose of carrying on his business under this agreement. It is either one of the rights or a part of the source or one of the capital assets in the business of the assessee. Which ever way one looked at it, the sum of Rs. 25,00,000 must be referable to a capital asset.

Concurring view

[Per Cunliffe, J.] The maxim in equity which considers as done that which ought to be done is almost invariably applied to cases in which some default or fraud has taken place for which reason the assistance of the Court is asked. The whole of this transaction could be regarded as being nothing more or less than executory trust. The deposit of the draft so-called trust deed was in law a direction to create an executory trust. Executory trusts are exceedingly common in the United Kingdom. The directions to create them are usually found in wills and marriage settlements and often covenants to settle after acquired property have been confirmed. Where too, the creator of the trust nominates himself as a trustee for the cesti que trust, the Courts have always looked generously upon the intention of the declaration. It is quite true that covenants to settle usually only effect corpus and not income, but effect has been given where a plain intention is shown to trusts with income alone; for trusts and legal estates are governed by the same rules. It is quite true that a voluntary covenant to create a trust is not enforceable, but if the whole of the circumstances of the instant case, were examined, it would be seen that there was a valid contract between the Government and the assessee enforceable in law from which this voluntary trust sprang and the true test was whether, on the whole construction of the letters passing between the parties and also of the draft trust deed, there was an intention to give third parties immediate equitable rights. That test was fulfilled.

The Commissioner, however, contended that any question of a trust in India is controlled by the provisions of the Indian Trusts Act of 1882. That was quite true if the trust in question did not happen to be a charitable trust. But the preamble to that Act has been interpreted to exclude all charitable trusts from the operation of the statute. The arrangement in question came well within the definition of a charitable trust.

It was true that the assessee having regard to his covenant with the Chief Secretary received his salary and his position in a fiduciary capacity alone, but as that salary was not income derived from property held on trust he could not be considered as able to obtain the benefit of exemption. It was with reluctance that this assessment was upheld.

[Per Pratt, CJ]

Under the circumstances, it was clear that the money was the personal income of the assessee and only became trust money, if at all, when paid into the separate account for the purposes of the boat club.

The exemption set forth in sub-section (3)(i ) of section 4 of the 1922 Act had no application since the emoluments in question were not income derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes.

The position would have been different had he accepted the office on condition that he should draw no salary. It was open to him to accept the appointment without pay, and to leave the University with liberty to devote the emoluments, which would ordinarily be paid to a Lecturer and Professor to charitable purposes, if they thought fit.

He made no such agreement.

He could not, therefore, claim as of right exemption from income-tax with respect to a portion of his income, which he devoted to charitable purposes under an agreement with the Local Government, even if he had created a trust with respect thereto.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The AAC allowed the appeals and held that the assessee was entitled to exemption from income-tax under section 2(15) and 11.

On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal set aside the order of the AAC and restored that of the ITO holding that the business undertaking carried on by the assessee was one of the objects of the trust, and, therefore, the assessee was not entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 2(15), read with section 11.

HELD: In AddI. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1980] 121 ITR 1 (SC) it has been held by the Supreme Court that if the dominant or primary purpose of the assessee trust was charitable, the subsidiary objects would not militate against its charitable character and the purpose of the assessee would not be any the less charitable. It is not necessary that the accomplishment of the object or the means to carry out the object should not involve an activity for profit.

As laid down by the Supreme Court an activity involved in carrying out charitable purpose must not be motivated by a profit objective but it must be undertaken for the purpose of advancement or carrying out the charitable purposes. It would not be correct to draw invariably an inference that whenever an activity is carried on which yields profit, the activity must be deemed to be for profit and the charitable purpose involves a carrying on of activity for profit. In other words, the object must be of general public utility, that is, it must not involve the carrying on of any activity for profit, but if for advancement of that object it becomes necessary to carry on any activity for profit, such an activity could not detract from the charitable purpose. That the Legislature did not intend to debar a trust created for charitable purpose from holding property under trust including a business undertaking is clearly borne out by the language of section 11(4) which lays down that for the purpose of this section property held under trust includes a business undertaking so held. Thus, taking into consideration the provisions of section 11(4), it is clear that a business undertaking can be held for charitable purpose but the object of the trust must not be the carrying on of any activity for profit.

In the instant case, the question as to what were the object of the trust was to be decided on the interpretation of the various clauses of the trust deed itself.

In the instant case the J.K. Charitable Trust made the donations to both the petitioner-trusts with the specific direction that they would constitute part of the corpus of the donee-trust, and the petitioners accepted the donations subject to that condition. These donations were hence outside the purview of section 12(2) and could not themselves be deemed to be income from property held under trust within the meaning of section 11. Now, voluntary contributions to be of any use of section 11 or 12 must have money value; they will either be of money or money's worth in the shape of shares, securities, movable or immovable properties. If the legislative intent was to exempt income earned from property received by a trust in the form of voluntary contributions, there was no point in enacting section 12(1), because income from such property held by a trust would be income from property held under trust within the meaning of section 11 and 'would be liable to be delt with thereunder income from property held under trust exempt under section 11(1) only to the extent to which it is applied for charitable or religious purposes, except to the limited extent to which accumulation is permitted by that section. Reading section 12(1) to deal with the same kind of income, namely, income from property held under trust, would nullify the conditions and limitations placed by section 11, because under section 12(1) such income is unconditionally exempt from being included in the total income. This will create an impasse in the working of the Act. A construction which creates serious difficulties and anomalies in the working of inter-linked provisions of a statute is to be avoided.

The fact that section 12(1) is confined to voluntary contributions only does not advance the argument, because in the case of a charitable trust the constitution of its endowment or initial corpus is also from voluntary contributions. When a charitable or religious trust is created, the properties which constitute its initial corpus come by way of voluntary contributions from the settlors. The income of all such properties is already with in the purview of section 11.

The construction placed on section 12 is in consonance with the scheme underlying Chapter III. Sections 4(3)(i) and (ii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, exempted income from property of charitable and religious trusts without any restriction upon accumulation of income. The Act of 1961 engrafted restrictions upon accumulation of income. Section 11(1) granted exemption to such income as was actually applied or utilised for religious or charitable purposes. Accumulation was permitted to a limited extent on certain conditions. In order to prevent evasion by a trust of the restrictions upon accumulation, by instead of actually applying its income to religious or charitable purpose, it making a voluntary contribution of its income to other similar trusts, section 12(2) was enacted. Without it, a trust, by making voluntary contribution to a charitable or religious trust, could claim exemption under section 11(1) by saying that it had actually applied its income for religious and charitable purposes though that income remained accumulated in the hands of the receiving trust. The receiving trust, although accumulating the income so received would claim exemption under section 12(1) on the ground that it was derived from a voluntary contribution. To defeat this device for accumulating income, section 12(2) provided that contributions constituting income will be deemed to be income from property within the meaning of section 11, so that such contributions may become subject to the purview of section 11. The idea was to catch accumulations of income. Section 12(2) did not seek to convert a capital receipt into an income receipt. It has no application where what is received is, in its true nature and character, capital in the hands of the receiving trust. Sub-section (2) of section 12 speaks of contributions, and deems the contributions themselves to be income from property under section 11. In other words, what was income in the shape of voluntary contributions under section 12(1) is converted by sub-section (2) into income from property for purposes of section 11.

The contributions made by the J.K.Charitable Trust to the petitioner-trusts . formed part of the petitioners’ capital or corpus. They did not constitute income in the hands of the petitioners within the meaning of section 12(1). These contributions were not covered by section 12(2), and could not themselves be dealt with as if they were income from property held under trust for purposes of section 11. Of course, the income that the petitioners might earn or derived from the properties which constituted these contributions would be income from property held under trust and would be directly governed by section 11. The dividend income received by the petitioner-trust on the shares initially donated by the J.K. Charitable Trust to the petitioners would be governed by section 11.

In the result both the petitions succeed and were allowed. The ITO was directed not to include the value of the shares, etc., received by the petitioners by way of donations from the J.K. Charitable Trust as petitioners’ income, but to treat the dividend income as governed by section 11.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

It would be irrelevant in considering the true nature of the transaction, to project the somewhat legalistic consideration that a managing agency is not transferable. It is because it is not directly transferable, that the arrangement incorporated in the agreement was effected. It would be difficult to regard such a transaction relating to a managing agency as a trading transaction. Whether a particular receipt is capital or income from business, has frequently engaged the attention of the courts . It may be broadly stated that what is received for loss of capital is a capital receipt: what is received as profit in a trading transaction is taxable income. But the difficulty arises in ascertaining whether what is received in a given case is compensation for loss of a source of income, or profit in a trading transaction. Cases on the borderline give rise to vexing problems. The Act contains no real definition of income; indeed it is a term not capable of a definition in terms of a general formula. Section 2(6C) of 1922 Act catalogues broadly certain categories of receipts which are included in income. It is again not predicated that the income must necessarily have a recurrent quality. On reference : HELD: As regards the point regarding material before Tribunal for finding that payment by the company any to the firm was not collusive, it is well-settled that the apparent state of affairs is to be presumed to be real until the contrary is shown. It is equally well settled that good faith and the genuineness of a transaction are also to be presumed until the contrary is proved. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.

A partnership firm was formed by four brothers. No deed of partnership was said to have been executed in respect of this firm. The firm was appointed the chief agent an insurance company as from 1-9-1950. On 17-2-1951, the aforesaid brothers executed a declaration of trust whereby they declared that they and all persons thereafter becoming the trustees would hold the said business of the chief agency of the said company and all the benefits and profits to arise from the said business upon trust for public charitable purposes. The said declaration of trust was registered with the Registrar of Assurances.

The assessee claimed that as from 17-2-1951, the income from agency business should be assessed in the hands of the trustees and should be allowed exemption under section 4(3)(i). The ITO, however, made the assessment in the status of an unregistered firm. The ITO held that there was no charitable trust created by the deed dated 17-2-1951. On appeal, the AAC reversed the findings of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that there was no proper and valid contract between the insurance company and the trustees as such; that the letter of appointment was only a service agreement; that there had been no transfer of property to the trustees wholly for charitable purposes; that the alleged transfer of the agency agreement did not amount to the transfer of property. The Tribunal also held that before the income of a trust for charitable purposes was exempt from tax, it must satisfy the conditions laid down in section 4(3)(i), i.e., and in the instant case the business not being carried on the course of carrying out the primary purpose of the trust, the income was not exempt form liability to pay tax.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Three different amounts for three different purposes and an immovable property was settled on assessee-trust - It was provided in trust deed that income, profits and interest from one of aforesaid amounts and premises were to be utilised for maintenance, up-keep and improvement of aforesaid premises - It was also mentioned in trust deed that trustees had power to amalgamate such contributions or donations either with corpus or income, profits and interest income of trust premises or trust - Income received from aforesaid premises, which became surplus after meeting maintenance expenses, etc., was to be spent for charitable purposes described under trust deed - Whether such expenditure on charitable purposes out of income from trust premises was exempt under section 11 - Held, yes.

FACT: The assessee-trust was created by a deed and the settlor settled three different amounts for three different purposes together with an immovable property known as N. Hall. Under clause 3(a) of trust deed it was the income, interest and profits of the trust premises and the sum of Rs. 12,000, being a portion of the trust funds, would be used for the maintenance and upkeep of the trust premises including the said N. Hall and for ordinary and extra-ordinary repairs to the same and for improvement and betterment of the said trust premises. There was a proviso to clause 3(a) in which it was mentioned as to what would happen if the income of the said Hall was insufficient for the above purpose. It was mentioned in the said proviso that if the said Income, interest, profits and rents were insufficient for any of the purposes mentioned in clause 3(a), the trustees would have power to use the corpus of the said sum of Rs. 12,000 or use the income, interest and profits of the sum of Rs. 38,000 which was a portion of the trust fund. This sum of Rs. 38,000 had been settled separately on trust in clause 3(c) of the trust deed. Another sum which was settled on trust was Rs. 10,000 which had been referred to in clause 3(b) of the trust deed. The said clause laid down that the income, interest and profits of the said sum of Rs. 10,000 would be used for the upkeep and maintenance of educational institutions. There was a proviso in clause 3(b) which laid down as to what would happen if income, interest and profits be insufficient for meeting the expenses of the said educational institutions. It was laid down therein that the trustees would have power to use the corpus of the said sum of Rs. 10,000 or to use the income, interest and profits of the said sum of Rs. 38,000 [which had been settled separately in clause 3(c)]. The sum of Rs. 38,000 settled under clause 3(c) was in the first place to be applied for meeting the deficit which might arise under clauses 3(a) and 3(b) and the surplus was to be used for charitable purposes. It was also provided under the trust deed that the trustees had the power to amalgamate such contributions or donations either with the corpus or the income, profits and interest of the trust premises or the trust. The trustees were also empowered to amalgamate into one of the trust funds allocated for various purposes. In the relevant assessment year the assessee incurred certain expenditure towards charitable purposes mentioned in the trust deed and claimed exemption under section 11. The ITO disallowed it on the ground that the income of the assessee was mainly from N. Hall and this could have been spent only on the maintenance or up-keep of the aforesaid premises as described in the deed and, therefore, as the same had not been spent for the object of trust, the same was not to be exempted. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals), however, allowed the assessee’s claim, holding that reading all the clauses together, there was no prohibition in the trust deed for the utilisation of the income from the Hall for charitable purposes other than for the maintenance and upkeep and for improvement and betterment of the trust premises as provided in clause 3(a) ; consequently, it could not be said that the said expenditure had not been incurred by the assessee In accordance with the provisions of the trust deed. He, therefore, deleted the said disallowance and directed the ITO to allow deduction of the said amount in computing the total income.
