There were two groups of partners who constituted the managing agency firm BK. The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

Section  11, read with section  13, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust –Exemption of income from property held under (Violation of section 13(1)(c)) - Assessment years  2014-15 and 2015-16 - Assessee, a charitable trust registered under Societies Registration Act, engaged in imparting education, was denied exemption under section 11 on ground that it had paid honorarium and incurred travel expenses in favour of Chairperson, Vice Chairperson and other trustees in violation of section 13(1)(c) - Assessing Officer alleged that such payments were not in accordance with charitable objectives and treated entire income as taxable - Whether Assessing Officer had nowhere made any analysis of remuneration/ honorarium paid to members of Management Committee vis-à-vis their services utilized for benefit of Society - Held, yes - Whether further, Assessing Officer had not assigned any reason as to why he was departing from principle of consistency where such honorarium and traveling expenses had been allowed in earlier years - Whether therefore, disallowance made by Assessing Officer was not justified - Held, yes [Para 12.1][In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was a Charitable Trust imparting education. It was registered under Societies Registration Act. The assessee had filed its return of income declaring 'nil' income for assessment years 2014-15 and 2015-16 respectively.

■

The case of the assessee for both the years was selected for scrutiny assessment and notices under section 143(2) were issued.

■

The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee had violated section 13(1)(c) read with section 13(3) by making payments of honorarium to the Chairperson, Vice Chairperson, General Secretary, Finance Secretary of the assessee trust. He had also observed that assessee had provided travelling facility to these persons and, therefore, this was not part of its objectives. He thus harboured the belief that assessee was not acting for charitable objective, hence not entitled for benefit of section 11.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) did not bring any relief to the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

If scheme of Section 11 is being perused, then it would reveal that income derived from the property held under the Trust wholly for charitable or religious purpose, if applied to the extent of 85 per cent on its objectives, then such income will not fall in the total income assessable of an assessee. In other words, if Rs.100 is being derived from the property held under the Trust and Rs.85 is being applied towards the charitable objective of the Trust, then nothing will be taxable upon such a ‘Charitable Society’ or Trust. However, section 13 has contemplated certain exceptions. [Para 12]

■

made whether any portion of the income arising from the settled properties or from properties otherwise transferred is includible in the total income of the charitable or religious trust. If it is found by keeping in view the provisions of sections 60 to 63 that it is not so includible, then such income does not qualify for any relief in limine under this section. It shall have to be discarded altogether in the calculation of 15 per cent of the income eligible of being accumulated. [Para 36] In the instant cases, there was no doubt that the object of the market committees established under the U.P. Krishi Mandi Utpadan Adhiniyam, 1964 was to regulate the entire marketing of agricultural and some other produce from the stage of procuring till it reached the ultimate consumer, which was squarely covered within the meaning of the expression "advancement of any object of general public utility" contained in section 2(15). [Para 40]

It was contended by the revenue that the assessees were established with profit motive because they were not rendering free services but were charging cess/fees for their services and, therefore, they were not established for charitable purposes. There was no merit in that contention. The cess/fees were charged by the assessees from the purchasers in the market area at the rate prescribed by the State Government for the purpose of carrying out the object of the Act. As held by the Apex Court in the cases of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Mfrs. Association [1980] 121 ITR 1/[1979] 2 Taxman 501 and DIT v. Bharat Diamond Bourse [2003] 259 ITR 280/ 126 Taxman 365 , where the dominant purpose of a trust/institution is charitable, incidentally if some profit is made and the said profit is used for charitable purposes, the said trust/institution does not cease to be established for charitable purposes. In the case of the assessees, the dominant object was to regulate procurement and supply of agricultural and some other produce and to meet the expenses required for achieving the said object, the Legislature has empowered the assessees to levy cess/fees. Moreover, surplus remaining in the market fund was ploughed back for carrying out the object for which those mandi samitis was established. Thus, the surplus remaining in the market fund was neither distributed nor accumulated as profit. In those circumstances, it could not be said that the assessees were established with profit motive so as to deny registration under section 12A/12AA. [Para 41]

It is pertinent to note that prior to 1-4-1984, the words used in section 2(15) were "advancement of any other object of general public utility not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit". By the Finance Act, 1983 with effect from 1-4-1984, the Legislature has omitted the words "not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit" from section 2(15 ). Thus, after 1-4-1984, even if there is some profit in the activity carried on by the trust/institution, so long as the dominant object is of general public utility, it cannot be said that said trust/institution is not established for charitable purposes. [Para 42]

It was contended by the revenue that even if the assessees were covered under section 12A, they would still not be entitled to exemption because their income was neither derived from the property held under trust nor their income was from voluntary contributions made to the institution. There was no merit in that contention because the expression ‘property’ used in section 11 is of wide amplitude and it includes the business undertaking itself. The word ‘property’ in section 11 includes immovable and movable property like money, shares, securities, etc. Therefore, where a trust/institution fulfils all the conditions mentioned in section 12A/12AA, registration cannot be denied on the ground that some conditions of sections 11 and 12 are not fulfilled. Even after registration, unless the conditions set out in sections 11 and 13 are complied with, no benefit would be available to the registered trusts or institutions. Therefore, in the facts of the instant case, the decision of the Tribunal that the assessees, who had fulfilled all the conditions, were entitled to registration, could not be faulted. The contention of the revenue that the assessees were not registered as institution and, hence, not entitled to registration, was also without any merit, because there is no requirement under the Act that an institution constituted for advancement of any object of general public utility must be registered as a trust. [Para 44]

When such activity was done by the trustees, then it was quite clear, that the business so done was the business of the trust and once it was the business of the trust business itself would be the property held under trust. So far as the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64, were concerned, the very words of clause 2(j) make it apparent that the object of carrying on the business of manufacturing and marketing the products by using the patents and inventions was to make profit so as to raise funds for the fulfilment of the aims and objects of the trust. If that was so, such an activity could not be regarded as a charitable purpose in view of the definition of that expression in section 2(15) of the 1961 Act. As under section 11(1) of the 1961 as it then existed, only income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes has to be excluded from computation of total income of the previous year, the trustees could not be able to get the benefit of this provision for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64, because, the carrying on of the business was an activity for profit.

Note: The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee and partly in favour of the revenue.

rental income from the property earned by the assessee during the assessment years in question cannot also be sustained, the same having suffered tax in the hands of the late Nizam. Accordingly it was held that, on the facts and circumstances of the case, the rent received by the trust from the property during the assessment years 1971-72 and 1972-73, except for one month, could not be assessed under the head "Income from other sources" or under any other head. Further deed of trust specifically provided for payment of remuneration to the trustees, not exceeding Rs. 15,000 per annum for the services expected of and rendered by them. The remuneration paid to the trustees, therefore, constituted an overriding title in respect of that part of the income of the trust. In other words, the Income of the trust liable to tax in the hands of the trustees was ascertainable only after deducting from the total income of the trust, the remuneration payable to the trustees. The remuneration payable to the trustees was not different in character from the payments required to be made to the beneficiaries in terms of the trust. The amounts for remuneration paid to the trustee, therefore, constituted deductible expenditure from the income of the trust.

The Tribunal allowed 5 per cent of the total receipts of income by the trust towards expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively for earning the income under section 57. Section 19(i) also permitted deduction of a reasonable sum expended by the trustees for the purpose of realising interest on securities. Interest on securities also formed part of the income of the trust. The Tribunal, however, lost sight of the same. 7½ per cent of the net receipts of the income of the trust after deducting from its total income the remuneration paid to the trustees constitutes reasonable expenditure for administering the trust under sections 57(i ) and 19(i).

HEADNOTE: I. Section  11,  read with section  12,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  341,  read with section  335  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Charitable or religious trust  -  Exemption of income from property held under (Rental income)  - Assessment year  2013-14  - Assessee, a charitable trust claimed exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Assessing Officer denied exemption by treating assessee as an AOP on ground that assessee had earned substantial rental income by leasing its immovable properties which amounted to a commercial activity inconsistent with its charitable character - It was noted that trust deed contained a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon Board of Trustees - It was also noted that trustees were merely authorised to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with funds of trust for effectuating charitable objects of trust - Furthermore, Income and Expenditure Account demonstrated that receipts of trust, whether derived from grants, donations, interest or rental income, were applied only towards charitable objects of trust - Whether thus, income derived from property held under trust, including rental income, did not lose benefit of exemption under section 11 and section 12 merely because such income arises from leasing of trust property, so long as it is applied towards charitable purposes for which trust has been established - Held, yes - Whether since leasing of trust property was only an incidental mode of augmenting resources to fulfil charitable objects, same could not be construed as an independent commercial object of trust and assessee could not be denied exemption under sections 11 and 12 - Held, yes [Para 8.6] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a charitable trust claimed exemption under sections 11 and 12.

■

The Assessing Officer denied exemption by treating the assessee as an Association of Persons (AOP) on ground that assessee had earned substantial rental income by leasing its immovable properties which amounted to a commercial activity inconsistent with its charitable character.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the assessee’s claim on ground that the Assessing Officer had not brought cogent material to show that the assessee’s activities ceased to be charitable.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: (i) Rental income and leasing of properties

■

The principal basis adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) for allowing the assessee's claim is the observation that one of the objects of the trust was to lease out properties and earn rental income. However, on a careful examination of the original trust deed as well as the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the Tribunal finds that the observation is factually incorrect and contrary to the material available on record. The original trust deed, enumerates the charitable objects of the trust, namely: (i) genetic research and agricultural education; (ii) conservation of land, water and genetic resources; (iii) sustainable agriculture and environmental protection; (iv) family planning and population control; and (v) improvement of the status and literacy of women. Subsequently, by way of the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the additional charitable objects of Relief to the Poor and Education were incorporated. Significantly, neither the original trust deed nor the addendum includes, as an object of the trust, carrying on the activity of leasing or renting of immovable properties for earning rental income. [Para 8.2]

■

What is, however, contained in the trust deed is a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon the Board of Trustees. Clause VIII merely authorises the trustees to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with the funds of the trust for effectuating the charitable objects of the trust. Such an enabling clause cannot be elevated to the status of an independent charitable object. The power to acquire and manage trust properties is only incidental to the effective administration of the trust and to facilitate the attainment of its charitable purposes. Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that leasing of properties itself constituted one of the objects of the trust is clearly erroneous and is not borne out from the trust deed. [Para 8.3]

■

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 10(1) , read with section 2(1A), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(viii), read with section 2(1), of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Agricultural income - Assessment year 1942-43 - Assessee company entered into a managing agency agreement with  another company which derived income from several sources, one of which being agriculture, and was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(viii) of 1922 Act - In terms of said agreement, assessee was to annually receive a fixed commission from principal company’s net profits subject to a minimum sum - During relevant year received commission and claimed exemption under section 4(3)(viii) of 1922 Act in respect of income that was attributable to agricultural income of principal company - Tribunal rejected assessee’s claim - Whether if in any given year there was no agricultural income, remuneration with a minimum sum would still have to be paid to assessee out of profits earned through other activities of principal company, and, therefore, said sum could not necessarily be connected with agricultural income of principal company - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, conclusion of Tribunal was correct - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a managing agent of another company and the terms and conditions of management were embodied in an agreement. In terms of clause 2 of the said agreement, the assessee annually received from the principal company a commission fixed at 10 per cent of the net profits of the principal company subject to a minimum of Rs. 10,000. The principal company derived its income from several sources, one of which was the manufacture of sugar. The cane that was used in the manufacture was partly grown on the company’s own farms and partly bought from outside. A part of the company’s income from that source, i.e., the part that was attributable to the manufacture from the cane grown on the company’s farms, was exempted from income-tax, under section 4(3)(viii) of the 1922 Act as agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1) of the 1922 Act. The assessee, during the relevant year, received from its managing agency commission and contended that a part of the managing agency commission that it received, i.e., such part calculated at 10 per cent of the agricultural income of the principal company, was also agricultural income in its own hands and exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(viii) of the 1922 Act. The ITO rejected the assessee’s claim and included the amount, subject to certain adjustments, in the assessee’s total income, computed for the purposes of the assessment. On appeal, the AAC also upheld the said inclusion. On further appeal, the Tribunal sustained the AAC’s view.

On reference :

HELD: Under the agreement the managing agents could be participators in profits, if they divided in a stated percentage an agreed fund. They could not be participators of the profits divisible amongst the shareholders constituted one fund and they got a percentage of a fund which was differently calculated and, therefore, in fact a different fund. The ten per cent, were not necessarily payable out of the profits. The annual net profits. The net profits were again, not what one ordinarily finds in the company's balance sheets. They are net profits only for the purpose of calculation, to be worked out strictly on the lines specifically mentioned in that clause. It was obvious that several deductions which are not permitted under the clause would be made in preparing the balance sheet and ascertaining the net profits of a commercial corporation. Moreover, the commission was not in any year to amount to a sum less than Rs. 10,000. Therefore, if in any year the company made no profits, the sum had to be paid by the principal company, even out of its capital. If in any given year there was no agricultural income, the remuneration, with a minimum of Rs. 10,000, will still have to be paid out of the profits earned through the other activities of the principal company. It was therefore clear that, on the face of this clause itself, there was nothing to connect it necessarily with the agricultural income of the principal company.

In the instant case, the managing agents would receive the remuneration irrespective of the nature of the business of the principal company. They were paid for their work as managing agents. The assets of the principal company were not vested in them. They were not the persons who could sue for amounts due to the principal company in their own name. They were only agents for management. It seemed therefore clear that, under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the balance of the agricultural income in the hands of the principal company was not to be divided between the principal agency and the managing agents in a stated proportion.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922] - Hindu undivided family - Assessable as - Assessment year 1939-40 - Assessee was karta of HUF - He entered into partnership representing beneficial interest of HUF - Said partnership firm purchased a mill - Later on, partnership firm promoted a company which took over said mill - Company so promoted, appointed partnership firm as its managing agent - Pursuant to said agreement, firm received managing agency commission from company time to time which was divided between partners thereof - During assessment year in question, assessee claimed that his share of managing agency commission belonged to him individually, and therefore, it could not be included in his assessment made as karta of HUF - Revenue authorities rejected assessee's claim - Whether since managing agency was acquired with assistance of HUF's property, i.e. mill in which assessee as karta was beneficially interested, income derived by him from managing agency was to be regarded as income of HUF of which he was karta - Held, yes

FACT: Three brothers formed a partnership, and HD held his share in this partnership as karta. In the year 1918 the three brothers and five other persons purchased a mill in partnership. HD held his share in this partnership also as karta of the joint family. In the year 1920 the three brothers and the five other persons promoted a company and took over the said mill. Two documents were executed. One of these was an agreement between the new company and the eight vendors, that is to say the three brothers and the five other persons, for the purchase of the mills. The three brothers received by way of consideration, 1,000 shares in the new company and a sum of cash, and each brother held his 33 1/3 shares as karta of his respective joint family. Pursuant to the agreement, the said firm received the managing agency commission from the company time to time which was divided between the partners thereof, and the firm consisting of the three undivided families duly received their shares of the commission. The share of each family in the commission had been shown for income-tax purposes in the return of income made by the karta of the respective joint family up to and including the assessment year 1938-39. For the first time however in the return for the year 1939-40 the assessee objected to the inclusion in his assessment made as the karta of the family of the shares of the managing agency commission on the ground that it belonged to him individually. The Income-tax Officer overruled assessee's contention. The assessee's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was unsuccessful.

On reference :

HELD: There was no doubt, that the opportunity of becoming and of being actually appointed managing agents arose directly from the asset which was sold to the new company, viz., the mills, which in part was joint family property.

It was provided by the articles of association of the new company that the firm, should be appointed managing agents, and that this arrangement was part and parcel of the arrangements, whereby the Mills, in which the assessee admittedly held a share as karta, were sold by the partnership to the new company. If the partners should sell or assign their right to remuneration, as per clause 14 of the managing agency agreement it could not be said that the portion of the proceeds of sale attributable to HD's share, did not pass to him as joint family property. The managing agency was derived from or acquired with the assistance of joint family property, that is to say, the mills in which HD as karta was beneficially interested.

Accordingly, share income received by 'HD' from managing agency was income of HUF of which he was karta.

Decision was in favour of revenue.

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with section 19 of Bombay Trust Act, 1950 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1964-65 to 1969-70, 1972-73 and 1973-74 - Lands of some villages were said to have been granted by one Mughal Emperor for upkeep of Roza in year 1670 under a Sanad and grants were confirmed by sanads issued during British regime - A suo motu enquiry was started under section 19 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 - As a result of that inquiry, Dy. Charity Commissioner made an order directing that assessee- Roza Trust be registered as a Public Trust - On appeal Charity Commissioner confirmed order of Dy. Charity Commissioner - He held that assessee-trust was a public trust and lands of villages were properties of said trust - Question for consideration was as to whether income from lands in question was income of assessee-Roza Trust assessable in hands of said trust and exempt under section 11 or whether it was assessable in hands of Sajjadanashin of Trust i.e., ‘SM’, as income from his private property - Tribunal on material before it, which included orders made by Dy. Charity Commissioner and Charity Commissioner, documents such as Sanad issued by Mughal Emperor and Sanads of Government, Survey Settlement register and historical account given in text-books, came to finding that these lands of four villages belonged to assessee-trust - Whether while it is true that tax authority, during assessment proceedings, can always inquire into question of ownership of property and decide issue in context of relevant provisions of said Act, in order to ascertain income of the assessee for bringing it to tax, it will not be open for tax authorities to ignore relevant evidence of statutory registration of a public trust and fact of the properties having been registered as properties of such public trust under provisions of Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 - Held, yes - Whether finding of Charity Commissioner in an inquiry 
under section 19 of Bombay Public Trust operates as findings in rem and cannot be ignored by authorities under Income-tax Act - Held, yes - Whether Sajjadanashin of Roza Trust was spiritual leader and integral part of Roza Trust and, therefore, provision for Sajjadanashin was not a provision for man but for institution and therefore, expenses incurred on 
 Sajjadanashin by assessee-trust could not be held to be expenses for private property - Held, yes - Whether Tribunal was justified in holding that income from lands in question was assessable in hands of assessee-trust and not in hands of Sajjadanashin and further that trust was entitled to exemption in respect of income spent as ‘Madad-E-Maash’ on maintenance of Sajjadanashin, his family and descendants - Held, yes - Whether amount received by Sajjadanashin was to be taxed as income in his hands - Held, yes

The assessee was a trustee of a trust. Under a clause of the trust-deed, one-third of the income of the trust was to be paid to the trustees as their remuneration. The trustees had, however, by a resolution given up their right to receive the remuneration and had resolved that, that part of the income of the trust be also spent on the charitable objects of the trust. The resolution was adopted several years prior to the accounting years relevant to the assessment years in question and the question of the taxability of remuneration had been agitated in some earlier years and it was held that the same was not taxable. On receipt of information, that it had been held in the case of another trustee that such remuneration was taxable, the Assessing Officer reopened the assessee’s assessment under section 147(a). On appeal, the AAC held that there was no failure on the part of the assessee to disclose the material facts which were already known to the department and, therefore, the assessment could not be reopened under section 147(a) and if, at all, a reassessment was necessary, it could be done only under section 147(b) for which the limitation had expired. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal had reversed the order of the AAC holding that the ITO was justified in initiating reassessment proceedings under section 147(a) and that the matter be restored to the AAC to decide on merits the question of includibility of the remuneration payable to the assessee as a trustee.

On reference :

atha business was earmarked for application of charitable objects would not render business itself being considered as incidental to attainment of objects of trust [CIT v. Mehta Charitable Prajnalay Trust [2012] 28 taxmann.com 73/[2013] 214 Taxman 88 (Delhi), SLP granted inMehta Charitable Prajnalaya Trust v. CIT [2017] 82 taxmann.com 149/248 Taxman 145 (SC)]. Exploitation rights - The right to exploit space on either side of an overbridge for advertisements is a "property" [A. J. Patel v. CIT [1974] 97 ITR 683 (Bom.)].

Religious offerings - Offerings received by a religious teacher from his disciples would not constitute "property held under trust" [Swami Narsingh Giri v. CIT [1971] 79 ITR 544 (All.)].

INCOME

Commercial sense - It is not the 'total income' as would be assessed by the ITO that is relevant for the purpose of investing the funds of the trust or assessing the income of the trust. Taking into account the purpose for which the conditions of section 11(1)(a) are imposed, it would be clear that 'income' to be considered will be that which is arrived at in the context of what is available in the hands of the assessee subject to an adjustment of any expenses extraneous to the trust [CIT v. P. S. G. & Sons Charities [1997] 223 ITR 831 (Mad.)].

Grants - Where assessee-society was acting as a nodal agency receiving grant from Government of India and State Governments and distributed to district authorities for implementation of various schemes of Government of India and supervising execution of schemes, grants received by assessee should not be considered either as income or for ascertaining amount expanded or amount to be accumulated [CIT v. State Urban Development Society [2011] 11 taxmann.com 458 (P&H)]. Also see, DIT v. Gujarat State Council for Blood Transfusion [2014] 41 taxmann.com 449/221 Taxman 126 (Guj.).

Legal expenses - Legal expenses incurred by a charitable institution for defending its president from criminal charges are allowable as a permissible deduction while computing its income [Ananda Marga Pracharaka Sangha v. CIT [1994] 76 Taxman 88 (Cal.)].

Refund of income-tax - Refund of income-tax can by no stretch of imagination be held as income derived from property held under the trust and, hence, will not be covered u/s 11(2) [CIT v. Hamdard Dawakhana (Wakf) [2002] 120 Taxman 186 (Delhi)].

Returned amounts - Only the income spent on charitable or religious purposes is excluded from the total income of the trust and when that amount is returned by the beneficiaries of the trust, the receipt in the hands of the trust can only be its income of the years in which it is received; it cannot have any different character [CIT v. Cutchi Memon Union [1985] 20 Taxman 386/155 ITR 51 (Kar.)].

Taxes - Payment of taxes under VDIS is to be deducted before arriving at commercial income of assessee-trust that is available for application to charitable purposes [DIT v. National Association of Software & Services Companies [2012] 21 taxmann.com 213/208 Taxman 178 (Delhi)].

APPLICATION OF INCOME

General - If section 11(1)(a) has been fully exploited and there is still accumulated income left to be dealt with, section 11(2) can be pressed in service and if it is complied with, such additional accumulated income beyond the prescribed percentage can also earn exemption u/s 11(2) [Addl. CIT v. A. L. N. Rao Charitable Trust [1995] 83 Taxman 252 (SC)].

'Applied' need not be equated with 'spent' - The word 'applied' does not necessarily mean 'spent'. Even if the amount has been earmarked for the purposes of the institution and allocated, it may be deemed to have been applied [CIT v. Radhaswami Satsang Sabha [1954] 25 ITR 472 (All.)].

Both revenue and capital expenditure are covered - As far as the objects of the trust are concerned, the application of the amount can be for revenue or capital purposes [CIT v. Kannika Parameswari Devasthanam & Charities [1982] 133 ITR 779 (Mad.)].

Deemed income - Deemed income (i.e., tax deducted at source) is not to be taken into account for determining the application of income [CIT v. Jayashree Charity Trust [1986] 159 ITR 280 (Cal.)].

Donation - Donation of sale proceeds of capital asset made by charitable trust to another trust was to be allowed as 'application of income' for charitable purpose [PCIT v. St. Joseph's Monastery [2022] 137 taxmann.com 133 (Kar.)].

HEADNOTE: Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1950-51 - Managing agents of assessee company decided to voluntarily forgo part of its remuneration - In matter of assessment of managing agents High Court held that amount voluntarily forgone by managing agents could not be allowed as revenue deduction and accordingly, taxed entire amount of remuneration in their hands - Whether liability incurred by assessee company was not lesser amount but whole amount payable as remuneration and, hence, assessee was entitled to deduction of whole amount as managing agency remuneration - Held, yes

Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1950-51 - Whether on facts under head 'Business expenditure - Allowability of' amount voluntarily given up by managing agents and received as such by assessee could not be treated as receipt or income in hands of assessee and, hence, was not liable to income-tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee owned a textile mill. Under the agreement of managing agency, the managing agents of the mill were entitled to a remuneration of certain sum. The managing agents agreed to forgo a part of their remuneration. In the matter of assessment of the managing agents the High Court held that the amount voluntarily forgone by the managing agents was not allowable as revenue expenditure and accordingly, the whole amount was taxed in the hands of the managing agents. In the matter of the assessment of the assessee-company, it had at first claimed deduction of the sum which had actually been paid to the managing agents. At the stage when the matter was pending before the AAC, the assessee claimed a deduction of the whole sum contending that that was the amount which they were liable to pay to the managing agents and that was the amount which had been brought to assessment in the hands of the managing agents. The matter was ultimately carried to the Tribunal and the Tribunal relying upon the judgment of the High Court held that the effect of the voluntary giving up of a part of the commission by the managing agents was that the liability had been incurred first and then there was a giving up of commission and the liability that had been incurred by the company was for the whole amount and that was the amount for which deduction should have been allowed.

On reference:

HELD: The only possible view was that the liability incurred by the company was not the lesser amount but the whole amount and if that be the position, then the Department was justified in withholding full deduction.

The finding of the High Court in the earlier reference relating to the assessment of the managing agents was that the managing agents were not compelled under the provisions of any, agreement to give up the amount but it was voluntarily given up by them. That being the position, it was extremely difficult to see how that amount which was voluntarily given up by the managing agents and received as such by the company could be treated as receipt or income in the hands of the company.

Therefore, the assessee company was entitled to a deduction of the whole amount as managing agency remuneration and on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the payment made by the managing agents was not a revenue receipt of the assessee company and was not liable to income-tax.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

G.N. Joshi and R.J. Joshi for the Applicant.

Kolah and N.A. Palkhivala for the Respondent.

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment years 1977-78 to 1979-80 - Assessee-trust was denied exemption under section 11 as it derived income from letting out its hall as Kalyana Mandapam and furniture, utensils and decorative items, etc., at commercial rates - Whether since objects of assessee-trust were education and other objects of general utility and letting out of Kalyana Mandapam was not one of objects of assessee but was only activity carried on to fulfil its objects and income therefrom was not its business income but property income, Tribunal was correct in holding that assessee was entitled to exemption under section 11 - Held, yes

Section 57,  read with section 256, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income from other sources - Deductions - Whether following decision in CIT v. Trustees of H.E.H. The Nizam's Miscellaneous Trust [1986] 160 ITR 253 (AP), the High Court was right in dismissing revenue's application under section 256(2) and holding that 7½ per cent of net receipts of income of trust after deducting from its total income remuneration paid to trustees, constituted reasonable expenditure for administering trust under sections 57(i) and 19(i) - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 2(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 2(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] – Agriculture income – Assessment year 1938-39 – Whether where income received by wakf estate was within definition of agricultural income in section 2(1) of 1922 Act, sums drawn therefrom as remuneration by assessee (mutawalli of wakf estate) could not be regarded as agricultural income received by assessee – Held, yes

FACT: The assessee the hereditary Mutawalli of a wakf estate, received remuneration under the scheme of management and claimed that the income thus, received by him was agriculture income and, therefore, same was exempt from taxation. The High Court rejected the assessee's claim.

On appeal to the Privy Council:

HELD: Under the scheme the assessee had only powers of management of the wakf estate and that these powers were limited in certain respects by the control of a committee of management. The recovery of the rent depends on the rights of the wakf estate, and on the assessee's performance of his duties of management as Mutawalli, and the amount of his remuneration did not depend either on the nature of the properties or assets which constitute the wakf estate, nor on the amount of the income derived therefrom by the wakf estate. If, as might possibly happen, the whole or a portion of the wakf property ceased to be represented by agricultural lands, it was clear that the remuneration fixed by article 15 of the scheme would not be affected.

Thus, the High Court was right in holding that, albeit the income received by the wakf estate was within the definition of agricultural income in section 2(1), the sums drawn therefrom as remuneration by the assessee were not agricultural income received by the assessee.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

On 24-10-1944, the settlor, executed a trust deed in respect of shares of certain company. The provisions of the trust deed were that the income from the trust property was to belong to him during his lifetime. On his death the income was to go to the wife if she survived him. By clause 1(b) of the trust deed, settler's wife was entitled to the net income 'during her lifetime without power of anticipation or alienation'. After the death of the survivor of the settlor and his wife, the net income was to go, after payment of certain remuneration to the trustees, to certain charitable trusts which the settlor had created previously for the maintenance of those trusts. If after the utilisation of the income from the trust properties for the benefit of those specified charitable trusts, any income was available, it was to be utilised for the maintenance of any nursing home, hospital or any institution for medical relief. The trust deed came to be modified on 15-7-1953, by which the settlor relinquished his entire life interest in the income from the trust properties.

After this relinquishment the income from the trust fund was continued to be paid to his wife until the death of settlor. No amount was paid to settler's wife after the death of the settlor.

On 20-5-1955, the wife of settler executed a deed whereby she in her turn relinquished and surrendered her life interest with a view to accelerating the subsequent trust in favour of charity.

In these circumstances the assessee trustees claimed that the income derived from the property had under trust was wholly for religious and charitable purpose and therefore clearly covered under provisions of section 4(3)(i) of the Act of 1922 and applied for refund. However the ITO observed that the interest for life allowed by the settlor to his wife, was of a restricted nature inasmuch as it was definitely laid down that she had no power to anticipate or alienate her interest, though she would be perfectly justified in refusing to become a beneficiary in her place. He therefore, he held that the declaration dated 25-5-1955 made by her was void and, as such, the income of the trust would, in law, revert to the executors/legal heirs of the settlor. Hence the refund applied for by the trustees was not in order as the properties were not held for charitable purpose. Accordingly he rejected the claim for refund which was upheld by the AAC. On further appeal the Tribunal held that after the deed of release and surrender dated 20-5-1955, the disposition in favour of charity came into operation and the income was thereafter received by the trustees who held the property under trust which was admittedly wholly for religious or charitable purposes within the meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

On reference:

Following the decision of the High Court in the case of CIT v. Madras Stock Exchange Ltd. [1976] 105 ITR 546, it was held that the object of the assessee did not involves carrying on of an activity for profit and, therefore, the objects of the assessee society constituted 'charitable purposes' as defined in section 2(15) entitling it to exemption under section 11.

As regards the applicability of section 28(iii), the underlying idea behind the said section is that there must be a business from which income is derived and that in the course of such business specific services must be rendered for its members. The concept behind section 28(iii) is to cut at the mutuality principle being relied on in support of a claim for exemption, when the assessee was actually deriving income or making profits as a result of rendering specific services for its members in a commercial way.

Section 2(24)(v) provides that income includes any sum chargeable to Income-tax under clause (iii) of section 28. The definition would apply so as to bring to tax the income as a business income, only if the income was not covered by any exemption available under the Act. Section 28(iii ) cannot be read in isolation, but has to be read with the other provisions of the Act. In the case of activity carried on by an entity like the present assessee, which, as it is now well settled exists for a charitable purpose, the impact of section 11 read with section 2(15) has to be taken into account. Wherever there is no activity designed for making profit it would not fall within the scope of this definition and the exemption under section 11 in its full force would apply. It was already seen that the instant was held to be brought within the scope of exemption from assessment, the question of taxing the income would arise if the profit-making activity was the means by which the object of public utility was sought to be achieved. This was not a case where the object of public utility was sought to be achieved by these activities. Therefore, the fact that there was income does not by itself solve the problem. The profit-making was only an incident and not the means of achieving the object of public utility. So long as the object was charitable and so long as the income was not earned from an activity which was by itself designed to achieve the object of general public utility, the exemption cannot be denied. As the facts show, the assessee was actually required by the Government to take up some of the activities as a result of which it had received certain amounts from the members. In such a case, it could not consider that there could be any scope for the view that there was any activity for profit. This view was reinforced by a reference to section 10(23A). Under Section 10(23A), there is an exclusion from assessment of the income falling under certain categories. One of the categories is income derived from rendering any specific services. It is true that this provision deals only with institutions or associations having as their object the control, supervision, regulation or encouragement of certain professions. But in the instant case the question was whether receipts in consideration of services are taxable. This provision is relevant to show that Parliament does not always conceive such receipts to be taxable and that such receipts may be exempt under certain conditions. It is not, therefore, enough if there are receipts. Such receipts must be considered in the context of all the provisions of the Act.

Section 11(4) provides that for the purpose of this section 'Property held under trust' includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, even if there is a business, which yields income, so long as the business is held under trust, its income would be exempt from tax. It was not suggested that the properties were held otherwise than under trust. Section 28(iii) would not apply, to tax income from such a business, as otherwise, the benefit sought to be conferred under section 11 would be destroyed, and the exemption provision would be stultified.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 28(1), read with section 15 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1), read with section 7 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1940-41 and 1941-42 - Assessee-firm was constituted with a view to float a company and obtain its managing agency - Accordingly a company was floated and assessee was given managing agency with right to receive monthly allowance, commission on sale and on profits of company - During relevant assessment years assessee-firm received income for working as managing agents as well as for working as sole agents of company - Assessee’s claimed that amount so received should be treated as salary and assessed under section 7 was rejected by ITO - Whether mere appointment as a managing agent or working as such would not necessarily make person a servant of company - Held, yes - Whether in case of a firm, which can be constituted only for purpose of sharing profits of a business, work of managing agency must be held to be business of firm - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, profits which assessee-firm earned from their business of working as managing agents of company must be held to be their profits or gains from business, profession or vocation assessable to tax under section 10 of 1922 Act and not as salary under section 7 of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-firm was constituted with a view to float a private limited company. In pursuance of the deed of partnership, a private company S was actually floated and the managing agency of the company was obtained by the assessee-firm. The appointment of the assessee-firm as managing agents of the company S carried with it the right to receive an allowance of Rs. 1,000, a month, a commission of 1 per cent on all sales of the company’s products and a commission varying from 5 to 10 per cent on the profits of the company for working as such.

Consequently during accounting years relevant to the assessment years 1940-41 and 1941-42, the assessee received certain amounts by way of remuneration and commission. In addition, during both these years, the assessee-firm worked as the sole selling agents of the company and received commission on sales of sugar and income under some other heads. The ITO assessed this entire income of the assessee-firm in each of the years as income from business under section 10. The contention of the assessee-firm that the income received by it for working as managing agents as well as for working as sole agents, should be treated as assessed under section 7 was rejected by the ITO. The appeals to the AAC and to the Tribunal were also dismissed.

On reference :

HELD: The definition of managing agent makes it clear that a managing agent need not necessarily be a servant of the company whose affairs are managed by that managing agent. All that is needed is that the managing agents should have an agreement with the company under which he receives the right of management of the affairs of the company though this management of affairs of the company is to be under the control and direction of the directors except to the extent, if any, otherwise provided for in the agreement. Such an agreement may be entered into between a person who is already a servant of the company or it may be entered into between the company and some person who may not be a servant of the company. The mere appointment as a managing agent or working as such would not necessarily make the person a servant of the company. Whenever any one works as a managing agent of a company, that person must be reimbursed in some form or other for the work done by him. In a case where a managing agent happens to be a servant of the company, the payment to him of his salary as servant may compensate the person for the whole work done by him as the managing agent and the servant of the company and no separate or additional remuneration may be provided for working as managing agent. On the other hand, if the managing agent does not happen to be a servant of the company, then the payment would be made, under the agreement, for the work done as managing agent and not as salary for services rendered by him as a servant. It thus appears to be clear that, under the Indian Companies Act, a managing agent may either be a servant of the company or a mere agent without being a servant.

SECTION 11 OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CHARITABLE OR RELIGIOUS 
TRUST-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDER TRUST-
WHETHER HANDING OVER OF ACCUMULATED INCOME TO ANOTHER CHARIT-
ABLE TRUST WOULD AMOUNT TO APPLICATION OF INCOME FOR CHARITABLE PURPOSES-HELD, YES

In the instant case the person in receipt and control of the income was undoubtedly the officer commanding. Therefore, he was an assessee under the Act. ‘Dharat’ means weighing charges which in the instant case were levied by the assessee from the tenants of the land in addition to the rent which he received from them. It was admitted that they formed part of an agreement entered into with the tenants in that behalf. Section 2(1) of the 1922 Act defines agricultural income, which includes the performance by a cultivator, or receiver of rent in kind of any process ordinarily employed by a cultivator or receiver of rent-in-kind to render the produce raised or received by him fit to be taken to market. Accordingly, dharat income would clearly fall within the provision of this sub-clause and was, therefore, exempt from the provisions of the Act.

In the instant case, in the year 1924 a huge sum of Rs. 1,74,518, was paid as bonus to the regiment. Similarly in the years 1929 and 1930 sums to the extent of Rs. 6,000 odd and Rs. 35,000 odd, respectively, were shown as unparticularised. In 1931, Rs. 23,113 appeared to have been spent on ‘farewell to the Commander-in-Chief’. In 1926 the Mess car account took away Rs. 2,944. In 1931, Rs. 698 had been spent on a wedding party. Those disbursements would not justify the conclusion that the property was held in trust wholly for charitable purposes, nor could it be said to be so held in part as that question had been finally set at rest by the pronouncement of their Lordships of the Privy Council in Muhammad Ebrahim Raza Malak v. CIT AIR 1930 PC 226.

Further, it was admitted that the element of discretion of the Officer Commanding, who operated on the Stud Farm Fund in making those disbursements, as he thought fit, was not altogether excluded. This would bring the farm within the mischief of the rule enunciated by Morice v. Durham [1805] 32 ER 947. However, benevolent or liberal the objects of a trust may be, so long as the trustee has any discretion left in the matter, the trust cannot be supported as a charitable legacy. The court was alive to the fat that most of the objects of the Stud Farm were no doubt charitable even within the technical sense of the term but so long as the trust was not given a legal shape, by eliminating the element of discretion vesting in the Officer Commanding, it would not be able to claim the benefit of the exemption provided for in the Act.

The trust had to fail as a charitable trust for want of certainty as to its objects and that defect could not be cured so long as the Officer Commanding insisted on his discretion in the matter.

For those reasons the income was not exempt from taxation within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

Note: The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee.

persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity. The educational institution being run by the assessee was for the general benefit of the public and not for the benefit of any class or section of the public, as (a ) the institution was duly recognized by HNB Garhwal University and strictly followed all procedures with regard to admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum as laid down by the university, and (b) the nominees of State Government, HNB University and AICTE (functioning under the Human Resources Ministry) were on the governing body of the society and, therefore, the assessee had no choice in matters of admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum. The institute, was, in fact, State Government managed.

It was also found that the working system of the assessee was as per the guidelines laid down by the University. In respect of fixing and charging fees from students, the society management had no powers. Fee was being charged from students strictly as specified and laid down by the University. The governing body of the society had no powers to workout the cost and thereafter to add on the element of overheads and profits. Therefore, there was no question of building huge margins of profits in the fees structure as conceived by the Assessing Officer.

From a plain reading of the main objects given in the Memorandum, it could very well be discerned that the society had been formed with the sole objective of imparting and spreading computer education. Further, the assessee-society was virtually Government managed. Therefore, the question of functioning like a commercial profit making institution was totally unfounded. Thus, the fees charged by the assessee was simply receipt in the hands of the society and not profit.

Further, the assessee was rendering services of education to the general public. Therefore, its activities clearly fell within the ambit of charitable purpose as defined under section 2(15). Charging of fees does not in anyway dilute the aspect of charitable purpose. It is the end use and spirit and objective which matters.

In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had not been able to appreciate the difference in the words 'charitable purposes' as are used in the Act and the word 'charity' as had been used by the Assessing Officer in his order. The word 'charity' as used in English language and recognized in English law, implies as an act motivated by pity and may require benevolence to manifest it. However, exemption under section 11 has been prescribed with reference to 'charitable purposes' and not 'charity'. The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act.

Therefore, the property from which income was derived by the assessee was held under trust and such property was held for charitable purpose and the income derived from trust was property which was being applied for charitable purpose. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

HEADNOTE: Section 4 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 3 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1952-53 - Assessee company was managing agents of various companies including one 'G', in which assessee held a large block of shares - In 1951, board of directors of 'G' decided to terminate agency against payment of certain amount to assessee - Whether termination of managing agency in question had resulted in destruction of source of in come of assessee and, thus, amount received by assessee was capital receipt - Held, yes

Section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 66 of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - High Court - Reference to - Assessment year 1952-53 - Whether neither High Court nor Supreme Court has jurisdiction to reappreciate material on record to find out whether facts found by Tribunal are correct or not - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was acting as a managing agents of various companies including one 'G'. The assessee acquired a large block of shares in 'G'. In 1950, 'G' was converted into a public company. Thereafter, the assessee was not entitled to any commission on sales, etc., in view of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as amended in 1939. Hence, a fresh agreement was entered into between the assessee and the 'G' on 10-5-1960, under which the assessee company was entitled to an office allowance of Rs. 5,000 per month and a commission of 10 per cent of the net profits. The Board of directors of the Managed Company had taken a decision to terminate the agency of managing company. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed-company approved the resolution of the board of directors on 31-3-1951. That meeting also recommended a payment of Rs. 18 lakhs to the assessee as compensation. That resolution was communicated to the assessee on 3-4-1951, and the latter accepted it on 10-4-1951. In the assessment for the assessment year 1952-53, the ITO included aforesaid amount in the total income of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC held that the amount in question represented compensation received by the assessee company for the termination of its managing agency. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the transactions, whereby the managing agency of the company was terminated were genuine and real business transactions, that managing agencies held by the assessee represented sources from which it received is income by way of commission and, therefore, the termination of managing agency would represent destruction of a source of income. As a consequence of those findings, the Tribunal held that the receipt in question was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipt. On reference, the High court held that all the proceedings relating to the termination of the managing agency of the company were not genuine transactions. It further came to the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee were its stock-in-trade, and, therefore, the amount paid by the managing company to the assessee must be considered as a revenue receipt.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: It was wholly impermissible fort the High Court to disturb the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal. The Tribunal was the final fact-finding authority. The facts found by it could have been challenged only on certain recognised grounds. Neither the High Court nor the Supreme court has jurisdiction to reappreciate the material on record to find out whether the facts found by the Tribunal are correct or not. The High Court should not have taken upon itself the responsibility to go into the question whether the findings of fact reached by the Tribunal were correct. The only question that the High Court was called upon to determine was whether, on the facts found by the Tribunal, the receipt in question should not have been considered by the Tribunal as revenue receipt.

if the trustees were to spend the entire income or the entire corpus on non-charitable object mentioned in clause 4(1)(iv ), they would not be committing any breach of the terms and conditions of the trust and such expenditure on their part would be perfectly valid and proper. In view of this position which obtained very clearly under the indenture dated 12-6-1959, it seemed very clear that the trust could not be regarded as a trust having been created wholly for charitable purposes. The contention of the assessee was that this sub-clause (iv) should be regarded, if it all, as incidental or ancillary object and since the main or dominant object of the deed was to do charity and since several other sub-clauses of clause 4 indicated what those charitable objects were, it should be held that notwithstanding sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) the trust should be regarded as one having been created wholly for charitable purposes. It was not possible to accept this submission of the assessee. In the first place, there was nothing to indicate in clause 4(1) of the deed that the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv) thereof was incidental or ancillary to other objects mentioned in the other sub-clauses of clause 4(1). Secondly, clause 4(2) in terms elevated the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv ) to the same level as the other objects mentioned in sub-clauses of clause 4(1), for, under sub-clause (2) of clause 4, the trustees had been given liberty to utilise the corpus of the trust property or any part thereof for any one or more of the objects mentioned earlier and in such proportion as they might in their absolute discretion think fit. At least while conferring such power upon the trustees some indication could have been given by the settlors if they wanted to regard sub-clause (iv) as incidental or ancillary, but nothing of the kind had been done. In other words, sub-clause (2) of clause 4 had conferred absolute discretion upon the trustees to spend the entire corpus of the trust property or any part thereof upon any one or more of the objects mentioned in sub-clause (1) of clause 4. Further, it was not possible to accept the contention that sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) provided for management expenses, such as remuneration payable to the employees of the trust and that normally the trustees would have incurred such expenditure on the employees during the course of management of the trust. In fact, clause 4(1) separately provided for expenses for management and maintenance of the trust property. In terms, clause 4(1) provided that the trustees would pay out of the rents, profits, interest, dividends and income all outgoings payable in respect of the trust property including all ground rent, rates, taxes and costs of repairs of any immovable property forming part of the trust property, premium for insurance or any other costs, charges, expenses and outgoings of and incidental to the management and maintenance of the trust property and execution of the trusts therein contained including the wages and salaries of employees and it is after payment of such outgoings and other expenses that the trustees had been directed to spend the income of the trust property over the objects which have been specified in sub-clauses (i) to (vi) of clause 4(1). In a way this independent provision for meeting the expenses of the management and maintenance of the trust property including wages and salaries of the employees on the contrary suggested that the settlors had in mind while incorporating sub-clause (iv) in clause 4(1) that it was an independent object of the trust for which the trustees were given liberty to spend the income of the trust property. Having regard to the above position which contained very clearly on reading of the deed of trust as a whole, it was difficult to accept the contention that sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) should either be regarded as not providing any object at all or as providing for an incidental or ancillary object. It was clear that the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv) was also one of the independent objects on which the trustees had been given power to spend the income of the property or even the entire corpus of the trust property by virtue of clause 4(2) of the deed and if that be so, it was clear that the trust in question could not be regarded as being one created wholly for the purpose of the charitable objects.

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) – Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under – Assessment years 1952-53 to 1955-56 – Claim of assessee trust for exemption of its income under section 4(3)(i) was rejected by ITO on ground that business of trust carried on by managing trustee on behalf of trust fell within proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) and hence its business income was not exempt from taxation – Whether where trust carries on business and business itself is held in trust and income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for purpose of religious or charitable character, conditions prescribed under section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and income is exempt from taxation - Held, yes – Whether claim of exemption cannot be denied even if business were to be conducted by someone else acting on behalf of trust, and proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to such businesses as are not held under trust and, therefore, field of its operation is distinct and separate from that covered by main provision of section 4(3)(i) – Held, yes - Whether in view of aforesaid legal position, assessee being a religious and charitable trust, was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act for assessment years in question – Held, yes

HEADNOTE: Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 10(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Business income - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1953-54 - Assessee was managing agent of company F - It entered into agreement with 'M' who agreed to purchase entire holding of shares of assessee in company - 'M' also agreed to compensate assessee for loss of office - Subsequently, assessee tendered its resignation and 'M' was appointed as managing agent of company - Accordingly, assessee received sum on account of compensation for loss of office - Whether, on facts, amount of compensation for loss of office - Whether, on facts, amount of compensation received by assessee to relinquish managing agency could not be regarded as revenue receipt and, thus, it was not liable to tax - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a managing agent of a company F. The assessee entered into an agreement with 'M' who agreed to purchase entire holding of shares of assessee in company and to procure that principal company 'M' also agreed to compensate the assessee for loss of office after it submitted its resignation.

Subsequently, the assessee tendered its resignation and 'M' was appointed as managing agent of the company. Accordingly, the assessee received sum on account of compensation for loss of office. In the proceedings for the relevant assessment year the ITO, included this amount in the assessee's taxable income. On appeal the AAC modified the assessment holding that the sum received by the assessee as compensation for surrendering the managing agency, which was to enure for five years more, and which in normal course might have continued for another term of twenty years, was a capital receipt. On further appeals Tribunal confirmed the order of the AAC. On appeal to the Supreme Court :

1. The trust was receiving income out of certain assets which had been endorsed to the deities. Even after the vesting of the assets to the State, the income from those assets continued to flow for the purposes of the trust. It was not a case of capital value of asset being paid in annual instalments but a case of payment of income from the assets, as envisaged in section 24(3 ) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act. The annuity, therefore, continued to have the character of income.

2. The deed of relinquishment clearly showed that the remuneration payable to the assessee shall, instead of being paid to him, be used in a particular manner as per directions contained in the trust deed. It was a clear case of diversion of income after it accrued to the assessee. There is no merit in the argument that since the State was paying only net income, the question of payment of fifteen per cent out of it to the trustee did not arise.

Bihar Land Reforms Act did not bar such payment out of annuity paid. The remuneration was, accordingly, assessable in the hands of the assessee.

The provision of section 11 uses two expressions : (1) "total income" and (2) "income derived from property held under trust". Total income is an expression defined in the Act in section 2(45) as meaning the total amount of income referred to in section 5, computed in the manner laid down in the Act. However, there is no definition of "income". The words "income" is an expression of elastic ambit and the courts have always qualified their description by saying that it is not exhaustive.

In the absence of any definition of income" one has to proceed on the basis of it as a concept, as understood in general parlance. Income would ordinarily exclude a receipt by way of capital. Mere gross receipt cannot also be taxed as income. It may be broadly stated that what is taxed is not also any gross receipt. The receipt must be revenue in nature and is to be taxed after excluding the necessary outgoings.

Section 11 contemplates an application of the income from charitable purposes. The charity can accumulate 25 per cent of the income. The application as well as the accumulation has necessarily to be the income as accounted for in the accounts, and not as computed under the Act, subject of course to what is provided in sub-section (4) of section 11.

Taking into account the purpose for which the conditions of section 11(1)(a) are imposed, it would be clear that one has to consider the income as arrived at in the context of what is available in the hands of the assessee, subject of course to any adjustment for expenses extraneous to the trust. If the expression "income" is so understood, then one has to take the accounts of the assessee with reference to the receipts and deduct therefrom the expenses necessary for earning or looking after that income. The net amount that remains would be available for distribution or application for charitable purpose. In applying the income for charitable purpose, even capital expenditure may be incurred. Therefore, the nature of the expenditure in the hands of the entity which receives the money is not the criterion. So long as the assessee disburses the amount for capital or revenue purposes, whether the amounts are utilised for capital or revenue purposes by the charity concerned, the assessee would have complied with that part of the requirement of section 11, namely, application of the income for charitable purposes. The authorities will have to find out as to whether they are really charitable purposes or not. Subject to such examination, the application of the income for charitable purposes will have to be excluded and it is only the balance that would require examination for finding out whether the assessee has complied with the rule of accumulation to the extent of Rs. 10,000 or 25 per cent of the income, whichever is higher.

The Tribunal has in a way mixed up the notion of total income in understanding the expression "income from property held under trust". Section 14 occurs in the chapter "Computation of total income". It provides that all income for the purposes of charge of income-tax and computation of total income be classified under certain heads. Therefore, the computation under the different categories or heads arises only of the purposes of ascertaining the total income for the purposes of charge. Those provisions cannot be introduced to find out what the income derived from the property held under trust to be excluded from the total income is, for the purpose of the exemptions under chapter III.

The income from the properties held under trust would have to be arrived at in the normal commercial manner without reference to the provisions which are attracted by section 14. Twenty-five per cent thereof will have to be ascertained and if the assessee had accumulated more than twenty-five percent, then the consequences contemplated by section 11 will follow. The remand made by the Tribunal will, therefore, have to stand and the ITO will compute the income in the light of the above.

As regards the taxability of surplus derived from running the two schools, though the schools themselves did not appear to be held in trust, they were institutions brought into existence by the trust and, therefore, the income would be eligible for exemption. In fact, in the instant case, there was a finding by the Tribunal that the trust was not carrying on any business of running those schools. In view of this findings the exemption in its full amplitude as contemplated by section 10(22) would apply. The Tribunal had unfortunately not noticed this provision. It is for the ITO to consider this provision in the light of the judgment in Addl. CIT v. Aditanar Educational Institution [1979] 118 235 (Mad.).
