Note : The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Religious or charitable trust - Exemption of income from property held under - One N, who was interested in motor engineering and transport companies created a trust and purported to endow it with share held by him in certain transport companies - Contemplated institution was not to be brought into being immediately but companies in which N was interested were to have benefit of assets set apart by him - N was managing trustee and empowered to borrow to any extent on properties conveyed to trust not only for trust but for his own use trustees were empowered, so long as N held office of managing trustee, to sell immovable properties belonging to trust for purpose of floating other companies - Foundation of institution was apparently to be left over until companies had made sufficient money for purpose - N also reserved right to revoke trust at any time - Whether on facts properties in question were not held under trust for charitable purpose within meaning of section 4(3)(i) of 1922 Act - Held, yes

In the Circular No. 1132 issued by the CBDT, it has been clarified that the payment of a sum by one charitable trust to other for utilisation of the donee-trust towards its charitable objects is proper application of income for charitable purpose in the hands of donor-trust and donor-trust will not lose exemption under section 11 merely because the donee trustee did not spend the donation during the year of receipt itself. In the instant case, the buildings of the assessee-society were used by other societies for similar aims and objects of charitable nature and that being so, such use could very well be treated as use by the assessee-society in furtherance of its aims and objects for the purpose of exemption under section 11. Moreover, exemption under section 11 was allowed to the assessee-society for the assessment years 1992-93 and 1993-94 by the department in the similar facts and circumstances. As such, the Commissioner (Appeals) was fully justified in treating the use of assessee’s property by other societies for charitable purposes as charitable activity carried on by the assessee and accordingly in allowing exemption under section 11 as claimed. The impugned order was, therefore, upheld. [Para 7]

Agricultural and dairy activities were being carried on by the assessee’s society as separate business activities and the same, therefore, constituted ‘property held under trust’ of the assessee-society as provided in sub-section (4) of section 11 and income of the said activities, in any case, was to be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act, i.e., after deducting the expenditure incurred in connection with the said business. The assessee-society had derived income from the said activities and the amount being more than sufficient to cover the expenses incurred in connection with the said activities, the allowance of the same by the Commissioner (Appeals) as application of its income as claimed by the assessee hardly made any difference in the ultimate position so as to cause any grievance to the revenue. [Para 8]

Hence, the revenue’s appeal was to be dismissed.

in whose hands the income is assessable shall be entitled to receive the same on behalf of any person; if he is not so entitled, the provisions of the section cannot be invoked. So, it was contended that, as the properties vested in the managing trustee and he received the income in his own right and not on behalf of the beneficiaries, though for their benefit, the said income in the hands of the managing trustee fell outside the scope of section 41 of the 1922 Act. There were two answers to that contention. The doctrine of vesting is not germane to that contention. In some of the enumerated persons in the section the property vests and in others it does not vest, but they only manage the property. In general law the property does not vest in a receiver or manager but it vests in a trustee, but both trustees and receivers are included in section 41 of the 1922 Act. The common thread that passes through all of them is that they function legally or factually for others: they manage the property for the benefit of others. That the technical doctrine of vesting is not imported in the section is apparent from the fact that a trustee appointed under a trust deed is brought under the section though legally the property vests in him. In the case of a Muslim wakf the property vests in the Almighty; even so the mutawallis are brought under the section. A reasonable interpretation of the section is that all the categories of persons mentioned therein are deemed to receive the income on behalf of another person or persons or manage the same for his or their benefit. None of them has any beneficial interest in the income; he collects the income for the benefit of others. In that view, even if the nattamaigars were trustees in whom the properties of the Durgha vested, they should be deemed to have received the income only on behalf of the kasupangudars in definite shares.

The nattamaigars were only the managers of the properties in which the Durgha and the kasupangudars had beneficial interests. The properties did not vest in them. They receive the income therefrom on behalf of both of them. In terms of section 41 of the 1922 Act the nattamaigars were the managers of the properties on behalf of others and were entitled to receive the income therefrom on behalf of them. With the result, the income which they held on behalf of the kasupangudars could be assessed only in their hands in the manner prescribed thereunder.

What vested in the nattamaigars was not the properties of the Durgha but the management and administration thereof. It was therefore, held that the scheme did not vest the properties of the Durgha in the nattamaigars .

In the result, it was held that the High Court was right in holding that section 41 of the 1922 Act applied to the assessee. The appeals failed and were dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act. Therefore, the property from which income was derived by the assessee was held under trust and such property was held for charitable purpose and the income derived from trust was property which was being applied for charitable purpose. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly allowed the assessee's claim for exemption under section 11.

As regards the point regarding material before Tribunal for finding that payment by the company any to the firm was not collusive, it is well-settled that the apparent state of affairs is to be presumed to be real until the contrary is shown. It is equally well settled that good faith and the genuineness of a transaction are also to be presumed until the contrary is proved. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.

Clause (i) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 1922 Act deals with income derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation for religious or charitable purposes, while clause (ia) deals with income derived from business carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution. The two clauses, therefore, do not necessarily overlap. Clause (i) of sub-section (3) of section 4 of the 1922 Act, applies to cases where the business itself is held under trust for religious or charitable purposes, while clause (ia) applies only to such business as is carried on behalf of a religious or charitable institution which was not held under trust.

The Sabha, was clearly an institution having been brought about to effect the purpose and to carry out the objects for which the trust was founded. The word "applied" in clause means actually spent while, in clause (i) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act, the words used are "income applied or finally set the words "finally set apart" had not been repeated in clause(ia) at that sub-section. The word "applied" did not necessarily mean "spent". Even if it has been earmarked and allocated for the purposes of the institution, it may, be deemed to have been applied for its purposes. Neither the word "applied" nor the word "institution" is of any importance in this case, the case was governed by income from the property held under trust as laid down in section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act.

Therefore, it was held that the bhents (offerings) vested in the Sabha under a legal obligation wholly for religious or charitable purposes of the Sabha but the bhents could not be said to be income derived from property under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act. They would properly come under clause (ii) of that sub-section meaning thereby that they were income of a religious or charitable institution derived from voluntary contributions and applicable solely to religious or charitable purposes.

Further, the income derived from industrial and commercial concerns was the income from property held under trust wholly for religious or charitable purposes and was exempt from income-tax under section 4(3)(i) of the 1922 Act and it was, therefore, not necessary to apply to such income section 4(3)(ia) of the 1922 Act.

Income-tax is a levy on income. No doubt the Income-tax Act takes into account two points of time at which the liability to tax is attracted, viz., the accrual of the income or its receipt, but the substance of the matter is the income. If income does not result at all there cannot be a tax even though in book-keeping an entry is made about hypothetical income which does not materialise. Where income has in fact been received and is subsequently given up it remains the income of the recipient, even though given up and the tax with regard to it is payable. Where, however, the income can be said not to have resulted at all there is obviously neither accrual nor receipt of income even though an entry to that effect might in certain circumstances have been made in the books of account.

In the instant case, there was a custom in the market according to which commission agents realised Dharmada from their constituents. The constituents paid that amount to the commission agents knowing that the same was being collected over and above the commission which was payable by them to the commission agents. This amount, under the custom, had to be spent on charities. The amount was being paid by the constituents for being made a part of the fund which had already been established by the commission agent for purposes of charity. From the very beginning it was clear to both the parties, viz., the one paying Dharmada and the other receiving the same, that it was being received by the petitioner for being credited to an already existing fund for charity. Accordingly, when this amount reached the petitioner it did not in truth reach him as its income.

Merely because some discretion was given to the petitioner to spend the amount deposited with it on a charity of its own choice, it did not mean that either no trust was created or the trust so created was invalid. The finding recorded by the Additional Commissioner merely meant that the petitioner was free to apply the trust fund on a charity of its own choice. It did not mean that the petitioner could, if it so liked, appropriate the amount credited to Dharmada account for its own purposes. After all, if Dharmada was being collected for purposes of charity in accordance with a custom, its disposal was equally governed by the obligation created by that custom, i.e. , the amount was to be spent only for some charitable purpose.

In order to determine whether a particular receipt, by whatever name is termed, is or is not the income of an assessee its real nature and quality has to be considered. If it was received under a custom, the answer to the question would depend on the nature of obligation treated by that custom. In the instant case, it was not disputed that the petitioner received Dharmada under a custom according to which it was obligatory upon it to spend the amount so collected on charity alone. The petitioner had created a fund for that purpose and Dharmada collected by it had to be credited to that fund. In the circumstances, the amount so collected was not received by the petitioner as its income.

In view of aforesaid, instant petition was allowed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the petitioner.

The ITO had relied on the English law relating to charities to conclude that the object of promotion of sports was not charitable. However, it is well settled that the definition of charitable purpose in section 2(15) has a wider significance because of the use of the words ‘any other object of general public utility’. In fact, promotion of sports and athletic activities was one of the objects of the Government and there were ministries and directorates for this purpose in both the Central and the State Governments. Section 10(23) itself provides for exemption of income of any association or institu- tion having as its object the control, supervision, regulation or encourage- ment of various games because it was considered that such institutions should fiourish in public interest. It was a matter of public concern that there should be keen interest in sports not only in the interest of public health but also to see that sportsmen fared well in the world arena. It could not, therefore, be said that’ such an object would not qualify for exemption under section 11. Since the other objects of the assessee were also clearly charitable, the assessee would qualify for exemption under section 11. The finding of the first appellate authority on this point was, therefore, correct.

As regards the question whether the impugned income from the race meets and inter-venue betting was income from property or income from business it would be difficult to accept that the assessee was conducting a business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter- venue betting on two or three occasions in a year.

Even if the receipts did not constitute the corpus, there was certainly no quid pro quo in the arrangement between the assessee and the HRC as the asses- see was getting, from the said race meets and inter-venue betting, on almost certain profit from the HRC at practically no risk or cost to itself. The assessee had obtained a licence from the Government to conduct the races and inter-venue betting on the basis of a letter from the HRC. This licence itself could be treated as property and such property was obtained with the consent of the settlor-club and was contemplated even at the inception of the assessee-trust. Since the expression ‘property’ has the widest import for income-tax purposes, the impugned income would be income from property held under trust.

Alternatively. even if the impugned income was not income from property, it could only be treated as a voluntary contribution given by the HRC to the assessee. Though the form of such contribution indicated that the assessee itself had to conduct the races, the actual conduct was done by the HRC on behalf of the assessee merely as a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contribution did not have the character of income but was a capital receipt. The facts of the case did not justify the inference that the assessee-trust was in business for conducting horse races. It had neither the horses nor organisation nor any other equipment for that purpose. Consequently, since the impugned income was not income from business, the question of applicability of section 13(1)(bb ) did not arise.

For the foregoing reasons, the assessee-trust was an institution which satisfied the conditions of section 2(15) read with section 11. Since the ITO had not considered the requirements of accumulation, if there had been such accumulation, or application of sections 12, 12A and 13, the assessments were set aside for consideration of these aspects.

Assessee has not disputed the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) that rentals received from its Kalyanamandapams had to be considered under the head income from business. In fact the High Court while remitting the question back to the Commissioner (Appeals) for assessment years 1997-98, 1998-99 etc., had indicated that income of the assessee from the Kalyanamandapams was more in the nature of business income. Obviously, assessee cannot now raise a plea against the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that income of the assessee from renting out Kalyanamandapams were business income, and it has wisely done so. However, it is peeved on the view taken by the Commissioner (Appeals) that such business income could not be considered as income earned from a property held under the Trust, thereby disentitling the assessee from taking advantage of section 11(4). The Commissioner (Appeals) was of the opinion that Kalyanamandapams having being built by the assessee subsequent to its formation in the year 1959, could not be considered as property under trust. The assessee during the course of his arguments has stated that the land on which Kalyanamandapams were built was part of the original settlement and the building were built therein by the assessee from its income. Be that as it may, there is no dispute that the land and building was owned by the assessee society, whether it was part of original settlement or not. It is opined that, once income of a trust is used by it to acquire a property, the property so acquired will be property held under trust. Income from such property will be income from property under the trust. Thus, rental income received by the assessee from Kalyanamandapams though it was in the nature of income from business, such income was nothing but income from property held under trust.[Para 9]

Whether assessee could be denied exemption claimed by it under section 11(1) by virtue of sub-section (4A) thereof?

To answer the question, whether assessee can be denied the exemption claimed by it under section 11(1)(4A) it is to be seen whether renting out the Kalyanamandapams could be considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects of the assessee as they appear in its Memorandum of Association. By virtue of clause (d) of the objects clause, assessee can purchase, build and let out properties for its other purposes. The purpose mentioned in clause (a) clearly indicate promotion of any object which was wholly and solely charitable in nature. No doubt Commissioner (Appeals) had mentioned this to be a very wide expressions, disentitling it from claiming exemption under section 11. It is true that clause (a) is of a wide amplitude. However what needed to be remembered is that the assessee was having registration under section 12A since 11-4-1975, and such registration still continued. If the main object of the assessee was too wide, as mentioned by the Commissioner (Appeals), it would not have been given such registration. Having given such registration, which was alive since 1975, revenue cannot now turn back and say that the main object was very wide and assessee could not be given benefit of section 11(1). Activity of renting out Kalyanamandapams could be construed as only incidental to the attainment of its main object. Assessee therefore could take advantage of section 11(4). There is no dispute that assessee had maintained separate books for its Kalyanamandapams. The audited accounts filed along with its return clearly show separate income and expenditure for each of the activities, including Kalyanamandapams. Sub-section 4A would not apply to the assessee once its business is considered as incidental to the attainment of its main objects.[Para 10]

Whether predominant activity of assessee was charity and if so what was nature of charity?

In the instant case one of the two partners had received an extra remuneration for managing the estate which was in excess of that part of his income which he received as of right by virtue of the ownership of his share in the partnership. Such remuneration, even though the property managed was agricultural, was in the nature of "salary" as the term is used in Section 7. The mere fact that its ultimate source was agricultural property would not make it agricultural income because the payment was received not as part of his profit from the agricultural property, but as remuneration due to him for work done as manager of the property.

Therefore, the sum in question was not exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(vii).

On reference :

It was clear from the provision contained in clause 4(2) of the deed that the trustees had been given absolute discretion to utilise not merely the income but also the corpus of the trust property or any part thereof for any one or more of the objects mentioned in clause 4(1). In other words, it was clear that even if the trustees were to spend the entire income or the entire corpus on non-charitable object mentioned in clause 4(1)(iv ), they would not be committing any breach of the terms and conditions of the trust and such expenditure on their part would be perfectly valid and proper. In view of this position which obtained very clearly under the indenture dated 12-6-1959, it seemed very clear that the trust could not be regarded as a trust having been created wholly for charitable purposes.

The contention of the assessee was that this sub-clause (iv) should be regarded, if it all, as incidental or ancillary object and since the main or dominant object of the deed was to do charity and since several other sub-clauses of clause 4 indicated what those charitable objects were, it should be held that notwithstanding sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) the trust should be regarded as one having been created wholly for charitable purposes. It was not possible to accept this submission of the assessee. In the first place, there was nothing to indicate in clause 4(1) of the deed that the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv) thereof was incidental or ancillary to other objects mentioned in the other sub-clauses of clause 4(1). Secondly, clause 4(2) in terms elevated the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv ) to the same level as the other objects mentioned in sub-clauses of clause 4(1), for, under sub-clause (2) of clause 4, the trustees had been given liberty to utilise the corpus of the trust property or any part thereof for any one or more of the objects mentioned earlier and in such proportion as they might in their absolute discretion think fit. At least while conferring such power upon the trustees some indication could have been given by the settlors if they wanted to regard sub-clause (iv) as incidental or ancillary, but nothing of the kind had been done. In other words, sub-clause (2) of clause 4 had conferred absolute discretion upon the trustees to spend the entire corpus of the trust property or any part thereof upon any one or more of the objects mentioned in sub-clause (1) of clause 4. Further, it was not possible to accept the contention that sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) provided for management expenses, such as remuneration payable to the employees of the trust and that normally the trustees would have incurred such expenditure on the employees during the course of management of the trust. In fact, clause 4(1) separately provided for expenses for management and maintenance of the trust property. In terms, clause 4(1) provided that the trustees would pay out of the rents, profits, interest, dividends and income all outgoings payable in respect of the trust property including all ground rent, rates, taxes and costs of repairs of any immovable property forming part of the trust property, premium for insurance or any other costs, charges, expenses and outgoings of and incidental to the management and maintenance of the trust property and execution of the trusts therein contained including the wages and salaries of employees and it is after payment of such outgoings and other expenses that the trustees had been directed to spend the income of the trust property over the objects which have been specified in sub-clauses (i) to (vi) of clause 4(1). In a way this independent provision for meeting the expenses of the management and maintenance of the trust property including wages and salaries of the employees on the contrary suggested that the settlors had in mind while incorporating sub-clause (iv) in clause 4(1) that it was an independent object of the trust for which the trustees were given liberty to spend the income of the trust property. Having regard to the above position which contained very clearly on reading of the deed of trust as a whole, it was difficult to accept the contention that sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) should either be regarded as not providing any object at all or as providing for an incidental or ancillary object. It was clear that the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv) was also one of the independent objects on which the trustees had been given power to spend the income of the property or even the entire corpus of the trust property by virtue of clause 4(2) of the deed and if that be so, it was clear that the trust in question could not be regarded as being one created wholly for the purpose of the charitable objects.

A cursory perusal of the terms of the deed would show that the managing trustee was the heart and soul of the trust. The terms of the trust deed expressly provided for the trust funds being employed in any trade, industry or business, which meant that the trust could carry on the business just like an individual or a firm or a limited company. It was not the contention of the department that the trust was a mere fiction or that it was illusory. Thus, a valid trust had been constituted and the trust carried on the business during the relevant accounting years.

It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

Note: The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

The assessee carried on business as merchants and also as managing agents and agents of a many companies and firms. They were appointed as managing agents of company 'C' but there was nothing in the articles regarding their appointment for any fixed term of years. There was no contract actually executed between the company and the assessee for their services as managing agents of the company. It was not at the option of the company to very the remuneration from time to time and the assessees were at liberty to terminate their own appointment as managing agents at their option. On 16-01-1925 company 'C' was wound up voluntarily. Certain amount was paid to the assessee as compensation for their loss of office as managing agents of the company. The assessee claimed that sum as a receipt of casual non-recurring nature not arising from business or the exercise of a profession, vocation or occupation and so exempt under section 4(3)(vii)of the 1922 Act. The ITO considered the sum as a receipt from business and included it in their income for purposes of assessment. On appeal, the Assistant Commissioner upheld the assessment. On reference, the Commissioner also took the same view which was taken by the ITO.

No deeming provision is necessary to regard the money received by the trust from its beneficiaries as the income of the trust since section 11(1) itself contains sufficient indication to treat such moneys as income of the trust. Only the income to the extent that it is applied for charitable or religious purposes can be excluded from the total income of the assessee. When that amount is returned by the beneficiaries of the trust, the receipts in the hands of the trust can only be its income of the years in which it is received. If the contention of the assessee was accepted and such receipts were treated as not income of the trust, then it might as well defeat the very purpose of the trust. The trust in that event was not under the obligation to apply the money for the objects of the trust since by implication it ceased to be income of the trust. On the other hand, if the income was recycled by the trust for charitable or religious purposes, it was again and again entitled to the benefit of section 11. This was also the tenor of the circular, dated 24-1-1973, issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes.

Accordingly, the Tribunal was not justified.

(i) Rental income and leasing of properties

■

The principal basis adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) for allowing the assessee's claim is the observation that one of the objects of the trust was to lease out properties and earn rental income. However, on a careful examination of the original trust deed as well as the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the Tribunal finds that the observation is factually incorrect and contrary to the material available on record. The original trust deed, enumerates the charitable objects of the trust, namely: (i) genetic research and agricultural education; (ii) conservation of land, water and genetic resources; (iii) sustainable agriculture and environmental protection; (iv) family planning and population control; and (v) improvement of the status and literacy of women. Subsequently, by way of the Addendum/Rectification Deed, the additional charitable objects of Relief to the Poor and Education were incorporated. Significantly, neither the original trust deed nor the addendum includes, as an object of the trust, carrying on the activity of leasing or renting of immovable properties for earning rental income. [Para 8.2]

■

What is, however, contained in the trust deed is a separate enabling provision conferring powers upon the Board of Trustees. Clause VIII merely authorises the trustees to acquire, hold, manage or otherwise deal with land, buildings and other immovable properties with the funds of the trust for effectuating the charitable objects of the trust. Such an enabling clause cannot be elevated to the status of an independent charitable object. The power to acquire and manage trust properties is only incidental to the effective administration of the trust and to facilitate the attainment of its charitable purposes. Therefore, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that leasing of properties itself constituted one of the objects of the trust is clearly erroneous and is not borne out from the trust deed. [Para 8.3]

■

At the same time, the Tribunal also notices that the trust deed, along with the Addendum, has been the subject matter of adjudication in the preceding as well as subsequent assessment years. At no stage have the Revenue authorities questioned the charitable nature of the objects or recorded any finding that the activities of the trust were not genuine. The entire controversy is confined to the interpretation of the enabling clause empowering the trustees to acquire and manage immovable properties. [Para 8.4]

■

The record further reveals that the revenue has not brought any material to establish that the rental income earned by the trust was diverted for any non-charitable purpose or that the dominant character of the trust had ceased to be charitable. On the contrary, the Income and Expenditure Account demonstrates that the receipts of the trust, whether derived from grants, donations, interest or rental income, were applied only towards the charitable objects of the trust. Thus, the source from which the income was generated has not altered the fundamental charitable character of the institution. [Para 8.5]

■

It is a settled proposition of law that the decisive test is the dominant object of the institution and not the source of its income. Income derived from property held under trust, including rental income, does not lose the benefit of exemption under Section 11 and Section 12 merely because such income arises from leasing of trust property, so long as it is applied towards the charitable purposes for which the trust has been established. The leasing of trust property, in the facts of the present case, is only an incidental mode of augmenting resources to fulfil the charitable objects and cannot be construed as an independent commercial object of the trust. [Para 8.6]

■

Accordingly, while the Tribunal disagrees with the reasoning assigned by the Commissioner (Appeals) in holding that earning rental income was itself one of the objects of the trust, the Tribunal nevertheless upholds the ultimate conclusion that the assessee cannot be denied exemption on this ground. The reasoning adopted by the Commissioner (Appeals) is incorrect; however, the conclusion reached by him is sustainable on the basis that the rental income was merely incidental to the charitable activities and was admittedly applied towards the charitable objects of the trust. Consequently, the ground raised by the Revenue on this issue is devoid of merit and is dismissed. [Para 8.7]

■

Accordingly, the Tribunal concurs with the findings recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) on this issue. The ground raised by the Revenue challenging the allowability of exemption merely because the assessee earned rental income is devoid of merit and is, therefore, dismissed. [Para 8.8]

The assessee-firm, was the managing agent of a company. Under the provisions of the articles of association, the assessee was entitled to monthly remuneration from the date of the incorporation of the company and a commission of ten per cent on the net annual profits. On 15-6-1953, the assessee wrote to the company confirming the resolution of the latter nominating C as its ex-officio director on behalf of the managing agents and intimating that thereby they authorised C to draw the managing agency monthly allowance of Rs. 1,000 per month for his expenses to attend to all the matters relating to the managing agency affairs on behalf of the assessee. During the relevant accounting year, the assessee credited the sum of Rs. 12,000 in its books as managing agency commission from the company and debited C with that amount. In the circumstances the assessee did not include the said amount in its total income in the return. The ITO added this sum declining to accept the assessee's claim that the sum should not be regarded as an income or in any case should be viewed as an expenditure entitled to deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of 1922 Act. The AAC however accepted the assessee's appeal. The revenue made a successful appeal to the Tribunal which expressed its view that the receipt was by the assessee-firm primarily and the payment to C was only an application of that income.

On reference :

Section 11 contemplates the computation of the income, in order to find out whether the income has been applied for charitable purposes to the required extent. It is, therefore, necessary for the ITO to find out first what the property held in trust is. He will then have to ascertain the income derived from the said properties of the trust and after ascertaining the income, he will have to examine whether any part of the said income has been accumulated for application. Such accumulation could be only up to a maximum of 25 per cent of the income from the property or Rs. 10,000, whichever is higher. This provision itself shows that to the extent of 75 pr cent of the income, there has to be an application of the income for charitable purposes. It was in the context of the application of the income that the Tribunal in the instant case had observed that the expenditure in improving the property of the trust or maintaining it resulting in the income of the trust being maintained or even increased would have to be taken as application for charitable purposes. In coming to this conclusion, the Tribunal had mixed up two things relevant under section 11. Section 11 requires consideration of the objects of the trust and also of the income derived from the property held in trust. The income from the trust properties has to be applied on the objects of the trust. As far as the objects of the trust are concerned, the application of the amount can be for revenue or capital purposes. So long as the expenditure had to be incurred out of the income earned by the trust, even if such expenditure is for capital purposes on the objects of the trust, the income would be exempt. The Tribunal was, therefore, wrong in proceeding on the basis that improvement of a property held under trust would by itself come within the scope of the application of the income for charitable purposes. However, facts would have to be investigated to find out whether the assessee had, in incurring the expenditure of a capital nature, promoted the objects of the trust by applying the income to those objects. The ITO would have to go into this question, as the assessment itself had been set aside by the Tribunal and restored to his file. So long as the income derived from the property held under trust had been expended on the objects of the trust, the income would be exempt under section 11. If this was not done, then the income would not be exempt.

Section 11 provides that the income from any property held under trust for charitable or religious purpose is exempt from tax to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India. The question is, what does the word 'income' connote in the context of the exemption under section 11. On a reading of section 11(1)(a) and further from the consideration of the various decisions of the High Courts in this regard it is apparent that it is the real income which is to be taken into account. The question of deduction which is otherwise allowable in computing the income in a case not covered by section 11 cannot arise while deciding the percentage of application or accumulation. The question of deduction comes only when the income is otherwise chargeable to tax under the provisions of the Act. It cannot be disputed that section 11 has given a benefit to an assessee-trust which applies its income to charitable or religious purposes. If the entire income is applied to charitable purpose, the question of payment of any tax would not arise. If a trust desires to accumulate income in excess of the limits laid down in section 11(1), the conditions specified in section 11(2) have to be fulfilled in respect of the entire accumulation and not merely in respect of the accumulation in excess of 25 per cent of the income. Further, if the trust does not comply with the conditions laid down in section 11(2), the amount which becomes liable to assessment under section 11(3) is the entire income accumulated and not merely the income accumulated in excess of the limits specified in section 11(1). In other words, such an assessee loses the benefit of the accumulation permitted under section 11(1). The question of chargeability of a part of income to tax which is not exempt arises only when the accumulation is more than the permissible limit. While making assessment of the part of the income which is in excess of the specified percentage, such taxable income of a trust cannot be classified under different heads. It is only when any income is assessed under a particular head, that the question of allowing deduction under that head arises for consideration.

In a case where an assessee-trust has income from different sources and has applied such income and a part of such income comes within the ambit of taxation, it will not be possible for earmarking any part of such an income up to a particular head. The head of income is irrelevant unless the entire income comes from one specific head. Since the income from property held under trust has to be arrived at in a normal commercial manner and when the income from property held under trust as such is excluded, there is no scope for computating the income from property by applying the provisions of section 14. The provisions of section 14 cannot be pressed into service in such a case. Therefore, the question of allowing any statutory deductions as contemplated by the different provisions of the Act dealing with different heads of income in computing the income accumulated does not arise when the trust loses the benefit of accumulation.

Sub-section (1A) has been inserted in section 11 by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1971, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1962. Under section 11, income derived from property held under trust for charitable or religious purposes is exempt from income-tax to the extent such income is actually applied to such purposes during the previous year itself or within the three months next following. As 'income' includes 'capital gains', a charitable or religious trust would forfeit exemption from income-tax in respect of its income by way of capital gains unless such income is also applied to the purposes of the trust during the stipulated period. By sub-section (1A), it has been provided that, in a case where a capital asset being property held under trust for charitable or religious purposes is transferred and the whole or any part of the net consideration for the transfer (i.e., full value of consideration as reduced by the expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer) is utilised for acquiring another capital asset to be held as part of the corpus of the trust, the capital gain arising from the transfer will be regarded as having been applied to charitable or religious purposes. Where the whole of such net consideration is utilised in acquiring the new capital asset, the entire amount of the capital gain will be regarded as having been applied to charitable or religious purposes while, in a case where only a part of the net consideration is utilised for acquiring the new capital asset, so much of such capital gains as is equal to the amount, if any, by which the amount so utilised exceeds the aggregate of the cost of acquisition of the capital asset transferred and the cost of any improvements made to such asset, will be regarded as having been applied to such purposes.

The word ‘business’ is one of large and indefinite import. However, it connotes something which occupies the labour and attention of a person for the purpose of profit. Generally speaking, business is an activity of a commercial nature and means practically anything, which is an occupation as distinguished from a pleasure. If the transaction is a trading transaction or an adventure in the nature of trade, it will amount to business, whether it results in loss or profit. It also includes adventure in the nature of trade. The object of the definition of ‘business’ in the Act is to treat the receipts from an adventure also to tax just as the receipts from the trade profit are brought to tax. In each case, however, one has to determine the nature of transaction, its volume, frequency, continuity and regularity. There is no hard and fast rule for application that particular transaction is a business. Any transaction, whether it is continuously undertaken or isolated transaction, can be treated alike to hold that a particular transaction is a business. The activities of the trust, i.e., conducting of races and inter-venue betting, after obtaining licence from the State Government and income derived therefrom could not be called as income from the business of the trust for the reason that the same was being utilized to achieve the primary object of the trust.

The objects and legality of the trust and also the grant of licence by the State Government were not in dispute, except to the extent that the objects were distributive in nature and some of them were charitable and others were non-charitable in nature. But, once if it was found that promotion of sports and athletics which benefit a large number of people were charitable in nature and also of general public utility, that objection also would stand apart.

The trust had conducted these stray activities for the purpose of achieving its primary objects, i.e., relief to poor, education, medical aid, etc. Thus, the activities undertaken by the trust could not be called a business systematically organized. The transactions in conducting the races and inter-venue betting were being meant for achieving primary objects of trust and could not be called a business. The natural corollary that followed was that the income derived from such transactions could not be called an income from the business. Assuming that it was a business as contemplated under section 2(13), the same was exempted under section 11. Further, the submission that the income would be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust could not also be disbelieved. [Para 12]

The licence to run races and betting itself could be treated as property and the said property was obtained with the consent of the Hyderabad Race Club. The term ‘property’ itself has got widest import for income-tax purposes and inclusive of holding a licence. But, it is not every case of business which can be treated as property. If it were to be so treated, section 13(1)(bb) would lose its meaning. It may be that a business itself may be settled in trust of the trustees who may conduct a business on their own under the powers given to them in the trust deed. In the instant case, it was difficult to accept that the assessee-trust was conducting the business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter-venue betting for few occasions in a year. Thus, there could not be any doubt that the income derived by the trust for the relevant assessment years was from the property held under trust and as such it was exempted under section 11.

Assuming even if it was not treated as income from the property held under the trust, it could be treated as voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee-trust as contemplated under section 12. The conduct of the Hyderabad Race Club in respect of the transaction was only a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contributions could be characterized only as a capital receipt in the assessee’s hands. Thus, it could not be held that there had been business in the normal sense in such arrangement and in the facts and circumstances, it was not such a business which would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). It was only an activity which could constitute the property or an arrangement involved in transfer of funds from Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee’s institution in a form recognized by law and not shown to be colourable exercise or otherwise as contended by the revenue. Since it could not be said to be a business and the income derived could not be said to be a business income, the provisions of section 13(1)(bb) were not attracted. The assessee-trust was an institution, which satisfied the conditions under section 2(15), read with section 11 and as such, conclusion reached by the Tribunal should be upheld. [Para 13]

The assessee-trust was formed by a deed dated 15-6-1964 with the objects, inter alia, of acquiring and maintaining a charitable home in Bombay for providing temporary accommodation to persons for purposes of study, medical treatment and such other charitable purposes. For this purpose, the deed specifically authorised the trustees to raise contributions by written appeals, public entertainments and so on. On 5-7-1964, the trust organised a charity show, inviting contributions by way of tickets for the show and by priced advertisements in a souvenir. The total receipts came to Rs. 1,05,372 and the outgoings totalled Rs. 8,601. The balance of Rs. 96,771 was transferred to the corpus of the trust and invested in fixed deposits for subsequent use to fulfil its purposes. The ITO treated the collections as income from property held in trust under section 11(1)(a), and held that since it had been accumulated, exemption was available only to the extent of 25 per cent thereof. In appeal, the AAC held the entire receipts to be voluntary contributions, exempt under section 12(1) (as it then stood). On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the said contributions formed part of the trust capital and that hence the provisions of sections 11 and 12 did not apply. It also held that even if the receipts constituted income, they would be exempt under section 12(1).

On reference, the revenue argued that since the receipts were for a consideration, which was entertainment in the case of tickets for the show and advertisement in the case of souvenir, these could not be treated as voluntary contributions. The assessee countered this by arguing that no one would have paid the high price charged for the tickets and advertisements merely for the entertainment or the advertisement.

The assessee-firm was appointed an managing agent of a company. The managed company received a letter from another company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as its managing agents and requested that it may be so appointed. On 28-9-1943, the managed company decided to ask the assessee to retire from the managing agency business with effect from 30-9-1943, on receipt of compensation for the premature termination of the contract. This amount was paid to the assessee on 30-9-1943, and the assessee retired from the managing agency business with effect from that date. The majority of shareholders in company ‘J’ were the members of the assessee-firm. The assessee submitted a return without showing in the return the receipt of the said compensation. For the assessment year 1944-45, the ITO completed the assessment of the assessee without including the aforesaid amount of compensation. Subsequently, the successor ITO issued a notice to the assessee under section 34 of the 1922 Act calling upon the assessee to submit a return in respect of that amount. In response to the notice the assessee submitted the return but contended that the aforesaid receipt was capital in nature not liable to tax. However, the contention was rejected and receipt was subjected to tax. The Tribunal held that as there was merely a change in the personnel of the managing agency, there was no loss of office, which might entitle the managing agents to payment, which was held to be collusive and, therefore, there was no genuine termination of the managing agency and as such the payment was not ‘compensation for termination of the managing agency’. The Tribunal also held that the receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act as it was not casual and it did arise out of the business of the assessee, that the receipt was ‘foreseen, well planned and thought of’ and, therefore, the receipt was revenue receipt.

The issue is whether, on the facts and circumstances of the case and having regard to the terms of the trust deed, it can be said that the activities carried on by the assessee in the form of running of community hall, was itself held under the trust. [Para 6]

It is to be noted that section 11(1) grants exemption to the income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India. There is no exhaustive definition of the words "property held under trust" in the Act; however, sub-section (4) says that for the purposes of section 11, the words "property held under trust" includes "a business undertaking so held". [Para 7]

If a property is held under trust, and such property is a business, the case would fall under section 11(4) and not under section 11(4A). Section 11(4A) would apply only to a case where the business is not held under trust. Thus, there is difference between property or business held under trust and business carried on by or on behalf of the trust. [Para 8]

This distinction was recognized by the Supreme Court in the case of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1978] 121 ITR 1/[1979] 2 Taxman 501 wherein it was observed that if a business undertaking is held under trust for a charitable purpose, the income therefrom would be entitled to the exemption under section 11(1) of the Act. In the present case, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) is that running of community Hall was incidental to the object of the trust, it was not business commenced/carried on by the assessee. Though the business was commenced by the trust and it was carried on by the trust after its formation, it cannot be said to constitute property held under trust.

Under section 11(4), it is only the business which is held under the trust that would enjoy exemption in respect of its income Under section 11(1) and there is a distinction between the objects of a trust and the powers given to the trustees to effectuate the purpose of the trust. Though the objects of the trust were charitable, they were mere powers conferred upon the trustees to carry on the business and the profits from such business would benefit the charitable objects. The exemption Under section 11 cannot be granted on the reason that the business itself was not in existence at the time of formation of the trust and the property held under trust at the time of formation of the trust was not spelt out in the trust deed of the assessee.

The running of " Community Hall" was not at all in existence at the time of formation of the trust so as to say that the business is property held under trust. Thus, the activities relating to running of "Community Hall" was not even in the contemplation of the trust deed on the basis of which the society is formed and, therefore, could not have been settled upon trust. The business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the assessee. In this case, the activities viz., running of community hall, was carried on by the assessee for and on behalf of the trust and it was not business held under trust.

Section 11(1) of the Act confers exemption from tax only where the property is itself held under trust or other legal obligation; it does not apply to cases where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property but only the income derived for a charitable or religious purpose. Surplus funds of a trust, which was claimed to be exempt on the footing that it was property held under trust within the meaning of section 11(1) of the Act, was not property held under trust since the property from which the surplus was generated was itself not held under trust.

In other words, merely carrying on business for and on behalf of the charitable trust and applying the profits of the same for the object of the trust does not entitle for exemption under section 11(4) unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objects of the trust. [Para 9]

The provisions of sections 11 and 12 are applicable to income derived from property held under trust or other legal obligation for charitable or religious purposes. In addition to cases of regular trusts executed under trust deeds, other charitable or religious institutions of the nature of society, club, etc., are also entitled to the benefits under these sections inasmuch as the income derived by such institutions is from property held under trust or other legal obligations. For this purpose, it is not at all necessary that a trust deed is executed in a due manner. The legal obligation will attach to any property which is held by some persons or on behalf of others. In case of a charitable or religious institution, be it a club or a society or otherwise, the managing committee holds the property of the institution in trust for either the members as a whole or the charitable purpose for which the society has been formed.

In the instant case, the assessee was a society registered under the Karnataka Societies Registration Act. The main purpose for which the society was formed was towards charity. Hence, there was no doubt about the fact that the managing committee of the society held the assets of the society under implied trust towards fulfilment of the said charitable objects. In that way, the managing committee must be considered to be a ‘representative assessee’ for the purpose of sections 139(4A) and also 271(1)(a). Hence, the argument of the assessee that only trusts catering for religious or charitable purposes was under an obligation to file their returns of income under section 139(4A) and not other religious or charitable institutions, was not correct. Thus, all charitable trusts and institutions (including the assessee) are also bound by the provisions of section 139(4A).

Again, sections 160 and 161 are machinery sections and are not exhaustive of cases where trustees are liable to charge in respect of the income received by them on behalf of the beneficiary. Hence, it could not be said that the assessee, in the instant case, did not come within the description of ‘representative assessee’ as enunciated under section 160. The submission that merely being a charitable society, the assessee did not fall under the requirements of section 139(4A) was, therefore, rejected,

As regards the argument that no time-limit was prescribed in section 139(4A), the use of the expression call the provisions- of this Act shall so far as, apply as if it were a return required to be furnished under sub-section (1)’ requires the assessee to file its return of income within the time-limit as prescribed under section 139(1).

As regards the assessee ‘s contention about filing of application in Form No. 6, there was no mention about it in the relevant portion of the return. This indicated that most probably no such application had been filed However, it was also a fact that there might be existence of reasonable cause behind the delay and such delay might be condoned even without any application in Form No.6 being filed The assessee was undisputedly a charitable organisation and its income for the relevant year had also been ultimately found to be totally exempt under sections 11 and 12. It was also an acknowledged fact that a Chartered Accountant was looking after the entire affairs relating to filing of returns, etc., of the assessee. The delay in filing the return should, therefore, be considered to be attributable to the Chartered Accountant himself. Since the Chartered Accountant was no more, it was not possible to get at the exact reason behind the delay. At the same time again no liability could was prevented by reasonable cause from filing its return within the due date. The penalty was, therefore, cancelled

The trust deed was executed by the settlor with the intention that the income from the properties transferred should be utilised for the maintenance of his daughter S and the balance, if any, for charitable purposes. The properties had been transferred to be held in trust according to the terms mentioned in the trust deed. The Commissioner, after referring to the various clauses of the trust-deed had concluded that the trust could not by any accepted standards be regarded as a charitable trust for the reason that the purposes of the trust included maintenance and meeting the needs of any other relatives of the donor at the absolute discretion of the managing trustee and a trust created primarily for the benefit of the members of the settlor's family was not for charitable purposes. Clause 10 of the trust-deed gave to the managing trustee to have the final voice in all matters concerning the utilisation of the income and disposal of the trust property. It was open to the managing trustee to utilise the entire income for the maintenance and meeting the needs of any of the relatives of the donor at his absolute discretion. Besides, the individual shares of the persons on whose behalf the income was received, were also indeterminate.

Therefore, the assessee-trust was not a charitable trust and the writ was accordingly dismissed.

Under a Will of one 'W', the trustees of his estate were directed to carry on the 'Arya Vaidya Shala' and to maintain a hospital and a school conducted by 'W' and to apply 60 per cent of the income for the benefit of the hospital and the school and the rest for the benefit of two tavazhies. Exigibility to tax of 60 per cent of the income directed to be utilised for the hospital and the school was finally decided by this Court in CIT v. P. Krishna Warriar [1964] 53 ITR 176 (SC). In these appeals the dispute related to the special surcharge on income-tax and super-tax on the balance of the income directed to be given to the two thavazhies in the account years relevant to the assessment years 1957-58 to 1961-62.

After the original assessments were completed, on coming to learn that 15 per cent surcharge on tax should have been levied in respect of the total income of the trust, which in his view was unearned income, the ITO issued notices under section 34(1)(b) of 1922 Act and assessed the trustees to special surcharge under the Finance Act, 1957. The order was confirmed in appeal by the AAC and the Tribunal.

On reference, the High Court held that the share paid to the thavazies, being earned income, was not liable to surcharge. In the opinion of the High Court the case did not fall within the terms of section 41 of 1922 Act since the business of 'Arya Vaidya Shala' was property and the trustees did not carry on the business on behalf of any beneficiary.

An incorporated limited liability company 'L' had a subscribed capital consisting of preference shares, ordinary shares and deferred shares. The assessee-company became the managing agents of said company under an agreement. Subsequently, the assessee acquired its ordinary shares and preference shares. On 10-10-1947, the assessee made a further acquisition of some deferred shares. Thereafter, the assessee agreed to make over its managing agency to 'K'. The terms included that 'K' should take over the deferred shares and also pay the assessee a further sum of certain amount as compensation for loss of future remuneration to the assessee as managing agent. The assessee sold during the relevant assessment year, the ordinary and preference shares which resulted in a loss. After adjusting this loss on the extra amount received on the sale of deferred shares, there was a net profit. The assessee did not return the amount as its income for the year on the ground that it was a capital receipt. The revenue disagreed and brought the amount to tax treating it as income. The Tribunal concurred with that view. It also declined to a make a reference.

The assessee-company was acting as a managing agents of various companies including one 'G'. The assessee acquired a large block of shares in 'G'. In 1950, 'G' was converted into a public company. Thereafter, the assessee was not entitled to any commission on sales, etc., in view of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as amended in 1939. Hence, a fresh agreement was entered into between the assessee and the 'G' on 10-5-1960, under which the assessee company was entitled to an office allowance of Rs. 5,000 per month and a commission of 10 per cent of the net profits. The Board of directors of the Managed Company had taken a decision to terminate the agency of managing company. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed-company approved the resolution of the board of directors on 31-3-1951. That meeting also recommended a payment of Rs. 18 lakhs to the assessee as compensation. That resolution was communicated to the assessee on 3-4-1951, and the latter accepted it on 10-4-1951. In the assessment for the assessment year 1952-53, the ITO included aforesaid amount in the total income of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC held that the amount in question represented compensation received by the assessee company for the termination of its managing agency. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the transactions, whereby the managing agency of the company was terminated were genuine and real business transactions, that managing agencies held by the assessee represented sources from which it received is income by way of commission and, therefore, the termination of managing agency would represent destruction of a source of income. As a consequence of those findings, the Tribunal held that the receipt in question was a capital receipt and not a revenue receipt. On reference, the High court held that all the proceedings relating to the termination of the managing agency of the company were not genuine transactions. It further came to the conclusion that the managing agencies held by the assessee were its stock-in-trade, and, therefore, the amount paid by the managing company to the assessee must be considered as a revenue receipt.

The assessee-trust was created by an indenture dated 12-6-1959 for certain purposes. The settlors settled certain sum on the trust, and were also interested in a private limited company. The company was in occupation of certain premises, being a godown and 4 shops. The company had given the premises on leave and licence basis to TF Ltd. Subsequently, by another agreement dated 1-7-1959, the company allowed the trustees to occupy a portion of the shed subsequently, on 9-11-1959, a tripartite agreement was entered into between the company, the trustees and TF Ltd. under which the premises were given to TF. Ltd. on leave and licence for certain fee payable by the licensees to the trustees. During the assessment year 1960-61 the trustees had recovered and realised licence fee in respect whereof the trustees claimed exemption from tax under section 4(3)(i) as being the income from property held under trust or legal obligation for charitable purposes. The ITO took the view that the source of this income, namely, right to receive licence fees under the agreements dated 1-7-1959, and 9-11-1959, was not held by the assessee under a trust or other legal obligation and, therefore, the income that was received by the assessee was not saved from taxation under section 4(3)(i). He accordingly brought the said amount to tax. In appeal, the AAC accepted the claim of the assessee that the property from which the income had been derived was held under trust or legal obligation, but further took the view that in view of certain provisions which were contained in the objects clause read with clause 4(2) of the indenture dated 12-6-1959, the trust could not be regarded as having been created wholly for charitable purposes. He, thus, rejected the claim of the assessee of exemption under section 4(3)(i) in respect of that income earned by the assessee and confirmed the ITO's order. The Tribunal confirmed the order of AAC.

The assessee-trust was set up by a Race Club HRC for certain specified charitable purposes including promotion and encouragement of public activities in sports and games. The initial corpus of the trust was only a very small amount but an explanatory statement attached to the resolution of the club whereby the trust was created, clarified that further accretions to the corpus could be made through donations and conduct of races under the auspices of the trust. The assessee-trust was allowed the benefit of profits on races and inter-venue betting conducted under the auspices of the trust on a few days in a year. The assessee’s claim for exemption of such income under section 11 was rejected by the ITO on the grounds (i) that the assessee was not a charitable institution inasmuch one of its object was promotion of sports or athletic activities which could not be considered to be charitable, and (ii) that the assessee’s income from races and inter- venue betting as aforementioned was not income from property but income from business and was hit by the prohibition contained in section 13(1)(bb), disentitling the assessee from exemption under section 11. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee was a charitable trust and qualified for exemption under section 11 but that only income from the initial corpus was income from property held in trust and was eligible for exemption. In this view, he upheld the ITO’s disallowance of exemption in respect of income from races and inter-venue betting on ground (ii) supra.

On second appeal, the assessee argued that its aforementioned income from races and inter-venue betting under arrangement with the settlor- club was income from property held in trust and not business income, while the revenue contended that the assessee was not a charitable institution.
