The deceased had executed a will under which he created a trust in respect of all his properties and appointed the Official Trustee as the sole executor and trustee he directed that all his properties would vest in the Official Trustee on his death; who would sell his properties and invest the net realizations in Government approved securities and pay certain legacies out of the income from the investment. On the deceased's death, the assessee (i.e. Official Trustee) applied for and granted probate of the will.

The assessee's claim that for the assessment years 1962-63 to 1964-65 and 1966-67, he should be assessed only as a trustee and that income derived by him from the properties held for charitable purposes, could not be assessed was disallowed by the ITO who held that since all the immovable properties of the deceased had not been sold during the assessment years, the assessee could not be said to have discharged the executorial functions, and that, therefore, the assessee having acted only as an executor under the will of the deceased during the years in question the income was liable to be taxed in his hands only, under section 168, and not as a trustee. On appeal, the AAC observed that the deceased had clearly stated in the will that the assessee was to be the sole executor, that he should sell all the properties and the net realisations including the cash should be invested in Government securities and that, therefore, the assessee could not shed his character as an executor so long as he had not completed the sale of the properties. On further appeal, the Tribunal allowed assesee's claim holding that where the official trustee was appointed as a trustee by a testator under his will, there was no question of an executor functioning at all, that even if there was any executor he had to transfer the properties subject to the trust after obtaining the probate of the will to the trustee, that the directions contained in the will regarding the sale of the properties merely amounted to a direction for conversion of the properties from one kind to another, that the official trustee was bound to pay the legatees, carry out the duties such as discharge of the debt and payment of legacies, etc., as a trustee and that, therefore, the properties of the deceased had become vested in the assessee as trustee from the very inception and that in any event after the official trustee obtained probate of the will of the deceased he had ceased to be an executor and had assumed the character of a trustee. The Tribunal also upheld the claim of the assessee that the income from the properties held by him in trust in so far as it related to religious and charitable purposes was exempt from tax under section 11. It also held that the official trustee was a representative assessee as contemplated in sections 160(1)(iii) and 160(1)(iv) and as such he had to be assessed only in the manner indicated in section 161(1) and that the amounts disbursed by him to the various relatives of the deceased as per the terms of the will could not be aggregated together for the purpose of ascertaining the tax and that tax on such amounts had to be levied separately and the aggregate-tax had to be recovered from the assessee.

The assessee-firm was deriving income from managing agency and financing business. The assessee-firm was appointed as managing agent to a company under an agreement, dated 6-1-1948. The remuneration of the managing agent was fixed by clause 2 of the agreement which included, inter alia, 15 per cent commission on the net profits of the company (within the meaning of section 87(c)(3) of the Indian Companies Act, 1913), with a minimum profit of Rs. 25,000 in a year in case of inadequacy of profits’

The assessee-firm contended before the ITO that the minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 could be claimed by the assessee only if there was no loss to the managed company after charging such commission in the profit and loss account of the managed company, that in the assessment year in question, i.e., 1954-55, the managed company did not make any profit, and that no commission was, therefore, paid to the assessee-firm. But, on a scrutiny of the profit and loss account of the managed-company, the ITO found that the managed company made in the relevant year a profit of Rs. 5,571 before charging any commission payable to its managing agent, i.e., the assessee-firm. The ITO, therefore, held in his assessment order dated 30-3-1959, that, according to clause 2(b) of the managing agency agreement, the assessee-firm was entitled to a minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 from the managed company, that the assessee firm had earned the commission, and that if the assessee-firm chose not to claim the minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 from the managed company, it only meant a voluntary surrender of the amount by the assessee firm for extra-commercial consideration. He, accordingly, included the sum of Rs. 25,000 in the total income of the assessee-firm.

Against the said assessment order of the ITO the assessee-firm preferred an appeal to the AAC and contended that, on a correct interpretation of clause 2(b) of the managing agency agreement, the assessee-firm was entitled to a minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 only when the profit of the managed company exceeded Rs. 25,000, that since in the relevant year the managed company made a profit of only Rs. 5,571 before charging any commission payable to the assessee-firm, no commission had at all accrued to the assessee-firm, and that, therefore, the said amount ought not to have been included in the total income. The AAC by his order dated 4-9-1961, rejected the said contention, and held that on a plain reading of clause 2(b) of the managing agency agreement, it was clear that, in case of in adequacy of profits, the assessee-firm was entitled to the minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 and that as there was a profit of Rs. 5,571 in the profit and loss account of the managed company for the relevant year, the assessee-firm was entitled to the minimum commission of Rs. 25,000.

A second contention was urged before the AAC that, even if it was held that the minimum commission of Rs. 25,000 had accrued to the assessee-firm under clause 2(b) of the agreement, the said sum should have been held to be an admissible deduction, as the amount was surrendered or waived by the assessee-firm on grounds of commercial expediency. The AAC rejected this contention also on the ground that the surrender of managing agency commission was merely a gratuitous act in the circumstances of the case.

The Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the assessee.

The assessee-trust was created by a deed of trust by settlor for the benefit of her three unmarried daughters, who had equal shares in the income and corpus of the trust. Under the trust deed, the net income of the trust was to be divided in three equal parts and applied for the benefit of the three beneficiaries. After the trust had worked in the prescribed manner for 12 years, the trustees and the beneficiaries entered into three agreements whereby (i) the trustees decided to grant annuities of Rs. 5,000 per month to each of the three beneficiaries, (ii) the beneficiaries assigned their rights and shares in the residuary income, after the payment of aforesaid annuities, to a charitable trust, called J Trust, and (iii) the beneficiaries by separate deeds of gift gifted away their interest in the corpus of the trust property of the assessee-trust. It was contended before the ITO by the assessee-trust that only an annual amount of Rs. 1,80,000 should be appor-tioned amongst the three beneficiaries and the balance of income should be allocated to J Trust. The ITO however, held that the beneficiaries were not empowered to part with any portion of their rights under the original trust deed and that the income first accrued to the beneficiaries and thereafter was applied for charitable purposes and, therefore, it was a case of application of income and not of diversion of income by an over-riding title in favour of J Trust. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) the assessee contended, inter alia, that in view of section 11 and section 58 of the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, beneficiaries had the power to part with any portion of their interest and in fact the interest of the beneficiaries in the balance income of the assessee-trust in excess of Rs. 1,80,000 was effect-ively diverted at source and, therefore, it no longer belonged to them. The Commissioner (Appeals) accepted the assessee's contention and set aside the ITO's order.

The assessee, a registered firm, was appointed as the managing agents of a company. The duration of the managing agency period was 20 years. The managing agency agreement provided that the company would pay each year to the managing agents 5 per cent commission on the proceeds of the total sales of yarn and of all cloth sold by the company or three pies per pound avoirdupois on the sale, whichever the managing agents chose; that the company would also pay 10 per cent on the proceeds of sales of all other materials; that the mills were to pay to the managing agents each year after December 31, or such other date which the directors of the company may choose for the closing of the accounts. There was a further clause that if the net profits of the managed company were not sufficient to enable the directors to recommend a dividend of 8 per cent per annum on the paid up capital, then the managing agents were bound to forgo a portion of their commission up to one-third. On 9-12-1950, the managing agency agreement was modified as to the commission payable under it and that the managing agents had agreed to charge 3 per cent on sales instead of 5 per cent, for the year ending 31-12- 1950. A resolution was passed at the annual general meeting of the managed company on 22-4-1951, and it was ratified at an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed company on 7-10-1951. For the assessment years 1951-52 and 1952-53, the managing agents were taxed by the income-tax authorities on the basis that in those two years they had voluntarily relinquished a sum. These sums were added to the income of the managing agents for the purpose of income-tax. On appeal, the Tribunal held that the agreement between the managing agents and the managed company to receive remuneration at 3 per cent on the total sales was a valid one and took effect as from 1-1-1950. It also held that commission did not accrue as the managing agents were to get the amount of commission after the whole profit was determined at the end of the year. On reference, the High Court decided in favour of the managing agents.

The assessee society was a Charitable Institution registered under section 12AA. The main objects of the society were to provide education, medical relief to the poor and objects of general public utility. It was running lodging accommodations at two places and had two auditoriums and a ground, which had a commercial value to be let out for public functions, exhibitions, etc. The society maintained a swimming pool, recreation centers and gymnasium. Two schools and a home were also formed and maintained for the deprived children. Relief activities in times of flood and other natural calamities were also being carried out by the society. The Auditorium and the hall were let out to members and non-members. Rooms were also let out to members and non-members, which included providing of food.

The Assessing Officer held that the assessee was carrying on business activities. As regards the letting out of the Auditoriums, the ground and letting of rooms the society was charging rent as well as providing food and beverages to the persons, who were occupying such rooms. The assessee took contention that the income from these activities was not business income but income from the property. However, the contention of the assessee was rejected holding the view that letting out of the hall and the open space and hiring out rooms amounted to business and, hence, the income therefrom was assessable as business income. Thus, the Assessing Officer viewed that the assessee would be ineligible for exemption under sections 11 and 12.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) agreed with the assessee that the receipts from letting off of the rooms and the Auditorium constitute income from a house property and thus directed the Assessing Officer to grant the benefit under section 11.

On second appeal the Tribunal held that the question as to whether the assessee was earning income as incidental to the activities of the society or whether the assessee was really engaged in business activity was required to be examined by the Assessing Officer and for this the matter was deserved to be remitted back to the Assessing Officer to examine afresh in all these aspects.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust entered into an agreement with a private limited company for transfer of operations, management, and movable assets of hospital to it, since object of transfer agreement was to ensure that hospital was managed professionally and purpose of charity was not violated, assessee's claim for tax exemptions under sections 11 and 12 could not be denied

The assessee was a charitable trust enjoying exemption from tax in the earlier assessment years. During relevant assessment year, the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee was earning rental income from sub-letting the properties. According to the Assessing Officer, the said exercise done by the assessee for earning income was not incidental to the attainment of the object of the trust and, thus, income so earned was to be assessed as income from business by applying the provisions of section 11(4A).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that the provisions of section 11(4A) were not attracted and income earned from sub-letting the property was for the charitable object and hence, the exemption under section 11 was to be allowed. On revenue's appeal, the Tribunal held that to enable the trust to carry out its charitable object in effective manner if rental income was received by way of sub-letting, for that reason, the exemption could not have been denied by the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal :

Business held as property in trust

The business held as property under trust, i.e., held as corpus, is used as a ‘means’ of achieving the object of the trust. It is the medium through which the objects are accomplished. It produces or results in income, like any other property [Thiagarajar Charities v. Addl. CIT [1977] 92 Taxman 152 (SC)]

Sassoon & Company (Sasoons) were the managing agents of three companies. The Sassoons transferred their managing agencies of the said companies to other companies. The Sassoons executed in favour of the transferee companies formal deeds of assignment and transfer and received from them the net consideration of Rs. 75,77,693. This was taken by them to the "Capital Reserve Account". The accounts of the managing agency commission payable by the respective companies to the managing agents for the year 1943 were made up in the year 1944 and the transferee companies received from managed companies certain amounts as and by way of such commission.

For the assessment year 1944-45 the original income-tax assessment of the Sassoons were made on a total income of Rs. 46,48,483. This income however did not include any part of the managing agency commission received by the transferees. The entire amounts of the managing agency commission received by the transferees were assessed by the ITO for the assessment year 1945-46 as the income of the transferees. The Tribunal accepted the transferees' contention that the managing agency commission received by them should be apportioned on a proportionate basis and the transferees should be made liable to pay tax only on the commission earned by them during the period that they had worked as the managing agents of the respective companies.

The ITO discovered that the amounts of the managing agency commission earned by the Sassoons prior to the dates of the respective transfers were not brought to tax and therefore issued on 29-6-1946, notice under section 34 of 1922, Act upon the Sassoons on the ground that their income from the managing agency had escaped assessment, the amount proposed to be included was Rs. 28,51,934. According to ITO, such managing agency commission had accrued to the Sassoons for services rendered upto the dates of transfers so that on the dates on which the agencies were transferred the Sassoons were entitled to such remuneration from the managed companies. In spite of the objection of the Sassoons the ITO determined the said sum as their escaped incomes and assessed them accordingly. The AAC dismissed assessee's appeals. The Tribunal relied upon its order in the case of the transferees and confirmed the orders of the AAC. The Tribunal was of the opinion that the managing agency commission was earned for services rendered and therefore, it was taxed in the hands of the person who carried on the business of the managing agency and not in the hands of the person to whom it was assigned, and that therefore so far as the Sassoons were concerned the managing agency commission should be apportioned between them and their transferees. On references by the assessee and the Department, the decision of the High Court was against the contentions which had been urged both by the Sassoons and the Commissioner. The High Court adopted test of the services rendered by the Sassoons as well as the transferees during the whole of the year and considered the proportions of the services rendered by the Sassoons and the transferees as the managing agents of the companies as decisive of the portions of the managing agency commission earned respectively by each. The High Court held in substance that (1) the managing agency remuneration for the year in question accrued as the joint income of the both the assignor and the assignee and was apportionable between them, and (2) the assignee-companies received the assignor's share of the joint income by virtue of the assignments of the assignor's share and hence to that extent it was not their taxable income but continued to be the taxable income of the assignor. The income was held assessable to tax not on the basis of receipt but on the basis of accrual.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee, a trust existing for charitable purposes, gave interest-free loans to needy persons. When the loans were repaid, the ITO treated the repayments of such loans, received back by the assessee, as the assessee's income for the years in which sum repayments were made. On appeal, the AAC set aside the ITO's order on the ground that repayments of the loans did not constitute taxable income of the assessee and on further appeal, the Tribunal upheld the AAC's order.

On reference, the assessee contended that the money received from or returned by the beneficiaries could not be deemed to be the income derived from the property held under trust in the absence of any deeming provision in section 11.

TRUST

Other legal obligation - The words 'or other legal obligation' cover a case in which the trustees of the original settlement are bound to pay income to other trustees who in their turn are bound to apply it for purposes which are religious or charitable [Vallabhdas Karsondas Natha v. CIT [1947] 15 ITR 32 (Bom.); Sree Sree Iswar Gopal Jew v. CIT [1950] 18 ITR 743 (Cal.)].

Section 11 does not apply to a case where a trust or legal obligation is not created on any property, but only the income derived from any particular property or source is set apart and charged for a charitable or religious purpose. The expression 'legal obligation' cannot be separated from "property" itself, inasmuch as law enjoins that such property must be held under a trust or other legal obligation, and not the fund derived therefrom [CIT v. P. K. Barooah [1970] 77 ITR 967 (Gauhati)].

Wakfs and endowments are included - A trust under the Indian law would include Moslem wakfs and Hindu Endowments [Trustees of the 'Tribune', In re [1939] 7 ITR 415 (PC)].

Registration is not required - For purposes of section 11, there is no requirement under the law that a trust should be registered under the Societies Registration Act [CIT v. Arya Vysya Kalyana Nilaya Sangam [1986] 159 ITR 324 (AP)]. Also see, CIT v. Dr. (Miss) Chandrakanta Rohatgi [2006] 150 Taxman 19 (All.).

Determining nature of trust - Determination of nature of trust as wholly religious or wholly charitable or both charitable and religious is not a question of fact. It is but a question which requires examination of legal effects of the proven facts and documents, i.e., the legal implication of the objects of the trust as contained in the trust deed. It is only the objects of a trust as declared in the trust deed which would govern its right of exemption u/s 11 or 12 [CIT v. Dawoodi Bohara Jamat [2014] 43 taxmann.com 243/222 Taxman 228 (SC)].

'Property held under trust in part', meaning of - The expression 'in part' does not refer to an aliquot part; if half a house is held in trust wholly for religious and charitable purposes, the subject-matter of the trust is only the said half of the house, and that half is held wholly for religious and charitable purposes. The expression 'in part' therefore must apply to a case other than a property, a part of which is held wholly for religious or charitable purposes. The dichotomy between the two expressions 'wholly' and 'in part' is not based upon the dedication of the said property wholly for religious or charitable purposes or in part for such purposes [CIT v. P. Krishna Warrier [1964] 53 ITR 176 (SC)].

PROPERTY HELD UNDER TRUST [SECTION 11(4)]

Applicability - Section 11(4) would have no application in case of a charitable trust or institution falling within any of the heads of the definition 'charitable purpose' except under the head 'advancement of any other object of general public utility' [Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Manufacturers Association [1979] 2 Taxman 501 (SC)].

'Income', meaning of - The income spoken of in section 11(4) appears to be the gross income and not the net income of the business undertaking [CIT v. Birla Education Trust [1985] 21 Taxman 134 (Cal.)].

Business commenced by trustees - Since katha business was commenced by trustees with the aid and assistance of borrowings from sister concerns, it could not be case of 'property being held under trust' within the meaning of section 11(4) but would only be a case of business being carried on by and on behalf of trust and mere fact that whole or some part of income from katha business was earmarked for application of charitable objects would not render business itself being considered as incidental to attainment of objects of trust [CIT v. Mehta Charitable Prajnalay Trust [2012] 28 taxmann.com 73/[2013] 214 Taxman 88 (Delhi), SLP granted inMehta Charitable Prajnalaya Trust v. CIT [2017] 82 taxmann.com 149/248 Taxman 145 (SC)].

INCOME TAX: Where assessee-trust registered under section 12A/12AB carried out environmental protection activities and earned receipts mainly from contractual arrangements incidental to its objects, application of such receipts wholly for charitable purposes did not alter their charitable character, and exemption under section 11 could not be denied merely because income arose from such arrangements

in case of a trust or an institution having obtained registration u/s 12AA as well as approval u/s 10(23C)(vi), if registration is withdrawn at some point of time due to certain adverse findings, the withdrawal of approval u/s 10(23C)(vi) shall not be automatic but will depend upon whether these adverse findings also impact the conditions necessary to keep approval u/s 10(23C)(vi) alive.

3. Generation of surplus out of gross receipts A doubt has been raised whether generation of surplus out of gross receipts would necessarily 'breach' the threshold condition that the educational institution should exist 'solely for educational purpose and not for the purpose of profit'. Perusal of prescribed provisions clearly reveal that mere generation of surplus cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) on the ground that it amounts to an activity of the nature of profit making. In fact, the third Proviso to the said clause clearly provides that accumulation of income is permissible subject to the manner prescribed therein provided such accumulation is to be applied "wholly and exclusively to the objects for which it is established". Hence, it is clarified that mere generation of surplus by educational institution from year to year cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) if it is used for educational purposes unless the accumulation is contrary to the manner prescribed under law.

4. Collection of amounts under different heads of fee from students—

It has been brought to the notice that collection of small amounts from students by way of application fee, examination fee, fee for issuing transfer certificate, subscription fee for library etc. is being treated by some Assessing Officers as profit making activity resulting in denial of exemption u/s 10(23C)(vi). Collection of small and reasonable amounts under different heads of fee, which are essentially in the nature of fee connected with imparting education and do not violate any Central or State regulation does not, in general, represent a profit making activity. Hence, there is no justification for treating the charging of small amounts under different heads of fee as profit making activity unless the amount in the nature of 'capitation fee' is charged directly or indirectly.

5. Impact of extraordinary powers of the Managing Trustees to appoint remove or nominate other trustees.

5.1 Doubt has been expressed whether extraordinary powers to the Managing Trustees to appoint or remove other trustees and also to nominate their successor affect the nature of charitable activity of the trust and whether in such an eventuality, exemption can be denied.

5.2 There is no provision under the Act which calls for denial of exemption merely on account of appointment or removal of trustees. Although answer to such a situation would normally depend on the factual implication of such arrangement, the same should generally not be a ground for denying exemption unless the nature of activities of the trust or institution get changed or modified or no longer remain to exist 'solely for educational purpose and not for purposes of profit'. Courts have considered when it can be regarded that the income is applied wholly for charitable purposes or otherwise and have laid down the following principles or guidance.

In the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT[1976] 103 ITR 777 the Supreme Court held as follows: “If one of the objects of the trust deed is not of a religious or charitable nature and the trust deed confers full discretion on the trustees to spend the trust funds for an object other than of a religious or charitable nature, the exemption from tax under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, is not available to the assessee.

If the primary or dominant purpose of a trust is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but which is merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purpose would not prevent the trust from being a valid charity.” (pg. 777)

It must also be noted that the existence of a non-charitable object may not render the trust invalid if the trust deed itself provides that the trustees shall not carry out any object, which is held to be non-charitable. This concept was delivered by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case of CIT v. Mahendra Mohta Sewa Nidi[1985] 152 ITR 516 where it was held that:

“There was not only a positive command in the trust deed that the objects mentioned in it which were not found charitable should not be carried out by the trustees but also in fact no amount was actually spent on such an object. Therefore, the assessee was a charitable trust entitled to exemption under section 11.” (pg. 516)

It was also very well explained in The Law and Practice of Income-tax Volume 1 by Kanga, Palkhiwala & Vyas, page no. 516

“(iv) The property may be held upon trust to apply a specified part of the income to charitable purposes and the balance of the income to non-charitable purposes. 1 For instance, where a wakf is created with a direction to apply half of the income to charity and the other half for the benefit of the wakf’s descendants, the property is held in part only upon charitable trusts. 2 However, this type of cases where a specified part of the income is directed to be applied to charity should be distinguished from cases where a specified part of the corpus is held upon charitable trusts. Where a specified part of the income is set apart by the author of the trust for charitable purposes, the case falls within sub-section (1)(b),—property held in part only for charitable purposes. But where a definite specified part of the corpus itself is held upon charitable trust, the remainder of the corpus being settled upon non-charitable trusts, qua the portion of the corpus which is settled upon charitable trusts, the case falls within sub-seciton (1)(a), since that portion of the property is held under trust wholly for charitable purposes. In Chaturbhuj Vallabhdas v. CIT 3 a testator directed that three-fourths of his estate should be utilized for charity, while the remaining one-fourth was to be given in the discretion of the trustee to the testator’s descendants. Held, the three-fourths of the estate was property held in trust wholly for charitable purposes.”

While section 2(45) specifically defines 'total income', the expression used in section 11(1) is 'only income'. Accordingly, it would be incorrect to assign to the word 'income' used in section 11(1)(a), the same meaning as has been specifically assigned to the expression 'total income' in section 2(45). The CBDT in Circular No. 5P (LXX-6), dated 19-6-1968 has also adopted the same approach. Even in interpreting the several provisions of the Act, wherever the expression 'income' occurs, there has been some divergence in the meaning given to that expression on account of the particular context involved. In the context of section 11, which contemplates application or accumulation of income for charitable or religious purpose, it has necessarily to be the income as accounted for in the accounts and not a computed under the Act. Hence, for the purpose of section 11(1) the expression 'income' has to be understood in the popular or general sense, i.e., in the sense what is actually available in the hands of the assessee subject, of course, to any adjustment for expenses extraneous to the trust. It is only the income as available to the assessee and, over which the assessee has power to enjoy which can be applied or accumulated for charitable purposes. Moreover, wherever the statute contemplated the income being computed in the manner set out in the provisions of the Act, appropriate words are used. Such is not the case with section 11(1). Hence, income from the properties held under trust would have to be arrived at in the normal commercial manner without reference to the provisions which are attracted by section 14.

In other words, it would not be possible for such an institution to contend that since the income derived is used for charitable purpose, it is incidental to the attainment of the objectives, it should constitute charitable purpose (as was held by Supreme Court in Asstt. 1.2-4 Effects of the amendment- Note the following:

1.2-4a Taxability - Any trust or institution, which in the pursuit of its Other Objects, carries on any 'specified activity' and the proviso applies to it, from assessment year 2009-10, the object would not be considered as charitable purpose and, hence, it would not be eligible for the exemption of income applied towards the objects.

Accordingly, all the provisions of the Act relating to taxability, computation, payment of taxes, filing of returns, etc., would apply.

Depending on the nature of income, it will have to be classified under the applicable heads.

While computing its income, the relevant provisions of the Act will have to be applied for determining the income as well as allowability of expenses.

Such trusts or institutions will have to note the difference between deduction of expenses and application of income. To illustrate, while they were eligible for exemption, even capital expenditure could have been claimed as application of income. However, such a claim would not be allowable in computation of its income. Similarly, voluntary contributions were not considered as income earlier on account of the specific provisions. However, once it loses the exemption, such contributions may also be considered as income liable to tax.

1.2-4b Liability to FBT - An employer is liable to fringe benefits tax, in terms of the provisions of Chapter XII-H of the Act.

Section 115W(a) defining 'employer' excludes any person registered under section 12AA of the Act.

In terms of the amendment, any trust or institution, to which new proviso to section 2(15) applies, may no longer continue to have registration under section 12AA of the Act and, therefore, the trust or institution would be considered as employer.

If so, the trust or institution may be liable to FBT, subject to the provisions of Chapter XII-H of the Act.

1.2-4c Position in case of trusts or institutions having mixed objects - Section 11(1)(a) confers exemption to income applied wholly for charitable purposes.

Section 11(1)(b) of the Act confers exemption to income applied even partly for charitable purposes, in case of trusts or institutions established before 1st April, 1962.

There may be certain trusts or institutions, which may have its objects education and the Other Objects. They pursue both the objects and apply the income derived from the property on both the objects.

If the Other Objects do not constitute charitable purpose, on account of the applicability of the proviso, in terms of section 11(1)(a), it cannot be said that the income derived from the property held in trust is wholly applied towards charitable purposes.

Accordingly, such a trust or institution would lose the exemption under section 11.

Although, not intended, this is the result.

For continuation of the exemption, the trust or the institution will have to ensure that none of the objects is such that it cannot be considered as charitable purpose.

1.2-3 Irrespective of its application - The proviso stipulates that even if the income derived from disqualifying activities (carrying on any activity in the nature of trade or rendering any services in relation to the trade) are used for charitable purpose, the disqualifying activities would render Other Object as non-charitable purpose.

In other words, it would not be possible for such an institution to contend that since the income derived is used for charitable purpose, it is incidental to the attainment of the objectives, it should constitute charitable purpose (as was held by Supreme Court in Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust[2001] 115 Taxman 126/247 ITR 785).

1.2-4 Effects of the amendment - Note the following:

1.2-4a Taxability - Any trust or institution, which in the pursuit of its Other Objects, carries on any ‘specified activity’ and the proviso applies to it, from assessment year 2009-10, the object would not be considered as charitable purpose and, hence, it would not be eligible for the exemption of income applied towards the objects.

Accordingly, all the provisions of the Act relating to taxability, computation, payment of taxes, filing of returns, etc., would apply.

Depending on the nature of income, it will have to be classified under the applicable heads.

While computing its income, the relevant provisions of the Act will have to be applied for determining the income as well as allowability of expenses.

Such trusts or institutions will have to note the difference between deduction of expenses and application of income. To illustrate, while they were eligible for exemption, even capital expenditure could have been claimed as application of income. However, such a claim would not be allowable in computation of its income. Similarly, voluntary contributions were not considered as income earlier on account of the specific provisions. However, once it loses the exemption, such contributions may also be considered as income liable to tax.

1.2-4b Liability to FBT - An employer is liable to fringe benefits tax, in terms of the provisions of Chapter XII-H of the Act.

Section 115W(a) defining ‘employer’ excludes any person registered under section 12AA of the Act.

In terms of the amendment, any trust or institution, to which new proviso to section 2(15) applies, may no longer continue to have registration under section 12AA of the Act and, therefore, the trust or institution would be considered as employer.

If so, the trust or institution may be liable to FBT, subject to the provisions of Chapter XII-H of the Act.

1.2-4c Position in case of trusts or institutions having mixed objects - Section 11(1)(a) confers exemption to income applied wholly for charitable purposes.

Section 11(1)(b) of the Act confers exemption to income applied even partly for charitable purposes, in case of trusts or institutions established before 1st April, 1962.

There may be certain trusts or institutions, which may have its objects education and the Other Objects. They pursue both the objects and apply the income derived from the property on both the objects.

If the Other Objects do not constitute charitable purpose, on account of the applicability of the proviso, in terms of section 11(1)(a), it cannot be said that the income derived from the property held in trust is wholly applied towards charitable purposes.

Accordingly, such a trust or institution would lose the exemption under section 11.

Although, not intended, this is the result.

For continuation of the exemption, the trust or the institution will have to ensure that none of the objects is such that it cannot be considered as charitable purpose.

Courts have considered when it can be regarded that the income is applied wholly for charitable purposes or otherwise and have laid down the following principles or guidance.

In the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT[1976] 103 ITR 777 the Supreme Court held as follows:

Although, not intended, this is the result.

For continuation of the exemption, the trust or the institution will have to ensure that none of the objects is such that it cannot be considered as charitable purpose.

Courts have considered when it can be regarded that the income is applied wholly for charitable purposes or otherwise and have laid down the following principles or guidance.

In the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 777 the Supreme Court held as follows: "If one of the objects of the trust deed is not of a religious or charitable nature and the trust deed confers full discretion on the trustees to spend the trust funds for an object other than of a religious or charitable nature, the exemption from tax under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, is not available to the assessee.

If the primary or dominant purpose of a trust is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but which is merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purpose would not prevent the trust from being a valid charity." (pg. 777)

It must also be noted that the existence of a non-charitable object may not render the trust invalid if the trust deed itself provides that the trustees shall not carry out any object, which is held to be non-charitable. This concept was delivered by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case of CIT v. Mahendra Mohta Sewa Nidi [1985] 152 ITR 516 where it was held that:

"There was not only a positive command in the trust deed that the objects mentioned in it which were not found charitable should not be carried out by the trustees but also in fact no amount was actually spent on such an object. Therefore, the assessee was a charitable trust entitled to exemption under section 11." (pg. 516)

It was also very well explained in The Law and Practice of Income-tax Volume 1 by Kanga, Palkhiwala & Vyas, page no. 516

1.2-4d Generally - In the light of the amendments, any trust or institution claiming exemption under sections 11 to 13 will have to examine:

Whether objects include any object, which could be classified as the Other Object?

Whether it is pursuing any activity, which can be classified or has been classified as the Other Object?

Whether the activity pursued is correctly classified as the Other Object? Can it otherwise fall under the specific objects, namely: the relief of poor, education or medical relief?

Whether the activity involved in pursuit of the Other Objects is in the nature of trade?

Whether the activity involved in pursuit of the Other Objects amounts to rendering of services in relation to the trade? If so, whether it is for a consideration?

Whether newly inserted proviso to section 2(15) is applicable?

If not, the reasons thereof.

If yes, the implications, if any, in respect of the specific objects (the relief of poor or education or medical relief).

Whether income derived from the property held in trust can be and is also applied towards the objects, which do not constitute charitable purpose (in particular, on account of the applicability of the proviso)?

'Property', meaning of - The word 'property' in section 13(2) will have to be understood as having been used in its own generic sense to include 'movable and immovable property' [Agappa Child Centre v. CIT [1997] 92 Taxman 327 (Ker.)].

'Lending' and 'investment' - In the process of investment, the element or risk is involved and the expectation of return or profit is not assured and the depletion of capital itself is not an abnormal feature. In the case of lending, the return by way of interest is generally assured and the element of risk is minimal. When an amount is advanced on an agreed rate of interest, the transaction is within the fold of 'lending' and it cannot be considered as 'investment' [CIT v. Polisetty Somasundaram Charities [1990] 188 ITR 377 (AP)].

In the case of lending by trusts, clause (a) of section 13(2) will apply and not clause (h) [CIT v. Sarladevi Sarabhai Trust (No. 2) [1988] 40 Taxman 388 (Guj.)].

Relationship of borrower and lender must exist - For an amount to fall within the mischief of section 13(2)(a), there must be a loan. To constitute a loan, there must be a positive act of lending, coupled with an acceptance by the other side of the money as a loan. The relationship of borrower and lender must come into existence by the act of parties [CIT v. Nachimuthu Industrial Association [1983] 14 Taxman 224 (Mad.)].

Decision binding if the point is the same

2.38 Thus the principle of res judicata or estoppel though cannot strictly apply to the decisions rendered in proceedings under the Income-tax Act, they have a binding effect both on the assessee as well as the revenue, if the point on which the decision has been given is the same. On the basis of this principle the Madras High Court1 held that the decision on the question whether a certain trust is charitable or not, has nothing to do with the fluctuations in the income, and that such questions, if decided by a Court on a reference made to it, would be res judicata and the same question cannot be subsequently reagitated. It may be stated that in that case, the question was already considered by the Supreme Court2 as to whether the assessee would be entitled to exemption, wherein the claim for deduction of the donation made to the assessee-trust was rejected by the Supreme Court on the ground that the assessee-trust could not be held to be entitled to the benefit of exemption because some of the objects of the trust were not charitable and the trustees had discretion to spend the income of the trust on charitable and non-charitable objects. The matter turned on the finding already arrived at by the Supreme Court as to whether the trust in question was a charitable one or not and so the question of exemption was based on the previous finding regarding the nature of the trust.

The Supreme Court in CIT v. Durga Prasad More3, held that though neither the principle of res judicata nor the rule of estoppel was applicable to the assessment proceedings, the fact that the assessee included the income of the premises in his returns for several years after objecting to its inclusion in the year 1942-43, was a circumstance which the taxing authorities were entitled to take into consideration in the absence of any specific explanation and that the Tribunal was right in holding that the house property was not the trust property. The Supreme Court proceeded to consider the question as to whether the finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal was in any way vitiated and it was held that it was not in any way vitiated.

The term 'held wholly for charitable and religious purposes' as occurring in section 11 would mean that property in question is not assigned to any other purpose or used directly or indirectly either in the objects clause of the trust or by the trustees in practice. Assigning of corpus, i.e., capital asset wholly for the purpose of charitable work and not assigning for any non-charitable purpose would be sufficient compliance of provisions of section 11(1A). The Circular No. 72 of the Board further supports this proposition. If the assigner partly assigns the property for charitable work and partly for non-charitable work or the property after assigning or acquisition is partly assigned to charitable work and partly to non-charitable work then on transfer of such an asset, proportionate exemption to the extent asset is assigned for charitable work would be available and no exemption to capital gain in respect of that portion thereof which arises from that part of the property which is assigned for or held for non-charitable purposes, would be available. It is not the case that passive holding of the land or non-use of the land would mean that it is assigned or held for non-charitable purposes. Non-use of the land or passiveness of the land is not equivalent to its holding for non-charitable purposes which alone can forfeit the exemption as per sub-section (1A) of section 11 and Circular No. 72, dated 6-1-1972.

1.2-4c Position in case of trusts or institutions having mixed objects - Section 11(1)(a) confers exemption to income applied wholly for charitable purposes.

Section 11(1)(b) of the Act confers exemption to income applied even partly for charitable purposes, in case of trusts or institutions established before 1st April, 1962.

There may be certain trusts or institutions, which may have its objects education and the Other Objects. They pursue both the objects and apply the income derived from the property on both the objects.

If the Other Objects do not constitute charitable purpose, on account of the applicability of the proviso, in terms of section 11(1)(a), it cannot be said that the income derived from the property held in trust is wholly applied towards charitable purposes.

Accordingly, such a trust or institution would lose the exemption under section 11.

Although, not intended, this is the result.

For continuation of the exemption, the trust or the institution will have to ensure that none of the objects is such that it cannot be considered as charitable purpose.

Courts have considered when it can be regarded that the income is applied wholly for charitable purposes or otherwise and have laid down the following principles or guidance.

In the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT[1976] 103 ITR 777 the Supreme Court held as follows:

“If one of the objects of the trust deed is not of a religious or charitable nature and the trust deed confers full discretion on the trustees to spend the trust funds for an object other than of a religious or charitable nature, the exemption from tax under section 4(3)(i) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, is not available to the assessee.

If the primary or dominant purpose of a trust is charitable, another object which by itself may not be charitable but which is merely ancillary or incidental to the primary or dominant purpose would not prevent the trust from being a valid charity.” (pg. 777)

It must also be noted that the existence of a non-charitable object may not render the trust invalid if the trust deed itself provides that the trustees shall not carry out any object, which is held to be non-charitable. This concept was delivered by the Punjab and Haryana High Court in the case of CIT v. Mahendra Mohta Sewa Nidi[1985] 152 ITR 516 where it was held that:

“There was not only a positive command in the trust deed that the objects mentioned in it which were not found charitable should not be carried out by the trustees but also in fact no amount was actually spent on such an object. Therefore, the assessee was a charitable trust entitled to exemption under section 11.” (pg. 516)

It was also very well explained in The Law and Practice of Income-tax Volume 1 by Kanga, Palkhiwala & Vyas, page no. 516

“(iv) The property may be held upon trust to apply a specified part of the income to charitable purposes and the balance of the income to non-charitable purposes. 1 For instance, where a wakf is created with a direction to apply half of the income to charity and the other half for the benefit of the wakf’s descendants, the property is held in part only upon charitable trusts. 2 However, this type of cases where a specified part of the income is directed to be applied to charity should be distinguished from cases where a specified part of the corpus is held upon charitable trusts. Where a specified part of the income is set apart by the author of the trust for charitable purposes, the case falls within sub-section (1)(b),—property held in part only for charitable purposes. But where a definite specified part of the corpus itself is held upon charitable trust, the remainder of the corpus being settled upon non-charitable trusts, qua the portion of the corpus which is settled upon charitable trusts, the case falls within sub-seciton (1)(a), since that portion of the property is held under trust wholly for charitable purposes. In Chaturbhuj Vallabhdas v. CIT 3 a testator directed that three-fourths of his estate should be utilized for charity, while the remaining one-fourth was to be given in the discretion of the trustee to the testator’s descendants. Held, the three-fourths of the estate was property held in trust wholly for charitable purposes.”

The words 'applied or finally set apart for application' in the second part of clause (i) of section 4(3) of the 1922 Act [corresponding to section 11 of the 1961 Act] indicated that unless the income from the property was applied or finally set apart for religious or charitable purposes within the taxable territories, it did not earn the exemption. A different meaning should not be given to the expression 'applied or accumulated for application' in the first part of the clause; for, on principle, there could not be any possible distinction between income from property wholly held in trust or that which forms a part of the property held in trust. The words 'applied' and 'accumulated', therefore, meant 'applied or finally set apart'. 'Applied' meant that the income was actually applied for charitable or religious purposes in the taxable territories; and 'accumulated' meant that the income was set apart during the year for future spending on such purposes. The expression 'accumulated' for a purpose involved a conscious act in praesenti and posited a clear indication on the part of the trustee to set apart the income for that purpose.

11.4 Hitherto, section 13 provided that the income of a charitable or religious trust would not be exempt if any part of income or the property of the trust or institution was used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person such as the author of the trust or the founder of the institution, trustee of the trust or manager or relative of such person (hereinafter referred to as a 'specified person') or any concern in which any such person has a substantial interest.

Section 13 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2001-02 and a new sub-section (6) has been added which provides that a trust running an educational institution or a medical institution or a hospital shall not lose the benefit of exemption of any income other than the value of benefits of educational or medical facilities provided to the specified persons, solely on the ground that such benefits have been provided to specified persons. In other words, the value of any such income received from specified persons would be taxable, however, the other income would remain exempt.

The expression 'value' has been defined in Explanation to section 12(2) of the Act, as 'the value of any benefit or facility granted or provided free of cost or at concessional rate'.

The new provisions would apply only to charitable or religious trust running a hospital or a medical institution or an educational institution. They would not apply to all institutions eligible for exemption under section 11 of the Act, e.g. sanitariums, religious trusts, etc., would not get the benefits of the new provisions.

It appears that the value of facility provided to the specified persons would be taxable and no deduction shall be allowed in respect of expenses incurred in providing services to the specified person.

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill reads as follows -

"The existing provisions provide that the income of a charitable or religious trust will not be available if any part of such income or any property of the trust is used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person such as the author of the trust, trustee or any relative of such persons or any concerns in which such persons have a substantial interest (referred to as a specified person). It is proposed to insert a new sub-section in section 13 to provide that a trust running an educational institution or a medical institution or a hospital shall not lose the benefit of exemption of any income other than the value of benefits of educational or medical facilities provided to the specified persons, solely on the ground that such benefits have been provided to specified persons."

This gives an impression that the amendment is made for all categories of interested persons including concerns.

However, the residual category specified in section 13(3)(e), namely, 'any concern in which any person referred to in clauses (a), (b), (c), (cc) and (d) has a substantial interest' is not specifically mentioned in sections 12(2) and 13(6). Thus, it is not clear as to whether a trust will lose tax exemption if any benefit is given directly or indirectly to the residual category in section 13(3)(e).

3.2-6c Basic exemption

Section 11(1)(a) reads as follows:

"Income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India; and, where any such income is accumulated or set apart for application to such purposes in India, to the extent to which the income so accumulated or set apart is not in excess of fifteen per cent of the income from such property". The expression "such" means the purposes referred to in the earlier part of the section, that is, charitable or religious purposes. Hence, even the income accumulated or set apart has to be applied towards charitable or religious purposes in India. Now, the amendment states that any corpus donation shall not be treated as "application of income for charitable or religious purposes". Hence, if the accumulated income up to 15% is utilized by a charitable institution for giving corpus donation, then on a literal interpretation, the income could be regarded as applied towards non-charitable/religious purpose, thus, violating the condition that even accumulated income has to be applied towards charitable or religious purposes. A consequence would be that the income of the year to which the basic exemption pertains may become taxable in the said year. To illustrate, if the 15% basic accumulation of assessment year 2014-15 is utilised for grant of corpus donation in assessment year 2018-19, the exemption given in assessment year 2014-15 may be withdrawn on the basis of literal interpretation. This does not appear to be intended and a clarification from the CBDT or a statutory amendment will help in eliminating the exposure.

Income derived from the property held under trust for charitable or religious purposes to the extent such income is applied to such purposes in India, is to be excluded for the purposes of computing the income of the trust under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1961. The word ‘applied’ means ‘to put to use’ or ‘to turn to use’ or ‘to make use’ or ‘to put to practical use’. When the income of a trust is used or put to use to meet the expenses incurred for religious or charitable purposes, it is applied for charitable or religious purposes. The said application of the income takes place in the year in which income is adjusted to meet the expenses incurred for religious or charitable purposes. In other words, even if expenses for religious or charitable purposes have been incurred for the earlier year and the said expenses are adjusted to meet the expenses. In other words, even if expenses for charitable or religious purposes have been incurred for the earlier years and the said expenses are adjusted against the income of a subsequent year, the income of that year can be said to have been applied for charitable and religious purposes in the year in which the expenses incurred and adjusted [CIT v. There was a difference between a payment made as compensation for the termination of an agency contract and an amount paid as solatium for the cancellation of a contract entered into by a businessman in the ordinary course of business. In an agency contract, the actual business consists in the dealings between the principal and his customers, and the work of the agent is only to bring about that business. What he does is not the business itself but something which is intimately and directly linked up with it. The agency may, therefore, be viewed as the apparatus which leads to the business rather than the business itself. Considered in this light, the agency can be held to be of the nature of a capital asset invested in business. But this cannot be said of a contract entered into in the ordinary course of business. 3.8. Powers of Assessing Officer under Section 11(4)

Section 11(4) defines "property held under trust" and deals with the determination of income of a business undertaking. The term 'property held under trust' includes a business undertaking. Therefore, income from the business will qualify for an exemption, provided the said business is held under trust for charitable or religious purposes.

Where a claim is made that the income of such undertaking shall not be included in the total income of the persons in receipt thereof, the Assessing Officer shall have power to determine the income of such undertaking in accordance with the provisions relating to assessment. Where any income so determined is in excess of the income shown in the accounts of the undertaking, such excess shall be deemed to be applied to purposes other than charitable or religious purposes.

It may be noted that the Assessing Officer has the power to determine business income under section 11(4) as per the provisions of the Act, which would imply that all provisions of the Act shall apply. However, this power is available to the AO during the assessment proceedings, and there is no provision to suggest that the assessee is required to compute income in a manner other than applicable to charitable institutions under section 11.

The text of Section 11(4) is reproduced herein below:

(4) For the purposes of this section "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held, and where a claim is made that the income of any such undertaking shall not be included in the total income of the persons in receipt thereof, the Assessing Officer shall have power to determine the income of such undertaking in accordance with the provisions of this Act relating to assessment; and where any income so determined is in excess of the income as shown in the accounts of the undertaking, such excess shall be deemed to be applied to purposes other than charitable or religious purposes.

The Assessing Officer has been given the power to determine the income of such business in accordance with the provision of this act, but this subsection nowhere provides that the income shall be computed under the head Profits & Gains from Business. MoreovertheCBDT Circular No. 5-P(LXX-6) Dt. 19th June 1968 has clarified as under:

"In the case of a business undertaking, held under trust, its "income" will be the income as shown in the accounts of the undertaking"

Therefore, a legitimate claim can be made that the income of such business may not be included in the total income of the person receiving such income. 1.2 Section 11 of the Act provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent of the application of such income. Section 2(15) of the Act defines ‘charitable purpose’ and includes :

◆ Relief of the poor;

◆ Education;

◆ Medical relief; and

◆ The advancement of any other object of general public utility (‘the Other Object’).

1.2-1 Amendment in definition of charitable purpose - Finance Act, 2008 substitutes the above definition, effective 1st April, 2009, that is, assessment year 2009-10 and provides that if the pursuit of the Other Object involves carrying on of specified activities, it shall not be considered as charitable purpose, as stipulated in the proviso.

Newly inserted proviso to section 2(15) lays down the ‘specified activities’ and they are :

◆ Carrying on of any activity in the nature of trade, commerce or business (hereafter referred to as ‘the trade’); or

◆ Carrying on of any activity of rendering any service in relation to the trade, for a fee or cess or any other consideration.

The proviso further lays down that if the specified activities are pursued in pursuit of the Other Object, it would not be considered as a charitable purpose irrespective of the nature of use or application or retention of income arising from the specified activities.

1.2-2 Analysis of the amendment - It may be noted from the newly inserted proviso that—

1.2-2a Application of proviso restricted to the Other Object - Newly inserted proviso would apply only if the specified activities are carried out in the pursuit of the Other Objects.

If the specified activities are carried out in relation to the relief of poor, education or medical relief, it would still constitute charitable purpose. To illustrate, if a trust assists poor women to meet and market household products, being an object providing the relief to poor and in the process it, renders certain services in relation to the business or actually carries on any activity in the nature of business, the proviso would not apply and it cannot be said that it is not a charitable purpose.

Courts have considered the following objects as ‘education’.

◆ To set up a statutory board for promotion of education. 1

◆ To extend financial assistance to poor and deserving students by way of loans, scholarships, and grant for purchase of books and other educational requisites. 2

Courts have considered the following objects as ‘the relief of poor’.

◆ To form a Scheme to relieve poverty among unemployed agriculturists by providing them with work. 3

◆ To make provision of help for marriages or sacred thread ceremonies. 4

◆ To undertake rehabilitation of economically handicapped women and destitute by giving them suitable employment. 5

◆ To help poor and public utility bodies, such as, mosques, schools, water supply, etc. 6

Further, it may also be noted that the trusts or institutions claiming exemption under section 10(23C) of the Act may also be not affected inasmuch as the objects eligible for the said exemption, by and large, do not constitute the Other Objects.

1.2-2b Other Objects - Courts have considered, from time to time, various objects, for the purposes of classification, and have held that the objects listed in Annex 1.1 would constitute Other Objects.

Accordingly, in pursuit of the above objects, if a trust or institution carries out the specified activities, it may not constitute charitable purpose.

1.2-2c Pursuit of Other Objects to involve carrying on of the specified activities - The proviso would apply only if the pursuit of the Other Objects involves carrying on of the specified activities. In other words, the proviso would not apply if the pursuit of the Other Objects does not involve carrying on of the specified activities.

To illustrate, a trust owns a house property and allows the user thereof by a certain class of working persons, free of any cost. In such a case, it cannot be said that the trust is carrying on any activity in the nature of business. Accordingly, to such a trust the proviso would not apply and, therefore, its object would continue to be a charitable purpose.

1.2-2d Carrying on of any activity in the nature of trade - The proviso, as such, does not define ‘activity in the nature of trade’.

SALARY DUE [SECTION 15(a)]

"Due", implication of - The expression "due" shows that there should be an obligation on the part of the employer to pay that amount and a right on the part of the employee to claim the same (i.e., a vested right) [CIT v. L. W. Russel [1964] 53 ITR 91 (SC)].

Forgoing salary - A distinction has to be made in forgoing salary before it becomes due and in surrendering the same after it has become due or has accrued. In the former case, there will be no accrual of salary while in the latter case, it would be an application of the salary which had become due and payable [CIT v. Mehar Singh Sampuran Singh Chawla [1973] 90 ITR 219 (Delhi)].

Writing-off or waiver on the part of the assessee after the income from "Salaries" had become due to him cannot amount to anything more than disposal of the income. The concept of real income where the income falls under the head "Salaries" cannot help the assessee [CIT v. Bachubhai Nagindas Shah [1976] 104 ITR 551 (Guj.)].

ADVANCE SALARY [SECTION 15(b)]

'Paid' and 'allowed', meaning of - The expression "paid" takes in its sweep every receipt of contemplated payments to the employee whether it was due to him or not by the employer. Another expression "allowed", in the legal terminology, is equivalent to 'fixed, taken into account, set apart, granted' [CIT v. L. W. Russel [1964] 53 ITR 91 (SC)].

Termination of service - The agreement stated that the employer might terminate the services of the assessee by giving either 12 months' notice in writing or paying any salary in lieu thereof. Consequently, the employer, instead of giving notice in writing, has paid 12 months' salary and, therefore, the employee received 12 months' salary though he did not work for such period. By no stretch of imagination, it could be said that such payment was in consideration of the surrender by the recipient of his rights in respect of the office. Therefore, that amount held not to be treated as compensation for loss of employment but simply taxable as 'salary' u/s 15 [V. D. Talwar v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 122 (SC)].

Tips to employees - Tips, being voluntary amounts, that may or may not be paid by the customers for the services rendered to them would not fall within the ambit of section 15(b) since there being no vested right in the employee to claim any amount of tip from his employer or former employer. Consequently, tips are received by the employer in the fiduciary capacity as trustee for payments that are received from customers which they disburse to their employees for services rendered to such customers [ITC Ltd. v. CIT [2016] 68 taxmann.com 323/239 Taxman 372 (SC)].

The words "if not charged to income-tax" are wide enough to include cover those cases where the charge could or could not have been imposed [CIT v. Sardar Arjun Singh Ahluwalia [1999] 107 Taxman 246 (SC)].

Group company - Monies given by assessee-trust to sister concern purportedly for construction of hospital and which was kept lying unused with sister concern could not be regarded as having been applied for charitable purposes [CIT v. V. G. P. Foundation [2003] 134 Taxman 663 (Mad.)].

Improvement of property - Expenditure on improvement of a property held under trust would by itself not come within the scope of 'application of income' for charitable purposes [CIT v. Kannika Parameswari Devasthanam & Charities [1982] 133 ITR 779 (Mad.)].

Incomes exempt u/s 10 - While computing exempt income u/s 11, incomes which are exempt u/s 10 are to be excluded [DIT v. Jasubhai Foundation [2015] 58 taxmann.com 218 (Bom.)].

Interest on corpus donations - Where assessee received corpus donation on which it earned interest, assessee's claim for exemption in respect of interest so earned was also to be allowed [CIT v. Provision - Where an amount was set apart as provision in the accounts of the assessee and the finding of fact was that the amount was not actually applied for charitable or religious purposes, assessee would not be entitled to exemption u/s 11 in respect of that amount [Nachimuthu Industrial Association v. CIT [1999] 235 ITR 190 (SC)].

Repayment of borrowed funds - Repayment of funds borrowed for construction of building could be treated as 'application of income' for charitable purposes and, thus, entitling assessee to exemption [CIT v. Janmabhumi Press Trust [2000] 242 ITR 457 (Kar.); DIT v. Span Foundation [2009] 178 Taxman 436 (Delhi); DIT v. Govindu Naicker Estate [2009] 315 ITR 237 (Mad.)].

11.4 Hitherto, section 13 provided that the income of a charitable or religious trust would not be exempt if any part of income or the property of the trust or institution was used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person such as the author of the trust or the founder of the institution, trustee of the trust or manager or relative of such person (hereinafter referred to as a 'specified person') or any concern in which any such person has a substantial interest.

Section 13 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2001-02 and a new sub-section (6) has been added which provides that a trust running an educational institution or a medical institution or a hospital shall not lose the benefit of exemption of any income other than the value of benefits of educational or medical facilities provided to the specified persons, solely on the ground that such benefits have been provided to specified persons. In other words, the value of any such income received from specified persons would be taxable, however, the other income would remain exempt.

The expression 'value' has been defined in Explanation to section 12(2) of the Act, as 'the value of any benefit or facility granted or provided free of cost or at concessional rate'.

The new provisions would apply only to charitable or religious trust running a hospital or a medical institution or an educational institution. They would not apply to all institutions eligible for exemption under section 11 of the Act, e.g. sanitariums, religious trusts, etc., would not get the benefits of the new provisions.

It appears that the value of facility provided to the specified persons would be taxable and no deduction shall be allowed in respect of expenses incurred in providing services to the specified person.

The Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill reads as follows -

"The existing provisions provide that the income of a charitable or religious trust will not be available if any part of such income or any property of the trust is used or applied directly or indirectly for the benefit of any person such as the author of the trust, trustee or any relative of such persons or any concerns in which such persons have a substantial interest (referred to as a specified person). It is proposed to insert a new sub-section in section 13 to provide that a trust running an educational institution or a medical institution or a hospital shall not lose the benefit of exemption of any income other than the value of benefits of educational or medical facilities provided to the specified persons, solely on the ground that such benefits have been provided to specified persons."

This gives an impression that the amendment is made for all categories of interested persons including concerns.

However, the residual category specified in section 13(3)(e), namely, 'any concern in which any person referred to in clauses (a), (b), (c), (cc) and (d) has a substantial interest' is not specifically mentioned in sections 12(2) and 13(6). Thus, it is not clear as to whether a trust will lose tax exemption if any benefit is given directly or indirectly to the residual category in section 13(3)(e).

11.4-1 Amendment of section 12 - A new sub-section (2) has been inserted in section 12 with effect from the assessment year 2001-02. It provides that the value of any medical or educational services made available by any charitable or religious trust running a hospital or medial institution or an educational institution to any specified person shall be deemed to be the income of such trust or institution derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes during the previous year in which such services are so provided and shall be chargeable to income-tax notwithstanding the provisions of section 11(1).

Charitable purpose [Section 2(15)]

1.2 Section 11 of the Act provides for exemption in respect of income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent of the application of such income.

Section 2(15) of the Act defines ‘charitable purpose’ and includes :

◆ Relief of the poor;

◆ Education;

◆ Medical relief; and

◆ The advancement of any other object of general public utility (‘the Other Object’).

1.2-1 Amendment in definition of charitable purpose - Finance Act, 2008 substitutes the above definition, effective 1st April, 2009, that is, assessment year 2009-10 and provides that if the pursuit of the Other Object involves carrying on of specified activities, it shall not be considered as charitable purpose, as stipulated in the proviso.

Newly inserted proviso to section 2(15) lays down the ‘specified activities’ and they are :

◆ Carrying on of any activity in the nature of trade, commerce or business (hereafter referred to as ‘the trade’); or

◆ Carrying on of any activity of rendering any service in relation to the trade, for a fee or cess or any other consideration.

The proviso further lays down that if the specified activities are pursued in pursuit of the Other Object, it would not be considered as a charitable purpose irrespective of the nature of use or application or retention of income arising from the specified activities.

1.2-2 Analysis of the amendment - It may be noted from the newly inserted proviso that—

1.2-2a Application of proviso restricted to the Other Object - Newly inserted proviso would apply only if the specified activities are carried out in the pursuit of the Other Objects.

If the specified activities are carried out in relation to the relief of poor, education or medical relief, it would still constitute charitable purpose. To illustrate, if a trust assists poor women to meet and market household products, being an object providing the relief to poor and in the process it, renders certain services in relation to the business or actually carries on any activity in the nature of business, the proviso would not apply and it cannot be said that it is not a charitable purpose.

Courts have considered the following objects as ‘education’.

◆ To set up a statutory board for promotion of education. 1

◆ To extend financial assistance to poor and deserving students by way of loans, scholarships, and grant for purchase of books and other educational requisites. 2

Courts have considered the following objects as ‘the relief of poor’.

◆ To form a Scheme to relieve poverty among unemployed agriculturists by providing them with work. 3

◆ To make provision of help for marriages or sacred thread ceremonies. 4

◆ To undertake rehabilitation of economically handicapped women and destitute by giving them suitable employment. 5

◆ To help poor and public utility bodies, such as, mosques, schools, water supply, etc. 6

Further, it may also be noted that the trusts or institutions claiming exemption under section 10(23C) of the Act may also be not affected inasmuch as the objects eligible for the said exemption, by and large, do not constitute the Other Objects.

1.2-2b Other Objects - Courts have considered, from time to time, various objects, for the purposes of classification, and have held that the objects listed in Annex 1.1 would constitute Other Objects.

Accordingly, in pursuit of the above objects, if a trust or institution carries out the specified activities, it may not constitute charitable purpose.

1.2-2c Pursuit of Other Objects to involve carrying on of the specified activities - The proviso would apply only if the pursuit of the Other Objects involves carrying on of the specified activities. In other words, the proviso would not apply if the pursuit of the Other Objects does not involve carrying on of the specified activities.

To illustrate, a trust owns a house property and allows the user thereof by a certain class of working persons, free of any cost. In such a case, it cannot be said that the trust is carrying on any activity in the nature of business. Accordingly, to such a trust the proviso would not apply and, therefore, its object would continue to be a charitable purpose.
