In this case, the Court observed that the language of section 11(1)(a) makes it clear that the income derived from the property held under trust wholly for charitable and religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India, is excluded. When once the income from the property, as such, is excluded, there is no question of computing the income from the property by applying the provisions of section 14.

(c)

`Income' must be understood in a commercial sense and not the `total income' as assessed

It is not the `total income' as would be assessed by the ITO that is relevant for the purpose of investing the funds of the trust or assessing the income of the trust. Taking into account the purpose for which the conditions of section 11(1)(a) are imposed, it would be clear that `income' to be considered will be that which is arrived at in the context of what is available in the hands of the assesse subject to an adjustment of any expenses extraneous to the trust – CIT v. P.S.G. & Sons Charities 1996 Tax LR 477 (Mad.), See also – CIT v. Programme for Community Organisation [1997] 228 ITR 620/141 CTR 502 (Ker.).

(d)

Heads of income under section 14 have no relevance and question of allowing statutory deductions will not arise

The word 'income' in section 11(1)(a) must be understood in a commercial sense [Cir. No. 5-P(LXX-6) Dt. 19th June 1968] and five heads of income as per section 14 are not applicable. Since the five heads of income under section 14 do not apply to a trust registered under section 12AB, there is no income to be computed under the head of business and profession.

The `income' contemplated by the provisions of section 11 is the real income and not the income as assessed or assessable. Since the income from property held under trust has to be arrived at in a normal commercial manner and when the income from property held under trust as such is excluded, there is no scope of computing the income from property by applying the provisions of section 14 of the Act. Therefore, the question of allowing any statutory deductions as contemplated by the different provisions of the Act dealing with different heads of income in computing the income accumulated does not arise when the trust loses the benefit of accumulation – DIT (Exmp) v. Girdharilal Shewnarain Tantia Trust [1993] 71 Taxman 150/199 ITR 215 (Cal.).

Therefore income in the case of charitable institutions is to be computed in a commercial sense and not under five heads of income, including profit and gains from business.

Should Parking Charges, Toll Charges and Driver Batta be included in the Gross amount for arriving at the service tax component in the case of Rent-a-Cab and Tourist Operator Services ?

Really no, but to be on safe side, in your agreement or terms and conditions, you should indicate ‘scope of service’ and say that other expenses are not part of the service. However, for administrative convenience, you will first pay and then recover on actual basis. This will make things a little more safe and you will fall within the definition of ‘pure agent’ in respect of those charges.

If a Rent-a-Cab operator takes a vehicle from some other Rent-a-Cab operator for few days/trips, is the latter liable to collect service tax from the former ?

Legally, he is also liable since as per section 65(105)(o ), any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a rent-a-cab scheme operator in relation to the renting of a cab is ‘taxable service’.

Change of category of service

There is no law that if you make a mistake, you should continue with the mistake for rest of life and it can never be corrected.

If a Rent-a-Cab operator takes a vehicle from person, say X who is not Rent-a-Cab operator (X has purchased a vehicle out of his savings and loan and given the vehicle to a rent-a-cab operator for some revenues which are not related to the actual amounts earned by the vehicle). X is not engaged in travel business at all.

If control of vehicle is handed over, VAT is payable and not service tax. If control over vehicle is retained by X (e.g., his own driver), then it can come under ‘supply of tangible goods for use’ and service tax will be payable.

There is a specified violation if the income of a trust is applied otherwise than for the objects of the charitable institution.

Paraphrasing, Explanation(a) applies if all the following conditions are fulfilled:

The income is applied;

The Explanation applies to charitable trusts as well as religious trusts.

‘In relation to’ is explained by Supreme Court in Doypack Systems (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Union of India (1988) 36 ELT 201 (SC) as follows:

“The expression ‘in relation to’ (so also ‘pertaining to’), is a very broad expression which pre-supposes another subject-matter. These are words of comprehensiveness which might both have a direct significance as well as an indirect significance depending on the context”. It may be noted that the words ‘in relation to’ have been given a wide meaning and would cover any service directly or indirectly provided in relation to the trade.

For a consideration

The service must be for a consideration, whether called fee or cess or by any other name. It appears that the other consideration stated in the proviso must take its colour from ‘fee or cess’, having regard to the principles of ejusdem generis.

In relation to the trade and for a consideration

It appears that the proviso does not contemplate that the services must be provided to any person or persons. It will be suffice if the services rendered are generally in respect of any trade, business or commerce, whether given to any person or class of persons or generally for the benefit of any particular trade, business or commerce or otherwise.

To illustrate, if a chamber of commerce renders services to anyone and everyone in respect of any particular activity relating to the trade, for consideration, it could be said that the chamber renders services in relation to the trade.

If a chamber of commerce agrees to promote the trade, pursuant to a specific contribution made by the members or the persons engaged in the trade, it could be said that the chamber renders services in relation to the trade and for a consideration.

However, if a trade body generally promotes the trade or industry out of its own funds, whether provided by the members or otherwise, though, it may constitute service, it may not be regarded as a service for consideration.

Following relevant extract from the reply of the Finance Minister to debate in the Lok Sabha on 29-4-2008 on the Finance Bill, 2008 may also be noted :

“6. I once again assure the House that genuine charitable organisations will not in any way be affected. In other words, it would not be possible for such an institution to contend that since the income derived is used for charitable purpose, it is incidental to the attainment of the objectives, it should constitute charitable purpose (as was held by Supreme Court in Asstt. 1.2-4 Effects of the amendment - Note the following:

1.2-4a Taxability - Any trust or institution, which in the pursuit of its Other Objects, carries on any ‘specified activity’ and the proviso applies to it, from assessment year 2009-10, the object would not be considered as charitable purpose and, hence, it would not be eligible for the exemption of income applied towards the objects.

Accordingly, all the provisions of the Act relating to taxability, computation, payment of taxes, filing of returns, etc., would apply.

Depending on the nature of income, it will have to be classified under the applicable heads.

While computing its income, the relevant provisions of the Act will have to be applied for determining the income as well as allowability of expenses.

Such trusts or institutions will have to note the difference between deduction of expenses and application of income. To illustrate, while they were eligible for exemption, even capital expenditure could have been claimed as application of income. However, such a claim would not be allowable in computation of its income. Similarly, voluntary contributions were not considered as income earlier on account of the specific provisions. However, once it loses the exemption, such contributions may also be considered as income liable to tax.

1.2-4b Liability to FBT - An employer is liable to fringe benefits tax, in terms of the provisions of Chapter XII-H of the Act.

Section 115W(a) defining ‘employer’ excludes any person registered under section 12AA of the Act.

In terms of the amendment, any trust or institution, to which new proviso to section 2(15) applies, may no longer continue to have registration under section 12AA of the Act and, therefore, the trust or institution would be considered as employer.

(b) Section 11(1) provides that subject to the provisions of sections 60 to 63, "the following income shall not be included in the total income of the previous year. . . ." The reference in clause (a ) is invariably to "Income" and not to "total income". The expression "total income" has been specifically defined in section 2(45) as "the total amount of income computed in the manner laid down in this Act". It would, accordingly, be incorrect to assign to the word "income", used in section 11(1)(a), the same meaning as has been specifically assigned to the expression "total income" vide section 2(45).

(c)

In the case of a business undertaking, held under trust, its "income" will be the income as shown in the accounts of the undertaking. Under section 11(4), any income of the business undertaking determined by the ITO, in accordance with the provisions of the Act, which is in excess of the income as shown in its accounts, is to be deemed to have been applied to purposes other than charitable or religious, and hence it will be charged to tax under sub-section (3). As only the income disclosed in the account will be eligible for exemption under section 11(1), the permitted accumulation of 25 per cent will also be calculated with reference to this income.

(d)

Where the trust derives income from house property interest on securities, capital gains, or other sources, the word "income" should be understood in its commercial sense, i.e., book income, after adding back any appropriations or applications thereof towards the purposes of the trust or otherwise, and also after adding back any debits made for capital expenditure incurred for the purposes of the trust or otherwise. It should be noted, in this connection, that the amounts so added back will become chargeable to tax under section 11(3) to the extent that they represent outgoings for purposes other than those of the trust. The amounts spent or applied for the purposes of the trust from out of the income, computed in the aforesaid manner, should be not less than 75 per cent of the latter, if the trust is to get the full benefit of the exemption under section 11(1).

(e)

To sum up the business income of the trust, as disclosed by the accounts plus its other income computed as above, will be the "income" of the trust for the purposes of section 11(1). Further, the trust must spend at least 75 per cent of this income and not accumulate more than 25 per cent thereof. The excess accumulation, if any, will become taxable under section 11(1).

It may be noted that under sections 11 to 13, there are specific references where the sections applicable under the head 'Profits & Gains of Business or Profession' are also made applicable to the computation of income under section 11. In other words, unless specifically provided, the provision of the head 'Profits & Gains of Business or Profession' shall not apply to Charitable Institutions.

The Finance Act, 2018 inserted Explanation 3 to Section 11(1) to apply the following two provisions to charitable and religious institutions:

(i)

Disallowance for payment without TDS deduction under sub-clause (ia) of clause (a) of section 40.

(ii)

Disallowance for cash payment above Rs. 10,000/- under sub-section (3) and (3A) of section 40A.

The text of Explanation 3 to Section 11(1) is reproduced as under:

"Explanation 3 - For the purposes of determining the amount of application under clause (a) or clause (b), the provisions of sub-clause (ia) of clause (a) of section 40 and sub-sections (3) and (3A) of section 40A, shall, mutatis mutandis, apply as they apply in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits & Gains of business or profession".

In light of the above, it is very clear that the statute specifically provides that some provisions applicable to business entities are required to be made applicable to charitable entities. In other words, unless specifically provided no provision corresponding to section 14 and five heads of income shall apply to charitable institutions.

3.2-6c Basic exemption

Section 11(1)(a) reads as follows:

"Income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India; and, where any such income is accumulated or set apart for application to such purposes in India, to the extent to which the income so accumulated or set apart is not in excess of fifteen per cent of the income from such property". The expression "such" means the purposes referred to in the earlier part of the section, that is, charitable or religious purposes. Hence, even the income accumulated or set apart has to be applied towards charitable or religious purposes in India. Now, the amendment states that any corpus donation shall not be treated as "application of income for charitable or religious purposes". Hence, if the accumulated income up to 15% is utilized by a charitable institution for giving corpus donation, then on a literal interpretation, the income could be regarded as applied towards non-charitable/religious purpose, thus, violating the condition that even accumulated income has to be applied towards charitable or religious purposes. A consequence would be that the income of the year to which the basic exemption pertains may become taxable in the said year. To illustrate, if the 15% basic accumulation of assessment year 2014-15 is utilised for grant of corpus donation in assessment year 2018-19, the exemption given in assessment year 2014-15 may be withdrawn on the basis of literal interpretation. This does not appear to be intended and a clarification from the CBDT or a statutory amendment will help in eliminating the exposure.

Hence, even under the pre-amendment law, such corpus donations were not permitted out of income accumulated under section 11(2).

If it is held that such donation is income, then on account of the amendment, the corpus donation given will not be regarded as application of income resulting in taxation of the ostensible corpus donation in the year of receipt.

Management, Maintenance and Repair Services

As per section 65(64) of the Finance Act, 1994 (as amended w.e.f. 16-6-2005 and by the Finance Act, 2006 w.e.f. 1-5-2006), "management, maintenance or repair" means any service provided by—(i) any person under a contract or an agreement; or (ii) a manufacturer or any person authorised by him, in relation to, (a) management of properties, whether immovable or not (b) maintenance or repair of properties whether immovable or not; or (c) maintenance or repair including reconditioning or restoration, or servicing of any goods or equipment, excluding motor vehicle.

In many cases, housing societies collect the charges from members which are termed as ‘maintenance’ charges. Hence, it is alleged that the housing society provides management, maintenance or repair.

As discussed above, the activities undertaken by housing society are a bundle of various activities, some of which might fall under ‘management, maintenance or repair’ services. However, a service can be taxed if it is predominantly a taxable service. In Daelim Industrial Co. v. CCE 2003 STT 438 = 155 ELT 457 = 57 RLT 636 = 3 STR 124 (CEGAT), it was held that a works contract on turnkey basis is not a consultancy contract. A works contract cannot be vivisected and part of it subjected to tax (SLP filed by department dismissed by SC - [2004] 170 ELT A181). This was followed in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE [2005] 1 STT 183 = 2004 (174) ELT 322 = 60 RLT 505 = 3 STR 223 (CESTAT), in respect of design element of works contract.

The principle that a contract cannot be vivisected is applicable to all services.

D.O. letter No. 334/4/2006-TRU, dated 28-2-2006 states as follows, ‘Often services provided consist of more than one service. In such cases, it is important to decide, for the purpose of classification of services, whether each element of the transaction should be treated separately or as a single composite transaction, albeit, made up of two or more separate services. A composite service, even if it consists of more than one service, should be treated as a single service based on the main or principal service and accordingly classified. The decision is to be made on question of facts and law. It will not make a difference if the tax rates of the components are the same as that of the principal service. The problem may arise when some elements are taxable and others are exempt. While taking a view, both the form and substance of the transaction are to be taken into account. The guiding principle is to identify the essential features of the transaction. The method of charging does not in itself determine whether the service provided is a single service or multiple services’.

Thus, a service can be taxed only if it is predominantly a taxable service.

The so called ‘service’ provided by housing society is not predominantly a ‘management, maintenance or repair’ service.

Hence, in my view, the service of housing society cannot be classified under that head.

Introduction

1. The recent decision of the CBEC to omit clause (v), which provided exemption from service tax for activities related to advancement of any other object of general public utility upto the prescribed monetary limits from the definition of 'charitable activity' from 1-4-2013 is an instance, which indicates CBEC's unfair treatment of charities, which enures to the welfare of the people of the country in terms of Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution of India ["the Constitution" for short].

The primary objective of any tax law and its administration is to raise revenue for funding Governmental expenditure, which, inter alia, is to be spent for the peoples' welfare. An important source of revenue to the Govt. is service tax. Article 38 in Chapter IV of the Constitution, titled Directive Principles of State Policy provides that the State shall, amongst others, provide that the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice shall ensue to all institutions of social life. This directive of the Constitution is being fulfilled by direct expenditure as also by tax foregone in the form of exemptions and deductions in tax legislations, which cost to the Govt. some financial burden as cash expenditure.

This position is well recognized in most of the countries of the world. In this context, it may be appropriate to refer to the philosophy concerning concessions permissible for charitable contributions under the U.S. Internal Revenue Code. The House Ways and Means Committee, in one of its reports, has observed as under:—

"……The exemption from taxation of money or property devoted to charitable and other purposes is based upon the theory that the Government is compensated for the loss of revenue by its relief from financial burden, which would otherwise have to be met by appropriation from public funds and by the benefit resulting from the promotion of the general welfare".

2. Exemption of income of charitable bodies

2.1 Under the I.T. Act - The principle of giving tax benefits to charities and various objects of general public utility are well enshrined in the law relating to taxation of income. Section 2(15) of the I.T. Act, 1961 (Act) defines the term 'charitable purpose' (as amended) as under:—

"Charitable purpose includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, preservation of environment [including watersheds, forests and wildlife] and preservation of monuments or places or objects of artistic or historic interest and the advancement of any other object of general public utility".

To prevent the misuse of tax concessions for charities for business purposes, two provisos were added to this definition, which read as under:—

"Provided that the advancement of any other object of general public utility shall not be a charitable purpose, if it involves the carrying on of any activity in the nature of trade, commerce or business, or any activity of rendering any service in relation to any trade, commerce or business, for a cess or fee or any other consideration, irrespective of the nature of use or application or retention of the income from such activity:

Provided further that the first proviso shall not apply, if the aggregate value of the receipts from the activities referred to therein is twenty-five lakh rupees or less in the previous year."

Sections 11 and 10(23C) of the Act provide for exemption from tax of the incomes derived by charitable institutions on the fulfilment of the prescribed conditions.

For ensuring that undeserved institutions do not avail of tax benefits, the Act vide section 12A provides for registration of such institutions with the Chief Commissioners/Commissioners of Income-tax of the respective regions by making applications in the prescribed forms with relevant accounts and documents duly audited. Section 12AA prescribes the procedure for registration and lays down the time-limit within which the registration is to be granted. Sub-section (3) of section 12AA prescribes for cancellation of registration, if the activities of the Trust/Institution, which has been allowed registration, are found to be non-genuine or it is noticed that the activities of the institution are not being carried on in accordance with the objects of the trust/institution, as the case may be. Thus, I.T. Act has well-known law and procedure for giving tax benefits to charitable organizations, which are for the welfare and benefit of the people.

2.2 Under the Service Tax law - Regretfully, it is noticed that such important issue was being treated under the service tax legislation by the CBEC in a routine and arbitrary manner – not appreciating the spirit and purpose behind giving tax benefits to charitable institutions. In the pre 1-7-2013 period, the CBEC took a very narrow view regarding charitable activities, as could be seen from later discussion.

Income from incidental Business under section 11(4A)

The Text of Section 11(4A) is reproduced herein below:

(4A) Sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) or sub-section (3A) shall not apply in relation to any income of a trust or an institution, being profits and gains of business, unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objectives of the trust or, as the case may be, institution, and separate books of account are maintained by such trust or institution in respect of such business.

Business income shall be eligible for exemption under Section 11 if it is incidental to the attainment of objectives of the trust and separate books of account are maintained by the trust in respect of such business. We need to understand the meaning of business incidental to the attainment of main objects.

In the case of Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 115 Taxman 126/247 ITR 785/165 CTR 681, the Supreme Court held that a business whose total income is utilised for the purposes of achieving the objects of the trust should be considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects.

In the case of CIT v. Janakiammal Ayyandar Trust [2005] 277 ITR 274 (Mad.), the Supreme Court ruling was reaffirmed where the seemingly unrelated business of manufacturing paper cap was held to be incidental as the entire income was applied for charitable purposes. The Madras High Court referred to the Apex Court in Thanthi Trust (supra) holding section 11(4A) of the Act, as amended in 1992.

The High Court of Delhi in the case of Pr. CIT v. Servants of People Society [2021] 133 taxmann.com 244/[2022] 284 Taxman 461 held that where main object of assessee-society was running a printing press and publishing a newspaper and profit so generated was being ploughed back for charitable activities and Commissioner itself had granted registration to assessee under section 12A, recognition under section 10(23C)(vi) and exemption under section 80G, mischief of proviso to section 2(15) was not attracted and findings of Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal that assessee/society did not carry on any business, trade or commerce with intent of earning/distributing profit and was thus entitled to exemption under section 11(1) was agreeable.

3.11. Incidental business does not fall under the Scope of Business

Incidental business activity to achieve charitable objectives does not fall under the coverage of Business.

The Supreme Court, in several cases, has held that any business activity integrally required for the dominant charitable activity is also a charitable activity. The Supreme Court of India, in the case of Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 777, held that an incidental business activity would also be treated as a charitable activity if it is necessary and incidental to the primary activity

In Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. Dy. GIT(E) [WP(C) No. 3147 of 2012, dated 4-7-2013] while considering whether the activities of ICAI fell within the proviso to section 2(15) as introduced with effect from 1-4-2009, this court, after considering the Supreme Court decision in the case of CST v. Sai Publication Fund [2002] 122 Taxman 437/258 ITR 70/177 CTR 1 held:

"Thus, if the dominant activity of the assessee was not business, then any incidental or ancillary activity would also not fall within the definition of business."

Hence the incidental business activity to feed charity cannot be classified as a business, and therefore, the income for such incidental business-like activity is to be computed in a commercial sense as per the normal scheme of taxation as applicable to a charitable trust and the provisions to compute income under the head profit and gains from business and profession shall not apply.

4. CONCLUSION

Based on the legal jurisprudence and provisions of the Income-tax Act as discussed above, it can be concluded that there is nothing in the statute that suggests that the income of the charitable institution shall be computed under the head `Profit & Gain from Business' nor it suggests that Tax Audit under section 44AB shall apply to charitable trusts. Sections 11 to 13 are independent of the five heads of income. As long as the registration under section 12AB is intact, the income cannot be computed under the five heads of income.

Brand owners hold intellectual property rights over the brand names, whereas other persons hold license granted by the State Government to manufacture under the brand name of the brand owner. The brand owner enters into an agreement with such manufacturers/licencee to grant permission to use their brand as well as also provide technical staff/assistance to maintain required quality. Property, risk and reward of the products so manufactured rest with such manufacturer/licensee. Such manufacturer/licensee pays on the agreed sum to the brand owner for grant of permission to use the brand name and the technical know-how. The Board through instruction F.No. 249/1/2006-CX.4, dated 27-10-2008 has clarified that in such cases brand owner provides taxable service, i.e., intellectual property service to licensee/manufacturer, on which service tax is chargeable on the gross amount charged by the brand owner.

Whether amount paid for booking of space and time for advertisement falls under advertising services?

No. The Government vide its Circular No. 341/43/96-TRU, dated 31-10-1996 has clarified that the amount paid by the advertising agency for space and time in getting the advertisement published in print media, i.e., news papers, periodicals, etc., or the electronic media, i.e., Doordarshan, private TV Channels, All India Radio, etc., will not be includible in the value of taxable service for the purpose of levy of service tax.

Whether ordinary transporters are different from courier services?

Yes. The Government has clarified vide its Circular No. 341/43/96-TRU, dated 31-10-1996 that the nature of business of a ‘courier agency’ is quite distinct from ordinary transporters, which carry goods from one place to another, whereas ‘courier agency’ delivers time sensitive documents, goods and articles.

Whether preservation of wasteland and bringing it into use falls under consulting engineer services?

No. In the case of CCE v. Nippon KOEI Co. Ltd. [2007] 8 STT 449 (Bang. - CESTAT), the Tribunal held that the appellants were carrying out ECO conservation works to preserve the wasteland and bringing it into use, especially for development of tribals. The said activity can’t be considered as activity coming within the ambit of ‘consulting engineer services’.

Whether facility of use of premises to the members by clubs falls under mandap keeper services?

No. In the case of Dalhousie Institute v. Asstt. Commissioner, Service Taxcell 2005 (180) ELT 18/1 STT 15 (Cal.), the High Court held that tax is recoverable from the ‘mandap keeper’ who is having a different and separate legal and physical entity, and lets out the mandap with commercial and trading object. Here the members have formed the petitioner No.1 to serve themselves mutually and for this purpose members are paying for such user and any amount of receipt alone, and not third party, therefore clubs are not liable to service tax as mandap keeper.

Whether services provided by managing director or the director of the company fall under the management or business consultant services?

The Board through Circular No. 115/09/2009-ST, dated 31-7-2009 has clarified that remuneration paid to the managing directors/directors of the companies whether whole-time or independent when being compensated for their performance as managing directors/directors would not be liable to service tax.

Whether photography service is taxable even if works contract tax is applicable?

Yes. In the case of Kerala Colour Lab Association v. Union of India 2003 (156) ELT 17/[2007] 8 STT 353 (Ker.), the High Court held that once we determine the taxable event as the service rendered, and not the sale of goods, irrespective of whether it is a works contract or contract for sale of goods, the taxable event would occur. The taxable event occurs because of the service rendered. Merely because the measure or valuation of tax is linked with gross consideration received in the transaction, it does not determine the nature of tax. The taxable event determines the true event of tax; the measure of tax does not determine the nature of tax, but the quantum of tax which can be levied and collected.

11. Proposals for Charitable & Religious Trust

11.1. Period of registration of smaller charitable trusts or institutions

Under the current provisions of the ITA, Section 12AB grants registration to charitable trusts or institutions for a period of five years, and where activities have not commenced at the time of application, provisional registration for three years. To ease compliance for smaller trusts or institutions whose total income before exemption does not exceed Rs. 5 crores in each of the two previous years preceding the year of application, it is proposed to extend the validity of registration from five years to ten years. However, this benefit shall not apply to trusts or institutions applying for registration for the first time, whether before or after commencing activities.

11.2. Rationalisation of 'specified violation' for cancellation of registration of trusts or institutions

Section 12AB(4), inter alia, provides that when the registration or provisional registration of a trust or institution has been granted, and the PCIT/CIT subsequently notices the occurrence of one or more specified violations during any previous year, the PCIT/CIT shall pass a written order cancelling the registration of such trust or institution if satisfied that one or more specified violations have taken place. The Explanation to Section 12AB(4) states that "specified violation", inter alia, includes cases where the application referred to in Section 12A(1)(ac) is incomplete or contains false or incorrect information. It is proposed that the Explanation to Section 12AB(4) be amended to clarify that an incomplete application for the registration of a trust or institution shall not be considered a specified violation for the purpose of cancellation by the PCIT/CIT.

11.3. Relaxation in the classification of specified persons

Section 13 of the ITA, inter alia, provides that Section 11 or Section 12 shall not apply to exclude any income from the total income of a trust or institution if such income enures to, or if any income or property of the trust or institution is used or applied, directly or indirectly, for the benefit of any person referred to in Section 13(3). Any person who has made a contribution to the trust or institution of more than Rs. 50,000 up to the end of the relevant previous year is regarded as a specified person. Additionally, the relatives of such substantial contributors and concerns in which they have a substantial interest are also considered specified persons. The Finance Bill 2025 proposes to amend Section 13(3) to provide that a person is to be treated as a substantial contributor under Section 13(3)(b) if his contribution during the previous year exceeds Rs. 1 lakh or his total contribution during the lifetime of the trust exceeds Rs. 10 lakhs. The relatives of substantial contributors shall no longer be treated as specified persons for the purposes of Section 13(3). Further, any concern in which a substantial contributor has a substantial interest shall no longer be included in the category of specified persons under Section 13(3).

In many instances, the specified domestic and international transactions occurring over several years are similar and repetitive in nature. These transactions involve the same enterprises, functions, asset and risk analysis (FAR), and the same ALP determination. This creates unnecessary compliance and administrative burdens for both assessees and the TPO.

Section 65 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Franchise service - Courier agency

5.10 Assessee was a courier agency with a wide network of above 45 hubs located at various stations in South India. Its agents were centered around these hubs and they collected and delivered time-sensitive letters/articles to consignees. With aid of this network, assessee acted as a courier agent and transported articles between hubs. Revenue demanded service tax from assessee in category of ‘Franchise service’ and also imposed penalty. It was found that under a standard agreement entered into with each appointed agent, the assessee and each courier agent attached to the hubs had a relation as between principal and agent. Assessee controlled and administered their activities. Those agents were not conferred with any representational right by assessee. They were entitled to use name of assessee only as an ‘authorised agent’. Registration certificates issued to those agents carried endorsement that they were agents of assessee; that they returned courier charges received from clients to assessee, while retaining their expenses and remuneration and there was no payment of fee to assessee as required by section 65(47 ).

The Tribunal held that from 16-6-2005, the franchise service involves provision of a service associated with a particular person by trade mark, service mark, trade name or logo. The registration certificates issued to the agents carried the endorsement that they were agents of the assessee. The so-called franchisees being agents who undertook the work of courier agency on behalf of the assessee, it could not be held that any other service was involved in the transactions or that there was a different person receiving the service. It was further submitted that the agents were not doing business on their own account; that they were required to use consignment notes and stationery of the assessee, with the consignment notes bearing the name of the assessee; that no fee was paid by the agents and they only made a deposit with the assessee called trade deposits; that the agents paid service tax on the charges they collected from their clients, and returned the balance after retaining their expenses and remuneration; that the assessee did not impart any skill, technical know-how or managerial expertise to the agents; and, thus, there was no service rendered by the assessee to its agents to be taxed under the category ‘Franchise service’. "Franchise means an agreement by which the franchisee is granted representational right to sell or manufacture goods or to provide service or undertake any process identified with franchisor, whether or not a trade mark, service mark, trade name or logo or any such symbol as the case may be, is involved." On the basis of facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal held that it could be said that assessee undertook only courier agency’s service, engaging several agents who did not operate as ‘principals’ and, therefore, neither those agents were franchisees nor assessee, a franchisor. Accordingly, the Tribunal set aside the impugned order and allowed the appeal filed by the assessee.

CIT [2004] 90 ITD 493 (Hyd.), the issue came up before the regular bench of the Tribunal in Hyderabad. The exemptions were forfeited by virtue of section 13( l)(c ). The assessee contended that for the purposes of computing income from various projects, grants received from foreign donors could not be included in the income liable to tax, as such receipts would not be considered as income for the purposes of section 11. It was held that project grants did not form a part of the income of the assessee nor they form a part of the corpus. Voluntary contributions covered by section 12 are those contributions freely available to the assessee without any stipulation, which the assessee can utilise towards its objectives according to its own discretion and judgment. Tied-up grants for a specified purpose would only mean that the assessee which was a voluntary organisation, had agreed to act as a trustee of a special fund granted by donor with the result that it need not be pooled or integrated with the assessee’ s normal income or corpus. The Tribunal relied upon the findings of Nirmal Agricultural Society v. ITO [1999] 71 ITD 152 (Hyd.). Some relevant extracts are as under:

"The grants received from foreign donor were for specific purposes. The grants which were for specific purposes did not belong to the assessee-society, such grants did not form corpus of the assessee or its income. Those grants were not donations to the assessee so as to bring them under the purview of section 12. Voluntary contributions covered by section 12 are those contributions freely available to the assessee without any stipulation, which the assessee can utilise towards its objectives according to its own discretion and judgment. Tied-up grants for a specified purpose would only mean that the assessee which was a voluntary organisation, had agreed to act as a trustee of a special fund granted by donor with the result that it need not be pooled or integrated with the assessee ‘s normal income or corpus..." (p. 153)

Similarly, in Sukhdeo Charity v. CIT [1984] 149 ITR 470 /19 Taxman 222 (Raj.), the issue of whether specific grants were income or not was also discussed. It was observed that if the motive and intention of the donor play an important role in the utilization of the donation, then it cannot be considered as voluntary in nature. The word ‘ voluntary ’ in its very inception connotes the absence of any obligation on the part of the donor.

In the above case, the Court referred to the case of CIT v. Shri Billeswara Charitable Trust [1984] 145 ITR 29/16 Taxman 259 (Mad.).

In the above case, the Court ruled that a grant received for specific purposes cannot by any stretch of imagination be said to be income as envisaged by section 12(1). Because the word ‘ voluntary ’ in its very inception connotes the absence of an obligation on the part of the donor.

This circular was withdrawn vide Circular No. 96/7/2007-ST, dated August 23, 2007. Instead, the department has issued the following clarification :— Elucidation of the concept ‘charitable’

6. The service tax legislation does not contain any definition of what could be considered as charitable. However, the Income-tax law has a definition of this phrase. There is a judicial definition also. Its coverage has been comprehensively extended by the Courts (including the Apex Court) in a number of cases coming up before them, as can be seen from the discussion to follow.

Section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 defines ‘charitable purpose’ as relief of the poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general ‘public utility’. Besides this statutory definition, the concept of charity has been widely accepted in judicial decisions in the context of conferring benefit of exemption from tax. Thus, relief of a public character to the poor is a charitable activity.

In India as well as in England, the object of ‘relief of the poor’ has always been recognized as a charitable purpose. Dealing with the scope of these words, the Supreme Court in Dharmadeepti v. CIT [1978] 114 ITR 454 observed that they include the expression ‘to give charity’ also. Thus, the object of giving charity falls within the ambit of the expression ‘relief of the poor’ used in section 2(15).

However, relief to the poor is only one facet of charitable purpose - not the primary one or the main one, as has been said in the CBEC’s circulars.

Providing education is another aspect of charitable activity for the public. In CIT v. Bar Council, Madras [1943] 11 ITR 1 (Mad.), the activity of giving facilities for legal education and training of the advocates has been held to be an educational purpose.

In Ecumenical Christian Centre v. CIT [1983] 139 ITR 226/[1982] 8 Taxman 175 (Kar.), the main objects of the assessee were diffusion of useful knowledge, publication of journal and books and promotion of search for truth. After referring to the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Lok Shikshana Trust, the Court held that the objects of diffusion of useful knowledge, publication of journals and promotion of search for truth are directly related to education. The High Court adopted a broader approach by accepting the principle that over and above normal schooling, other means of rendering scholastic instruction are also included in the definition of ‘education’ under section 2(15).

Similarly, providing medical relief has been considered to be covered under the definition of ‘charitable purpose’ under section 2(15) (supra) and accepted by the courts.

The residuary part of the definition has been held to be of very wide amplitude. One of the conditions precedent for a trust/institution to be for charitable purpose under section 2(15) is that the beneficiary thereof should be general public and that the object should not be such as resulting in private gains. The scope of the term ‘general public’ is by itself extremely wide but it is almost impossible for a particular charitable trust/institution to cover more than a section of the public. The application of the expression ‘Object of general public utility’ is not, therefore, restricted to such objects as are beneficial to the whole mankind. It is sufficient if the intention is to benefit a section of the public, provided it is well-defined and identifiable by some common quality of impersonal nature, as distinguished from specified individuals.

The classic elucidation of this phrase has been given by Lord, Macnaghten in Commr. for Special Purposes of Income-tax v. Remsel, 1891 AC 531 at 583 thus:—

"Where four principal divisions were said to be comprised-trusts for the relief of poverty, trusts for the advancement of education, trusts for the advancement of religion and trusts for other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the preceding heads. The definition in this Act makes the significant change when it speaks of ‘public utility’ and this gives a guidance to the whole meaning and purpose of the exemption [see Fazlul Rabbi Pradhan v. State of West Bengal AIR 1965 SC 1722]."

General public utility has been regarded as an important consideration in determining whether an activity is charitable or not. [This aspect has been included in describing activity of a charitable nature in the service tax law also section 65(25a)( supra). The courts’ interpretation of ‘charitable’ in the context of advancement of any other object of general public utility could be seen from some of the decisions mentioned hereinafter.

CONCEPT OF ACCRUAL OF INCOME

Sachin Vasudeva*

In this article, the author discusses the concept of accrual of income in the context of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and distinguishes it from the concept of revenue recognition as per the accountancy principles. He also casts a glance at the impact of RBI directions on the concept of accrual of income as applicable to Non-Banking Financial Companies - EDITOR

Meaning of Accrual

1. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the meaning of the word ‘accrue’ is ‘to fall as a natural growth or increment; to come as an accession or advantage’. It indicates a right to receive. Thus, it is manifest that if a person acquires a right to receive income, the income can be said to accrue to him, though it may be received later on. Unless and until there is created in favour of a person a debt due by somebody, it cannot be said that he has acquired a right to receive the income or that income has accrued to him. A mere claim to income without an enforceable right thereto cannot be regarded as accrued income for the purpose of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’).

According to Kanga & Palkhivala (7th edition, the page 170), the question of accrual of income has three aspects: the time of accrual, the person to whom the income accrues, and the place of accrual. These three aspects are considered below:

(i) Time of accrual of income - Income can be said to accrue only when the assessee acquires a right to receive that income. If, however, the income is foregone before it accrues, it cannot be taxed at all because the act of surrender prevents the accrual of income.

(ii) Person to whom income accrues - The question as to whom a particular item of income accrues is distinct and different from the question as to when the income accrues. In the case of E.D. Sassoon & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 27, the Apex Court held that ". . . in order that the income can be said to have accrued to or [been] earned by the assessee it is not only necessary that the assessee must have contributed to its accruing or arising by rendering services or otherwise but he must have created a debt in his favour. . . ." However, the question whether the proposition that no income accrues to a person unless a debt is created in his own favour is of general application and would depend upon the facts of the case.

(iii) Place of accrual of income - The question should be decided on the facts of each case in the light of commonsense and plain thinking, and too much importance should not be attached to, nor too much emphasis laid upon, the niceties of verbal definitions.

Some important judicial pronouncements

2. The concept of accrual of income under the income-tax law can be understood in the light of the following decisions :

(i) In the case of CIT v. K.R.M.T.T. Thiagaraja Chetty & Co. [1953] 24 ITR 525, the Apex Court, while deciding whether the managing agency commission payable to the assessee would be taxable in the hands of the assessee in the relevant year as the company had resolved to keep the amount in the suspense account without paying it, held that ". . .The computation of profits, whenever it may take place, cannot possibly be allowed to suspend their accrual. In the case of an income where there is a condition that the commission will not be payable until the expiry of a definite period of the making of the account, it might be said with some justification, though we do not decide it, that the income has not accrued, but there is no such condition in the present case. Clauses 7 and 8 of the agreement which relate to the payment of the commission and the calculation of the profits mean no more than this that the commission will be quantified only after certain deductions have been made and not that the commission will not accrue until the profits have been ascertained. The quantification of the commission is not a condition precedent to its accrual. If the profits of the company are said to have accrued on the 31st of March, upon a parity of reasoning, it must be conceded that the commission also accrued on the same date. . . ." (p. 534)

Hitherto, there was no specific section for taxing the certain income of a charitable institution at a specific prescribed rate.

The Finance Bill, 2022 proposes to insert Section 115BBI with effect from the assessment year 2023-24 to provide that where the total income of any "specified charitable institution" includes any "specified income", the income-tax payable shall be the aggregate of:

3.9. Intent and purpose of Section 11(4)

In the case of CIT v. Birla Education Trust[1985] 21 Taxman 134/153 ITR 579/44 CTR 263, the Calcutta High Court explained the intent and purpose of section 11(4) of the Act. In this case, it was explained that special powers were given to the AO only to ensure that the trustees or any other vested group are not misusing the exemptions available to trusts by under stating the profits of business held under trust. The High Court also quoted the explanatory statements provided by the Ministry of Finance when the Finance Bill was placed before the Parliament in 1961. The relevant extract is as under:

"It is now settled that the speech of the mover of the Bill is relevant. In Varghese v. ITO, P.N. Bhagwati J., held (at p. 608):

"Now, it is true that the speeches made by the Members of the Legislature on the floor of the House when a Bill for enacting a statutory provision is being debated are inadmissible for the purpose of interpreting the statutory provision but the speech made by the mover of the Bill explaining the reason for the introduction of the Bill can certainly be referred to for the purpose of ascertaining the mischief sought to be remedied by the legislation and the object and purpose for which the legislation was enacted. This is in accord with the recent trend in juristic thought not only in Western countries but also in India, that interpretation of a statute being an exercise in the ascertainment of meaning, everything which is logically relevant should be admissible."

Smt. Tarakeswari Sinha participating in the debate on September 1, 1961, stated in relation to Sub-section (4) of Section 11:

"Suppose a factory has got a capacity for an annual income of Rs. 15 lakhs but for avoiding a particular portion of the tax, sometimes the trustees or the donors have manipulated the accounts. They say that the income of the factory is only Rs. 10 lakhs and not Rs. 15 lakhs, thus avoiding tax payment on Rs. 5 lakhs which goes to their own pocket. For plugging this hole, actually powers were taken by the income-tax authorities to scrutinise the accounts to find out that the income shown in the books is the correct and has not been more. That was the only safeguard that has been provided by the sub-clause."

Thus, Sub-section (4) was intended to uncover tax evasion by manipulation of the account books. It was not intended to apply to application or expenditure of income by the business undertaking. As already seen, the non-application of income for purposes of the trust was dealt with by Sub-section (3) of Section 11.

It appears to us that Sub-section (4) was intended for a different contingency. It was meant to cover a different situation. It was not intended to apply to application of income.

Under Sub-section (4), the ITO can determine the income and compare it with the income appearing in the accounts. The income spoken of in Sub-section (4) appears to us to be the gross income and not the net income of the business undertaking. The net income is computed after granting the admissible deductions. The deductions admissible from income of a business undertaking are not always the same as application of income wholly for charitable or religious purposes. They may or may not be admissible deduction from business income under the provisions relating to assessment of income. Yet they are entitled to exclusion under Sub-section (1) of Section 11 because they represent application of income wholly for charitable or religious purposes.

Here, the ITO has to scrutinise the accounts and see if there is suppression of income or manipulation of accounts with a view to conceal income. He could see whether there are items which are deemed to be income under some provision of the I.T. Act and which have not been accounted for in the books of the undertaking, or there may be some receipts which are really in the nature of income and which have not been reflected in the accounts. This interpretation of Sub-section (4) of Section 11 is in consonance with the legislative intent as disclosed by the Finance Minister who spoke in Parliament while this provision was under consideration."

In light of the above, it is clear that there is no provision under section 11(4) to suggest that tax audit under section 44AB is applicable or that the AO is required to apply the provisions applicable to business assessees under section 44AB.

Statutes are considered to be in pari materia to pertain to the same subject-matter, when they relate to the same person or thing, or to the same class of persons or things, or have the same purpose or object. Obviously, law relating to levy of Income-tax and service tax are in pari materia and, hence, definition of ‘charitable purpose’ given in the Income-tax Act will be relevant for the purposes of service tax also. 9. M/s. A Pvt. Ltd. let out its premises to M/s. B Pvt. Ltd. Company A is one of the shareholders in Company B. Company A does not charge any rental to Company B for the first year trial run of business of Company B. What will be tax implications under income-tax law as well as service tax law ?

Insofar as service tax law is concerned, since there appears to be no consideration (assuming that there is no control also giving suspicion as to hidden consideration), there cannot be any charge of service tax.

However, section 22 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 deals with charge of tax under the head 'Income from House Property' and tax is levied on annual value, which is expected rent (as computed) or actual rent, whichever is higher. Hence, deemed annual value would be liable to income-tax law.

SERVICE TAX - AMENDMENT IN NEGATIVE LIST - SERVICES BY GOVERNMENT - WHETHER MCA FEES, REGISTRATION FEES, ETC., LIABLE TO SERVICE TAX ?

The first issue is whether these payments are for a 'service' or not ? In our view, service means any activity carried out by one person for another for consideration. The MCA filing fees, land registration charges, RTO license fee, etc., are not activities carried out for consideration but mere statutory fee charged by Departments/Government for assessee's compliance with law. The same does not amount to 'service' and is, therefore, not liable to service tax even after proposed amendment referred to by you.

(a)

Aspects of general public utility have been considered as charitable since long under the English law. The Statute of Elizabeth as per its preamble enumerated the following purposes as charitable:—

"The relief of aged, impotent and poor people; the maintenance of sick and mined soldiers and mariners; the maintenance of schools of learning, free schools and scholars in universities; the repair of bridges, ports, havens, causeways, churches, sea-banks and highways; the education and preferment of orphans; the relief, stock or maintenance of houses of corrections; the marriage of poor maids; the supportation, aid and help of young tradesman, handicraftsmen, and person decayed; the relief or redemption of prisoners or captives; the aid or ease of any poor inhabitants concerning payment of taxes; the setting out of soldiers."

(b)

Though the statute was repeated by the Mortmain and Charitable Uses Act, 1888 the preamble to the statute (supra) was retained in section 13(2) of the repealing Act!

(c)

The concept of charity developed in the Mortmain and Charitable Uses Act, 1888 (C.42) S. 13(2) under the four principle heads as defined or classified has been explained by Lord Macnaghten in the classic case of Commissioners for Special Purposes of Income-tax v. Pemsel [1891] AC 531, for the majority.

The dictum of Lord Macnaghten was as follows:

"Charity" in its legal sense comprises four principal divisions: trusts for the relief of poverty, trusts for the advancement of education, trusts for the advancement of religion, and trusts for other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the preceding heads. The trusts last referred to are not the less charitable in the eye of the law because incidentally they benefit the rich as well as the poor, as indeed every charity that deserves the name must do, either directly or indirectly.

Apparently, denying the exemption to the bodies that are engaged in advancing the objects of general public utility, other than those mentioned in clauses (i) to (iv) in the definition of 'charitable activity', which are no less charitable, because the same fall under the residuary head.

Concluding remarks

7. Apparently, the dropping of clause (v) from the definition of 'charitable activity' in the Notification, dated 20-6-2012 (supra) is unfair and misconceived – more so when no justification has been given for omitting it from the definition. It would be a handicap for many charitable institutions, who are doing commendable work for public welfare. The CBEC, administering the Service Tax legislation, needs to be rational in dealing with this law. It cannot be impulsive in its decisions. Taking decisions on whims and fancies, without any solid grounds, besides affecting the functioning of the concerned Department, erodes the credibility of the Government.

If there is a belief that giving tax benefits under the Service-tax law would be misused, then precautions of the nature, as taken under the I.T. Act law relating to registration, audit, etc., can be introduced for the trusts/institutions, who wish to avail of the exemptionary benefit under Service-tax legislation. But having lukewarm attitude towards such institutions, firstly by taking a narrow view about the meaning of charitable activities in Circulars in pre 1-7-2012 regime and then prescribing a reasonable scheme on the pattern of Income-tax law and curtailing its ambit just after introduction of only 9 months of the new law indicates a wavering attitude towards activities, whose efficacy for the welfare and benefit of the people of the country is well-established in the implementation of the tax legislation not only in India but in practically most of the countries.

The author, in this article, has examined the Reference No. 076.01 in the CBEC’s Master Circular dated August 28, 2007 concerning the aspect relating to exemption from service tax to persons or body of persons engaged in any activity having objectives which are of a charitable nature and has convincingly demonstrated that the CBEC’s approach in the circular interpreting the words ‘charity’ and ‘charitable’ on the basis of dictionary meaning and discarding the definition given in the Income-tax Act, 1961 is narrow and archaic in nature not in tune with the advancement of time and discard of definition as given in the Income-tax Act is not conforming with the collective functioning in the Department of Revenue in the Government of India and, therefore, the circular needs to be reviewed.

Introduction

1. Services rendered by clubs or associations to their members are taxable under the provisions of the Finance Act, 1994, vide section 65(105)( zzze). Taxable service concerning these has been defined to mean any service provided or to be provided to its members, by any club or association in relation to provision of services, facilities or advantages for a subscription or any other amount.

‘Club or association’ - Meaning of

2. Club or association has been defined in section 65(25a) (inserted by the Finance Act, 2005 with effect from June 16, 2005) to mean any person or body of persons providing services, facilities or advantages, for a subscription or any other amount, to its members, but does not include—

(i)any body established or constituted by or under any law for the time being in force; or

(ii)any person or body of persons engaged in the activities of trade unions, promotion of agriculture, horticulture or animal husbandry; or

(iii)any person or body of persons engaged in any activity having objectives which are in the nature of public service and are of a charitable, religious or political nature; or

(iv)any person or body of persons associated with press or media.

Thus, rendering of a service which is in the nature of public service and is of a ‘charitable’ nature, is exempt from levy of service tax.

Meaning of ‘charitable’

3. The Finance Act, 1994 as amended from time to time does not contain any definition of the word ‘charitable’. Hence, it has to be interpreted as per the accepted rules for interpretation of statutes. Interpretation or construction, according to Salmonds is "the process by which Courts seek to ascertain the meaning of the Legislature through the medium of authoritative forms in which it is expressed" (vide Salmonds ‘Jurisprudence’ 11th edition page 152). Legislation in the present time is generally driven by some policy to curb "some public evil or to effectuate some public benefit. The exemption aforesaid from service tax for charitable bodies is, apparently, intended to effectuate public benefit which such bodies are promoting. Referring to concessions permissible for charitable contributions under the U.S. Internal Revenue Code, the House Ways and Means Committee in one of its reports has made the following observations:

"...The exemption from taxation of money or property devoted to charitable and other purposes is based upon the theory that the Government, is compensated for the loss of revenue by its relief from financial burden which would otherwise have to be met by appropriation from public funds and by the benefit resulting from the promotion of the general welfare."

Such adjustment is permissible only if the proportionate service tax is also refunded to the person from whom the amount was received.

Such adjustment is permissible only if refund is given to the person for non-provision of service. If refund is given for some other reason, such adjustment is not permissible.

Tax on Management Consultant’s Services was introduced with effect from 16-10-1998. But the Finance Act, 2006, w.e.f. 1-5-2006 had specified the area of consultancy. For the words "relating to conceptualising, devising, development, modification, rectification or upgradation of any working system of any organisation", the words "in relation to financial management, human resources management, marketing management, production management, logistics management, procurement and management of information technology resources or other similar areas of management" had been substituted. In the clarification contained in the CBEC Circular, dated 27-6-2001, it was stated that term ‘management’ is generally understood to mean running the affairs of an organization in an organized and systematic manner. To be able to do this efficiently and effectively, management typically involves carrying out a host of activities, functions and tasks at different levels. Thus, the term ‘management’ encompasses both strategic and operational level functioning and would include tasks such as planning, organizing, staffing, directing, controlling and co-ordinating. Management also invariably involves designing organizational structure around functions such as marketing, manufacturing, research and development and finance and/or business area, such as product groups or geographical markets. Thus, management of any organization involves carrying out a wide variety of clearly defined activities across a number of organizational sub-units in a coherent and co-ordinated manner. Since the expression ‘management’ is an inclusive term, ‘management consultant’ would also be equally encompassing expression and would include any adviser, who renders services on any aspect of management10 .

In the case of Parasmal Bam v. CCE [2007] 7 STT 198 (New Delhi - CEGAT), a company had appointed assessee to advise it on matters relating to production, as well as on commercial, marketing, financial matters, etc. Consultancy bill issued by company to assessee pointed out that payment had been made to assessee for providing consultancy on various matters related to company’s affairs. So the question was whether payment made by company to assessee was towards professional charges? The Tribunal held that there is nothing in definition of ‘Management consultant’ that a management consultant should have any particular academic or professional qualification and years of experience in management gives person insight which an academician cannot gather. Therefore, lower authorities were held justified in holding assessee as a management consultant.

‘Charitable’ means ‘generous in giving to those in need’ or ‘of, or relating to, or connected with a charity or charities’. ‘Charity’ means giving voluntarily to those in need, alms-giving’ – Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Thus, the word ‘charity’ has narrow meaning in dictionary. However, the word has acquired a technical meaning in law, which is wide.

As per section 2 of Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief to poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility, but does not include a purpose which relates exclusively to religious teaching or worship. WHETHER TO ACCUMULATE PROJECT GRANTS UNDER SECTION 11(2) 9. There is a lot of confusion in this regard. Many NGOs treat such restricted grants as income for the purposes of section 11. The difficulty arises when they are unable to spend such contribution in the year of receipt as per the stipulation of the project agreement. For example, a 3 year grant is received in the first year. Now, if such grant is treated as income in the year of receipt, then 85 per cent of it has to be utilised in that year itself. But the project agreement allows only 33 per cent to be utilised in the first year. The assessee has to accumulate the income under section 11(2). There is no legal necessity for invoking section 11(2) when the grant by virtue of the project agreement was not available to the assessee for utilisation.

The above instance is of a specific grant where the instruction of the donor has to be complied with and, therefore, it cannot be treated as voluntary contribution. Such contribution should be kept in the donor account by applying principles of fund accounting. The application of such funds should be made from the donor/project account, so created. Such grant/contribution should not be included for the purposes of computing the total income under section 11.

The project contract/agreement and the ‘letter of intent/instruction ’ from the donor is of paramount importance.

LEGISLATIVE PRECEDENCE

10. It is important to have a look at the legislative precedence. The Income-tax Act till April 1, 1973 did not consider even voluntary contribution as a part of income. Only after 1-4-1973 , the scope of the Income-tax Act was broadened to include all kinds of income (capital or revenue) for the purposes of section 11. It may be noted that even corpus donation is included as a part of income and it is separately exempted under section 11(1)( d). However, the restricted grants still remain out of the purview of income, because a contractual liability cannot be treated as income. Therefore, even under the analogy of treating corpus contribution or capital receipts as income, the restricted funds should not be considered as income.

INCOME AND ITS UNCONDITIONALITY

11. Income traditionally has been considered as a surplus which is disposable at the hands of the recipient. Therefore, we have the concept of gross income to determine the net amount unconditionally available at the end for appropriations (all expenditure being a charge to income). In other words, any receipt which is subject to a charge can at best be considered as gross income even if we want to extend the definition of ‘income ’ to it. Only those receipts should be considered as income which can be appropriated in any manner and are not subjected to any charge or obligation. This is a fundamental requirement for determining income whether in business or charity.

Another trait of income is its availability to the organisation unconditionally. For instance, a voluntary contribution can be retained or used by the organisation and, therefore, the consequent use of fund is not relevant while treating it as income. Even today, an NGO can retain and accumulate the entire voluntary contribution received (it may have to pay taxes for retention of income above 15 per cent). But the point is that the discretion is available to the NGO, therefore, it fits into the definition of ‘income ’. In other words, the assets have certainly increased though they may or may not have been applied.

On the contrary, a grant based on a specific contract does not allow any freedom or discretion to the organisation as it comes as a legal obligation, which has to be supported by an legally enforceable matching liability. Therefore, there is no inflow or enhancement of asset.

There is no need to rule out the possibility of considering capital receipts as income. Whether revenue or capital, for a receipt to become income it has to be available to the recipient as surplus at its discretion, then only it can be subjected to tax. If a legal bondage or obligation is attached to it, then the net of such bondage or obligation can only be treated as income. Because we cannot treat something as income when it is not available or generated. If we treat contractual grants as income, we will be not only defying the law of natural justice but also create an overriding effect on the legal contracts, which may or may not permit an income or surplus. Incidentally, voluntary contracts do not permit a surplus. It is reiterated that irrespective of the tax laws such receipts have to be applied exactly the way specified in the contract and, therefore, the question of any individual or institutional income does not arise; which alone can be taxed or provided tax exemption with conditions to apply for charitable purposes.

The Apex Court has said that it is necessary to draw a line of distinction between what are the objects of the trust and what are the powers conferred upon the trustees for achieving objects. One should not mix the objects of the trust with the powers conferred upon the trustees as incidental to the carrying out of the objects of the trust - Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 777 (SC), Umaid Charitable Trust v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 55 (Raj.) and Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industries’ case ( supra). The powers should, under no circumstances, be confused with objects or purposes.

‘Public’ has various meanings. One of the meaning is - ‘a section of the community having a particular interest or in some special connection [Concise Oxford Dictionary]. As per section 12 of Indian Penal Code, ‘public’ includes any class of the public or any community.

Object beneficial to a section of the public is an object of ‘general public utility’ -Hiralal Bhagwati v. CIT [2008] 246 ITR 188 (Guj.).

In Municipal Council, Alleppey v. Manager, Bombay Co. Ltd. AIR 1950 TC 103, it was held that public includes a section of public. Hence, a canteen run by company exclusively for its employees and which is not open to general public is ‘public’ [ Aiyar’s Law Lexicon 1999 edition page 1554].

Even if only a section of public is benefited by land acquisition, the purpose would still be ‘public purpose’ - Secy. of State v. N. Gopala Aiyar AIR 1930 Mad. 798, Srinivasa Ayyangar v. S. Ramalinga Iyer AIR 1931 Mad. 78

Land acquisition for a particular co-operative society if for public purpose - Musamiyam Imam Haridarbux Razvi v. State of Gujarat AIR 1971 Guj. 158.

Thus, ‘public’ includes a ‘section of public’.

What is meaning of ‘charitable’ ? - ‘Charitable’ means ‘generous in giving to those in need’ or ‘of, or relating to, or connected with a charity or charities’. ‘Charity’ means giving voluntarily to those in need, alms-giving - Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Thus, the word ‘charity’ has narrow meaning in dictionary. However, the word has acquired a technical meaning in law, which is wide.

Hence, the wide meaning should apply and not narrow dictionary meaning [However, department is of the view that narrow meaning should apply -CBE&C, vide circular No. 84/2/2006-ST, dated 19-9-2006 and Ref. Code 076.01/23-8-07 of CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/2007-ST dated 23-8-2007 - see discussions below under Whether public charitable trust is automatically excluded].

Any object of ‘general public utility’ will be a ‘charitable purpose’, as discussed below.

As per section 2 of Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief to poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility, but does not include a purpose which relates exclusively to religious teaching or worship. As per section 2(15) of Income-tax Act, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, and the advancement of any other object of general public utility. Preamble to Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920 also indicates that trust created for public purpose comes under purview of that Act.

Public does not refer to whole of mankind or all people in the country. It is sufficient if the intention is to benefit a section of the public as distinguished from specified individuals. The section of community sought to be benefited should be identifiable by some common quality of public or impersonal nature. The expression ‘general public utility’ include all objects which promote the welfare of general public. When an object is to promote or protect the interest of a particular trade or industry, that object would be charitable purpose, but not so, if it seeks to promote the interest of those who conduct the said trade or industry - CIT v. Andhra Chamber of Commerce [1965] 55 ITR 722 (SC).

Advance of any object of benefit to the public or section of public, as distinguished from benefit to an individual or group of individuals would be a charitable purpose - CIT v. Ahmedabad Rana Caste Association [1983] 140 ITR 1 (SC) [affirming CIT v. Ahmedabad Rana Cast Association [1973] 88 ITR 354 (Guj.), Andhra Chamber of Commerce case (supra).

In CIT v. Bar Council of Maharashtra [1981] 6 Taxman 1 (SC), it was held that purpose of State Bar Council is to ensure quality services of competent lawyers, to spread legal literacy, promote law reforms and provide legal assistance to poor. Such purpose is the advancement of the object of general public utility and it will be a charitable purpose. It was also held that a trust can carry on business for purpose of earning profit, to be utilised exclusively for charitable purposes.

The foregoing discussion, showing how the courts have interpreted the concept of charity in the context of income-tax legislation, clearly shows that the concept of ‘charity’ has to be pragmatically and widely construed - not narrowly as has been done by the CBEC in its circulars (supra).

Flaws in the CBECs’ circulars

8. These are as under :

(A) Discarding of the interpretation of the concept of ‘charity’ in the Income-tax Act is wrong

There is apparent flaw in the CBEC’s circular when it says that the exemption under the Income-tax Act on the ground of being a public charitable institution is of no consequence or relevance for service tax purposes.

This view, it needs to be said, is misconceived and opposed to judicial thinking for the reasons mentioned hereinafter :

(i)The CBEC’s circulars categorically say that for determining whether activities carried on by an undertaking are of a charitable nature or not, definition under the Income-tax Act is of no consequence. This is, apparently, a mistaken notion. For understanding the meaning of these words, reference to other statutes ‘in pari materia’, i.e., statute forming part of the same system can be looked into. In the absence of a statutory definition (which is not there in the service tax provisions relating to charitable purpose/nature), it is open to look for the meaning by reference to definitions in the sister legislation (which the Income-tax Act is vis-á-vis Service Tax legislation). Resort to adoption of dictionary meaning or meaning in common parlance is to be taken if there is no definition in the Act or in sister legislation. Hence, to say that exemption in income-tax is of no consequence for service tax purposes, is, prima-facie, a misconception.

(ii)Viscount Salmond in a passage in AG HRH Prince Earnest Augustus of Hanover [1957] 1 All ER 49, page 53 (HL) has said that ‘I consider it my right and duty to examine every word of a statute in its context and I use context in its widest sense as including . . . . . . other statutes in pari materia’. The application of this rule of construction has the merit of avoiding any apparent contradiction between a series of statutes dealing with similar subjects. Certainly, income-tax and service tax are in pari materia. The structuring of the two legislations is on similar lines. Hence, it cannot be said that the concept of ‘charitable purpose’ under the Income-tax Act is of no consequence under the service tax provisions.

(B) Reference to dictionary meaning when the words can be interpreted with the help of other Acts, pari-materia seems incorrect
