On reference :

It was clear from the provision contained in clause 4(2) of the deed that the trustees had been given absolute discretion to utilise not merely the income but also the corpus of the trust property or any part thereof for any one or more of the objects mentioned in clause 4(1). In other words, it was clear that even if the trustees were to spend the entire income or the entire corpus on non-charitable object mentioned in clause 4(1)(iv ), they would not be committing any breach of the terms and conditions of the trust and such expenditure on their part would be perfectly valid and proper. In view of this position which obtained very clearly under the indenture dated 12-6-1959, it seemed very clear that the trust could not be regarded as a trust having been created wholly for charitable purposes.

The contention of the assessee was that this sub-clause (iv) should be regarded, if it all, as incidental or ancillary object and since the main or dominant object of the deed was to do charity and since several other sub-clauses of clause 4 indicated what those charitable objects were, it should be held that notwithstanding sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) the trust should be regarded as one having been created wholly for charitable purposes. It was not possible to accept this submission of the assessee. In the first place, there was nothing to indicate in clause 4(1) of the deed that the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv) thereof was incidental or ancillary to other objects mentioned in the other sub-clauses of clause 4(1). Secondly, clause 4(2) in terms elevated the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv ) to the same level as the other objects mentioned in sub-clauses of clause 4(1), for, under sub-clause (2) of clause 4, the trustees had been given liberty to utilise the corpus of the trust property or any part thereof for any one or more of the objects mentioned earlier and in such proportion as they might in their absolute discretion think fit. At least while conferring such power upon the trustees some indication could have been given by the settlors if they wanted to regard sub-clause (iv) as incidental or ancillary, but nothing of the kind had been done. In other words, sub-clause (2) of clause 4 had conferred absolute discretion upon the trustees to spend the entire corpus of the trust property or any part thereof upon any one or more of the objects mentioned in sub-clause (1) of clause 4. Further, it was not possible to accept the contention that sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) provided for management expenses, such as remuneration payable to the employees of the trust and that normally the trustees would have incurred such expenditure on the employees during the course of management of the trust. In fact, clause 4(1) separately provided for expenses for management and maintenance of the trust property. In terms, clause 4(1) provided that the trustees would pay out of the rents, profits, interest, dividends and income all outgoings payable in respect of the trust property including all ground rent, rates, taxes and costs of repairs of any immovable property forming part of the trust property, premium for insurance or any other costs, charges, expenses and outgoings of and incidental to the management and maintenance of the trust property and execution of the trusts therein contained including the wages and salaries of employees and it is after payment of such outgoings and other expenses that the trustees had been directed to spend the income of the trust property over the objects which have been specified in sub-clauses (i) to (vi) of clause 4(1). In a way this independent provision for meeting the expenses of the management and maintenance of the trust property including wages and salaries of the employees on the contrary suggested that the settlors had in mind while incorporating sub-clause (iv) in clause 4(1) that it was an independent object of the trust for which the trustees were given liberty to spend the income of the trust property. Having regard to the above position which contained very clearly on reading of the deed of trust as a whole, it was difficult to accept the contention that sub-clause (iv) of clause 4(1) should either be regarded as not providing any object at all or as providing for an incidental or ancillary object. It was clear that the object mentioned in sub-clause (iv) was also one of the independent objects on which the trustees had been given power to spend the income of the property or even the entire corpus of the trust property by virtue of clause 4(2) of the deed and if that be so, it was clear that the trust in question could not be regarded as being one created wholly for the purpose of the charitable objects.

"Agricultural income" is defined in section 2(1) of 1922 Act as any rent or revenue derived from land which is used for agricultural purposes, and the question, therefore, which arose for determination was whether any portion of the remuneration received by the assessee was rent or revenue derived from land which was used for agricultural purposes. It was clear that the remuneration received by the assessee was under a contract between it and the principal company for services to be rendered by the assessee as the managing agents of the principal company. That contract had nothing whatever to do with the income earned by the principal company from agricultural sources. It was also clear from the contract that what the principal company contracted with the managing agents was to pay them a sum of Rs. 10,000 or ten percent of the profits computed in a particular manner whichever sum was larger.

In the instant case, it was perfectly evident that what the assessee was going to share in was an artificial fund which first came into existence. They received ten per cent of that fund. After that had been ascertained the usefulness of that fund disappeared and a new fund came into existence by a different computation which was to be divisible amongst the shareholders as their own profits.

If the income is agricultural income, it bears an indelible impression upon it and is exempt from tax. But on the construction of the contract, the remuneration of the assessee was for its services as the managing agents of the principal company; that was the character of its income. The character of its income was not that part of it was rent or revenue from land which was used for agricultural purposes. Therefore, the income received by the assessee from the principal company which was proportionate to the agricultural income earned by the principal company was not agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(1) of the Act 1922, and was not exempt from assessment under the provision of section 4(3)(viii) of the 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

The assessee, a registered charitable trust, was running a Skin Institute which was providing medical facility in the field of skin and also carried out research fully recognised by the Board and offered courses of dermatology. The patients were divided into three categories, being free category, subsidised category and paying category. No consultation fees was charged from free category patients. The assessee-trust filed a return for the assessment year 1992-93 declaring nil income claiming exemption under section 10(22)/11. The Assessing Officer observed that 50 per cent of income generated by the trust was given to Dr. ‘P’, founder and managing trustee, and that the assessee denied to have received any donation, whereas in the profit and loss account it had claimed to have received donation, which in fact was sale proceeds of the medicines. The Assessing Officer denied exemption claimed by the assessee. On appeal, the assessee contended that Dr. ‘P’ had no income from trust except that he was charging 50 per cent of the income for rendering medical services to the trust, but he was not charging anything for managerial or administrative services and it was by mistake that medicine sale proceeds had been shown as donation. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejecting the assessee’s contention, upheld the Assessing Officer’s order.

The ITO had relied on the English law relating to charities to conclude that the object of promotion of sports was not charitable. However, it is well settled that the definition of charitable purpose in section 2(15) has a wider significance because of the use of the words ‘any other object of general public utility’. In fact, promotion of sports and athletic activities was one of the objects of the Government and there were ministries and directorates for this purpose in both the Central and the State Governments. Section 10(23) itself provides for exemption of income of any association or institu- tion having as its object the control, supervision, regulation or encourage- ment of various games because it was considered that such institutions should fiourish in public interest. It was a matter of public concern that there should be keen interest in sports not only in the interest of public health but also to see that sportsmen fared well in the world arena. It could not, therefore, be said that’ such an object would not qualify for exemption under section 11. Since the other objects of the assessee were also clearly charitable, the assessee would qualify for exemption under section 11. The finding of the first appellate authority on this point was, therefore, correct.

As regards the question whether the impugned income from the race meets and inter-venue betting was income from property or income from business it would be difficult to accept that the assessee was conducting a business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter- venue betting on two or three occasions in a year.

Even if the receipts did not constitute the corpus, there was certainly no quid pro quo in the arrangement between the assessee and the HRC as the asses- see was getting, from the said race meets and inter-venue betting, on almost certain profit from the HRC at practically no risk or cost to itself. The assessee had obtained a licence from the Government to conduct the races and inter-venue betting on the basis of a letter from the HRC. This licence itself could be treated as property and such property was obtained with the consent of the settlor-club and was contemplated even at the inception of the assessee-trust. Since the expression ‘property’ has the widest import for income-tax purposes, the impugned income would be income from property held under trust.

Alternatively. even if the impugned income was not income from property, it could only be treated as a voluntary contribution given by the HRC to the assessee. Though the form of such contribution indicated that the assessee itself had to conduct the races, the actual conduct was done by the HRC on behalf of the assessee merely as a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contribution did not have the character of income but was a capital receipt. The facts of the case did not justify the inference that the assessee-trust was in business for conducting horse races. It had neither the horses nor organisation nor any other equipment for that purpose. Consequently, since the impugned income was not income from business, the question of applicability of section 13(1)(bb ) did not arise.

For the foregoing reasons, the assessee-trust was an institution which satisfied the conditions of section 2(15) read with section 11. Since the ITO had not considered the requirements of accumulation, if there had been such accumulation, or application of sections 12, 12A and 13, the assessments were set aside for consideration of these aspects.

Subba Rao, J.—In the town of Nagore in Tanjore District, Madras State, there is a Durgha consecrated to Hazerath Sayed Shahul Hameed Quadir Ali Ganja Savoy Andavar, who lived some 400 years ago. The said Durgha receives large income from immovable properties endowed to it and the offerings in cash and kind made by the devotees. The Durgha and its properties are now being administered under a scheme settled by the Madras High Court on March 16, 1955. Under the scheme the management of the administration of the affairs of the said Durgha vests hereditarily in 8 trustees called nattamaigars, who constitute a board of trustees. The said board of trustees shall from among themselves elect one as a managing trustee and he shall hold office for a term of 3 years. The managing trustee shall at the end of each Fasli prepare a balance-sheet verified by the manager and ascertain the net amount available for payment to kasupangudars, who are the descendants of Saiyed Muhammed Eusoof, the foster-son of the saint. The managing trustee shall declare the amount due to each of the kasupangu (share) and shall allocate the amount to each kusupangudar (sharer) in the list to be prepared for that purpose in each year. He shall pay the amount to each kasupangudar in accordance with the list. It is said that at present there are 640 kasupangudars. Briefly stated under the scheme the management of the properties of the Durgha, both movable and immovable, vest in nattamaigars, and the kasupangudars are entitled to the surplus in accordance with their shares.

For the assessment years 1953-54 and 1954-55 the Income-tax Officer assessed the surplus income in the hands of the managing trustee as an association of persons. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on appeal, confirmed the same. On further appeal, the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal took the same view. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal submitted the following question for the opinion of the High Court of Madras under section 66(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1922, hereinafter called the Act:

"Whether the provisions of section 41 can be said to apply to the assessees in this case ?"

A Division Bench of the High Court, which heard the reference, held that the managing trustee qua the surplus income managed the property and derived the income on behalf of the kasupangudars and that the assessment should be made on the said managing trustee to the extent of the interest of each of the kasupangudars in the income received by him. In the result it answered the question in the affirmative and in favour of the assessee. The Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras, on a certificate of fitness granted by the High Court, has preferred the present appeals against the said order.

The learned Additional Solicitor-General, appearing for the revenue, contended that the nattamaigars being trustees, the properties of the Durgha vested in them and, therefore, they or the managing trustee administered the trust properties in their own right and not on behalf of the kasupangudars and hence section 41 of the Act did not apply, with the result the Income-tax Officer had rightly assessed the surplus income in the hands of the trustees as an association of persons.

Mr. A.V. Viswanatha Sastri, learned counsel for the assessee-respon-dent, argued, on the other hand, that the nattamaigars of the Durgha were not trustees as understood in the law of trust but were only managers managing the properties on behalf of the Durgha and kasupangudars. On that assumption, his argument proceeded, as the nattamaigars, as managers, held the surplus on behalf of the kasupangudars for distribution in definite shares, section 41 of the Act was attracted.

At the outset we may make it clear that in this appeal we are concerned only with the surplus remaining on hand with the nattamaigars after meeting the expenses of the Durgha.

The problem presented in these appeals falls to be decided on a true construction of section 41 of the Act. The material part of section 41 reads:

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-trust established with main object of establishing educational institutions and providing scholarships, was also running Kalyana Mandapam within boundaries set out in trust deed and surplus generated out of this activity had been utilized by assessee in furtherance of other charitable purposes viz. payment of school fees, contribution to relief funds etc., assessee's claim of deduction under section 11 could not be usurped merely on finding that assessee's activities resulted into surplus funds for assessee

Following the decision of the High Court in the case of CIT v. Madras Stock Exchange Ltd. [1976] 105 ITR 546, it was held that the object of the assessee did not involves carrying on of an activity for profit and, therefore, the objects of the assessee society constituted 'charitable purposes' as defined in section 2(15) entitling it to exemption under section 11.

As regards the applicability of section 28(iii), the underlying idea behind the said section is that there must be a business from which income is derived and that in the course of such business specific services must be rendered for its members. The concept behind section 28(iii) is to cut at the mutuality principle being relied on in support of a claim for exemption, when the assessee was actually deriving income or making profits as a result of rendering specific services for its members in a commercial way.

Section 2(24)(v) provides that income includes any sum chargeable to Income-tax under clause (iii) of section 28. The definition would apply so as to bring to tax the income as a business income, only if the income was not covered by any exemption available under the Act. Section 28(iii ) cannot be read in isolation, but has to be read with the other provisions of the Act. In the case of activity carried on by an entity like the present assessee, which, as it is now well settled exists for a charitable purpose, the impact of section 11 read with section 2(15) has to be taken into account. Wherever there is no activity designed for making profit it would not fall within the scope of this definition and the exemption under section 11 in its full force would apply. It was already seen that the instant was held to be brought within the scope of exemption from assessment, the question of taxing the income would arise if the profit-making activity was the means by which the object of public utility was sought to be achieved. This was not a case where the object of public utility was sought to be achieved by these activities. Therefore, the fact that there was income does not by itself solve the problem. The profit-making was only an incident and not the means of achieving the object of public utility. So long as the object was charitable and so long as the income was not earned from an activity which was by itself designed to achieve the object of general public utility, the exemption cannot be denied. As the facts show, the assessee was actually required by the Government to take up some of the activities as a result of which it had received certain amounts from the members. In such a case, it could not consider that there could be any scope for the view that there was any activity for profit. This view was reinforced by a reference to section 10(23A). Under Section 10(23A), there is an exclusion from assessment of the income falling under certain categories. One of the categories is income derived from rendering any specific services. It is true that this provision deals only with institutions or associations having as their object the control, supervision, regulation or encouragement of certain professions. But in the instant case the question was whether receipts in consideration of services are taxable. This provision is relevant to show that Parliament does not always conceive such receipts to be taxable and that such receipts may be exempt under certain conditions. It is not, therefore, enough if there are receipts. Such receipts must be considered in the context of all the provisions of the Act.

Section 11(4) provides that for the purpose of this section 'Property held under trust' includes a business undertaking so held. Therefore, even if there is a business, which yields income, so long as the business is held under trust, its income would be exempt from tax. It was not suggested that the properties were held otherwise than under trust. Section 28(iii) would not apply, to tax income from such a business, as otherwise, the benefit sought to be conferred under section 11 would be destroyed, and the exemption provision would be stultified.

On reference : HELD: As regards the point regarding material before Tribunal for finding that payment by the company any to the firm was not collusive, it is well-settled that the apparent state of affairs is to be presumed to be real until the contrary is shown. It is equally well settled that good faith and the genuineness of a transaction are also to be presumed until the contrary is proved. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.

3.8. Powers of Assessing Officer under Section 11(4)

Section 11(4) defines "property held under trust" and deals with the determination of income of a business undertaking. The term 'property held under trust' includes a business undertaking. Therefore, income from the business will qualify for an exemption, provided the said business is held under trust for charitable or religious purposes.

Where a claim is made that the income of such undertaking shall not be included in the total income of the persons in receipt thereof, the Assessing Officer shall have power to determine the income of such undertaking in accordance with the provisions relating to assessment. Where any income so determined is in excess of the income shown in the accounts of the undertaking, such excess shall be deemed to be applied to purposes other than charitable or religious purposes.

It may be noted that the Assessing Officer has the power to determine business income under section 11(4) as per the provisions of the Act, which would imply that all provisions of the Act shall apply. However, this power is available to the AO during the assessment proceedings, and there is no provision to suggest that the assessee is required to compute income in a manner other than applicable to charitable institutions under section 11.

The text of Section 11(4) is reproduced herein below:

(4) For the purposes of this section "property held under trust" includes a business undertaking so held, and where a claim is made that the income of any such undertaking shall not be included in the total income of the persons in receipt thereof, the Assessing Officer shall have power to determine the income of such undertaking in accordance with the provisions of this Act relating to assessment; and where any income so determined is in excess of the income as shown in the accounts of the undertaking, such excess shall be deemed to be applied to purposes other than charitable or religious purposes.

The Assessing Officer has been given the power to determine the income of such business in accordance with the provision of this act, but this subsection nowhere provides that the income shall be computed under the head Profits & Gains from Business. MoreovertheCBDT Circular No. 5-P(LXX-6) Dt. 19th June 1968 has clarified as under:

"In the case of a business undertaking, held under trust, its "income" will be the income as shown in the accounts of the undertaking"

It was contended by the revenue that the assessees were established with profit motive because they were not rendering free services but were charging cess/fees for their services and, therefore, they were not established for charitable purposes. There was no merit in that contention. The cess/fees were charged by the assessees from the purchasers in the market area at the rate prescribed by the State Government for the purpose of carrying out the object of the Act. As held by the Apex Court in the cases of Addl. CIT v. Surat Art Silk Cloth Mfrs. Association [1980] 121 ITR 1/[1979] 2 Taxman 501 and DIT v. Bharat Diamond Bourse [2003] 259 ITR 280/ 126 Taxman 365 , where the dominant purpose of a trust/institution is charitable, incidentally if some profit is made and the said profit is used for charitable purposes, the said trust/institution does not cease to be established for charitable purposes. In the case of the assessees, the dominant object was to regulate procurement and supply of agricultural and some other produce and to meet the expenses required for achieving the said object, the Legislature has empowered the assessees to levy cess/fees. Moreover, surplus remaining in the market fund was ploughed back for carrying out the object for which those mandi samitis was established. Thus, the surplus remaining in the market fund was neither distributed nor accumulated as profit. In those circumstances, it could not be said that the assessees were established with profit motive so as to deny registration under section 12A/12AA. [Para 41]

It is pertinent to note that prior to 1-4-1984, the words used in section 2(15) were "advancement of any other object of general public utility not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit". By the Finance Act, 1983 with effect from 1-4-1984, the Legislature has omitted the words "not involving the carrying on of any activity for profit" from section 2(15 ). Thus, after 1-4-1984, even if there is some profit in the activity carried on by the trust/institution, so long as the dominant object is of general public utility, it cannot be said that said trust/institution is not established for charitable purposes. [Para 42]

It was contended by the revenue that even if the assessees were covered under section 12A, they would still not be entitled to exemption because their income was neither derived from the property held under trust nor their income was from voluntary contributions made to the institution. There was no merit in that contention because the expression ‘property’ used in section 11 is of wide amplitude and it includes the business undertaking itself. The word ‘property’ in section 11 includes immovable and movable property like money, shares, securities, etc. Therefore, where a trust/institution fulfils all the conditions mentioned in section 12A/12AA, registration cannot be denied on the ground that some conditions of sections 11 and 12 are not fulfilled. Even after registration, unless the conditions set out in sections 11 and 13 are complied with, no benefit would be available to the registered trusts or institutions. Therefore, in the facts of the instant case, the decision of the Tribunal that the assessees, who had fulfilled all the conditions, were entitled to registration, could not be faulted. The contention of the revenue that the assessees were not registered as institution and, hence, not entitled to registration, was also without any merit, because there is no requirement under the Act that an institution constituted for advancement of any object of general public utility must be registered as a trust. [Para 44]

In terms of clause 2 of the said agreement, the assessee annually received from the principal company a commission fixed at 10 per cent of the net profits of the principal company subject to a minimum of Rs. 10,000. The principal company derived its income from several sources, one of which was the manufacture of sugar. The cane that was used in the manufacture was partly grown on the company’s own farms and partly bought from outside. The assessee, during the relevant year, received from its managing agency commission and contended that a part of the managing agency commission that it received, i.e., such part calculated at 10 per cent of the agricultural income of the principal company, was also agricultural income in its own hands and exempt from taxation under section 4(3)(viii) of the 1922 Act. The ITO rejected the assessee’s claim and included the amount, subject to certain adjustments, in the assessee’s total income, computed for the purposes of the assessment. On appeal, the AAC also upheld the said inclusion. On further appeal, the Tribunal sustained the AAC’s view.

HELD: Under the agreement the managing agents could be participators in profits, if they divided in a stated percentage an agreed fund. They could not be participators of the profits divisible amongst the shareholders constituted one fund and they got a percentage of a fund which was differently calculated and, therefore, in fact a different fund. The ten per cent, were not necessarily payable out of the profits. The annual net profits. The net profits were again, not what one ordinarily finds in the company's balance sheets. They are net profits only for the purpose of calculation, to be worked out strictly on the lines specifically mentioned in that clause. It was obvious that several deductions which are not permitted under the clause would be made in preparing the balance sheet and ascertaining the net profits of a commercial corporation. Moreover, the commission was not in any year to amount to a sum less than Rs. 10,000. Therefore, if in any year the company made no profits, the sum had to be paid by the principal company, even out of its capital. If in any given year there was no agricultural income, the remuneration, with a minimum of Rs. 10,000, will still have to be paid out of the profits earned through the other activities of the principal company. It was therefore clear that, on the face of this clause itself, there was nothing to connect it necessarily with the agricultural income of the principal company.

In the instant case, the managing agents would receive the remuneration irrespective of the nature of the business of the principal company. They were paid for their work as managing agents. The assets of the principal company were not vested in them. They were not the persons who could sue for amounts due to the principal company in their own name. They were only agents for management. It seemed therefore clear that, under the terms of the managing agency agreement, the balance of the agricultural income in the hands of the principal company was not to be divided between the principal agency and the managing agents in a stated proportion.

General - If section 11(1)(a) has been fully exploited and there is still accumulated income left to be dealt with, section 11(2) can be pressed in service and if it is complied with, such additional accumulated income beyond the prescribed percentage can also earn exemption u/s 11(2) [Addl. Deemed income - Deemed income (i.e., tax deducted at source) is not to be taken into account for determining the application of income [CIT v. Jayashree Charity Trust [1986] 159 ITR 280 (Cal.)].

Donation - Donation of sale proceeds of capital asset made by charitable trust to another trust was to be allowed as 'application of income' for charitable purpose [PCIT v. St. Joseph's Monastery [2022] 137 taxmann.com 133 (Kar.)].

3.2-6c Basic exemption

Section 11(1)(a) reads as follows:

"Income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes, to the extent to which such income is applied to such purposes in India; and, where any such income is accumulated or set apart for application to such purposes in India, to the extent to which the income so accumulated or set apart is not in excess of fifteen per cent of the income from such property". The expression "such" means the purposes referred to in the earlier part of the section, that is, charitable or religious purposes. Hence, even the income accumulated or set apart has to be applied towards charitable or religious purposes in India. Now, the amendment states that any corpus donation shall not be treated as "application of income for charitable or religious purposes". Hence, if the accumulated income up to 15% is utilized by a charitable institution for giving corpus donation, then on a literal interpretation, the income could be regarded as applied towards non-charitable/religious purpose, thus, violating the condition that even accumulated income has to be applied towards charitable or religious purposes. A consequence would be that the income of the year to which the basic exemption pertains may become taxable in the said year. To illustrate, if the 15% basic accumulation of assessment year 2014-15 is utilised for grant of corpus donation in assessment year 2018-19, the exemption given in assessment year 2014-15 may be withdrawn on the basis of literal interpretation. This does not appear to be intended and a clarification from the CBDT or a statutory amendment will help in eliminating the exposure.

3.2-6d Secondary application under section 11(2) - In this case, Explanation to section 11(2) already provides that any amount credited or paid to any other charitable institution registered under section 12AA or covered by section 10(23C)(iv)/(v)/(vi)/(via) shall not be treated as application of income. Hence, even under the pre-amendment law, such corpus donations were not permitted out of income accumulated under section 11(2).

3.2-6e Corpus donations given out of corpus donation received - In some cases, the corpus donations received are utilized to give corpus donations to other institutions.

The tax department, often contends that the original corpus donation received is in essence not a corpus donation but income [see Tewari Charitable Trust v. DIT(E) [2014] 49 taxmann.com 45 (Mum. - Trib.); Dharma Pratishthanam v. ITO [1985] 11 ITD 40 (Delhi-Trib.); ITO v. Abhilash KumariPublicCharitableTrust [1987] 28 TTJ 523 (Delhi-Trib.)]. If it is held that such donation is income, then on account of the amendment, the corpus donation given will not be regarded as application of income resulting in taxation of the ostensible corpus donation in the year of receipt.

However, if such corpus donation cannot be treated as income, then it appears that the amendment would not apply. This is because, the Explanation 2 refers to any amount paid or credited to any other charitable institution "out of income referred to in clause (a) or clause (b) read with Explanation 1" of section 11(1). In other words, the Explanation 2 covers only income referred to in section 11(1)(a) and (b) and not section 11(1)(d). Therefore, it could be argued that corpus donations exempt under section 11(1)(d) are not covered under the NewExplanation 2.

3.3 Mandatory application by a charitable institution upon change or modifications of objects [Section 12A(1)(ab)]

Section 12A provides for conditions to be satisfied by a charitable institution for availing of exemption under sections 11 and 12. Hitherto, there was no explicit provision in the Act which mandated a charitable institution to approach for fresh registration in the event of adoption on undertaking modifications of the objects after the registration had been granted.

Section 12A(1)(ab) has been inserted with effect from assessment year 2018-19 to provide that where a charitable institution has been granted registration under section 12AA or section 12A and subsequently, it has adopted or undertaken modification of the objects which do not conform to the conditions of registration, it shall be required to take fresh registration.

Further, section 12AA(1) and (2) dealing with the procedure for registration and time limit for registration by the Commissioner have been amended to include an application for registration referred to in section 12AA(1)(ab).

The charitable institution has been granted registration under section 12AA or has obtained registration at any time under section 12A.

(c)

Such modifications do not conform to the conditions of registration.

If the aforesaid conditions are satisfied, the charitable institution shall not be eligible for exemption under sections 11 and 12 unless the following conditions are fulfilled :

The institution has made an application for its registration.

Even if the receipts did not constitute the corpus, there was certainly no quid pro quo in the arrangement between the assessee and the HRC as the asses- see was getting, from the said race meets and inter-venue betting, on almost certain profit from the HRC at practically no risk or cost to itself. The assessee had obtained a licence from the Government to conduct the races and inter-venue betting on the basis of a letter from the HRC. This licence itself could be treated as property and such property was obtained with the consent of the settlor-club and was contemplated even at the inception of the assessee-trust. Since the expression ‘property’ has the widest import for income-tax purposes, the impugned income would be income from property held under trust.

Alternatively. even if the impugned income was not income from property, it could only be treated as a voluntary contribution given by the HRC to the assessee. Though the form of such contribution indicated that the assessee itself had to conduct the races, the actual conduct was done by the HRC on behalf of the assessee merely as a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contribution did not have the character of income but was a capital receipt. The facts of the case did not justify the inference that the assessee-trust was in business for conducting horse races. It had neither the horses nor organisation nor any other equipment for that purpose. Consequently, since the impugned income was not income from business, the question of applicability of section 13(1)(bb ) did not arise.

Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

However, benevolent or liberal the objects of a trust may be, so long as the trustee has any discretion left in the matter, the trust cannot be supported as a charitable legacy. The court was alive to the fat that most of the objects of the Stud Farm were no doubt charitable even within the technical sense of the term but so long as the trust was not given a legal shape, by eliminating the element of discretion vesting in the Officer Commanding, it would not be able to claim the benefit of the exemption provided for in the Act.

The trust had to fail as a charitable trust for want of certainty as to its objects and that defect could not be cured so long as the Officer Commanding insisted on his discretion in the matter.

It is not an invariable canon of construction that the proviso in a statute should be read as a qualification or limitation upon the effect of the main enactment. The function of the proviso is very often to deal with an excepted class of cases, which may be within the principal enactment but for it. It would not however be correct to say that a proviso should always be assumed to be and read as an exception. A substantive provision may also appear in the form of a proviso and if the clear meaning of the proviso establishes that it is not a qualifying clause of the main provision it is bound to be given effect without straining to attribute to it the character of a segment of that main enactment. The unambiguously clear language of the main provision cannot be controlled or overridden by mere implication from the existence of a proviso unless the words of the proviso have necessarily that effect. The meaning of the proviso should be derived from its own terms without any predilection that the subject-matter of the proviso is already covered by the main provision and that its object is to exclude something out of that main provision.

The word "property" in section 4(3)(i) includes business. Income from business held in trust for a religious or charitable purpose applied or earmarked for application for the purpose of the trust falls within the exemption provided for under section 4(3)(i). A business owned and carried on by the trust is of course held in trust. A trust is an institution which has no corporate personality. It is not a legal person. The word "trust" is a convenient and a compendious description of the trustees, the beneficiaries and the subject-matter of the trust. The trustees of a trust in India have no title to the trust properties; the properties only vest in them for administration and management. The instrumentality of the trustees to hold and manage trust properties should not cause any misapprehension of the real position of the trustees vis-a-vis the trust. They occupy a representative position representing the trust and they are not strangers to the trust. When the trustee acts, it is only the trust that acts, as the trustee fully represents the trust. A business carried on behalf of a trust rather indicates a business which is not held in trust, than a business of the trust run by the trustees.

Thus, proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) does not restrict the operation of the main provision in section 4(3)(i). If a trust carries on business and the business itself is held in trust and the income from such business is applied or accumulated for application for the purpose of the trust, which must of course be of a religious or a charitable character, the conditions prescribed in section 4(3)(i) are fulfilled and the income is exempt from taxation. This exemption cannot be defeated even if the business were to be conducted by somebody else acting on behalf of the trust. Proviso (b) to section 4(3)(i) has application only to businesses which are not held in trust, and the field of its operation is, therefore, distinct and separate from that covered by section 4(3)(i).

In view of aforesaid, the assessee trust was entitled to exemption under section 4(3)(i) for assessment years in question.

1.2-1 Amendment in definition of charitable purpose - Finance Act, 2008 substitutes the above definition, effective 1st April, 2009, that is, assessment year 2009-10 and provides that if the pursuit of the Other Object involves carrying on of specified activities, it shall not be considered as charitable purpose, as stipulated in the proviso.

Newly inserted proviso to section 2(15) lays down the ‘specified activities’ and they are :

◆ Carrying on of any activity in the nature of trade, commerce or business (hereafter referred to as ‘the trade’); or

◆ Carrying on of any activity of rendering any service in relation to the trade, for a fee or cess or any other consideration.

The proviso further lays down that if the specified activities are pursued in pursuit of the Other Object, it would not be considered as a charitable purpose irrespective of the nature of use or application or retention of income arising from the specified activities.

1.2-2 Analysis of the amendment - It may be noted from the newly inserted proviso that—

1.2-2a Application of proviso restricted to the Other Object - Newly inserted proviso would apply only if the specified activities are carried out in the pursuit of the Other Objects.

If the specified activities are carried out in relation to the relief of poor, education or medical relief, it would still constitute charitable purpose. To illustrate, if a trust assists poor women to meet and market household products, being an object providing the relief to poor and in the process it, renders certain services in relation to the business or actually carries on any activity in the nature of business, the proviso would not apply and it cannot be said that it is not a charitable purpose.

Courts have considered the following objects as ‘education’.

◆ To set up a statutory board for promotion of education. 1

◆ To extend financial assistance to poor and deserving students by way of loans, scholarships, and grant for purchase of books and other educational requisites. 2

Courts have considered the following objects as ‘the relief of poor’.

◆ To form a Scheme to relieve poverty among unemployed agriculturists by providing them with work. 3

◆ To make provision of help for marriages or sacred thread ceremonies. 4

◆ To undertake rehabilitation of economically handicapped women and destitute by giving them suitable employment. 5

◆ To help poor and public utility bodies, such as, mosques, schools, water supply, etc. 6

Further, it may also be noted that the trusts or institutions claiming exemption under section 10(23C) of the Act may also be not affected inasmuch as the objects eligible for the said exemption, by and large, do not constitute the Other Objects.

1.2-2b Other Objects - Courts have considered, from time to time, various objects, for the purposes of classification, and have held that the objects listed in Annex 1.1 would constitute Other Objects.

Accordingly, in pursuit of the above objects, if a trust or institution carries out the specified activities, it may not constitute charitable purpose.

1.2-2c Pursuit of Other Objects to involve carrying on of the specified activities - The proviso would apply only if the pursuit of the Other Objects involves carrying on of the specified activities. In other words, the proviso would not apply if the pursuit of the Other Objects does not involve carrying on of the specified activities.

To illustrate, a trust owns a house property and allows the user thereof by a certain class of working persons, free of any cost. In such a case, it cannot be said that the trust is carrying on any activity in the nature of business. Accordingly, to such a trust the proviso would not apply and, therefore, its object would continue to be a charitable purpose.

An analysis of the reasons given by the ITO disclosed no grounds to support the view that remuneration at a rate exceeding 10 per cent of the net profit was excessive or unreasonable. The contract with the Government was for the assessee an important contract requiring constant and vigilant application and supervision by a person well acquainted with the practical details of the business. If the management of the assessee as prudent businessman for advancing the interest of the assessee bona fide regarded 30 per cent of the net profits as reasonable remuneration, the revenue authorities were not justified in reviewing their opinion and reducing the rate of remuneration. It was true that if, on a consideration of the relevant materials, the Tribunal was of the opinion that a particular remuneration stipulated to be paid was not bona fide or is unreasonable, the High Court in exercising its advisory jurisdiction had no power to interfere with that opinion. But the material circumstances relating to the nature of the contract, the services to be performed and the nature of the duties by the employee were not at all taken into account by the Tribunal and the income-tax authorities. Therefore, the disallowance of a sum of out of the remuneration paid to 'T' was not justifiable ?

The contract under which the assessee was appointed managing agent for the 'N' was to enure till 1960, but it had to be prematurely terminated because the Government of Madras exercising its powers under 1949 Act had compulsorily acquired the electricity undertaking. With the acquisition of that undertaking the right of the assessee as managing agent ceased. Under section 15 of the 1449 Act, the Government was bound to pay compensation which would include compensation for termination of the managing agency agreement. The assessee received sum as compensation for termination of the agency, computed in the manner laid down in section 15 of that Act. Prima facie, such a receipt, being in lieu of extinction of an asset of the assessee, was a capital receipt.

Turning to the facts of the instant case, it must in the first instance be observed that it was for the revenue to establish that a particular receipt was income liable to tax, and beyond stating that the assessee was the managing agent of the 'N' and of two other companies, there was no other evidence about the nature of the business of the two other companies of which the assessee was the managing agent, about their relative importance qua the managing agency of the 'N' and whether by reason of the extinction of the managing agency of the 'N' any enduring asset was lost to the assessee, or its trading organisation was adversely affected. The ITO observed that the 'assessees business of managing agency as such had not come to an end', the assessee still continues as 'managing agents of other companies'. Even after surrender of one of the agencies, the assessee carried on business as before, its structure not being affected' and therefore 'the receipt was to be considered as revenue'.

Hence, the compensation received for taking over the 'N' was a capital receipt not liable to be taxed, and on the materials placed the Supreme Court did not disagree with the High Court.

The appeal therefore failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Income-tax is a levy on income. No doubt the Income-tax Act takes into account two points of time at which the liability to tax is attracted, viz., the accrual of the income or its receipt, but the substance of the matter is the income. If income does not result at all there cannot be a tax even though in book-keeping an entry is made about hypothetical income which does not materialise. Where income has in fact been received and is subsequently given up it remains the income of the recipient, even though given up and the tax with regard to it is payable. Where, however, the income can be said not to have resulted at all there is obviously neither accrual nor receipt of income even though an entry to that effect might in certain circumstances have been made in the books of account.

In the instant case, there was a custom in the market according to which commission agents realised Dharmada from their constituents. The constituents paid that amount to the commission agents knowing that the same was being collected over and above the commission which was payable by them to the commission agents. This amount, under the custom, had to be spent on charities. The amount was being paid by the constituents for being made a part of the fund which had already been established by the commission agent for purposes of charity. From the very beginning it was clear to both the parties, viz., the one paying Dharmada and the other receiving the same, that it was being received by the petitioner for being credited to an already existing fund for charity. Accordingly, when this amount reached the petitioner it did not in truth reach him as its income.

Merely because some discretion was given to the petitioner to spend the amount deposited with it on a charity of its own choice, it did not mean that either no trust was created or the trust so created was invalid. The finding recorded by the Additional Commissioner merely meant that the petitioner was free to apply the trust fund on a charity of its own choice. It did not mean that the petitioner could, if it so liked, appropriate the amount credited to Dharmada account for its own purposes. After all, if Dharmada was being collected for purposes of charity in accordance with a custom, its disposal was equally governed by the obligation created by that custom, i.e. , the amount was to be spent only for some charitable purpose.

In order to determine whether a particular receipt, by whatever name is termed, is or is not the income of an assessee its real nature and quality has to be considered. If it was received under a custom, the answer to the question would depend on the nature of obligation treated by that custom. In the instant case, it was not disputed that the petitioner received Dharmada under a custom according to which it was obligatory upon it to spend the amount so collected on charity alone. The petitioner had created a fund for that purpose and Dharmada collected by it had to be credited to that fund. In the circumstances, the amount so collected was not received by the petitioner as its income.

In view of aforesaid, instant petition was allowed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the petitioner.

INCOME DERIVED FROM VOLUNTARY CONTRIBUTION - SUB-SECTION (1) [AS IT STOOD AT RELEVANT TIME]

220. R.B. Shreeram Religious & Charitable Trust v. CIT [1998] 99 Taxman 318/233 ITR 53 (SC)

The phrase 'income derived from voluntary contribution' in sub-section (1) of section 12 refers to income in the form of voluntary contributions received by the recipient, religious or charitable trust. It has no reference to the income which may later on be derived from such voluntary contributions as and when such contributions are invested.

Board's Circular No. 2-P(LXX-5), dated 15-5-1963, it was explained that a religious or charitable trust, claiming exemption under section 11(1), must spend at least 75 per cent of its total income for religious or charitable purposes. In other words, it was not permitted to accumulate more than 25 per cent of its total income. The question has been reconsidered by the Board and the correct legal position is explained below.

(b) Section 11(1) provides that subject to the provisions of sections 60 to 63, "the following income shall not be included in the total income of the previous year. . . ." The reference in clause (a ) is invariably to "Income" and not to "total income". The expression "total income" has been specifically defined in section 2(45) as "the total amount of income computed in the manner laid down in this Act". It would, accordingly, be incorrect to assign to the word "income", used in section 11(1)(a), the same meaning as has been specifically assigned to the expression "total income" vide section 2(45).

(c)

In the case of a business undertaking, held under trust, its "income" will be the income as shown in the accounts of the undertaking. Under section 11(4), any income of the business undertaking determined by the ITO, in accordance with the provisions of the Act, which is in excess of the income as shown in its accounts, is to be deemed to have been applied to purposes other than charitable or religious, and hence it will be charged to tax under sub-section (3). As only the income disclosed in the account will be eligible for exemption under section 11(1), the permitted accumulation of 25 per cent will also be calculated with reference to this income.

(d)

Where the trust derives income from house property interest on securities, capital gains, or other sources, the word "income" should be understood in its commercial sense, i.e., book income, after adding back any appropriations or applications thereof towards the purposes of the trust or otherwise, and also after adding back any debits made for capital expenditure incurred for the purposes of the trust or otherwise. It should be noted, in this connection, that the amounts so added back will become chargeable to tax under section 11(3) to the extent that they represent outgoings for purposes other than those of the trust. The amounts spent or applied for the purposes of the trust from out of the income, computed in the aforesaid manner, should be not less than 75 per cent of the latter, if the trust is to get the full benefit of the exemption under section 11(1).

(e)

To sum up the business income of the trust, as disclosed by the accounts plus its other income computed as above, will be the "income" of the trust for the purposes of section 11(1). Further, the trust must spend at least 75 per cent of this income and not accumulate more than 25 per cent thereof. The excess accumulation, if any, will become taxable under section 11(1).

3.3. Applicability of provisions of PGBP to Charitable Institutions

To compute income under section 11(4) or under 11(4A), there is no mention of computing income under the head 'Profits & Gains of Business or Profession'. It may be noted that under sections 11 to 13, there are specific references where the sections applicable under the head 'Profits & Gains of Business or Profession' are also made applicable to the computation of income under section 11. In other words, unless specifically provided, the provision of the head 'Profits & Gains of Business or Profession' shall not apply to Charitable Institutions.

The Finance Act, 2018 inserted Explanation 3 to Section 11(1) to apply the following two provisions to charitable and religious institutions:

(i)

Disallowance for payment without TDS deduction under sub-clause (ia) of clause (a) of section 40.

(ii)

Disallowance for cash payment above Rs. 10,000/- under sub-section (3) and (3A) of section 40A.

The text of Explanation 3 to Section 11(1) is reproduced as under:

"Explanation 3 - For the purposes of determining the amount of application under clause (a) or clause (b), the provisions of sub-clause (ia) of clause (a) of section 40 and sub-sections (3) and (3A) of section 40A, shall, mutatis mutandis, apply as they apply in computing the income chargeable under the head "Profits & Gains of business or profession".

In light of the above, it is very clear that the statute specifically provides that some provisions applicable to business entities are required to be made applicable to charitable entities. In other words, unless specifically provided no provision corresponding to section 14 and five heads of income shall apply to charitable institutions.

3.4. Provisions of Chapter IV-D, i.e., sections 28 to 44D are not applicable while computing income falling under Chapter III :

Applicability of the provision - Where income is receivable by the trustees, on behalf of an unrecognised provident fund or an unapproved superannuation fund, gratuity fund, pension fund or any other fund created bona fide by a person carrying on a business or profession exclusively for the benefit of persons employed in such business or profession are concerned, they will continue to be charged to tax in the manner prescribed by section 164(1)(iv), as hitherto. Similarly, in the cases of registered societies, trade and professional associations, social and sports clubs, charitable or religious trusts, etc., where the members or trustees are not entitled to any share in the income of the association of persons, the provisions of section 167A will not be attracted and, accordingly, tax will be payable in such cases at the rate ordinarily applicable to the total income of an association of persons and not at the maximum marginal rate.—Circular : No. 320, dated 11-1-1982.

Bar Council of Maharashtra [1981] 6 Taxman 1 (SC), it was held that purpose of State Bar Council is to ensure quality services of competent lawyers, to spread legal literacy, promote law reforms and provide legal assistance to poor. Such purpose is the advancement of the object of general public utility and it will be a charitable purpose. It was also held that a trust can carry on business for purpose of earning profit, to be utilised exclusively for charitable purposes. In Management of Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Chief Inspecting Officer AIR 2005 SC 1433, it was held that dominant purpose should be found out. If the dominant purpose is appearing as charity, then it will be admissible to benefit of a charity, even if other object ancillary or incidental to dominant purpose, is no charitable If charity is incidental purpose, it will not be ‘charitable purpose’ - relying on Addl. Gujarat Maritime Board [2008] 166 Taxman 58 (SC), American Hotel & Lodging Association Educational Institute v. CBDT [2008] 170 Taxman 306 (SC).

In Gujarat Maritime Board’s case (supra), it was held that Gujarat Maritime Board established for purpose of development of minor ports is ‘charitable purpose’ - relying on CIT v. Andhra Pradesh State Road Corporation [1986] 25 Taxman 63A (SC), where it was held that corporation established for providing efficient transport system having no profit motive, is not liable to Income-tax even if it earns income.

Earning surplus does not mean it is not charitable purpose - Mere earning surplus does not mean the activity is not for charitable purpose. In American Hotel & Lodging Association Educational Institute’s case (supra ) in respect of an educational institute, it was observed as follows, ‘In deciding the character of the recipient (charitable trust), it is not necessary to look at the profits of each year, but to consider the nature of activities undertaken. . . . If after meeting expenditure, surplus remains incidentally from the activity carried on by educational institution, it will not cease to be one existing solely for educational purpose. In other words, existence of surplus from the activity will not mean absence of educational purpose - relying on Aditanar Educational Institution v. Addl. CIT [1997] 90 Taxman 528 (SC).

RENT-A-CAB SERVICE

Should Parking Charges, Toll Charges and Driver Batta be included in the Gross amount for arriving at the service tax component in the case of Rent-a-Cab and Tourist Operator Services ?

Really no, but to be on safe side, in your agreement or terms and conditions, you should indicate ‘scope of service’ and say that other expenses are not part of the service. However, for administrative convenience, you will first pay and then recover on actual basis. This will make things a little more safe and you will fall within the definition of ‘pure agent’ in respect of those charges.

If a Rent-a-Cab operator takes a vehicle from some other Rent-a-Cab operator for few days/trips, is the latter liable to collect service tax from the former ?

Legally, he is also liable since as per section 65(105)(o ), any service provided or to be provided to any person, by a rent-a-cab scheme operator in relation to the renting of a cab is ‘taxable service’.

Change of category of service

If a person who is actually carrying out Rent-a-Cab services, has so far been registered as Tourist Operator Services, can he get an endorsement for ‘Rent- a-Cab Service’ in his registration after explaining the registration under the wrong heading previously?

There is no law that if you make a mistake, you should continue with the mistake for rest of life and it can never be corrected.

If a Rent-a-Cab operator takes a vehicle from person, say X who is not Rent-a-Cab operator (X has purchased a vehicle out of his savings and loan and given the vehicle to a rent-a-cab operator for some revenues which are not related to the actual amounts earned by the vehicle). X is not engaged in travel business at all.

If control of vehicle is handed over, VAT is payable and not service tax. If control over vehicle is retained by X (e.g., his own driver), then it can come under ‘supply of tangible goods for use’ and service tax will be payable.

For this we have arrangement/agreement with FFMC, who has authorized us for this limited purpose only. We exchange money at prevalent market rate provided to us by the FFMC. There is no in-built consideration whatsoever. In other words the service is absolutely free of any charge.

INCOME/PROPERTY DEEMED TO HAVE BEEN USED/APPLIED FOR BENEFIT OF INTERESTED PERSONS [SECTION 13(2)]

'Property', meaning of - The word 'property' in section 13(2) will have to be understood as having been used in its own generic sense to include 'movable and immovable property' [Agappa Child Centre v. CIT [1997] 92 Taxman 327 (Ker.)].

'Lending' and 'investment' - In the process of investment, the element or risk is involved and the expectation of return or profit is not assured and the depletion of capital itself is not an abnormal feature. In the case of lending, the return by way of interest is generally assured and the element of risk is minimal. When an amount is advanced on an agreed rate of interest, the transaction is within the fold of 'lending' and it cannot be considered as 'investment' [CIT v. Polisetty Somasundaram Charities [1990] 188 ITR 377 (AP)].

In the case of lending by trusts, clause (a) of section 13(2) will apply and not clause (h) [CIT v. Sarladevi Sarabhai Trust (No. 2) [1988] 40 Taxman 388 (Guj.)].

Relationship of borrower and lender must exist - For an amount to fall within the mischief of section 13(2)(a), there must be a loan. To constitute a loan, there must be a positive act of lending, coupled with an acceptance by the other side of the money as a loan. The relationship of borrower and lender must come into existence by the act of parties [CIT v. Nachimuthu Industrial Association [1983] 14 Taxman 224 (Mad.)].

Lending of income/property - The mere circumstance that a partnership concern was not in a position to pay the amounts due to the assessee-partner on the date of his retirement from the partnership firm and the fact that the amounts were shown in the books of account as due to the assessee, could not convert the amounts due as moneys of the assessee lent to the firm [CIT v. Nachimuthu Industrial Association [1983] 14 Taxman 224 (Mad.)].

Personal surety given by director of a company to which assessee-trust had advanced loan could be considered to be adequate security for allowance of exemption u/s 11 [CIT v. Shri Ram Smarak Nidhi [2004] 141 Taxman 297 (Delhi)].

Where assessee-society had advanced certain sum to its treasurer without any surety and no interest had been charged on a loan outstanding against treasurer nor any provision for accrued interest was made, assessee was not entitled to exemption u/s 11 in view of provisions contained in section 13(1)(c) and 13(2)(a) [CIT v. Audh Educational Society [2011] 15 taxmann.com 235/203 Taxman 166 (All.)].

Making available any property without adequate compensation - Where the assessee, a public charitable trust, purchased a refrigerator even before the trust buildings were completed and kept it at the disposal of the managing trustee, and it was found that the assessee never even thought of charging adequate rent or other compensation from the trustee, the case would be hit by the prohibition contained in section 13(2)(b), and the assessee-trust would not be entitled to exemption u/s 11 [Agappa Child Centre v. CIT [1997] 92 Taxman 327 (Ker.)].

The assessee-company was acting as a managing agents of various companies including one 'G'. The assessee acquired a large block of shares in 'G'. In 1950, 'G' was converted into a public company. Thereafter, the assessee was not entitled to any commission on sales, etc., in view of the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, as amended in 1939. Hence, a fresh agreement was entered into between the assessee and the 'G' on 10-5-1960, under which the assessee company was entitled to an office allowance of Rs. 5,000 per month and a commission of 10 per cent of the net profits. The Board of directors of the Managed Company had taken a decision to terminate the agency of managing company. An extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the managed-company approved the resolution of the board of directors on 31-3-1951. That meeting also recommended a payment of Rs. 18 lakhs to the assessee as compensation. That resolution was communicated to the assessee on 3-4-1951, and the latter accepted it on 10-4-1951. The assessee was a registered society duly incorporated and registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1862. The society was formed with the main aim and object of advancement, promotion and spread of computer education, higher professional education, management studies and the establishment and support of colleges, schools, reading rooms, etc., in this regard. The income which the assessee received in the form of tuition fee and other receipts could not have been received but for the organization and, therefore, the tuition fee and other receipts derived from other organizations was income derived from property held under trust. Such tuition fee and other receipts, received by the assessee were directly and substantially arising from the organization, which was the property held under the trust. The Assessing Officer's assertion that whatever property in the shape of office building, furniture, computer was simply an application of income was not sustainable. It is well-settled that property acquired by an organization from its own income is also a property held under trust. Thus, fixed assets and current assets held by the assessee as on 31-3-1999 and 31-3-2000 were properties held under trust. Further, the Delhi Bench of the Tribunal in the assessee's own case vide order dated 15-12-2003 had held that department cannot guide a charitable institution as to how it should carry on its charity. It is sufficient compliance with the relevant provisions of law in case surplus of the institution is utilized into activities of the institution and does not find its way to the pocket of the persons who were running the society/institution. There was no allegation by the department that the funds had been siphoned off. Therefore, the Commissioner should not have withdrawn the registration granted to the assessee under section 12AA.

According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee was charging hefty fee from students and imparting education in return and, thus, it was a case of sound business proposition in which the assessee was engaged with the motive of earning profit and not doing any charity.

The educational institution being run by the assessee was for the general benefit of the public and not for the benefit of any class or section of the public, as (a ) the institution was duly recognized by HNB Garhwal University and strictly followed all procedures with regard to admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum as laid down by the university, and (b) the nominees of State Government, HNB University and AICTE (functioning under the Human Resources Ministry) were on the governing body of the society and, therefore, the assessee had no choice in matters of admissions, charging of fees and course curriculum. The institute, was, in fact, State Government managed.

It was also found that the working system of the assessee was as per the guidelines laid down by the University. In respect of fixing and charging fees from students, the society management had no powers. Fee was being charged from students strictly as specified and laid down by the University. The governing body of the society had no powers to workout the cost and thereafter to add on the element of overheads and profits. Therefore, there was no question of building huge margins of profits in the fees structure as conceived by the Assessing Officer.

From a plain reading of the main objects given in the Memorandum, it could very well be discerned that the society had been formed with the sole objective of imparting and spreading computer education. Further, the assessee-society was virtually Government managed. Therefore, the question of functioning like a commercial profit making institution was totally unfounded. Thus, the fees charged by the assessee was simply receipt in the hands of the society and not profit.

Further, the assessee was rendering services of education to the general public. Therefore, its activities clearly fell within the ambit of charitable purpose as defined under section 2(15). Charging of fees does not in anyway dilute the aspect of charitable purpose. It is the end use and spirit and objective which matters.

In the assessment order, the Assessing Officer had not been able to appreciate the difference in the words 'charitable purposes' as are used in the Act and the word 'charity' as had been used by the Assessing Officer in his order. The word 'charity' as used in English language and recognized in English law, implies as an act motivated by pity and may require benevolence to manifest it. However, exemption under section 11 has been prescribed with reference to 'charitable purposes' and not 'charity'. The expression 'charitable purpose' has been defined by way of inclusive definition "relief of poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general utility". In this definition per se is stated as constitution of a charitable purpose and there are no conditions prescribed such as imparting education for fee or at subsidized price. Thus, education may not be regarded as charitable activity in popular sense; it is a charitable purpose as defined in the Act.
