HELD: The definition of managing agent makes it clear that a managing agent need not necessarily be a servant of the company whose affairs are managed by that managing agent. All that is needed is that the managing agents should have an agreement with the company under which he receives the right of management of the affairs of the company though this management of affairs of the company is to be under the control and direction of the directors except to the extent, if any, otherwise provided for in the agreement. Such an agreement may be entered into between a person who is already a servant of the company or it may be entered into between the company and some person who may not be a servant of the company. The mere appointment as a managing agent or working as such would not necessarily make the person a servant of the company. Whenever any one works as a managing agent of a company, that person must be reimbursed in some form or other for the work done by him. In a case where a managing agent happens to be a servant of the company, the payment to him of his salary as servant may compensate the person for the whole work done by him as the managing agent and the servant of the company and no separate or additional remuneration may be provided for working as managing agent. On the other hand, if the managing agent does not happen to be a servant of the company, then the payment would be made, under the agreement, for the work done as managing agent and not as salary for services rendered by him as a servant. It thus appears to be clear that, under the Indian Companies Act, a managing agent may either be a servant of the company or a mere agent without being a servant.

‘N’ was the karta of a joint Hindu family. The joint family properties included a building which had been set apart for use of pilgrims visiting the town. Subsequently the family properties were partitioned under a partition deed between ‘N’ and his adopted son, ‘R’ as also minor, ‘D’ the adopted some of his pre-deceased son. Under that partition the building in question was directed to be maintained by ‘N’ with the income from certain lands over which he had been given a life-interest. Later on N died. At the time of his death he was a partner in the firm having a 3/16th share in the profits and losses of the said firm. The accountable persons filed an estate duty return admitting a net dutiable estate including the share capital and the share of profit and interest of the deceased in the managing agency firm, but did not include the value of the share of the deceased in the goodwill of the said managing agency firm. It also did not include the value of the building. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty, however, proposed to value of building at Rs. 62,000 and 3/16th share in the goodwill of the firm and to include the same in the estate of the deceased. The accountable persons objected to this proposal and contended that the value of the building could not be included in the estate of the deceased because it had been set apart only for charitable purposes, with regard to the goodwill, it was contended that in the case of managing agency business, there was no goodwill at all, and that in fact the accountable persons had not obtained any amount from the firm towards the value of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the firm. The Assistant Controller, however, overruled these objections and held that the building was not a trust property and that it was owned by the deceased at the time of his death, and, therefore, its value was includible in the estate of the deceased. On the question of goodwill, the Assistant Controller held that the managing agency firm did possess goodwill and on the death of the deceased the accountable persons were entitled to 3/16th share in the goodwill of the business of the firm and as such a sum being the value of the 3/16th share had to be included in the estate of the deceased.

On appeal, the Appellate controller upheld the order of the assistant controller and reduced the value of the building.

On further appeal the Tribunal upheld the order of the Appellate Controller in respect of inclusion of value of building holding that a mere provision for the maintenance of the building by the deceased and thereafter by others could not amount to creation of a trust with reference to the building and that the exclusive use of the building from 1942 to 1958, for religious and charitable purposes did not amount to a permanent dedication of the building as a trust property. As regards the inclusion representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm, the Tribunal held that goodwill cannot be associated with the business of managing agency firm because the managing agency business is governed by the terms of the agreement between the managing agency firm and the company and the right of managing agency was more personal and could not pass on to a successor. The Tribunal also held that no share in the goodwill of the business passed to the accountable persons on the death of the deceased and that in any event no amount was actually paid to the accountable persons by way of the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the business. In that view the Tribunal deleted the sum representing the deceased’s share in the goodwill of the managing agency firm.

Management, Maintenance and Repair Services

As per section 65(64) of the Finance Act, 1994 (as amended w.e.f. 16-6-2005 and by the Finance Act, 2006 w.e.f. 1-5-2006), "management, maintenance or repair" means any service provided by—(i) any person under a contract or an agreement; or (ii) a manufacturer or any person authorised by him, in relation to, (a) management of properties, whether immovable or not (b) maintenance or repair of properties whether immovable or not; or (c) maintenance or repair including reconditioning or restoration, or servicing of any goods or equipment, excluding motor vehicle.

In many cases, housing societies collect the charges from members which are termed as ‘maintenance’ charges. Hence, it is alleged that the housing society provides management, maintenance or repair.

As discussed above, the activities undertaken by housing society are a bundle of various activities, some of which might fall under ‘management, maintenance or repair’ services. However, a service can be taxed if it is predominantly a taxable service. In Daelim Industrial Co. v. CCE 2003 STT 438 = 155 ELT 457 = 57 RLT 636 = 3 STR 124 (CEGAT), it was held that a works contract on turnkey basis is not a consultancy contract. A works contract cannot be vivisected and part of it subjected to tax (SLP filed by department dismissed by SC - [2004] 170 ELT A181). This was followed in Larsen & Toubro Ltd. v. CCE [2005] 1 STT 183 = 2004 (174) ELT 322 = 60 RLT 505 = 3 STR 223 (CESTAT), in respect of design element of works contract.

The principle that a contract cannot be vivisected is applicable to all services.

D.O. letter No. 334/4/2006-TRU, dated 28-2-2006 states as follows, ‘Often services provided consist of more than one service. In such cases, it is important to decide, for the purpose of classification of services, whether each element of the transaction should be treated separately or as a single composite transaction, albeit, made up of two or more separate services. A composite service, even if it consists of more than one service, should be treated as a single service based on the main or principal service and accordingly classified. The decision is to be made on question of facts and law. It will not make a difference if the tax rates of the components are the same as that of the principal service. The problem may arise when some elements are taxable and others are exempt. While taking a view, both the form and substance of the transaction are to be taken into account. The guiding principle is to identify the essential features of the transaction. The method of charging does not in itself determine whether the service provided is a single service or multiple services’.

Thus, a service can be taxed only if it is predominantly a taxable service.

The so called ‘service’ provided by housing society is not predominantly a ‘management, maintenance or repair’ service.

Hence, in my view, the service of housing society cannot be classified under that head.

Conclusion

CASE LAWS WITH REGARD TO THE PROJECT GRANTS 7. In Society for Integrated Development in Urban and Rural Areas (SIDUR) v. Dy. CIT [2004] 90 ITD 493 (Hyd.), the issue came up before the regular bench of the Tribunal in Hyderabad. The exemptions were forfeited by virtue of section 13( l)(c ). The assessee contended that for the purposes of computing income from various projects, grants received from foreign donors could not be included in the income liable to tax, as such receipts would not be considered as income for the purposes of section 11. It was held that project grants did not form a part of the income of the assessee nor they form a part of the corpus. Voluntary contributions covered by section 12 are those contributions freely available to the assessee without any stipulation, which the assessee can utilise towards its objectives according to its own discretion and judgment. Tied-up grants for a specified purpose would only mean that the assessee which was a voluntary organisation, had agreed to act as a trustee of a special fund granted by donor with the result that it need not be pooled or integrated with the assessee’ s normal income or corpus. The Tribunal relied upon the findings of Nirmal Agricultural Society v. ITO [1999] 71 ITD 152 (Hyd.). Some relevant extracts are as under:

"The grants received from foreign donor were for specific purposes. The grants which were for specific purposes did not belong to the assessee-society, such grants did not form corpus of the assessee or its income. Those grants were not donations to the assessee so as to bring them under the purview of section 12. Voluntary contributions covered by section 12 are those contributions freely available to the assessee without any stipulation, which the assessee can utilise towards its objectives according to its own discretion and judgment. Tied-up grants for a specified purpose would only mean that the assessee which was a voluntary organisation, had agreed to act as a trustee of a special fund granted by donor with the result that it need not be pooled or integrated with the assessee ‘s normal income or corpus..." (p. 153)

Similarly, in Sukhdeo Charity v. CIT [1984] 149 ITR 470 /19 Taxman 222 (Raj.), the issue of whether specific grants were income or not was also discussed. It was observed that if the motive and intention of the donor play an important role in the utilization of the donation, then it cannot be considered as voluntary in nature. The word ‘ voluntary ’ in its very inception connotes the absence of any obligation on the part of the donor.

In the above case, the Court referred to the case of CIT v. Shri Billeswara Charitable Trust [1984] 145 ITR 29/16 Taxman 259 (Mad.).

In the above case, the Court ruled that a grant received for specific purposes cannot by any stretch of imagination be said to be income as envisaged by section 12(1). Because the word ‘ voluntary ’ in its very inception connotes the absence of an obligation on the part of the donor.

3.9. Intent and purpose of Section 11(4)

In the case of CIT v. Birla Education Trust[1985] 21 Taxman 134/153 ITR 579/44 CTR 263, the Calcutta High Court explained the intent and purpose of section 11(4) of the Act. In this case, it was explained that special powers were given to the AO only to ensure that the trustees or any other vested group are not misusing the exemptions available to trusts by under stating the profits of business held under trust. The High Court also quoted the explanatory statements provided by the Ministry of Finance when the Finance Bill was placed before the Parliament in 1961. The relevant extract is as under:

"It is now settled that the speech of the mover of the Bill is relevant. In Varghese v. ITO, P.N. Bhagwati J., held (at p. 608):

"Now, it is true that the speeches made by the Members of the Legislature on the floor of the House when a Bill for enacting a statutory provision is being debated are inadmissible for the purpose of interpreting the statutory provision but the speech made by the mover of the Bill explaining the reason for the introduction of the Bill can certainly be referred to for the purpose of ascertaining the mischief sought to be remedied by the legislation and the object and purpose for which the legislation was enacted. This is in accord with the recent trend in juristic thought not only in Western countries but also in India, that interpretation of a statute being an exercise in the ascertainment of meaning, everything which is logically relevant should be admissible."

Smt. Tarakeswari Sinha participating in the debate on September 1, 1961, stated in relation to Sub-section (4) of Section 11:

"Suppose a factory has got a capacity for an annual income of Rs. 15 lakhs but for avoiding a particular portion of the tax, sometimes the trustees or the donors have manipulated the accounts. They say that the income of the factory is only Rs. 10 lakhs and not Rs. 15 lakhs, thus avoiding tax payment on Rs. 5 lakhs which goes to their own pocket. For plugging this hole, actually powers were taken by the income-tax authorities to scrutinise the accounts to find out that the income shown in the books is the correct and has not been more. That was the only safeguard that has been provided by the sub-clause."

Thus, Sub-section (4) was intended to uncover tax evasion by manipulation of the account books. It was not intended to apply to application or expenditure of income by the business undertaking. As already seen, the non-application of income for purposes of the trust was dealt with by Sub-section (3) of Section 11.

It appears to us that Sub-section (4) was intended for a different contingency. It was meant to cover a different situation. It was not intended to apply to application of income.

Under Sub-section (4), the ITO can determine the income and compare it with the income appearing in the accounts. The income spoken of in Sub-section (4) appears to us to be the gross income and not the net income of the business undertaking. The net income is computed after granting the admissible deductions. The deductions admissible from income of a business undertaking are not always the same as application of income wholly for charitable or religious purposes. They may or may not be admissible deduction from business income under the provisions relating to assessment of income. Yet they are entitled to exclusion under Sub-section (1) of Section 11 because they represent application of income wholly for charitable or religious purposes.

Here, the ITO has to scrutinise the accounts and see if there is suppression of income or manipulation of accounts with a view to conceal income. He could see whether there are items which are deemed to be income under some provision of the I.T. Act and which have not been accounted for in the books of the undertaking, or there may be some receipts which are really in the nature of income and which have not been reflected in the accounts. This interpretation of Sub-section (4) of Section 11 is in consonance with the legislative intent as disclosed by the Finance Minister who spoke in Parliament while this provision was under consideration."

In light of the above, it is clear that there is no provision under section 11(4) to suggest that tax audit under section 44AB is applicable or that the AO is required to apply the provisions applicable to business assessees under section 44AB.

Where a settlor creates a trust, it lies within his power to also make a provision as to the management of the trust property. It is perfectly permissible for a settlor to nominate any person as trustees for first trustees and where there were more than one trustee, a managing trustee. It is also within his power to regulate the appointment of trustees in future as well as the managing trustee. There is no prohibition in law if the settlor himself takes over the function of the managing trustee after the trust has come into being. When the settlor himself becomes a trustee or managing trustee a change undergoes in his capacity from one of an owner of property to that of trustee holding the trust property for the benefit of the beneficiaries or for the purpose of working out the directions in the deed of trust. If for such work, any remuneration is provided for by the terms of the trust deed, that would not, amount to the reservation of any interest for the purposes of section 12(1).

The Department was, therefore, not entitled to rely on clauses 6 and 19 to contend that there was reservation of interest of the trust property and, therefore, the value of Kale Bhawan was liable to be treated as a part of the dutiable estate.

There could hardly be any doubt that clause 23 of the trust deed was a repository of the express power of revocation which could be exercised after the period of 10 years from the date specified therein and if the trust could not function for any reason. It could not be held that merely because in the case of a public trust a power to revoke is reserved by the settlor, such property must be deemed to pass on the death of the settlor for the purposes of section 12(1). When section 12(1) refers to the reservation by the settlor of the right to exercise the power of revocation, it obviously presupposes that such a power of revocation can be validly and legally reserved by the settlor. In other words, even if the document of trust does contain a clause expressly reserving the power of revocation if in law such a power of revocation is impossible to the either reserved or exercised, the Department would not be entitled to rely on the latter part of section 12(1) merely because in the settlement the settlers purported to reserve the power of revocation.

It cannot be disputed that once a trust for a charitable purpose is created in a given case, the trust fund can grow and grow to a size much larger than what was endowed originally by the settlement in the given case. Donations may be given to the trust or immovable property may be gifted to the trust by persons who want their property to be utilized for the same purpose for which the trust is created. Whether the trust is in favour of an idol and is of a religious nature or whether the trust is intended to achieve charitable purposes would in that context be wholly irrelevant. The real question is whether in such a case, it would be permissible for a settlor to revoke the trust so as to undo the trust itself and thus affect not only the trust property settled by him but certain other properties also which may have been endowed in favour of the trust or dedicated to that charity. There is no express provision of law permitting this to be done. On first principles, permitting such a power to be exercised by the settlor would open the floodgates of a device which would enable people to use the creation of the trust as a means for getting back larger property than what was originally settled as trust property.

There is unanimity in the view that in the case of a charitable endowment or trust once the dedication is completed there is no power of revocation left with the settlers. Even though in a given case the settlor has reserved the power to revoke the trust, such a reservation would be wholly invalid and the power cannot be invoked so as to undo the settlement.

Apart from the general principle that in the case of a public trust, where dedication is complete, a power of revocation does not vest in the settlor, in so far as the instant trust was concerned there could not be any ground which could be wholly irrelevant because there were overriding provisions of the Bombay Public Trusts Act under which a public trust was not being given effect to, the Charity Commissioner could step in and see that the trust funds were applied to a charitable purpose. It was, therefore, clear that the so-called power of revocation was wholly redundant and ineffective. If the power of revocation was redundant and ineffective and indeed wholly invalid the mere reservation of a power by a clause in the trust deed could not attract the applicability of the provisions of section 12(1).

15. Overriding effect to provisions of Section 115BBI

Hitherto, there was no specific section for taxing the certain income of a charitable institution at a specific prescribed rate.

The Finance Bill, 2022 proposes to insert Section 115BBI with effect from the assessment year 2023-24 to provide that where the total income of any "specified charitable institution" includes any "specified income", the income-tax payable shall be the aggregate of:

(a)

the amount of income-tax calculated at the rate of 30% on the aggregate specified income; and

(b)

the amount of income tax with which the assessee would be chargeable if the assessee's total income is reduced by the aggregate specified income referred to in clause (a).

Section 115BBI provides that the income which does not enjoy exemption under section 11 is taxable at the rate of 30%. On the other hand, proviso to section 164(2) providing for taxation of a charitable trust at maximum marginal rate (MMR) is not deleted. Hence, literally, both the provisions apply to a trust. Thus, it was not clear whether section 115BBI or section 164(2) should apply to a trust for taxation of certain incomes.

The Finance Bill (Lok Sabha) provided that notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of the Act, the specified incomes shall be taxable under Section 115BBI. Thus, the provisions of section 115BBI would have an overriding effect over anything contrary contained in the Act. Hence, the provisions of section 115BBI shall now prevail for the rate of tax in case of income specified therein.

Introduction

1. In India, the organisations which carry out their activities without profit motive have always been provided concessions in the form of exemptions in taxes or other concessions like providing of land, water and electricity. Whether CTs are liable to pay ST?

2. The answer is yes. Refer to charging sections, i.e., Section 66B which reads as follows:

'66B. There shall be levied a tax …. provided ….. by oneperson to another…….

What is a "person"?

3. 'Person' has been defined in section 65B. It includes the following entities:

an individual

a Hindu Undivided Family

a company

a society

a limited liability partnership

a firm

an association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not

Government

a local authority

As can be seen, the term "person" is wide enough and includes Association of Persons, whether incorporated or not.

Does it mean that CTs will have to pay ST on services provided by them?

4. Yes. Section 66D containing Negative List (NL) is not having any specific reference to services provided by CTs. Hence, services provided by CTs are taxable.

Whether CTs will have to pay ST on all the types of services provided by them?

5. No. For the purpose of determining tax liability, one will have to refer to Notification No. 25/2012 whereunder various types of services have been declared exempt.

Whether there are any exemptions for services provided by CTs?

6. Yes. Clause No. 4 of Notification No. 25/2012 provides as follows:

Services by an entity registered under section 12AA of the Income-tax Act, 1961(43 of 1961) by way of charitable activities;

As can be seen from above, exemption granted has two important conditions to be complied with, viz., (i) CT should have been registered under section 12AA of the Income-tax Act, and (ii) the activities carried on should be charitable activities. There were two groups of partners who constituted the managing agency firm BK. The shares of the two groups in that firm were equal. One group consisted of four members of the S family and the other consisted of four members of the G family. An agreement was duly executed between the company and the firm on 2-5-1935 appointing the firm as managing agents. The firm continued to function as the managing agents of the company till 1943, when disputes arose between the S group and the G group of partners. As a result of an arbitration on award, the managed company was to be given over exclusively to the G group. Provision was made for the purchase of the shares of the S Group by the G Group. After the interest of the Group S had ceased in the company, the managing agency was also to go to the Group G exclusively. A reconstituted firm in the name BR was brought into existence. The partners of this firm were the members of the G group alone. On 31-1-1944, the company recognized this new firm as its managing agents. This was objected to by S Group. The Company overruled the objections of the S group and terminated the managing agency of the firm BK. With effect from 30-9-1944. The S group required the company to pay damages and compensation for the alleged wrongful termination of the managing agency which was to last for a period of 99 years. The company relied to the S Group that their claim for compensation was misconceived as the managing agency was terminated due to quarrels between the two groups of partners themselves. Thereupon notices were given to the company both by the S group and by the G group, claiming compensation. Ultimately, the disputes were referred to the arbitration of M. Before the arbitration award the two-Groups settled their disputes inter se amicably. Under this settlement the S group was to receive compensation in the sum of rupees eight lakhs for the premature and wrongful termination of the managing agency. This amount was fixed irrespective of whatever amount may ultimately be awarded by the arbitrator as compensation for the wrongful termination of the managing agency. In pursuance of this agreement, the G group, on 19-2-1948, paid rupees eight lakhs to the S group. In due course the arbitrator, M, delivered his award and awarded a sum of rupees 18,90,000 to the managing agency firm as compensation for the wrongful and premature termination of the managing agency. Rupees eight lakhs having already been paid to the S group in full settlement of their share of the compensation, the balance, namely, Rs. 10,90,000 fell to the share of G group. Out of this amount each one of the four members of that group got Rs. 2,72,500. The ITO without giving any reason treated Rs. 2,72,500 in the hands of each one of the four partners as a revenue receipt and subjected the same to tax. On appeal the AAC held that the receipt was not a revenue receipt but a capital receipt. Since the similar amount of Rs. 8 lakhs in the hands of the S was not treated as a revenue receipt. On revenue’s appeal, the Tribunal asked for a remand report. In the remand report the ITO recorded the findings that the actual work of management was done by R in his capacity as an ex officio director of the company and not as a partner of the managing agency firm; that the payment made to managing agents was for past services and did not represent. Compensation for depriving the managing agents of a source of income; that there was collusion between the company and the managing' agents in making the payment; and that even if it was accepted that the managing agents rendered any service the payment represented remuneration in a commuted and consolidated form and was accordingly taxable as income. Thereafter, the Tribunal reversed the findings of the ITO and concluded that R worked on behalf of the managing agents of the company and not as a director of the company. He was the only adult male member of the G group of partners in the managing agency firm and it was provided in the partnership deed itself that he would be in charge of the business of the firm. The Tribunal also held that the payment made to the firm was not for past services; That there was no collusion between the managing agents and the company; and that there was no clause in the managing agency agreement for premature termination of the managing agency and the termination of the managing agency was wrongful as held in the award of M. In the result the Tribunal concluded that the amount received by the managing agency firm was a capital receipt not liable to tax.

Generation of surplus out of gross receipts A doubt has been raised whether generation of surplus out of gross receipts would necessarily 'breach' the threshold condition that the educational institution should exist 'solely for educational purpose and not for the purpose of profit'. Perusal of prescribed provisions clearly reveal that mere generation of surplus cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) on the ground that it amounts to an activity of the nature of profit making. In fact, the third Proviso to the said clause clearly provides that accumulation of income is permissible subject to the manner prescribed therein provided such accumulation is to be applied "wholly and exclusively to the objects for which it is established". Hence, it is clarified that mere generation of surplus by educational institution from year to year cannot be a basis for rejection of application u/s 10(23C)(vi) if it is used for educational purposes unless the accumulation is contrary to the manner prescribed under law.

4. Collection of amounts under different heads of fee from students—

It has been brought to the notice that collection of small amounts from students by way of application fee, examination fee, fee for issuing transfer certificate, subscription fee for library etc. is being treated by some Assessing Officers as profit making activity resulting in denial of exemption u/s 10(23C)(vi). Collection of small and reasonable amounts under different heads of fee, which are essentially in the nature of fee connected with imparting education and do not violate any Central or State regulation does not, in general, represent a profit making activity. Hence, there is no justification for treating the charging of small amounts under different heads of fee as profit making activity unless the amount in the nature of 'capitation fee' is charged directly or indirectly.

5. Impact of extraordinary powers of the Managing Trustees to appoint remove or nominate other trustees.

5.1 Doubt has been expressed whether extraordinary powers to the Managing Trustees to appoint or remove other trustees and also to nominate their successor affect the nature of charitable activity of the trust and whether in such an eventuality, exemption can be denied.

5.2 There is no provision under the Act which calls for denial of exemption merely on account of appointment or removal of trustees. Although answer to such a situation would normally depend on the factual implication of such arrangement, the same should generally not be a ground for denying exemption unless the nature of activities of the trust or institution get changed or modified or no longer remain to exist 'solely for educational purpose and not for purposes of profit'. Hence denial of exemption would not be justifiable only on the ground of induction of new trustees or removal of existing ones. - Circular No. 14/2015, dated 17-8-2015.

Conclusion

5. The above circular is just an explanation. This is issued to show the fact that the law governing the Income-tax Act and the law governing the service tax are separate and the governance of service tax does not depend on the Income-tax Act and for the purpose of word not defined in the Finance Act, 1994, it is not necessary to follow the Income-tax Act. This is the first time that it is mentioned that a specific dictionary has to be consulted for this purpose.

This is very casual approach to deal with a controversy. It will itself generate some other controversies. Our law makers have been following this method since the inception of service tax. There has been a need to clarify the meaning of the term ‘commercial concern’ since long time and how it is so far dealt with is not a very pending issue. The same process is adopted again by our law makers while defining the word ‘charitable’. They had given a very confusing clarification instead of defining the word in very clear terms.

The Text of Section 11(4A) is reproduced herein below:

(4A) Sub-section (1) or sub-section (2) or sub-section (3) or sub-section (3A) shall not apply in relation to any income of a trust or an institution, being profits and gains of business, unless the business is incidental to the attainment of the objectives of the trust or, as the case may be, institution, and separate books of account are maintained by such trust or institution in respect of such business.

Business income shall be eligible for exemption under Section 11 if it is incidental to the attainment of objectives of the trust and separate books of account are maintained by the trust in respect of such business. We need to understand the meaning of business incidental to the attainment of main objects.

In the case of Asstt. CIT v. Thanthi Trust [2001] 115 Taxman 126/247 ITR 785/165 CTR 681, the Supreme Court held that a business whose total income is utilised for the purposes of achieving the objects of the trust should be considered as incidental to the attainment of the objects.

In the case of CIT v. Janakiammal Ayyandar Trust [2005] 277 ITR 274 (Mad.), the Supreme Court ruling was reaffirmed where the seemingly unrelated business of manufacturing paper cap was held to be incidental as the entire income was applied for charitable purposes. The Madras High Court referred to the Apex Court in Thanthi Trust (supra) holding section 11(4A) of the Act, as amended in 1992.

The High Court of Delhi in the case of Pr. CIT v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 777, held that an incidental business activity would also be treated as a charitable activity if it is necessary and incidental to the primary activity

In Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. Dy. GIT(E) [WP(C) No. 3147 of 2012, dated 4-7-2013] while considering whether the activities of ICAI fell within the proviso to section 2(15) as introduced with effect from 1-4-2009, this court, after considering the Supreme Court decision in the case of CST v. Sai Publication Fund [2002] 122 Taxman 437/258 ITR 70/177 CTR 1 held:

"Thus, if the dominant activity of the assessee was not business, then any incidental or ancillary activity would also not fall within the definition of business."

Hence the incidental business activity to feed charity cannot be classified as a business, and therefore, the income for such incidental business-like activity is to be computed in a commercial sense as per the normal scheme of taxation as applicable to a charitable trust and the provisions to compute income under the head profit and gains from business and profession shall not apply.

Based on the legal jurisprudence and provisions of the Income-tax Act as discussed above, it can be concluded that there is nothing in the statute that suggests that the income of the charitable institution shall be computed under the head `Profit & Gain from Business' nor it suggests that Tax Audit under section 44AB shall apply to charitable trusts. Sections 11 to 13 are independent of the five heads of income. As long as the registration under section 12AB is intact, the income cannot be computed under the five heads of income.

6. The service tax legislation does not contain any definition of what could be considered as charitable. However, the Income-tax law has a definition of this phrase. There is a judicial definition also. Its coverage has been comprehensively extended by the Courts (including the Apex Court) in a number of cases coming up before them, as can be seen from the discussion to follow.

Section 2(15) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 defines ‘charitable purpose’ as relief of the poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general ‘public utility’. Besides this statutory definition, the concept of charity has been widely accepted in judicial decisions in the context of conferring benefit of exemption from tax. Thus, relief of a public character to the poor is a charitable activity.

In India as well as in England, the object of ‘relief of the poor’ has always been recognized as a charitable purpose. Dealing with the scope of these words, the Supreme Court in Dharmadeepti v. CIT [1978] 114 ITR 454 observed that they include the expression ‘to give charity’ also. Thus, the object of giving charity falls within the ambit of the expression ‘relief of the poor’ used in section 2(15).

However, relief to the poor is only one facet of charitable purpose - not the primary one or the main one, as has been said in the CBEC’s circulars.

Providing education is another aspect of charitable activity for the public. In CIT v. Bar Council, Madras [1943] 11 ITR 1 (Mad.), the activity of giving facilities for legal education and training of the advocates has been held to be an educational purpose.

In Ecumenical Christian Centre v. CIT [1983] 139 ITR 226/[1982] 8 Taxman 175 (Kar.), the main objects of the assessee were diffusion of useful knowledge, publication of journal and books and promotion of search for truth. After referring to the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Lok Shikshana Trust, the Court held that the objects of diffusion of useful knowledge, publication of journals and promotion of search for truth are directly related to education. The High Court adopted a broader approach by accepting the principle that over and above normal schooling, other means of rendering scholastic instruction are also included in the definition of ‘education’ under section 2(15).

Similarly, providing medical relief has been considered to be covered under the definition of ‘charitable purpose’ under section 2(15) (supra) and accepted by the courts.

The residuary part of the definition has been held to be of very wide amplitude. One of the conditions precedent for a trust/institution to be for charitable purpose under section 2(15) is that the beneficiary thereof should be general public and that the object should not be such as resulting in private gains. The scope of the term ‘general public’ is by itself extremely wide but it is almost impossible for a particular charitable trust/institution to cover more than a section of the public. The application of the expression ‘Object of general public utility’ is not, therefore, restricted to such objects as are beneficial to the whole mankind. It is sufficient if the intention is to benefit a section of the public, provided it is well-defined and identifiable by some common quality of impersonal nature, as distinguished from specified individuals.

The classic elucidation of this phrase has been given by Lord, Macnaghten in Commr. for Special Purposes of Income-tax v. Remsel, 1891 AC 531 at 583 thus:—

"Where four principal divisions were said to be comprised-trusts for the relief of poverty, trusts for the advancement of education, trusts for the advancement of religion and trusts for other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the preceding heads. The definition in this Act makes the significant change when it speaks of ‘public utility’ and this gives a guidance to the whole meaning and purpose of the exemption [see Fazlul Rabbi Pradhan v. State of West Bengal AIR 1965 SC 1722]."

General public utility has been regarded as an important consideration in determining whether an activity is charitable or not. [This aspect has been included in describing activity of a charitable nature in the service tax law also section 65(25a)( supra). The courts’ interpretation of ‘charitable’ in the context of advancement of any other object of general public utility could be seen from some of the decisions mentioned hereinafter.

As regards the point regarding material before Tribunal for finding that payment by the company any to the firm was not collusive, it is well-settled that the apparent state of affairs is to be presumed to be real until the contrary is shown. It is equally well settled that good faith and the genuineness of a transaction are also to be presumed until the contrary is proved. It followed that if the department wanted to challenge the fact that the payment of compensation for the premature termination of the managing agency, which was based upon a resolution of the company terminating the tenure of the firm, and the amount of compensation, which as determined by the award of M, were not genuine but collusive transactions, it was for the department to have materials before itself for those findings. The department’s counsel had not been able to point out any materials on the basis of which the ITO could come to the conclusion that the termination of the managing agency or the payment of compensation were collusive transactions. With regard to the other part of the counsel’s argument that the work done by R was not in his capacity as a partner but as a director, the position was also the same. Under the memorandum and articles of association of the company as well as under the terms of the managing agency agreement the work of management of the company was to be done by the firm and not by the directors. The directors were only to exercise supervision in respect of the actual management of the company by the firm. Under the deed of partnership of the managing agency firm, R was to do the work, as the other partners of the G group were women and a minor. It followed that prima facie been though R might also be a director of the company, whatever was done by him in the course of the management of the company, was done by him as a partner and not as a director. If the department wanted to controvert this position, it was for the department to have materials before it on the basis of which it could displace the prima facie case. Here also, department’s counsel had not been able to point any material on the basis of which it could be held that the work done by R was not as a partner but as a director. The assessee could not be required to prove the negative. It followed that the Tribunal was fully justified in coming to the conclusion that the payment of compensation for the termination of the managing agency was not due to any collusion and that the managing agency firm did actually do management work of the company. Besides, the proceeding before the Court was a reference under section 66(1). The only question or questions which the court had jurisdiction to decide were questions which had been actually referred. The point argued had not been referred though, it might be said to be implied in the question which had been actually referred. It followed that the questions, not having been actually referred, any argument on these questions was not open to counsel, and the court was not called upon to decide the correctness or otherwise of the conclusions of the Tribunal on those questions. However, on the footing, that the questions might be implied in the question referred, the Court had considered the same and the Court was satisfied that the conclusions reached by the Tribunal on those points were correct.

As regards the point that since payment of compensation was in presence of an agreement, it was in the nature of revenue, it was to be mentioned that under the agreement the termination of the managing agency was contemplated only in the case of the winding up of the company and no other case of premature termination was contemplated at all. The appointment as managing agents was to run for ninety-nine years and even beyond. After the expiry of the term, the managing agents were removable, if at all, only by a three-fourths majority of the shareholders. They were actually removed long before the expiry of ninety-nine years, and it could not be said that the termination was as contemplated by the agreement but the payment was wholly outside the agreement. The contract in the instant case was an agency agreement. Such agreements have been distinguished from trading contracts. Agency agreements have been described as an apparatus making it possible to earn income. They have been treated as capital assets and termination of an agency agreement has been held to be destruction of a capital asset. Anything paid for destruction of such an asset partakes of the nature of capital gain and not income. By payment of compensation, the Company took, in a sense, an assignment of the right of the managing agency which was to continue for a term of ninety-nine years. The termination of the agency agreement in lieu of payment of compensation was payment made to managing agency for the extinction of its capacity to make income so far as the business of this particular managing agency firm was concerned. This principle was enunciated by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Vazir Sultan & Sons [1959] 36 ITR 175 /[1959] Supp. 2 SCR 375.

CONCEPT OF ACCRUAL OF INCOME

Sachin Vasudeva*

In this article, the author discusses the concept of accrual of income in the context of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and distinguishes it from the concept of revenue recognition as per the accountancy principles. He also casts a glance at the impact of RBI directions on the concept of accrual of income as applicable to Non-Banking Financial Companies - EDITOR

Meaning of Accrual

1. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, the meaning of the word ‘accrue’ is ‘to fall as a natural growth or increment; to come as an accession or advantage’. It indicates a right to receive. Thus, it is manifest that if a person acquires a right to receive income, the income can be said to accrue to him, though it may be received later on. Unless and until there is created in favour of a person a debt due by somebody, it cannot be said that he has acquired a right to receive the income or that income has accrued to him. A mere claim to income without an enforceable right thereto cannot be regarded as accrued income for the purpose of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (‘the Act’).

According to Kanga & Palkhivala (7th edition, the page 170), the question of accrual of income has three aspects: the time of accrual, the person to whom the income accrues, and the place of accrual. These three aspects are considered below:

(i) Time of accrual of income - Income can be said to accrue only when the assessee acquires a right to receive that income. If, however, the income is foregone before it accrues, it cannot be taxed at all because the act of surrender prevents the accrual of income.

(ii) Person to whom income accrues - The question as to whom a particular item of income accrues is distinct and different from the question as to when the income accrues. In the case of E.D. Sassoon & Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 27, the Apex Court held that ". . . in order that the income can be said to have accrued to or [been] earned by the assessee it is not only necessary that the assessee must have contributed to its accruing or arising by rendering services or otherwise but he must have created a debt in his favour. . . ." However, the question whether the proposition that no income accrues to a person unless a debt is created in his own favour is of general application and would depend upon the facts of the case.

(iii) Place of accrual of income - The question should be decided on the facts of each case in the light of commonsense and plain thinking, and too much importance should not be attached to, nor too much emphasis laid upon, the niceties of verbal definitions.

Some important judicial pronouncements

2. The concept of accrual of income under the income-tax law can be understood in the light of the following decisions :

(i) In the case of CIT v. K.R.M.T.T. Thiagaraja Chetty & Co. [1953] 24 ITR 525, the Apex Court, while deciding whether the managing agency commission payable to the assessee would be taxable in the hands of the assessee in the relevant year as the company had resolved to keep the amount in the suspense account without paying it, held that ". . .The computation of profits, whenever it may take place, cannot possibly be allowed to suspend their accrual. In the case of an income where there is a condition that the commission will not be payable until the expiry of a definite period of the making of the account, it might be said with some justification, though we do not decide it, that the income has not accrued, but there is no such condition in the present case. Clauses 7 and 8 of the agreement which relate to the payment of the commission and the calculation of the profits mean no more than this that the commission will be quantified only after certain deductions have been made and not that the commission will not accrue until the profits have been ascertained. The quantification of the commission is not a condition precedent to its accrual. If the profits of the company are said to have accrued on the 31st of March, upon a parity of reasoning, it must be conceded that the commission also accrued on the same date. . . ." (p. 534)

‘Public’ has various meanings. One of the meaning is - ‘a section of the community having a particular interest or in some special connection [Concise Oxford Dictionary]. As per section 12 of Indian Penal Code, ‘public’ includes any class of the public or any community.

Object beneficial to a section of the public is an object of ‘general public utility’ -Hiralal Bhagwati v. CIT [2008] 246 ITR 188 (Guj.).

In Municipal Council, Alleppey v. Manager, Bombay Co. Ltd. AIR 1950 TC 103, it was held that public includes a section of public. Hence, a canteen run by company exclusively for its employees and which is not open to general public is ‘public’ [ Aiyar’s Law Lexicon 1999 edition page 1554].

Even if only a section of public is benefited by land acquisition, the purpose would still be ‘public purpose’ - Secy. of State v. N. Gopala Aiyar AIR 1930 Mad. 798, Srinivasa Ayyangar v. S. Ramalinga Iyer AIR 1931 Mad. 78

Land acquisition for a particular co-operative society if for public purpose - Musamiyam Imam Haridarbux Razvi v. State of Gujarat AIR 1971 Guj. 158.

Thus, ‘public’ includes a ‘section of public’.

What is meaning of ‘charitable’ ? - ‘Charitable’ means ‘generous in giving to those in need’ or ‘of, or relating to, or connected with a charity or charities’. ‘Charity’ means giving voluntarily to those in need, alms-giving - Concise Oxford Dictionary.

Thus, the word ‘charity’ has narrow meaning in dictionary. However, the word has acquired a technical meaning in law, which is wide.

Hence, the wide meaning should apply and not narrow dictionary meaning [However, department is of the view that narrow meaning should apply -CBE&C, vide circular No. 84/2/2006-ST, dated 19-9-2006 and Ref. Code 076.01/23-8-07 of CBE&C Circular No. 96/7/2007-ST dated 23-8-2007 - see discussions below under Whether public charitable trust is automatically excluded].

Any object of ‘general public utility’ will be a ‘charitable purpose’, as discussed below.

As per section 2 of Charitable Endowments Act, 1890, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief to poor, education, medical relief and the advancement of any other object of general public utility, but does not include a purpose which relates exclusively to religious teaching or worship. As per section 2(15) of Income-tax Act, ‘charitable purpose’ includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, and the advancement of any other object of general public utility. Preamble to Charitable and Religious Trusts Act, 1920 also indicates that trust created for public purpose comes under purview of that Act.

Public does not refer to whole of mankind or all people in the country. It is sufficient if the intention is to benefit a section of the public as distinguished from specified individuals. The section of community sought to be benefited should be identifiable by some common quality of public or impersonal nature. The expression ‘general public utility’ include all objects which promote the welfare of general public. When an object is to promote or protect the interest of a particular trade or industry, that object would be charitable purpose, but not so, if it seeks to promote the interest of those who conduct the said trade or industry - CIT v. Andhra Chamber of Commerce [1965] 55 ITR 722 (SC).

Advance of any object of benefit to the public or section of public, as distinguished from benefit to an individual or group of individuals would be a charitable purpose - CIT v. Ahmedabad Rana Caste Association [1983] 140 ITR 1 (SC) [affirming CIT v. Ahmedabad Rana Cast Association [1973] 88 ITR 354 (Guj.), Andhra Chamber of Commerce case (supra).

In CIT v. Such purpose is the advancement of the object of general public utility and it will be a charitable purpose. It was also held that a trust can carry on business for purpose of earning profit, to be utilised exclusively for charitable purposes.

The Apex Court has said that it is necessary to draw a line of distinction between what are the objects of the trust and what are the powers conferred upon the trustees for achieving objects. One should not mix the objects of the trust with the powers conferred upon the trustees as incidental to the carrying out of the objects of the trust - Yogiraj Charity Trust v. CIT [1976] 103 ITR 777 (SC), Umaid Charitable Trust v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 55 (Raj.) and Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce & Industries’ case ( supra). This is so because the powers relate to the method and manner of its actual working or functioning, whereas the objects indicate its ultimate goal or achievements. The powers should, under no circumstances, be confused with objects or purposes.

11.2 The CBEC has made confusing observations in its Circular F. No. 137/50/2008-CX.4, dated 28-4-2008, where it has observed about bodies like CII thus :—

The word ‘business’ is one of large and indefinite import. However, it connotes something which occupies the labour and attention of a person for the purpose of profit. Generally speaking, business is an activity of a commercial nature and means practically anything, which is an occupation as distinguished from a pleasure. If the transaction is a trading transaction or an adventure in the nature of trade, it will amount to business, whether it results in loss or profit. It also includes adventure in the nature of trade. The object of the definition of ‘business’ in the Act is to treat the receipts from an adventure also to tax just as the receipts from the trade profit are brought to tax. In each case, however, one has to determine the nature of transaction, its volume, frequency, continuity and regularity. There is no hard and fast rule for application that particular transaction is a business. Any transaction, whether it is continuously undertaken or isolated transaction, can be treated alike to hold that a particular transaction is a business. The activities of the trust, i.e., conducting of races and inter-venue betting, after obtaining licence from the State Government and income derived therefrom could not be called as income from the business of the trust for the reason that the same was being utilized to achieve the primary object of the trust.

The objects and legality of the trust and also the grant of licence by the State Government were not in dispute, except to the extent that the objects were distributive in nature and some of them were charitable and others were non-charitable in nature. But, once if it was found that promotion of sports and athletics which benefit a large number of people were charitable in nature and also of general public utility, that objection also would stand apart.

The trust had conducted these stray activities for the purpose of achieving its primary objects, i.e., relief to poor, education, medical aid, etc. Thus, the activities undertaken by the trust could not be called a business systematically organized. The transactions in conducting the races and inter-venue betting were being meant for achieving primary objects of trust and could not be called a business. The natural corollary that followed was that the income derived from such transactions could not be called an income from the business. Assuming that it was a business as contemplated under section 2(13), the same was exempted under section 11. Further, the submission that the income would be treated as income derived from the property held under the trust could not also be disbelieved. [Para 12]

The licence to run races and betting itself could be treated as property and the said property was obtained with the consent of the Hyderabad Race Club. The term ‘property’ itself has got widest import for income-tax purposes and inclusive of holding a licence. But, it is not every case of business which can be treated as property. If it were to be so treated, section 13(1)(bb) would lose its meaning. It may be that a business itself may be settled in trust of the trustees who may conduct a business on their own under the powers given to them in the trust deed. In the instant case, it was difficult to accept that the assessee-trust was conducting the business in horse racing merely because it took the benefit of a race meet or inter-venue betting for few occasions in a year. Thus, there could not be any doubt that the income derived by the trust for the relevant assessment years was from the property held under trust and as such it was exempted under section 11.

Assuming even if it was not treated as income from the property held under the trust, it could be treated as voluntary contribution given by the Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee-trust as contemplated under section 12. The conduct of the Hyderabad Race Club in respect of the transaction was only a fiduciary for the benefit of the assessee. Such voluntary contributions could be characterized only as a capital receipt in the assessee’s hands. Thus, it could not be held that there had been business in the normal sense in such arrangement and in the facts and circumstances, it was not such a business which would be hit by section 13(1)(bb). It was only an activity which could constitute the property or an arrangement involved in transfer of funds from Hyderabad Race Club to the assessee’s institution in a form recognized by law and not shown to be colourable exercise or otherwise as contended by the revenue. Since it could not be said to be a business and the income derived could not be said to be a business income, the provisions of section 13(1)(bb) were not attracted. The assessee-trust was an institution, which satisfied the conditions under section 2(15), read with section 11 and as such, conclusion reached by the Tribunal should be upheld. [Para 13]

The assessee-firm was appointed an managing agent of a company. The managed company received a letter from another company ‘J’, which offered itself to work as its managing agents and requested that it may be so appointed. On 28-9-1943, the managed company decided to ask the assessee to retire from the managing agency business with effect from 30-9-1943, on receipt of compensation for the premature termination of the contract. This amount was paid to the assessee on 30-9-1943, and the assessee retired from the managing agency business with effect from that date. The majority of shareholders in company ‘J’ were the members of the assessee-firm. The assessee submitted a return without showing in the return the receipt of the said compensation. For the assessment year 1944-45, the ITO completed the assessment of the assessee without including the aforesaid amount of compensation. Subsequently, the successor ITO issued a notice to the assessee under section 34 of the 1922 Act calling upon the assessee to submit a return in respect of that amount. In response to the notice the assessee submitted the return but contended that the aforesaid receipt was capital in nature not liable to tax. However, the contention was rejected and receipt was subjected to tax. The Tribunal held that as there was merely a change in the personnel of the managing agency, there was no loss of office, which might entitle the managing agents to payment, which was held to be collusive and, therefore, there was no genuine termination of the managing agency and as such the payment was not ‘compensation for termination of the managing agency’. The Tribunal also held that the receipt was not exempt under section 4(3)(vii) of the 1922 Act as it was not casual and it did arise out of the business of the assessee, that the receipt was ‘foreseen, well planned and thought of’ and, therefore, the receipt was revenue receipt.

Flaws in the CBECs’ circulars

8. These are as under :

(A) Discarding of the interpretation of the concept of ‘charity’ in the Income-tax Act is wrong

There is apparent flaw in the CBEC’s circular when it says that the exemption under the Income-tax Act on the ground of being a public charitable institution is of no consequence or relevance for service tax purposes.

This view, it needs to be said, is misconceived and opposed to judicial thinking for the reasons mentioned hereinafter :

(i)The CBEC’s circulars categorically say that for determining whether activities carried on by an undertaking are of a charitable nature or not, definition under the Income-tax Act is of no consequence. This is, apparently, a mistaken notion. For understanding the meaning of these words, reference to other statutes ‘in pari materia’, i.e., statute forming part of the same system can be looked into. In the absence of a statutory definition (which is not there in the service tax provisions relating to charitable purpose/nature), it is open to look for the meaning by reference to definitions in the sister legislation (which the Income-tax Act is vis-á-vis Service Tax legislation). Resort to adoption of dictionary meaning or meaning in common parlance is to be taken if there is no definition in the Act or in sister legislation. Hence, to say that exemption in income-tax is of no consequence for service tax purposes, is, prima-facie, a misconception.

(ii)Viscount Salmond in a passage in AG HRH Prince Earnest Augustus of Hanover [1957] 1 All ER 49, page 53 (HL) has said that ‘I consider it my right and duty to examine every word of a statute in its context and I use context in its widest sense as including . . . . . . other statutes in pari materia’. The application of this rule of construction has the merit of avoiding any apparent contradiction between a series of statutes dealing with similar subjects. Certainly, income-tax and service tax are in pari materia. The structuring of the two legislations is on similar lines. Hence, it cannot be said that the concept of ‘charitable purpose’ under the Income-tax Act is of no consequence under the service tax provisions.

(B) Reference to dictionary meaning when the words can be interpreted with the help of other Acts, pari-materia seems incorrect

Introduction

1. The recent decision of the CBEC to omit clause (v), which provided exemption from service tax for activities related to advancement of any other object of general public utility upto the prescribed monetary limits from the definition of 'charitable activity' from 1-4-2013 is an instance, which indicates CBEC's unfair treatment of charities, which enures to the welfare of the people of the country in terms of Directive Principles of State Policy in the Constitution of India ["the Constitution" for short].

The primary objective of any tax law and its administration is to raise revenue for funding Governmental expenditure, which, inter alia, is to be spent for the peoples' welfare. An important source of revenue to the Govt. is service tax. Article 38 in Chapter IV of the Constitution, titled Directive Principles of State Policy provides that the State shall, amongst others, provide that the State shall strive to promote the welfare of the people by securing and protecting as effectively as it may a social order in which justice shall ensue to all institutions of social life. This directive of the Constitution is being fulfilled by direct expenditure as also by tax foregone in the form of exemptions and deductions in tax legislations, which cost to the Govt. some financial burden as cash expenditure.

This position is well recognized in most of the countries of the world. In this context, it may be appropriate to refer to the philosophy concerning concessions permissible for charitable contributions under the U.S. Internal Revenue Code. The House Ways and Means Committee, in one of its reports, has observed as under:—

"……The exemption from taxation of money or property devoted to charitable and other purposes is based upon the theory that the Government is compensated for the loss of revenue by its relief from financial burden, which would otherwise have to be met by appropriation from public funds and by the benefit resulting from the promotion of the general welfare".

2. Exemption of income of charitable bodies

2.1 Under the I.T. Act - The principle of giving tax benefits to charities and various objects of general public utility are well enshrined in the law relating to taxation of income. Section 2(15) of the I.T. Act, 1961 (Act) defines the term 'charitable purpose' (as amended) as under:—

"Charitable purpose includes relief of the poor, education, medical relief, preservation of environment [including watersheds, forests and wildlife] and preservation of monuments or places or objects of artistic or historic interest and the advancement of any other object of general public utility".

To prevent the misuse of tax concessions for charities for business purposes, two provisos were added to this definition, which read as under:—

"Provided that the advancement of any other object of general public utility shall not be a charitable purpose, if it involves the carrying on of any activity in the nature of trade, commerce or business, or any activity of rendering any service in relation to any trade, commerce or business, for a cess or fee or any other consideration, irrespective of the nature of use or application or retention of the income from such activity:

Provided further that the first proviso shall not apply, if the aggregate value of the receipts from the activities referred to therein is twenty-five lakh rupees or less in the previous year."

Sections 11 and 10(23C) of the Act provide for exemption from tax of the incomes derived by charitable institutions on the fulfilment of the prescribed conditions.

For ensuring that undeserved institutions do not avail of tax benefits, the Act vide section 12A provides for registration of such institutions with the Chief Commissioners/Commissioners of Income-tax of the respective regions by making applications in the prescribed forms with relevant accounts and documents duly audited. Section 12AA prescribes the procedure for registration and lays down the time-limit within which the registration is to be granted. Sub-section (3) of section 12AA prescribes for cancellation of registration, if the activities of the Trust/Institution, which has been allowed registration, are found to be non-genuine or it is noticed that the activities of the institution are not being carried on in accordance with the objects of the trust/institution, as the case may be. Thus, I.T. Act has well-known law and procedure for giving tax benefits to charitable organizations, which are for the welfare and benefit of the people.

2.2 Under the Service Tax law - Regretfully, it is noticed that such important issue was being treated under the service tax legislation by the CBEC in a routine and arbitrary manner – not appreciating the spirit and purpose behind giving tax benefits to charitable institutions. In the pre 1-7-2013 period, the CBEC took a very narrow view regarding charitable activities, as could be seen from later discussion.

3. Earlier in 2007 renting of immovable property was introduced vide Notification Number 23/2007-ST. After reading the above definition it was clear that the service of renting of immovable property by a religious body or to a religious body was not chargeable to service tax.

So, if any religious body like a trust or a religious institution rented any immovable property or if any person rented immovable property to such religious body then it would not be treated as service of renting of immovable property.

The expression religious body is neither defined in the Act nor is being explained in any circular. The word 'religious' means 'connected with religion or with a particular religion' (Oxford Advanced Learners Dictionary).Thus, the body in question must be engaged in some religious activity like maintenance of temples/churches/mosques or organising religious functions. One can interpret these words to include any person whether incorporated or unincorporated who has the intention of carrying out religious activity. A charitable trust cannot be treated as a 'religious body' unless it is authorised to engage in any religious activity as its main activity.

In other words, we can say that under the old law if any of the following activities were carried out by a religious body, it was exempt from tax:

(a)

Renting activities of immovable property by a religious body

-

Renting of parts of any religious place to banks for operating branch offices.

-

Renting of any religious place to private persons for the purposes of any function which includes marriage, Havans, Keertan, etc.

-

Renting of any immovable property (even otherwise than part of religious place) for earning profit or otherwise etc.

(b)

Renting activities of immovable property to a religious body

-

Religious body renting an immovable property for conduct of religious events like Annual Samagam, Havans anywhere in India.

Religious body opening school or hospital at a rented place anywhere in India

Religious body of one State can get on rent an immovable property from another State

Decision binding if the point is the same

2.38 Thus the principle of res judicata or estoppel though cannot strictly apply to the decisions rendered in proceedings under the Income-tax Act, they have a binding effect both on the assessee as well as the revenue, if the point on which the decision has been given is the same. On the basis of this principle the Madras High Court1 held that the decision on the question whether a certain trust is charitable or not, has nothing to do with the fluctuations in the income, and that such questions, if decided by a Court on a reference made to it, would be res judicata and the same question cannot be subsequently reagitated. It may be stated that in that case, the question was already considered by the Supreme Court2 as to whether the assessee would be entitled to exemption, wherein the claim for deduction of the donation made to the assessee-trust was rejected by the Supreme Court on the ground that the assessee-trust could not be held to be entitled to the benefit of exemption because some of the objects of the trust were not charitable and the trustees had discretion to spend the income of the trust on charitable and non-charitable objects. The matter turned on the finding already arrived at by the Supreme Court as to whether the trust in question was a charitable one or not and so the question of exemption was based on the previous finding regarding the nature of the trust.

The Supreme Court in CIT v. Durga Prasad More3, held that though neither the principle of res judicata nor the rule of estoppel was applicable to the assessment proceedings, the fact that the assessee included the income of the premises in his returns for several years after objecting to its inclusion in the year 1942-43, was a circumstance which the taxing authorities were entitled to take into consideration in the absence of any specific explanation and that the Tribunal was right in holding that the house property was not the trust property. The Supreme Court proceeded to consider the question as to whether the finding of fact arrived at by the Tribunal was in any way vitiated and it was held that it was not in any way vitiated.

It is the ultimate accountability of the managing director to the company which determines the character of relation between the managing director and the company. Therefore, remuneration to the managing directors should be held assessable under the head "Salaries" [CIT v. B. P. Dalmia [1993] 71 Taxman 52 (Cal.)]. In common parlance, the whole-time director may not be an employee but even then, the character of the receipt or remuneration having come within the definition of salary u/s 17(1)(iv) being a fee or remuneration in whatever name it is called and not being excluded by the Explanation 2 to section 15, the remuneration received by the assessee cannot be treated to be anything other than income under the head "Salaries" [Sajid Mowjee v. ITO [2005] 148 Taxman 502 (Cal.)].

Commission paid to the non-executive or independent directors to attend Board meetings as well as of various Committees not to be treated as salary [CIT v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. [2018] 92 taxmann.com 30/254 Taxman 370 (Bom.)].

SALARY DUE [SECTION 15(a)]

"Due", implication of - The expression "due" shows that there should be an obligation on the part of the employer to pay that amount and a right on the part of the employee to claim the same (i.e., a vested right) [CIT v. L. W. Russel [1964] 53 ITR 91 (SC)].

Forgoing salary - A distinction has to be made in forgoing salary before it becomes due and in surrendering the same after it has become due or has accrued. In the former case, there will be no accrual of salary while in the latter case, it would be an application of the salary which had become due and payable [CIT v. Mehar Singh Sampuran Singh Chawla [1973] 90 ITR 219 (Delhi)].

Writing-off or waiver on the part of the assessee after the income from "Salaries" had become due to him cannot amount to anything more than disposal of the income. The concept of real income where the income falls under the head "Salaries" cannot help the assessee [CIT v. Bachubhai Nagindas Shah [1976] 104 ITR 551 (Guj.)].

ADVANCE SALARY [SECTION 15(b)]

'Paid' and 'allowed', meaning of - The expression "paid" takes in its sweep every receipt of contemplated payments to the employee whether it was due to him or not by the employer. Another expression "allowed", in the legal terminology, is equivalent to 'fixed, taken into account, set apart, granted' [CIT v. L. W. Russel [1964] 53 ITR 91 (SC)].

Termination of service - The agreement stated that the employer might terminate the services of the assessee by giving either 12 months' notice in writing or paying any salary in lieu thereof. Consequently, the employer, instead of giving notice in writing, has paid 12 months' salary and, therefore, the employee received 12 months' salary though he did not work for such period. By no stretch of imagination, it could be said that such payment was in consideration of the surrender by the recipient of his rights in respect of the office. Therefore, that amount held not to be treated as compensation for loss of employment but simply taxable as 'salary' u/s 15 [V. D. Talwar v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 122 (SC)].

Tips to employees - Tips, being voluntary amounts, that may or may not be paid by the customers for the services rendered to them would not fall within the ambit of section 15(b) since there being no vested right in the employee to claim any amount of tip from his employer or former employer. Consequently, tips are received by the employer in the fiduciary capacity as trustee for payments that are received from customers which they disburse to their employees for services rendered to such customers [ITC Ltd. v. CIT [2016] 68 taxmann.com 323/239 Taxman 372 (SC)].

ARREARS OF SALARY [SECTION 15(c)]

Pre-conditions - Twin conditions are to be satisfied for applicability of section 15(c), i.e., arrears of salary were paid or allowed in the PY by the employer or on his behalf and such arrears were not charged to income-tax for any earlier PY. The words "if not charged to income-tax" are wide enough to include cover those cases where the charge could or could not have been imposed [CIT v. Sardar Arjun Singh Ahluwalia [1999] 107 Taxman 246 (SC)].
